It is the fundamentals of his country, as opposed to the food. And as his hard currency dries up, the smuggling will-you know the smugglers want hard currency." So, the sanctions were working before they were so heedlessly abandoned.
The last major argument that the government has is that we must go in because Kuwaitis are being wiped out and nothing we could do could be anywhere near as bad.
I quote from an article in today's Edmonton Journal. "Brothers pray for safety of parents still in Kuwait". I quote from the article:
Two brothers from Kuwait prayed for their parents' safety
Wednesday night, listening to the TV in horror as American
bombers attacked Iraq.
January 17, 1991

Said and Sadi Karaman left their parents, a brother, and a sister in Kuwait City when they came to Canada on student visas in January.
Although a letter two weeks ago indicated their parents were fine, repeated attempts to reach them on the phone Wednesday night failed.
"I just want my parents here," said Said, 21, his voice shuddering.
Although he was angry when the Iraqis invaded, the Kuwaiti people could have solved their own problem, Sadi said.
"(The attack) isn't going to liberate Kuwait. It's going to be war. The peaceful solution would have been better."
That is the only Kuwaiti I have seen directly quoted in my hometown newspaper.
The last argument the government may have used is that the Canadian people were behind this. But, they are not. They are opposed to it. In my riding I have had 36 phone calls; three favour war, 33 are against. I have had six letters; one was for, five were against, not counting the letter I read into the record the other night.
In conclusion, and I am sorry I have not been able to lay before the House all the evidence I had hoped to in these brief 10 minutes. I would just say that what Canada is embarked upon at this time is a terrible and tragic mistake. It was wrong two days ago. It was wrong yesterday. It is wrong today. We must withdraw from that war and we must do everything we can to bring that war to a halt as quickly as possibly we can.

Madam Speaker, in congratulating the hon. member for Edmonton East for his very impressive speech, I would like to ask him to expand for a moment on his concluding remarks when he was pulling his argument together and tell the House and the people watching this debate whether, in his opinion, we would be in this terrible mess tonight if the sanctions would still be applied tonight in the Middle East.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. Had the sanctions been allowed to continue to bite ever deeper-first into Saddam Hussein's national Iraqi economy, but more importantly, into his ability to maintain his warmaking capacity-there would have been no need for war.
The current director of the CIA, in testimony in the United States, two former chairmen of the CIA, two former directors of the American joint chiefs of staff, all
Government Orders
testifying before various congressional committees, said the sanctions would in all probability work. In fact, they were already working. For whatever reason, that considered and informed opinion was deemed wrong. I have yet to hear any opinion expressed in this House to the contrary to which I would lend anything close to the same credibility.

Madam Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would tell us what kind of a serious situation we might face in a year if we were to give Saddam a year or perhaps two years in order to prepare his war machine, to continue to prepare for a battle which he seemed to be prepared to take on regardless of the consequences.
I am surprised to find a gentleman of that party at probably the only time in my life that I will hear him quoting such sources as the CIA and the joint chiefs of staff of the United States of America as his authorities to build his arguments. But, perhaps it occurs to the hon. member that things change, that the statements he was quoting earlier were subsequently proven incorrect. No, I do not suggest that the hon. member would ever listen to that kind of an argument.
Madam Speaker, there are members in this House, including members of the party of the member who just spoke, who say that this is not our war.
When is it our war? Is it when they move into Saudi Arabia? Is it when they move into Jordan? Is it when they try to move into Israel? When is it our war? When is it that the interests of Canada, of the United Nations and of world peace are not our interests?

I attempt, whenever I am mounting an argument, to cite the most credible sources I can find. That is how I attempt, logically, to examine a question.
I am sorry, but again I say I have heard nothing in this House that bears anywhere close to the credibility or indeed the fullness of the testimony of these gentlemen before the various American congressional committees. And, as to the question of what would happen in a year, I would just give him two brief quotes. One is from General David Jones, and I quote:
In the area of military hardware, we and our allies can repair and
replace our equipment as needed, while time works against the Iraqi
armed forces.

Government Orders
The current director of the CIA, William Webster, said in his testimony of December 5, and I quote:
At current rates of depletion, we estimate Iraq will have nearly
depleted its available foreign exchange reserves by next spring.
It is the foreign exchange reserves they use to buy the bootlegged, strategic material on the black market which the hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs was talking about. If they do not have the foreign exchange, they do not have the means to make war.

Madam Speaker, I submit to this House that Saddam Hussein is an evil that has advanced so far the world could wait no longer to take decisive action.
I know all Canadians tonight are thinking of our Armed Forces, men and women who are certainly putting their lives at stake in defence of freedom and in defence of world order. Certainly this is not a case, as the opposition and a great many others would have us believe, of a war for oil only.
On August 2 of this past year Iraq brutally invaded Kuwait, deploying more than 150,000 soldiers, 1,200 tanks, and some 1,000 armoured vehicles. Swiftly capturing Kuwait City, Iraq began a systematic ravaging of Kuwait's resources and population.
In fact the independent human rights organization, Amnesty International, recently documented a long list of cases of torture, rape, brutality, and so on inflicted on the Kuwaiti people. Canada is part of the United Nations sanctioned alliance which has been sending a clear message to Saddam Hussein that acts of armed aggression are no longer tolerated by the international community.
Over a three-month period, the United Nations Security Council has adopted 12 resolutions with respect of the Iraqi aggression in Kuwait. The debate in the House of Commons that began on Tuesday is on a government motion reaffirming Canada's commitment to United Nations resolution 678. I support whole heartedly the motion. Canada, as a member of the United Nations sanctioned alliance, has sent a message to Saddam Hussein that it would use military force if Iraq did not withdraw from Kuwait. As of last night, the United Nations coalition moved to make good on that pledge.
I strongly disagree with the Leader of the Loyal Opposition who indicated that at the first sign of military action Canada should withdraw from the gulf. With your friends you stand shoulder to shoulder, especially in hard
times, and I can assure the House that Canada is not a fair weather friend. Prior to the outbreak of hostilities in the Persian Gulf, many voices were raised saying that any military action in the gulf would be a United States action. Nothing could be further from the truth.
The force present in the gulf representing more than 30 nations is sanctioned by the 12 resolutions of the United Nations Security Council and is backed by near unanimous support. The world is united in its condemnation of the Iraqi aggression against Kuwait and the Iraqi aggression against the rule of international law.
Canada's role in the region and its support of resolution 678 are based solidly on our historical commitment to the United Nations as the preferred instrument for preserving international peace and security. Indeed, the actions of Canada and all nations currently in the Persian Gulf have been under the auspices of the United Nations. In terms of the military action that commenced January 16 under UN resolution 678, the charter of the United Nations clearly provides for the kind of action which has been taken in the region in the past. The United Nations was unable to undertake such measures because of the constraints of the cold war. The effect had been to prevent any direct intervention by the United Nations.
As it stands now, there is no contradiction between Canada's present role in the gulf and the peacekeeping roles we have undertaken in the past. Where Canadians are having a problem with Canada's present role is that Canadians are not used to sending ships, planes, and soldiers to areas where conflict threatens. We are used to our military forces putting on blue United Nations helmets and going to places where cease-fires had been declared and where we were enforcing a truce and not preventing a war.
However, just as the United Nations role is evolving in the post cold war period, so is Canada's role as a peacemaker. Interestingly enough, the idea of peacekeeping as Canadians have come to know was at one time new. When Lester B. Pearson designed the first United Nations force which helped to end the Suez crisis, there were many voices raised opposing what Canada was doing in that particular situation. Those same voices said that Suez was none of our business. The voices of doubt were wrong then, and they are most certainly wrong now. From the courage shown by most Canadians then a great United Nations tradition was
January 17, 1991

born and a long and honourable Canadian commitment was made to peacekeeping.
The crisis in the gulf is taking place in a new international climate brought about by the end of the cold war. The acquisition of territory by brute force has represented a dangerous behaviour for most of this century. Iraq's actions represented a fundamental challenge to the international community in an era where the end of the old superpower rivalries had opened the way for a more co-operative and harmonious approach to resolving international problems and protecting peace and security.
At the present juncture, Canada and the world community, working through the United Nations, have invested heavily in a collective international response to Iraq and with good reason, apart from forcing Saddam Hussein to comply with international law, the success of the current undertaking could serve as a model for future meaningful collective security actions.
The United Nations followed a balanced, carefully considered course of action and sought Iraq's unconditional withdrawal from Kuwait, preferably as a result of political and economic pressure. With the passing of the January 15 deadline, the United Nations sanctioned alliance took decisive action.
Those who still insist that the United Nations alliance should have waited for economic sanctions to work have their heads buried deeply in the sand. The bottom line is that Iraq had no intention of withdrawing of its own volition from Kuwait.
Canadians are by nature a peaceful people and beyond any doubt did not want to see a war in the Persian Gulf. The prospect of war in the gulf disturbs me deeply and personally, as I have three grandsons who are of military age: 18,19, and 22. Believe me, nothing would have been more welcome than a resolution of the crisis without conflict.
However, what has to be seriously considered is the fact that peace is not accidental. It must be constructed and maintained, and sometimes at a tremendous cost. The protection and maintenance of international law and order and the containment of a dangerous renegade
Government Orders
country are interests worth fighting for. What is happening in the gulf will work in the way its founders envisage.
Canada's role in international conflict has been one of creative diplomacy tied to the United Nations. Our most creative diplomacy has been in the building of international institutions founded on shared principles, on the rule of law, and on the creation of collective powers to respond when these principles were violated.
These are the achievements of our diplomacy that we must now defend. If we do otherwise, our diplomacy will have failed, not just in this current crisis but in what we have been doing for 45 years.
Some Canadians wish we were not in the Persian Gulf. We all share that sentiment. We wish Iraq had not invaded Kuwait, but responsible nations must deal with facts, not wishes. Regardless of how well intended, Canada is a responsible nation. The fact remains that the peace was not kept. Iraq did invade Kuwait. Canada, along with over 30 nations, is in the gulf to seek peace and defend order, just as we have done in the past.
Iraq's invasion of Kuwait is a crucial test of the United Nations in the post cold war world. Anything less than full support for United Nations resolution 678 would betray over 40 years of hope for the United Nations charter and its collective security provisions. If we succeed in the gulf, the signal will be clearly sent for all to witness that war as an instrument of foreign policy will not work.
What is at stake in the Persian Gulf is not territory or oil, but the preservation of the rule of international law. For these reasons and more, I am supporting our government's motion reaffirming Canada's commitment to United Nations resolution 678.

Madam Speaker, we all know where the question and comment come from, since we are in that period, when I say: Ask not what the country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country. What we can do for our country tonight and in weeks to come is probably put aside our partisanship politics and speak as one voice in this House in support of our troops who are there.
I am pleased that all members who spoke from the three parties, as well the independent members, have

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
been doing that. If they did not verbalize it, I know it was in their hearts because I have spoken to them outside the House also.
The question is: How can we support our forces now? I am glad everyone is recognizing the danger that our troops are in and the importance of showing them that we are solidly behind them. However, there are other foot soldiers there who maybe we have forgotten. It reminded me of the foot soldiers when we were watching the TV in the lobby last night. A CBC reporter from a hotel in Baghdad was reporting, and all of a sudden the TV went blank. Immediately everyone was horrified that the hotel was bombed or struck and that this reporter's life may have been in danger. Thank God his life was not in danger.
Watching in the lobby today, similar incidents are happening. Reporters with gas masks on are reporting to us that 10 missiles landed in Israel. In our support of the troops let us not forget these other important foot soldiers who are there, men and women. If it were not for them, we would not know what is happening in the gulf today.
I want to ask a question of the hon. member, though. Has his government given any support to the media personnel who are over there reporting to us in this excellent manner?

Madam Speaker, as far as support, I am not privy to what has been taking place over there. I certainly pay great tribute to the people in the media who have been giving us a very vivid and frightening picture of what took place last night, today and I guess tonight. If there is any need for support, there is no doubt that the government will do everything possible.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask a question of a very respected colleague. I am sure he truly believes in what he said, but I will say that I vociferously disagree with he has said. That is certainly allowed.
I understand that this day is soon going to draw to a close, but I want to touch on the the issue of sanctions one more time and whether they would work, did not work, or could not work. My colleague from Edmonton gave more proof as to the plausibility of sanctions
working. Certainly the Secretary of State for External Affairs suggested that undetected products were going through and therefore the sanctions were not working. This depends on reports from an ambassador from Asia. It did not cite the country, nor did the minister.
Sanctions are working no matter what anybody says. The government said that it is time to end the sanctions and that one of its reasons is that with sanctions Saddam Hussein would take the food from the children and give it to the soldiers. I guess our response to that is: let's bomb the heck out of them, let's just bomb them and continue to bomb. Is that the solution to the problem?
Given the choice, most people would prefer hunger to death. Once again, I ask the member, as we have asked so many people: What was wrong with sanctions? What was wrong with giving them the appropriate time, whatever that time might be?

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie, sanctions do work but they do not work very fast. In this particular case, there have been months in which sanctions have been applied, in which every opportunity was given to Saddam Hussein and his government, although he is really a one-man government and a real dictator. Apparently he felt that the coalition of the United Nations was bluffing. Every action was taken.
What is Canada going to do? Canada has made a modest contribution of 2,200 personnel, give or take, none of whom are ground troops. Our navy and our air force are there to protect and to assist.
I would point out to hon. members and to that saintly group in the comer, who seems to think that it has a corner on all morality, that a great many other countries are supporting the position Canada has taken. Canada has 2,200 troops at stake there. The United States has probably a half a million. Even the opposition in Great Britain, the Hon. Neil Kinnock has supported the present situation of using force. Australia, another Labour government, socialist government, has us supported it whole-heartedly. But the saintly NDP would have us withdraw our troops and sit back like cowards, and then, when the war is all over, we would get up and wave the Canadian flag and say: "Now we are able to help you. Wipe the blood and sweat of your face", and so on.
January 17, 1991

Madam Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to speak to the people of Canada and to the residents of the riding of Saint-Maurice.
First, allow me to offer my best wishes and congratulations to the new Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for Beausejour, who was recently elected to the House of Commons. As you know, he represented my riding for 23 years. He is a close friend whom I have known for 20-odd years, and I want to offer him my best wishes on his return to the House of Commons.
Madam Speaker, I know that in your capacity as member for Saint-Hyacinthe you too would like to express your heart felt sentiments about the war that has broken out in the Middle East. I know you would be able to reach deep into our hearts by your humanitarian observations. Knowing you as we do, we are also convinced that without political partisanship you would be in a position to tell the House how important it is that international order be maintained.
That being so, Madam Speaker, I should like to point out two things. This House is made up of three parties and a few independent members who have already expressed their views. Some of our colleagues took a partisan approach, others were more generous in their remarks.
However, my father taught me that great occasions in life enable us to differentiate men from children. All partisanship aside, Madam Speaker, I became aware of that after the appeal of the Prime Minister as I watched the behaviour of the three main parties. The Canadian public has been able to see how the government, the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party behaved.
They found that the members of the Liberal Party of Canada who make up the Official Opposition were able to a certain extent to rise above partisan politics. Through their leader, they said that what really mattered, under these very serious circumstances, was Canada's reputation.
In this respect, even if I do not usually share the views of the Official Opposition, I must recognize that the
Government Orders
members of the Liberal Party were able to show restraint.
I wish I could say the same thing about my socialists colleagues of the New Democratic Party. Unfortunately, again, they decided as usual to criticize the government's position. They proved to be unable to show common sense and to recognize that Canada's national interest transcended partisan considerations. Such was the behaviour of the New Democratic Party of Canada today. That, Madam Speaker, is the kind of medicine the citizens of Canada must sooner or later evaluate in relation to this whole matter of concern to them.
I would like to state briefly some of the feelings I experienced last August when I had the opportunity and the pleasure to travel to the Middle East with the hon. member for Western Arctic. On that occasion, we visited Israel, Palestine and Egypt at the very moment when Saddam Hussein was threatening Kuwait with possible sanctions. We went through some extremely difficult situations in that country.
One thing I learned, Madam Speaker, is that it is very difficult to separate the good from the bad. We met with Israelis and Palestinians, two peoples living in the same country but with very different objectives. They each had their own reason for wanting to live peacefully in the Middle East. Some will consider the Israeli as the good guys and the Palestinians as the bad guys. Others will do the exact opposite. But the truth is probably not that simple. What we are going through tonight seems even more complex, when we realize Israel did not reply to the first attacks againt its state.
Madam Speaker, for more than 40 years, experts have been predicting this war. For over 40 years, throughout the world, experts have said that some day the situation in the Middle East will get extremely explosive. This crucial time has come. And in this crucial crisis, Madam Speaker, our government and our people are left with but one option. We have the option of regrouping around our common denominator, the United Nations.
The United Nations have in their history gone through extremely difficult periods. However, they assured Palestinians in occupied territories minimal living conditions at a time when they were in a most difficult situation.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
The United Nations Agency for Palestinian Refugees is largely financed by the Government of Canada which is one of the largest contributors of the United Nations for Palestinians.
I think our government, in the last few years, was able to show flexibility. We are friends of Israel, of course, but we are also capable of compassion towards Palestinians.
Today, in spite of Canada's diplomatic action, in spite of the tens of millions of dollars we spent trying to insure peace in the Middle East, in spite of the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to the late Lester B. Pearson, in spite of all our efforts over decades, Madam Speaker, we have come to a point of no return. Saddam Hussein is putting us in a position where we cannot go back. Canada, America, the United Nations and the world have no choice. We have no choice in the matter and I think the position taken by our government and the one of the Liberal Party-and I will close my comments on that-is that of reason in supporting our troops and our government. I think that the New Democrats should, in all conscience, review their position, which is too partisan and, for now, totally out of synch.
Madam Speaker, I know my time is up. I thank you very much.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the House is aware, earlier this evening Iraq initiated an attack against Israel, a country that is not part of the coalition that is acting in concert to get Hussein out of Kuwait.
As a result of that heinous act, the opinions and sympathies of the Government of Canada have been made known to the Government of Israel. The Prime Minister had hoped and expected that he would have sufficient information about the events to come to the
House and report on the circumstances. As it is, the information is rather fragmentary. It is still incomplete and, for that reason, he is unable to come this evening.
Therefore, Madam Speaker, in view of the circumstances and the fact that the debate we are now having keeps changing in its parameters, hour by hour, minute by minute, I was going to suggest that, after discussions with the House leaders of hon. members, perhaps there might be a mood to suspend the sitting, as we did last night, and to return tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock.
That was the purpose, simply to inform, because some people had expected the Prime Minister to be here. He would have been here but, for the reasons I have just given, he was unable to do so. I rise on a point of order for the purposes of making that suggestion, for which there has been discussions among House leaders and on which I understood there was some agreement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we, too, recognize the horror which has occurred this evening and, in light of the changing situation and the unfortunate situation now, the escalation in hostilities, I think it is only appropriate that, until adequate information is made available, that we suspend until 10 o'clock. Presumably, we would then resume the debate at 10 o'clock tomorrow morning.

Madam Speaker, I would like more information about the proposal. Are we going to carry on with the debate on the same subject tomorrow at 10 o'clock? If so, I agree; otherwise, I refuse my consent. Could the Government leader answer this question?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it would be my intention to proceed under the existing Order tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock, which would mean the same question.

Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I rise because I feel that we are going to go through. Many would like to leave now, maybe tomorrow.
In all humility and as kindly as I can, I say to the House leader that next time that he wants to make a statement, it will only confuse and make life more difficult in the House. Just come and say so.
We are not fools. We will accept your making a statement. We know what is going on. But I do not think that using a point of order to make a statement is the right way.
Oh, oh!

Well, you do what you want, but you may need a lot of agreement. I say, kindly, to all of you, you may need a helluva lot more agreement than you think to terminate or to continue the debate. That is not the way to proceed.
You may disagree. Instead of saying, "come on," just listen. You may say, "I disagree," and that is it. I do not understand this kind of putting off any members with whom you disagree.
It is a tough enough time just to have an orderly debate, and I feel it get more and more difficult. That is all I am trying to put to the House.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:

As I said before-and I should not have to repeat this, the hon. member should accept my word-we will return to this existing order of the House tomorrow morning at 10 o'clock.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that these lessons of morality are out of place tonight.

If the House leader wants to play smart ass, he will not get anything.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:

On a point of order, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as being one of the others, as the parliamentary secretary referred to us, first of all I want to acknowledge that this Question Period and opportunity to present statements is the result of some generosity on all sides. January 17, 1991
Government Orders

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again the member from Edmonton anticipated what I was going to ask. I think that if the government removed the last few words of the motion, it could possibly accommodate the member from Edmonton. I said "could" possibly accommodate the member from Edmonton.

speechtext: Before we get into a great debate on that, let me, as I understand it, make clear what the procedure is. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am seeking clarification. There were suggestions that we delete some phrases; I am not certain which phrases, before we are asked for our consent for this motion. Could I have a clarification from the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader? What exactly is the wording of the motion we now have before us, for which there is a request for consent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to be really clear. The intention of this motion is to allow the House and the members of the House to have the normal members' statements, which would take place on a Friday, and also the normal Question Period which would take place on a Friday. That, notwithstanding the order made Wednesday, January 16, 1991, Statements by Members Pursuant to Standing Order 31 be called this day at 11 o'clock a.m., followed by Oral Questions at 11.15 o'clock a.m.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for taking the time of the House but, since this is the first time I have seen this sheet and the first time I have had this discussion, I want to be clear what we are agreeing to.
I want to ask the parliamentary secretary a question. Does this mean that we will cease discussion on the motion, prior to Question Period, that the House will then be suspended and we will resume on Monday? I am not clear as to what we are saying, in terms of the future of this debate.
Mr. Coopen Mr. Speaker, I am finding myself drawn into a rather interesting bit of negotiations and discussions here. I want to be very clear. As the situation is right now, if we do not agree to this motion, then we will continue with Motion No. 27 which would be uninterrupted until that debate collapses.
What I am suggesting to the House in making this offer is that we would interrupt debate to have members' statements and Question Period and then, at that point, we resume Government Orders and we have the traditional opportunity for the government to call whatever at that point. I say that simply because I would like to be in a position to not have the negotiations on the floor but to talk to any and all members, when we proceed at this point. I am not trying to restrict members. I think that Question Period has always been important to members of Parliament, on all sides of the House, and we do not want to take that away from members today.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
I believe that the wisdom that went into the drafting of this motion earlier was great and that the wording that is before us ought to be the wording that we now agree to. This provides us with a flexibility but, at this moment, I cannot agree to a motion that could end the debate on this critical issue.
I am willing to negotiate, as we always are, around the clock to try to facilitate the business of this House in a meaningful way and I would suggest that he seek unanimous consent for the motion that is in writing before us now.

There seem to be some misunderstandings. I think it would be better if we had the the next speaker. Then we could perhaps negotiate involving all of the parties, including the independent members, and come up with something we can all give unanimous consent to.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There has been a certain amount of anticipation of other people's helpful interventions already this morning. I might say the hon. member has anticipated the remark that I am about to make, which is a suggestion that we proceed with debate. We have an hon. member seeking the floor. It seems to me that hon. members may be veiy close to a resolution of this.

In view of the fact that there is not actually consent at the moment for the motion, I would propose to proceed with debate.
I am sure the parliamentary secretary, the House Leaders, and other members could have a discussion and they might be able to indicate to me at some appropriate point in a little while what has been agreed to.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker.
The last speaker last night was the the hon. member for Saint-Maurice. He had just finished his speech and we were just about to enter questions and comments. Even if he is temporarily absent, I had indicated I wanted to make a comment or two on the graciousness of his speech.
Madam Deputy Speaker, who was here last night, has just reminded me that there were two or three minutes remaining.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have some sympathy with the hon. member's request. I think that hon. members will remember that it has been customary in such cases when there is a break in the proceedings and at the recommencement of the proceedings, if the hon. member is not here, then we have to proceed to the next hon. member.
If it is any comfort to the hon. member for Saint-Denis, he has indicated what he would have like to have said. Perhaps there will be another occasion or another place where he can speak.
I have no questions for him. It is just a comment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that, but the hon. member is not here. He is no doubt on other business.

Mr. Speaker, last night I was about to speak when the House adjourned and this morning I was about to speak when we were interrupted by House procedure discussions. I feel as if I have been called back to the starting gate for the third time.
Government Orders
This has been a very emotional debate in the House. I appreciate those speakers who have stated that there should not be any politics involved in this issue and that we should be hitting the high road in this debate.
As I listened to the hon. member for Parry Sound- Muskoka last night, who is my neighbour geographically, I could not help but feel that our listening audience and our ratings last night would be considerably low because for the first time in history people are watching an actual war unfold. It is quite a change in modem technology.
My regret is that this debate did not take place last week. We were brought back here a week too late. A serious debate took place in the United States Congress a number of days ago and it voted last week. That is what we should have done. Nevertheless, we did not do it.
People wonder why there should be different points of views on this entire issue. We should not be surprised that there are because in the United States Senate the vote was very narrow: 52 to 47. Yet, when it was over, they joined forces to support their military community and those who are working to bring about a settlement of the Middle East situation.
There has been a great debate on this issue as to whether or not sanctions worked. I have a list here of the ways the sanctions were working. Others say they were not working. Others say there were extenuating circumstances that required the bringing about of the war at an early stage. However, that is all passe now. The event is upon us.
With regard to diplomacy, how can you practise diplomacy when you have a dictator who does not want to give in on anything? Therefore, the only thing we really had a hope of practising was the sanctions. As the war goes on and as the tyrannical dictatorship in that country finally realizes that it cannot continue, that is when you will get diplomacy.
We have had a long debate in the House, but I am sure that everybody, to the last individual, will support our forces in their efforts to bring about a settlement to this issue.
In speaking about our forces today and for the past number of days, the second field hospital unit, which is located on Base Petawawa just three miles from my home, has been getting ready to go to the Persian Gulf. I

Government Orders
understand from reports there will be possibly over 500 people who will go with it from all across Canada. We in the House want to say to them that we wish them well. We are proud of the way they are serving Canada, and we are proud of the way our Canadian forces always exercise three key points.
There is their ability as military personnel. The idea some people may have is that as soon as "military" is mentioned, that everybody is agressive. That is not the case. Our military is a professional community.
The forces are very good at diplomacy as well, and they have proven that time and time again in their United Nations work.
The third parameter is rather an odd one to attribute to people wearing the Canadian forces uniform, but it is true to a degree. That is, they are politicians too, because they have to work with people from other countries and they have to work to settle problems that face them from day to day, and month to month, individually. They have to provide advice to the civilian leadership of this country and they do it very well.
We have ships in the Middle East and have had them there for some time. We have 24 CF-18s there and a large number of ground support. To those people, we extend our appreciation for what they are doing. There is a lot of warmth in Canada for the service people who are over there now and certainly for those who will go hereafter.
Before the break at Christmas, I visited the town of Amprior and associated my remarks and support with a group that was sending Christmas packages to the entire crew of a ship. There are people as well who are organizing other events of communicating with our forces who are over there. I hope that will go on and I would encourage Canadians right across this nation to do that sort of thing. Get the names of people over there and send them letters and gifts of various kinds from time to time. It is very important to their morale.
This is a serious and a solemn issue and must be treated as such. We in the House must continue to take a very high road in that regard.
What we are witnessing today in the Persian Gulf is a high tech war of the kind that has never taken place before in world history. We are going to see more of this unfold in the days ahead.
As I was preparing this talk, I could not help but let my feelings wander back to the days when I was very active with the NATO parliamentary group here. I still am, but at that time I was leading the parliamentary group to international conferences with the 16 NATO countries. That was a tremendous experience because it taught me how to understand the culture of other nations, their political systems, the special things that affected them in relation to their economy, and, of course, their customs.
If we are going to be effective in the international community, the first thing that we must know is something about the other person's way of life. That is the bridge that we need in international affairs.
As I prepared this speech, I could not help but think of the tremendous amount of high tech military equipment that has been developed by precision science over a number of years that is in the NATO alliance and also situated within the Warsaw Pact. Nothing has had a greater impact on world history than the sudden collapse of the communist states in eastern Europe. It has brought about a relaxation of those horrendous groups, one facing the other in Europe. As we see this high tech unfolding today, can we imagine what we have been delivered from if a war had broken out between the NATO Alliance and the Warsaw Pact? It would have been devastating on world society.
I could not help but think of that great biblical verse that "God works in mysterious ways, his wonders to perform". I think that He has delivered us from that catastrophe.
Now, today, having been given the gifts to think, to work constructively, to work with other people on the face of this earth, we must bring forth our greatest qualities and our best efforts to improve the United Nations organization. We must put it in place as a very effective world referee-negotiator, diplomat, and the organization that will continue to support human rights, international boundaries, and international protocol.
This ongoing international issue in the Persian Gulf and the Middle East is one that has consumed every member of the House and, indeed, all Canadians. There are many times in the affairs of the human race when
January 17, 1991

peace does not come easily. I do not say this in a way that I mean to be insensitive nor, in any way, would I say it in order to create fear, because we do not need that at this time.
I had the honour and the privilege to travel to Dieppe for the anniversary of the Battle of Dieppe with the Hon. George Hees and a delegation from this Parliament. I believe it was in August 1987. The way that generals in those days ordered those young people to go into Dieppe in that raid was an inhuman act.
The veterans who were back there at that time were remembering that day and how real it was to them. The question mark is still on military minds as well as on everybody else's minds as to whether that raid should have even been ordered.
As one sees the markers of those young people, 18, 19, 20 and 21 years of age, it brings one back home with the sincere and deep feeling that we who hold the responsibility of public office, backed up by those well meaning people across our country, should be doing everything we possibly can to bring about effective diplomacy in this world. That is one of the most important things that this nation can practise. We must work with others to put even more teeth into the United Nations.
As I outlined, the high-tech military materiel is in place today, and will be in place in the future to a greater degree, and nothing is going to be more important to the human race than to have sensible people who can bring about a world policeman who is effective and who can settle disputes. Indeed, when force is necessary in the end, they must be prepared to support that too, as a world police organization.
We visited Normandy and Holland. Think of the impression that we can have on the world as a Canadian nation. On one of our NATO visits we had a Remembrance Day ceremony, even though it was not Remembrance Day, at a major cemetery in Holland. It was out in the country near a number of beautiful trees. As we looked down those rows of markers from the cenotaph where our ceremony was taking place, we saw coming in from the fields of the community the Dutch farmers in their farm clothing, with their hats in their hands. They stood around the cenotaph with us as we performed our wreath-laying ceremony and said our prayers.
Government Orders
Those are the things that have a great impact on an individual. Again, they send you home with the idea that you must try to be a better and more constructive person in the politics of your nation.
We have some great people in this House, on both sides. I wish this debate had taken place a week earlier, because it is now almost redundant, with the exception of the following through and the questioning of what is going on from day to day.
Let us make up our minds today, as we have in the past, to move forward in a constructive and effective way to be ready to practice diplomacy when the moment is right. Even now, we must look forward to the day when this war is over so that Canada will be in the forefront in an attempt to tone down and settle some of these horrendous problems in the Middle East that have been going on for 5,000 years. That is going to be a major role for this nation.
In the Korean conflict we joined with the other UN forces under the United Nations flag. That event was a success. In the Suez crisis we went in again under the United Nations flag. That proposal was brought about by that outstanding Canadian, Lester B. Pearson.
Lester B. Pearson was Prime Minister when I entered the House. He was a personal friend of mine. I had great admiration for him, and to me he was almost like a grandfather. He had a great effect on my thinking as a young parliamentarian. I have never forgotten many of the things that he said because he was a man of great common sense. Indeed, it was he and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent who can be credited with a major input into the founding of the United Nations organization in San Francisco on October 24, 1945.
We have to build on what they started. Indeed, it has been a tremendous achievement for Canadian statesmanship. That must go on and we must be prepared to tackle these issues seriously. Today, it is Iraq. Tomorrow, it will be someone else. The machinery must be in place, both from the human point of view and from an enforcement point of view, to settle those problems.
The United Nations was brought in with the idea of building a new world order. The respect for international boundaries became paramount and is still paramount today. That is what this present war is all about, that and economics. So, we must remain strong to the principles

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
of international order, respect for international boundaries and international protocol in the years to come.
Last night we saw the attack on Israel. It is madness, yes, but it is part of the failure of the human race. You cannot negotiate with a tyrant, but you can do everything possible to maintain international law.
I mentioned the other battles in world history where the UN flag was used to cover the entire forces which went into battle. I sincerely hoped that this present war could have been carried out under the United Nations flag. As it is, each nation is there under its own flag. In future, in order to strengthen the image and effectiveness of the United Nations, we should have these international conflicts under the command of the UN.
We can still have generals. We will have key people in place, but it will be an international order emanating from a unified group of nations under the UN. It will have to be a commitment on the part of all members of the United Nations, and their expertise and their input will have to be used to settle international problems.
I want to end with one very realistic saying. Tied up in the improvement and the sponsorship of UN forces in the future is the saying that I have heard on many occasions: "Wars are started by old men and fought by boys." Today, wars are fought by both boys and girls.
As we debate this issue of the war that is presently going on, let us look beyond the horizons and fully prepare ourselves for the challenges in the future. There will always be someone looking for world power. There will always be someone greedy. So, let us commit ourselves to improving the United Nations and international order in the world in the years to come as well as now.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for my very good friend who has many years of experience here. I listened to his speech with interest, particularly to that part about the United Nations and the honour Mr. Pearson brought to Canada with his participation in peacekeeping.
The purpose of my question is to try to clarify some of the confusion I see in this very serious issue in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition.
Is it the hon. member's position that, if the allies were there under the formal blue flag of the United Nations then some of the disagreement in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition about the motion of the government would disappear and thus there would be more of its members in favour of the government motion?

Madam Speaker, when I mentioned the governments, I did not put a Liberal label on them when I was talking about the United Nations and the input into it. I was trying to be broad and a bit statesman-like on these very important issues.
It was a Liberal government that committed forces to Korea under the United Nations. It was a Liberal government that asked that the Suez crisis be settled with the use of a United Nations force. I, and I am sure many others, would feel much more comfortable if this event were carried out under the United Nations flag. Having played a major role in the founding of the United Nations, if we do not support that organization and its flag over the years in these world controversies, then we are letting down those great statesmen before us.
I stated very clearly in my speech that in future contests I would prefer to see all forces under the United Nations' flag. We can still use the great expertise from those many nations to handle the UN force.
The hon. member was a classmate of mine. We came into the House together and he is very sensitive to this issue as well. He is very close to some of those great issues.
Canadian work within the international community over the years has been very important and it is important that we continue to support the UN flag. I would say to my hon. friend that it is not just a symbol I am talking about here. The message I am really trying to get across is that when we go into an international conflict without being under the United Nations flag, while our operations can still be very effective it tends to weaken the image of the United Nations organization in the eyes of the world. Our main aim under the United Nations is to

pull all nations and people of the world together to settle these conflicts.
We all know that half of the problem in settling disputes is that people will not talk to one another. However, if we have them in a major organization, then they will have to talk to one another and many of these disputes would not arise in the first place.
I am convinced that every party in the House should be aiming toward supporting the UN flag because that is the international organization we want to see handling all these great issues in the years to come.

Madam Speaker, my colleague has been in the House of Commons for a long time. As a result of this experience, I wonder if he would give me his comments and reactions to the following.
It seems to me that few people talk realistically about the casualties of war, how many people die, and how they die. For example, the Pentagon often refers to war with words such as outcomes and scenarios. I would like to compare that with recent remarks by Brigadier Patrick Cordingley, commander in chief of Britain's seventh division who said, while referring to this particular conflict:
It is going to be the sort of warfare people never realized, or could
have expected. The public is not prepared for what is about to
happen. And we have got to prepare the-public for a particularly
unpleasant war. They should be told there will be a lot of casualties.
I am assuming that he is talking not only about soldiers, our own and Iraq's, but as well about children, seniors, and many other people who will be the victims and casualties not only in terms of death but in terms of injuries.
A final quote from Admiral Gene Larocque of Washington's Centre for Defence Information, a military think-tank which opposes the gulf war. He has estimated that there will be several thousands of casualties for the Americans and the allies, but that the over-all casualties will probably exceed one-quarter of a million.
I am wondering if my hon. colleague would give me his reaction to those comments.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, that is an excellent question and those are excellent comments, because they fit right into the main thrust of my speech.
I said that what we are watching today is high-tech warfare. I mentioned what an horrendous calamity it would be for the human race if the war in Europe between the communist east and the free west had broken out because of all the high-tech equipment positioned within both of those camps over the years.
There is no question but that the person he quoted from the Pentagon was right on, because with the great destructiveness of high-tech equipment today tens of thousands of people can be killed in very short order. I do not think the nation has come to realize that the precise bombing going on with high-tech equipment, for example against Iraq today, is being done in order to try not to have great casualties in the civilian population. But that is not very much comfort. It is just lessening the problem a bit.
If there were some World War I veterans listening to my hon. colleague's question today and my remarks, they would probably say to us: "World War I and World War n were no picnics either". We cannot downplay that statement because the trench warfare in World War I was a disaster. We had people coming home who had been gassed. They had lung problems and physical problems the rest of their lives, lost limbs, and so on.
War is hell, no matter what generation it is in and no matter what kind of equipment is used. Today, we have equipment that can really destroy a whole nation and indeed the world. This is why I am saying what I am thinking today and that is why that I have changed the thrust of my debate.
I have tried to bring a different perspective to it by saying that it is time all free nations and responsible nations of the world get with it and decide that they are going to support a very strong United Nations organization, and that organization must be prepared at all times to police international problems and to negotiate international problems.
Yes, at some stage down the road force may become necessary in any event, but at least the best we can do as human beings is try to lessen the problems. No matter how hard we work to bring about a world order, we are not going to get perfection. But, if we do not try, we will not even come close to it.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
I thank the hon. member for that very important question because it really ties in with the great destructive forces available to mankind today in a war.
If ever there were a time in the world history that we need sanity among people, responsible leadership within our nations, responsible members of Parliament who are willing to stand up and be counted on the issue of enforcing international law through the United Nations and to support the UN and indeed reform the UN, if we can make it a better body, than it is now. We must be looking at that as well.
That is why I emphasize the importance of Canada being at the forefront and centre in any conferences or meetings that take place to try to lessen the problems in the Middle East and bring about some solutions. We are not going to be perfect at that either, because other people have not been perfect for 5,000 years, but at least we can improve the situation. The important thing is that we all act like responsible individuals, bring world order back, and be prepared to settle these issues in the future.
Finally, the underlying factor is that under the UN flag the nations of the world must commit themselves to the United Nations and add strong support to bring about future peace in the world. If we do not have peace, if we are going to stand alone out there, we all are going to go down together if we do not act responsibly from this day on with high-tech warfare.

Madam Speaker, when I stand today to talk about the motion before this House, I find it very difficult. Obviously the situation has changed tremendously from when this motion was first brought forward.
I know everyone in this House and in this country wants us as members of Parliament to do everything possible to bring peace to the world. Really, that is what we are talking about today and that is what we have been talking about for the last few days: to bring about an international order which will bring peace to this world. When we talk about this motion, we are talking about bringing peace to the world.
We must recognize that it was almost six months ago that Iraq breached the international peace agreement by invading Kuwait in an unqualified and unprovoked act of
aggression. That was when the war began. That was last August 2.
The UN Security Council, the international group of nations empowered to maintain law and order in the world, passed a resolution at that time condemning Iraq, demanding that Iraq withdraw from Kuwait and that both sides negotiate. That was the initial reaction. That was back on August 2. Iraq did not comply. We are all aware of that today.
That was followed by economic sanctions and the authority given to the allied forces and member nations to enforce those sanctions. I for one was a firm believer that those sanctions were going to work. I think everyone in this House believed those sanctions were going to work.
However, most of us recognize the ineffectiveness of those sanctions, the fact that those sanctions were hurting the civilians. They were hurting many people, but effectively they were not doing anything to the military powers within Iraq.
As we have gone along in this course of events, many resolutions have been put forward by the United Nations. In fact there have been 12 in all. They relate to the unacceptable breach of the UN, the holding of foreign nationals, Iraq's liability under the fourth Geneva convention as it relates to war crimes, altering the sovereign position of Kuwait, and destroying Kuwait's records. Those are atrocities that the international peacekeeping organization and the world cannot tolerate.
Canada has been very involved in those resolutions and those attempts to bring peace to the world.
Mr. Coopen I rise on a point of order, Madam Speaker. I believe you will find unanimous consent for the following motion:
That, notwithstanding the Order made Wednesday, January 16,

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Could there be a decision whether we resume debate after Question Period?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can confirm that immediately following Question Period at twelve o'clock noon we will be returning to Motion No. 27, the one presently before the House.
January 17, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand there is unanimous consent for the parliamentary secretary to move the motion, and I understand that there is consent to approve the motion. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

Madam Speaker, I think Canada as a countiy has been very involved in this process of negotiation, debate and attempt to resolve this problem peacefully. Canada was a co-sponsor and co-draftee of virtually all those motions. Canada has played a very responsible role as a member of the UN.
The UN agreed by resolution 678 to allow Iraq one final opportunity, a time frame when Iraq would not be attacked. As a gesture of goodwill by the international community, Iraq was allowed seven more weeks to comply with that August 2 resolution to withdraw from Kuwait.
The UN as the keeper of law and order in the world was forced to respond. Canada is a member of the UN, in fact a founding member, as has been mentioned quite often in this House recently. Yet, as much as we dislike the actions that will have to be taken-in fact I do not think it is too strong to say that we hate the actions taken-we have an obligation to maintain law and order in the world.
Force is not something that is taken lightly, nor can it be offered in a way that it implies an empty threat. I think that is one thing we must recognize. It is a last resort. I feel we have explored all the options possible to us. When we look at the events which have taken place over the last days, weeks, and months; when peaceful negotiations were taking place; when discussions were taking place to try to resolve this situation; when leaders of nations on an individual basis and even collectively, and even Secretary-General of the United Nations, Javier Perez de Cuellar, said there was no reason to have any real hope, Iraq had never mentioned it was prepared to withdraw from Kuwait.
There are questions that we as Canadians must ask ourselves. What course is right for Canada in the cause for peace? Will Canada stand and be counted? Will we continue to support the international coalition, or will
we stand aside and hope that others uphold the rule of law?
Collective security is what this crisis is all about. It is important to be clear that it is not about the defence of democracy. It is not about oil, nor is it about supporting Washington. The principle at issue is simple and straightforward. Collective security and the defence and construction of an international order where aggression is rejected are what this principle is about and what the United Nations resolutions are all about.
Canada does not have a policy of war.
Canada has a policy of peace. Our policy has been designed to achieve a peaceful solution to the international crisis. If we check the speeches of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the other day, which stated all the things that have been offered and all the attempts that have been made, there is only one person who can realistically offer peace to the world today. That man is Saddam Hussein.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must interrupt the hon. member. He can continue when debate resumes.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today on behalf of an overwhelming number of my constituents who support the government's action in the Persian Gulf and to say how proud they are of our armed forces personnel who are involved.
What concerns me is that the member for Okanagan- Shuswap, who has often criticized us for not listening to the majority of our constituents, is toeing his party line and is not supporting the United Nations action.
In a poll done in his constituency yesterday by radio station CJIB, when asked the question: "Are you in favour of UN action", 390 people said yes and 43 said no. That is 90 per cent in favour. When is the member going to listen to the overwhelming majority of his constituents?

January 17, 1991

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as this made-for-TV war unfolds, the still, small voice for peace becomes harder and harder to hear amid the din of guns and planes.
During the first few days of conflict, it has not been the voice of Saddam Hussein that has been silenced, but the voices of an unknown number of innocent men, women and children.
Therefore, I would like to read from a letter sent to our Prime Minister by the Mennonite Central Committee on January 11.
"If now, in the hope filled post-cold war era, non-military methods are abandoned so readily, then the prospects for resolving other disputes by peaceful means are greatly diminished, allowing militarism to continue with its exploitive, destructive and death-dealing effects".
These are the words of a people who have done much thinking about the issues of war and peace over the last 450 years. I beg all hon. members to pay them some heed.

Madam Speaker, on hearing of last night's attack on Israel, my first thoughts were for friends in Israel, that they and other Israelis had not been hurt.
We now know, of course, that innocent victims have died and our hearts go out to them and their families. We hope that Israel and Israelis will be spared further attack.
This unprovoked aggression reminds us of the tremendous price Israel pays simply to exist, and I am sure that everyone in this House supports Israel's right to defend itself.
Yesterday morning, we were hoping against all hope that this would be a short war. Today, things are not so optimistic. Saddam Hussein has now had the opportunity to see the destruction that this war will bring. Is it too much to hope that he may now be open to appeals to withdraw from Kuwait and bring an early end to this war?

Madam Speaker, nothing more graphically illustrates the international necessity of stopping Saddam Hussein than his reckless and cynical attack on Israel, its cities and its civilians. Saddam is callously trying to provoke a broadened war, one that could lead to a global conflagration.
Yesterday we heard some eloquent speeches in this House about the reported losses of Iraqi lives. While all members of this House are concerned about casualties and loss of life, be they Iraqi or otherwise, the deaths of his own people are of no consequence to this man.
Only the destruction of this man's military capability will restore international peace and security. I commend the Israeli government for its restraint to date, the courage of its people not to retaliate and urge them to continue to show restraint. The United Nations coalition will deal with Saddam, and the sooner the better for all.

Madam Speaker, last night SCUD missiles from Iraq rained down on Israel, proving Saddam Hussein is a man of his hateful word. He had sworn to attack this country which offered no other provocation than to exist. I vehemently condemn this villainous attack on Israel. This further act of aggression by Saddam Hussein is not going unanswered by the allied forces. Reports say the Iraqi Scud launch sites have either been destroyed or are under further attack by the allied forces, and rightly so. I commend Israel for her courageous restraint not to retaliate at once. I hope and pray Israel will continue to place her faith in the allied forces. I further pray that her citizens are not placed in greater peril. World sympathy goes out to the families of Israeli citizens lost last night. Our thoughts are with Israel and the allied forces striving to protect her.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, earlier this week, St. Thomas University in Fredericton established what they have called a Third Age Centre, under their Chair in Gerontology. Its mission is to give meaning to life at all ages but, particularly, to emphasize that as we get older we nonetheless continue to grow in value and potential as human beings.
In a recent essay, Rabbi Gunther Plaut of Toronto has warned against some attitudes that seem to say, in a society where new is considered better, the elderly are seen as so much extra baggage. In reality, the reverse is true. Never before have senior citizens had such an opportunity to exert their influence towards a better world.
There is truth about the wisdom of age. Never before has the world been in greater need of wise and mature judgment based on long and growing knowledge from real life experience. Especially in these recent days, as hostilities have erupted in the Persian Gulf, there is a world-wide frustration and dismay that mankind has not yet learned some of the most tragic lessons of history.

Madam Speaker, in response to the unfolding events in this tragic war in the Middle East, I want to express my personal and party's concern over the unnecessary and unwarranted attack by Iraq against the State of Israel. It is a shock to all of the people in Israel and certainly to the diaspora as well.
I want to comment, frankly, on the remarkable restraint shown by the leadership of the State of Israel in response to this attack. This restraint is a model, I think, for all of the nations involved to ponder and consider, because the most vulnerable, democratic country in the whole region is the only one that is apparently showing the kind of restraint necessary at this time.
I have members of my own family living there. They have been pioneers in that country since the early 1920s. I share, with other families, a deep concern not only for Israelis but for every human being in that region. Let us hope that the restraint shown by the Israeli government
will be a model for other nations in the region. Let us hope for a swift peace and let us hope for a peaceful future.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I know I am joined by all members of this House and, indeed, by all Canadians in conveying our deepest respect and appreciation at this special time for our young men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces who are serving in the Persian Gulf. As well as those in uniform, there are National Defence civilians in support of this very delicate operation, whose dedication and sacrifice have served us so admirably and we are sure will continue to do so.
From all of us, I am sure, well done.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, Canadian forces are now taking part in operations in the Persian Gulf. These men and women are outstanding in their professionalism and have a tremendous sense of duty. We have every reason to be proud of our people in the forces who are performing their duties with great zeal. I urge all Canadians to support our troops by sending them words of encouragement so they will feel truly supported by the Canadian people in their desire to carry out the missions with which they are entrusted.

Madam Speaker, it was my experience on July 12, 1990, as my colleagues and I sat on the Mount of Olives, overlooking the city of Jerusalem, that I had come to a land of beginnings, a land of great history. It was there that I truly felt the greatest sense of peace and personal satisfaction I have ever experienced in my travels around the world, never believing that this would be, as it is today, a land of anxiety, fear, confusion and chaos. I guess it is best reflected in the words of Dwight D. Eisenhower when he said: "When people speak to you about a preventative

war, you tell them to go and fight it. After my experience I have come to hate war. War settles nothing."
Tb those who have the responsibility for leadership in this war and the ceaseless quoting of the Pearsonian diplomacy, here is what he said: "The grim fact is that we prepare for war like precocious giants and for peace like retarded pygmies."
I have great hope for peace in the Middle East at this time. I would like to share my sorrow about what has happened there. Perhaps if tolerance persists as it is today, then we might have answers to this problem.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the unbelievable consequences of power in the hands of a madman returns to terrorize the free world. Saddam Hussein's unimaginable atrocities against innocent adults and children, his senseless eight-year war against his neighbours, and his continued refusal to respond to the diplomatic peace efforts of the past five and one half months, have pushed the free world into war.
It is my wish that others in the world who may be contemplating a similar course of action will learn of the senselessness of acts of aggression towards humanity.
I wish to commend the Israelis for their restraint in this crisis. The Israelis position is one that can best be appreciated by those currently immersed in the destruction caused by Saddam Hussein. Our prayers go out to them.
To the men and women of Canada's Armed Forces, a team which has continued to maintain a high level of military competence and tolerance, I offer my prayers as well. May they return home be without incident.

speakerposition: subtopic
Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, for decades Canadian women, in solidarity with other women around the world, have worked to encourage the use of non-violent strategies of conflict resolution and to end oppression and violence in all their forms.
Women have historically been the victims of war. Women have historically not had a voice in the decisions about wars in which they are the victims. They are the mourning mothers, here at home, or those with their children who are in the horrors of the theatres of war. Women have shown their commitment around the world to peace; women at Greenham Common in the U.K., for example, or Mothers of the Disappeared in Central America.
Today, women across Canada, through demonstrations, through writing letters, through attempting to contact their parliamentarians and through raising the consciousness of others in Canada are appealing to our government to include them in the decision making.
Members of Parliament across the country have been approached by women in Canada who are concerned and want their voices heard for peace. It is time all of us listened to the women of Canada.

Madam Speaker, when I woke up this morning I was sure that the news would tell me that Israel had retaliated against Iraq, resulting in a dramatic expansion of this horrible war. It did not happen.
I want to recognize the restraint shown by Israel by not responding to the attack by Iraq. There was no threat to Iraq from Israel. The attack was not even at military targets, but at highly populated areas in the heartland of Israel. The attack was simply an attempt to provoke a further expansion of the war.
We should remember that this restraint is even more profound and meaningful when we consider that since events during the Second World War, one of the main principles of Israel has been "never again". Never again will they not respond to aggression against the Jewish people.
January 17, 1991

The whole world breathed a sigh of relief when Israel broke that principle in the interest of containing this war. I know I speak on behalf of many Canadians when I say I am truly grateful to Israel, and I strongly urge them to continue to show this strength, even in the face of more attempts to provoke.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at this stage, we have to conclude that the government has dissipated Canada's reputation as a peacemaker in the world. That is a very sad conclusion.
It seems to us, now we are in this unwanted war, that our military efforts should be on the side of providing health, hospital and field medical services. Our role should be one that will increase and not demolish our credibility once the hostilities are over. This is a war. The solution of the problem in Kuwait is not by means of war and it is not a solution that a majority of Canadians support.
Canadians would want to see Canada involved in diplomatic efforts in order to bring an end to this unwanted and terrible situation which is deteriorating by the day.
