subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Last night Canadians were horrified to learn of the unprovoked attack by Iraq on Tel Aviv and Haifa, the two largest cities of Israel.
I am sure that all members of the House and all Canadians will share with me in expressing our deep sympathy and solidarity with our friends in Israel. It is clear that Israel has shown remarkable restraint in the face of a very real threat to its own people.
Oral Questions
Will the Prime Minister tell the House what decisions his government has made in response to the attack of last night?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the government indicated earlier this week, one of the reasons we have been supporting and been part of the international coalition, and the reason why Canada has stood steadfast with the United Nations, was to make sure that an unmistakable clear signal went out to Saddam Hussein about the resolve of this nation to defend international order. That includes standing firm against anybody who attacks a friendly state, such as the State of Israel.
Last night, in the face of this unprovoked attack, I communicated with the Government of Israel and then sent a letter to the Prime Minister in which I said:
You may be aware that I have strongly condemned Saddam Hussein's missile attack on your country tonight. However, I am writing to you to express my profound sympathy to you and to the people of Israel.
Canada deplores this criminal and unprovoked act. It demonstrates, if anyone was still in doubt, the threat that Saddam Hussein poses to international peace and security.
The attack on Israel was a clear attempt to provoke retaliation in order to bring your country into the war. I know this will not escape your government.
Our thoughts are with you tonight. I wish to express the sympathy of the Canadian Government to the victims and their families. I convey the best wishes of all Canadians to them for a speedy recovery.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been in touch with the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Israel. I spoke earlier today with the President of the United States. Canada will take all appropriate action to make sure that Saddam Hussein respects international law and order and the prescriptions of the United Nations, or suffers the consequences.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We
are glad to hear that the Prime Minister sent this message on behalf of the entire House and the Parliament of Canada, because yesterday's attack was entirely unjustified. We feel very deeply about these attacks that were absolutely unprovoked, and we were particularly impressed by the attitude taken by the Israeli government, both during the past few months when faced with verbal threats and yesterday, when those threats were actually carried out.

January 17, 1991
Oral Questions
However, I now want to ask the Prime Minister whether a decision has been made by the government to make available the kind of humanitarian aid Israel and the Israeli people might need in the present situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, late last night I spoke to the Israeli ambassador, and I told him that the government was prepared to provide any humanitarian aid Israel and the moderate Arab States affected by the situation might need.
This morning, the Secretary of State for External Affairs communicated directly with Mr. Levy, the Israeli Minister of Foreign Affairs, to express Canada's sympathy and offer any humanitarian aid his country might need to deal with problems caused by attacks by that dictator, Saddam Hussein.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have another question for the Prime Minister. As a result of last night's tragic attack on Israel, there were seven casualties. All members of the House know there are many Canadian nationals in Israel at this moment.
What steps has the government taken to ensure the safety of Canadians who are presently in Israel?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in Israel and elsewhere in the region, there are some 14,000 Canadians now.
We are naturally in more than daily contact with our embassies and posts. We have established a system of wardens, whereby members of the Canadian community in each of those countries, including Israel, help the Canadian Embassy keep track of the location and requirements of Canadians.
My information, as of this morning, from Israel and from other countries in the region is that no Canadians have been injured. All Canadians know how to have access to their embassy.
We have, in addition, yesterday established and published an 800 number in Canada for use by Canadians who have relatives or friends in the Middle East. That 800 number of course will work around the clock. I can report to the House that understandably it was very
actively used last night. By that means we hope to be able to respond immediately and fully to concerns on the part of Canadians who have family or friends in the region.

Madam Speaker, I would like to raise a question with either the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
The tragic attack last night in Israel demonstrates how this war carries with it the real potential of escalation and broadening of the conflict.
I would like to ask either of the two front-benchers: Will the United Nations Security Council or other agencies of the UN be seized of this particular issue, and will the Security Council be convened immediately to address this new escalation and broadening of the war which adds a new dangerous dimension to the whole conflict? Can the Secretary of State advise us of what role the United Nations and its agencies will be playing in response to this new development?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Secretary of State for External affairs was in touch yesterday with the Secretary-General of the United Nations, as we have been on a fairly regular basis from before the outbreak of hostilities, with a view to finding a formula that would persuade Saddam Hussein to respect the decisions of that international body.
We maintain that, if a signal from Saddam Hussein would have been his intention to respect the law and withdraw from Kuwait which he illegally occupied, it would have had a beneficial effect on the attitudes of the members of the Security Council. But we are now engaged in a campaign now and Canada is there with other members upholding the United Nations, making sure that his war machine will never again be used against innocent neighbours and against states in the region such as Israel.

Madam Speaker, we have heard that response before.
My more specific question is: Would the new dimension added to this conflict as result of the attack last night bring about a convocation of the Security Council to address that and to determine what means might be employed by the international body to try to limit the conflict?
January 17, 1991

In particular, in Canada's own case, in response to a question I raised yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the Government of Canada was interested in maintaining lines of communication so that signals could be transmitted.
We understand that the Secretary of State has ordered the expulsion of Iraqi diplomats. I would ask if he could confirm that. If that is the case, can he tell us what lines of communication the government would then be continuing so these signals might be passed back and forth so that whenever it is appropriate we can find a way of bringing this conflict to an end?
Right Hon, Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Madam Speaker, it may very well be a surprise to the hon. member, but it is a surprise to few others that there is a capacity for escalation in the activities of Saddam Hussein. He attacked Kuwait. That was an escalation. It is highly probable that had he not been stopped, he would have gone on to attack Saudi Arabia. He has made lethal threats through the peace against the State of Israel. Last night he began to carry out those threats. The hon. member should not pretend to be surprised by this escalation.
That capacity for escalation is precisely the reason that the United Nations was already seized of the grave threat that this aggression by Saddam Hussein posed to the world and was determined to take actions to stop it. We had hoped that we could stop it peacefully and diplomatically, but we were determined that we would stop it in any event.
When it became clear, first, that diplomacy had gone as far as it could and, second, that the time the people sought for the use of sanctions was being used to perfect chemicals weapons, to perfect biological weapons, to pollute the Persian Gulf, and also to extend the network of terrorist possibilities available to Saddam Hussein, then we believed it was time to act. That is the view of the United Nations. That is the view of the Security Council. The way to stop escalation is to stop Saddam Hussein.
An hon. member Right on.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. We join all members of the House and did so last night in decrying the particularly unjustified attack on Israel and, indeed,
Oral Questions
sadly the predictable attack. It has been one of the reasons why this party felt that getting into this war without having exercised all other options was exactly what this could lead to.
I want to add my voice to those who have said very sincerely to Israel that we admire their restraint and their contribution to the world community by trying to exercise restraint.
Hear, hear.

As has been mentioned earlier, of course, there are many Canadian families who have relatives and friends in Israel, as there are others in Canada who have relatives and friends in the region. I was pleased that the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned that there will be an 800 number.
I would just ask the Prime Minister again if there is other assistance that is being given to all those in Canada who have relatives and friends in the area? What is the Canadian government able to do for those people to allay their fears and make sure that communication is available to them?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that the consular number, the 800 number, is one important step because that allows individuals to identify precisely their concerns and allow us to respond.
But I think that the Leader of the New Democratic Party refers to another important element of this. There has been great restraint shown by Israel and the House respects and encourages that.
It also has to be said that there has been great restraint shown by the Arab countries and indeed by those of Arab origin in this country and that, too, should be encouraged by all of us in the House.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This should be recognized by us.
We have our consular people established as a task force, available to do everything that we can. This is not a traditional situation. If there are new or other things that need doing, I would hope that the Leader of the New Democratic Party and, indeed, others in the House, would suggest them to me. Within the range of our capacity, we will do everything that we can.

January 17, 1991
Oral Questions
As the Prime Minister has said, in terms of humanitarian assistance, we have communicated immediately to Israel and also to Jordan the willingness of the Government of Canada to be of extra help with regard to humanitarian requirements.

A supplementary, Madam Speaker. I appreciate the information the minister has given. I think it is useful, not just to us but to Canadians watching.
Of course one of the tragedies of this war is the displacement and hardship on civilians, all those who have not been involved in the conflict but certainly are victims.
We understand that Jordan has opened its borders and there are a number of refugees fleeing now and some who have fled there in the past. I understand that the United Nations has estimated there could be about 1.5 million refugees as a result of this war. I understand also that the United Nations has undertaken an augmented relief fund.
Can the minister tell the House what other humanitarian measures the Canadian government is going to take to assist these refugees, to assist victims of this war so that we can play our part in that aspect of humanitarian need?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The House will know that when this crisis was caused by the attack by Saddam Hussein against Kuwait, there were immediate impacts upon third countries, particularly caused by the outflow of refugees and the movement of displaced workers. Jordan was one of those and Egypt was another.
The package of actions the Prime Minister announced in early August included contributions in the neighbourhood of $75 million by the Government of Canada for humanitarian purposes. A little more than a third of that was directed to Jordan and a little less than a third of that to Egypt and contributions to other places in the world. That has already been done.
I am seeking to reach the foreign minister of Jordan by telephone this morning to communicate directly to him the Prime Minister's message to King Hussein, asking the Jordanians to indicate areas in which it would be helpful for Canada and, indeed, the rest of the world, but for Canada specifically, to offer further help. We
think that it is in these circumstances most efficient to respond to needs as they are identified by the countries which have to deal directly with the problem. We are doing that and we are prepared, again with in the limits known to the House, to consider other initiatives that would be helpful in the circumstances.

Madam Speaker, I have the following question for the minister. As he said in his reply to my colleague, there is a war on, and Canada supported that war. At the same time we must plan for peace, for the end of the war. I want to ask the minister whether Canada is now taking part in diplomatic initiatives within the United Nations or with other countries, first to find a way to end this war and second, to promote peace in the region in the future.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with respect, I must correct part of what the hon. member said. Canada supported the United Nations. Canada is supporting international law and order.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What Canada supports is the integrity and security of Kuwait, Israel and other countries that may be attacked by Saddam Hussein.
As for what may happen after the crisis, after the conflict, I have already had some conversations with the Secretary-General of the United Nations, in the course of which I advised him that the Prime Minister and myself were interested and determined to maintain close liaison with the Secretary-General and the United Nations on the subject of seeking ways to make speedy progress after the end of conflict.
This morning, I spoke to Dr. Abdel Mejuid, the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs. We discussed the situation in the region and other issues but we also talked about what would have to be done once peace is restored. A peacekeeping activity was mentioned in which Canada might play a role, and we also touched on other political and humanitarian questions.

Madam Speaker, as my leader and this government has said, we admire the incredible restraint that has been shown by Israel at this time in the face of, really, unprovoked attack.

I think that in the interests of peace in the Middle East, they even deferred their right to self-defence. That is quite an incredible undertaking, and I would presume that all of you as leaders, particularly sitting in the cabinet or ex-cabinet ministers, must know what it means to let their constituents down in a sense.
That is what the sense in Israel is right at this moment. I think and I hope they appreciate the interests of world peace.
I was listening carefully to the Minister of External Affairs whose courtesies I have appreciated. Can the government tell this House what further steps are being taken militarily and diplomatically by the United Nations to ensure that no further attacks will take place against Israel and to ensure the safety of Israel, which is presently being held hostage in the Iraq-Kuwait war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should tell my hon. friend that, as she might have noted from the response of the Government of Canada last night and from my remarks in the House of Commons some three days ago, this government has always taken as a matter of policy that the ultimate objective of Saddam Hussein would be an attack on Israel.
I conveyed to the House that this would be unacceptable to the Government of Canada. I indicated why it would be unacceptable. I indicated why we would resist it in all circumstances. For that reason, I communicated this morning with President Bush and had a lengthy conversation with him in regard to the present security status of Israel.
My hon. friend is quite right. Israel has exercised remarkable restraint. That restraint is not eternal. The coalition forces have, since that incident and will today, be taking action of such a persuasive nature against Iraq that we believe and hope that will obviate the need for the state of Israel to respond at an early moment.
I have always recognized that no one has the right to tell the state of Israel when and how it must defend itself. A nation of its suffering and of its extraordinary heritage, Israel always has the right to defend itself, and always has. I hope in the circumstances that the response of the great coalition, which seeks to preserve fundamental values, will persuade Israel that perhaps waiting
Oral Questions
at this moment is in its interest and in the interest of the cause of peace.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, I believe the government has noted Israel's tremendous patience. Let it not be tried any more.

The Canadian tradition has always been to help war victims. Sadly, innocent Israeli families are now in this tragic situation.
Does the government have other plans to help the people of Israel?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
This morning, the Secretary of State for External Affairs called Minister Levy of Israel to let him know that Canada is prepared to offer all available humanitarian resources, and that we would do so gladly and immediately.
The minister also told Mr. Levy, who voiced his appreciation, that the government also intended to offer its assistance to King Hussein and had also mentioned this to the Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs. Not only did Minister Levy agree but he was delighted with Canada's decision to maintain and intensify its humanitarian aid to Israel, Egypt and any other non-belligerents in the region.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Last night in response to the unjustified, unprovoked and callous attack upon Israel the Prime Minister said that Canada may play a new role with its allies in retaliatory action aimed at Iraq. I want to give the Prime Minister an opportunity now to tell Canadians specifically what he had in mind and if perhaps today he has issued new orders through the minister of defence to the chief of defence staff that could involve a change in position or mission for the Canadian forces or could, perhaps, mean sending additional Canadian forces to the gulf such as CF-18s or ground troops. Would he tell Canadians more specifically what he had in mind when he made that statement?

Oral Questions

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government has not, following a meeting of the cabinet this morning, issued new instructions to the military. We are examining all possibilities with our intelligence and military officials and with allies around the world. I referred to a conversation with President Bush this morning. There were conversations between the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the foreign minister of Egypt and with the foreign minister of Israel earlier today. We are examining all possibilities that would allow Canada to assist in a constructive and helpful way the prosecution of a very important initiative now under way in the Middle East.
Canada is not a superpower. Our military means are limited and we use them traditionally only with the greatest of care and reluctance. But I have no reluctance in telling you that while the mandate has not been defined because we are presently examining all of the options, Canada will not sit idly by in the face of unprovoked attack upon friendly countries. We are an ally and full partner in the coalition set up by the United Nations to drive Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. We will play a full and, if need be, a growing role and commit the necessary resources to ensure that justice is brought to that area of the world.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, the attack on Israel last night gives to that nation one of the most difficult dilemmas any country can face. It is a Hobson's choice. If they restrain themselves as they have and do not defend in order to protect the multilateral coalition, they may be encouraging Iraq and/or other countries to aggress or take advantage of the situation.
Might I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he has called in the ambassadors. If he has not, will he call in the ambassadors from the neighbouring states and tell them that any sign of harm or taking advantage of Israel's restraint will be taken most seriously by Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, both the Prime Minister and I last night communicated directly to the ambassador of Israel. I am now in the process of calling not the ambassadors, but the foreign ministers of countries in the region. In the conversation I have had so far with Egypt, certainly I was struck by the appreciation on the
part of Egyptian authorities of the restraint that has been shown by Israel, indeed the admiration, the sense that what Israel is doing in these circumstances, far from being a sign of weakness is a sign of the strength and maturity of that country.
Those are not just the sentiments of Canada. Those are the sentiments expressed this morning to me by the foreign minister of Egypt. But I will consider the proposal made by my friend and convene a meeting of the ambassadors to Canada of countries neighbouring Israel. They share, as we share, a profound interest in the integrity and stability of Israel, as they share a profound interest in stopping the one force that now most threatens to destabilize Israel, and that is Saddam Hussein.

Madam Speaker, I would like to direct my question also to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
We appreciate very much the statement he made earlier in answer to my leader that Canada is already reaching out to offer additional humanitarian aid to those countries that are immediately faced with such devastating humanitarian problems.
I would like to pursue that a little further. It has been estimated that about $1 million per day is being spent on this tragic war. I know that everyone in this House, regardless of our differences, pray for an early peace.
Since it is estimated by UN officials that about 1.5 million people may be displaced, coming I believe just from Iraq and Iran alone, and of course there are other humanitarian issues in that general area, will Canada plan to contribute at least as much as we have to the war effort, or perhaps more, to assist people devastated by war in those countries that are going to bear the brunt of the immediate refugee problems? Will we be able to provide practical help as quickly as possible by such means as transportation of personnel and direct assistance for teams of workers in refugee camps, as well as relief agencies?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are naturally looking at means by which we can help deal with a new refugee problem. The estimates she cites, in my judgment, may well be low. I think that the results of Saddam Hussein's
January 17, 1991

aggression could well, with respect to refugees, be more than 1.5 million displaced persons of which she speaks.
I have to say that the hon. member, and I hope members of her party, should stop citing just half the costs. Of course there are costs to war, but there have been extraordinary costs, not least to the Third World, as a result of this invasion of Kuwait by Saddam Hussein.
Among the things that happened were that thousands of people, people from the poorest countries, from Bangladesh, from the Philippines, from Sri Lanka, from countries in Africa, who were depending upon work in that region were forced to quit that region. That is causing right now immense problems. The longer Saddam Hussein is able to stay, the more time it is giving him. Time is what my hon. friend was asking for last week. The more time that it is given him, the longer those costs accumulate.
Obviously I cannot undertake to make the kind of expenditure the hon. member talks about, but I can certainly give her a commitment that Canada will play an active role with respect to response to the refugee problem.

Madam Speaker, I completely agree with the minister. Of course there are great humanitarian costs, and we do not begin to know them, sitting in our comfort here in Canada. We are just as concerned as he is with all aspects.
Just thinking ahead, as I know he is, and I am sure the Minister of Immigration is as well, I would like to ask this question. We know from past experience that the countries which receive refugees in the first and second stage of refugee movement are usually the countries left with permanent refugee camps and with stateless people. This is a great tragedy. I would hope that we would plan now-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member please put her question? This is getting into debate.

Yes, Madam Speaker. I am asking the minister if we will begin to plan now to be pro-active to try to prevent this from happening in the months ahead.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think that Canada's history has been one of being pro-active and helpful in refugee and refugee-like situations.
We are following this very carefully, and I stated that we would regard any humanitarian requests in a positive way.
We are, as my colleague has said, working with the UN Disaster Relief Organization. For the most part I believe that the UN is looking at potential repatriation as opposed to resettlement. But we are in constant touch. The situation is of course evolving all the time. It is our intention to continue to work with the United Nations on the humanitarian aspects and the refugee aspects, as well as in the military coalition.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
I am sure the minister knows, as does everybody in this House, that there are other Canadians who are deeply involved in this conflict. They are the families of the men and women who are bravely serving for Canada in the Persian Gulf.
I would like to ask the minister if he could give us his assurance in the House that the proper amount of planning and resources have been allocated to deal with the real needs of these families and help them cope with the anxiety. Could the minister give us some information on that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would be glad to respond to my hon. colleague, because I know he is very much concerned for the families in his area.
I am pleased to say that we have a family support system in place through our department. They have been operating for some time in Halifax, Esquimalt, and Cold Lake where the majority of personnel come from. That support system is working very effectively. I visited with them not long ago. They have counselling resources. In addition, each of the ships has set up a special group of the families related to those ships. They are providing support for the families. The spouses are meeting together.

January 17, 1991

I think it is working out very effectively. When I visited with them recently, certainly their response was very appreciative. We have also indicated to them that if additional resources are in any way required we will ensure that those are received.

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
The whole world held its breath last night, and thank God there was no use of chemical or nerve gas warfare in the attack. The next time we might not be so lucky.
My question therefore is for the Prime Minister. The Israeli Embassy today confirmed that there are people on the West Bank in the Gaza, men, women and children, who have not received gas masks.

We know there are men, women and children on the West Bank and in the Gaza strip who have not been given gas masks. Could the Prime Minister inform the House whether he is prepared to join his allies in seeing to it that gas masks are distributed to these men, women and children as soon as possible?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not have a specific response. I am aware of a Supreme Court decision, I believe in the State of Israel, which required that all citizens be provided with the necessary equipment. I know that the Government of Israel and the people of Israel are very principled-it is a very civilized country-and will want to make every effort to make sure that everybody receives these masks.
I can check into it immediately afterward and I would be happy to advise my hon. friend. The position of the Government of Canada, as conveyed officially, always was that the same benefits, of course, must apply to all citizens. We will look into it for the member and get back to her as quickly as we can.

specifically those sections dealing with international emergencies and war emergencies?

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Solicitor General.
I was advised yesterday by the President of the Canadian Arab Federation, Mr. James Kafieh that Canadians of Arab and Iraqi origin are, to quote Mr. Kafieh being "harassed and badgered" by the Security Intelligence Service.
Will the Solicitor General give his assurance that the Government of Canada, through the Security Intelligence Service, is not targeting for investigation Canadians solely on the basis of their ethnic or religious origin?
Can he reassure Arab Canadians that their rights will be protected and that they have not been placed under special surveillance by the Security Intelligence Service?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should perhaps respond to that, because I gave the assurance my hon. friend seeks in my speech to the House of Commons three days ago.
I indicated then that the invocation of the War Measures Act in the Second World War, which had imprisoned unfairly Japanese and Italian Canadians, was something that we had corrected and would never happen again. I gave Arab Canadians, particularly Iraqi Canadians, the assurance that that blot on our national history would never be repeated. I indicated to the House that the laws would apply fairly to all Canadians.
There will not be any special edicts of any kind and certainly no illegal, arbitrary or capricious actions taken against Canadians of Arab extraction, all of whom are deemed to be, like all of us, first-class citizens.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the UN resolutions on which this government has based Canada's involvement in this war were strictly limited to removing Iraq from Kuwait and to restoring the Government of Kuwait, as well as freeing the hostages and reparations.

In his statement the other night, George Bush clearly added to those objectives: to destroy the economic, military and political structure of Iraq and some say the agenda really is to destroy Saddam Hussein. Which is the agenda of this government? Is it George Bush's agenda, or is it the United Nations agenda?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there may come a day-and I hope it is soon-when the NDP will rid itself of this reflexive anti-American position on everything. I say it in all respect to my hon. friend. Well, for example, there is chuckling from the NDP. The socialist leader in Britain, Neil Kinnock, said that in the interests of distancing himself from the government, he did not propose to distance himself from his obligations to support the United Nations.
I say to my hon. friend that the United Nations has spoken clearly and effectively. Perhaps my hon. friend may care to read the objectives of the UN. Confronted with the intransigence of a dictator who invaded a friendly neighbour Arab state and who proved his criminality even further last night by attacking Israel, Canada is going to join with all members of the coalition to drive him out of Kuwait and to make sure that if we in the world community deals with him again, it will be in a position of his acceptance of the rule of international law. He will be held responsible for everything that is taking place.
Madam Speaker, this party has stood with him-
Oh, oh.
But, when the United States is wrong, this party and this country should stand and say to the United States that it is wrong. That is the situation we are in in this case.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member have a question?

Yes, I have, Madam Speaker.
My question is for the Prime Minister, whatever our differences on this issue, U.S. commanders are now saying that the control, communications and capacity of Saddam Hussein to wage war have been destroyed. Will this government join with all of us in this House and ask
Oral Questions
the United States administration to take a pause in the destruction and seek peace with Iraq in this war?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, is my hon. friend suggesting that with an attack against Israel last night, we should take a break and ask Saddam Hussein to be nice? This is absolutely preposterous.
What is even more serious is the suggestion that somehow we are in violation of resolution 678 and that the United States is doing something illegal. The resolution passed on November 29, 1990 does a number of things. It demands that Iraq comply fully with the resolutions. It authorizes member states co-operating with the Government of Kuwait to restore international peace and security in the area. It requests that all states provide appropriate support to restore international peace and security. That is exactly what we are in the process of doing. We have rallied to the call of the United Nations which is saying at this critical moment in the life of our organization, "Step forward those of you who believe in durable peace and freedom, step forward and defend the interests of the United Nations", and that is exactly what Canada is doing.

speakerposition: subtopic

In light of the critical situation and the sensitivity to testing a new generation of weapons, can the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicate to the House how Canada will vote today at the United Nations on this important issue.

I am very sad that this afternoon we would get to a point where harsh words would be shouted across that would be regretted by members who utter them. This could get the House into a situation which, to my feeling, would be very difficult for the rest of the country who is watching us.
There is a conflict in the Middle East, and this should not be a reason for us to create more of a conflict in the House of Commons.
I will recognize the hon. member for Calgary Northeast who has been most concerned with what has been going on in the last little while.
I see the hon. member for York South-Weston whose words I have chosen not to hear at one point. I think the wise thing for me to do would be to listen very quietly to the hon. member for Calgary Northeast and then for the House to resume debate.
Hopefully, the hon. member for York South-Weston will listen carefully to what his colleague from Calgary will have to say. Hopefully, he will change his mind about "not being finished".

speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the House agrees to a brief extension of Question Period, I would certainly take a moment to indicate that we are continuing to look at whether or not it is possible to make-

I am trying, Madam Speaker, despite shouts from the NDP, to respond to the question that was placed.
We are looking at ways in which the matter might be brought before either the CSCE or the United Nations in a way that would not encounter a veto by the Soviet Union.
In addition to that, the Prime Minister has written to Mr. Gorbachev. I have just written to the new Soviet foreign minister requesting an explicit and early response to the Prime Minister's letter. I am planning meetings in the next two or three days with representatives of leaders of the Baltic communities in Canada.
I know there have been meetings involving members of this House interested in this issue and the leaders of the Baltic community in Canada to see if there are practical ways in which we can bring our influence to bear on the Soviet Union.
There is now-at least there was at 11.30 and I think it is now in progress-a meeting involving three members of this House representing three parties with the Soviet ambassador to make it clear that the representations I had made to that ambassador that the failure of the Soviet Union to change its approach to the Baltic people will have an effect upon the range of its relations with Canada.
That is the message that I communicated, and that is the message being repeated by members of three parties in this House. I know the member's interest in these things, and I will naturally try to keep him advised as to developments in the issue.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to listen carefully, because this concerns him.
I do not have a broad experience of parliamentary debate in times of international crisis or wartime, but I am told that traditionally, for instance in Great Britain or France, when there is a crisis of this magnitude and those countries are involved, there is a refreshing lack of political partisanship. We see this happening across the world in other parliaments, with the exception of this one.
Perhaps the Chair could arrange for a meeting with certain leaders or certain groups.
I thought now that Canada was involved in a war, the debate in the House ought to rise above partisan considerations. Today, Madam Speaker, I am amazed to see that those partisan considerations are still there, especially in the attitude of the minister responsible. I would like some indication of what the precedents are in this respect. Madam Speaker, we have done eveiything we could to rise above partisan considerations. We have tried to be co-operative. Madam Speaker, the failure of the United Nations to handle this crisis-

Madam Speaker, the failure of the United Nations to handle this crisis would have severe impacts on the world. It might never again be able to play an effective role in responding to aggression. Success in this effort will provide a real prospect for collective security in the future. It is critical for countries like Canada even though we are a long way away. It is very critical for countries with small populations with two superpowers at their borders, but we have very limited capacity. We must preserve international law and order.
This is an opportunity for the United Nations to play the kind of role it was designed to perform. But it also puts the United Nations at risk. If the United Nations fails to live up to those principles, objectives and efforts for which so many people have fought so hard for so many years, what is the future for world peace, law and order? It is critical for the world order that we have peace in this particular situation.

tions from both the leaders of the parties involved and from private members as well. There have been most thoughtful contributions. Some of the contributions have been absolutely historic. We have had non-partisan contributions. We have had bipartisan contributions in the very best Canadian tradition. I wish to congratulate those who are responsible for the conduct of Canada's foreign policy.
Today, Madam Speaker, I propose to examine where we are, how we got here, the reaction from our riding and tell a couple of incidents about a young Canadian and a young Palestinian and to reflect on the Arab Canadian population of our country. To begin with, where we are. Israel today is exercising remarkable restraint. There is moral strength in exercising restraint.
As the Prime Minister correctly said today, Israel should not be unduly put to the test. However, I have been brought up to believe there is moral strength in exercising restraint and self-discipline and I congratulate the State of Israel for doing so.
I wish to associate myself with the Prime Minister's statement on the attack on Israel and I salute the Secretary of State for External Affairs who throughout this has exercised statesmanship of an historic character, particularly when he said: "the way to stop escalation is to stop Saddam Hussein and his ilk."
How did we get here? We got into the situation we are playing in the Middle East in the best Canadian tradition. I salute the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra for his historic and courageous contribution to the debate the other day in this House.
There are those who suggest that we are illegitimately with the United Nations. I quote the distinguished Canadian columnist, Jeffrey Simpson who wrote in today's Globe and Mail:
Keeping the peace under UN colours can involve a unified UN command, as in Korea, with strategic and operational authority given to the leading contributing country, the United States. Or it can be, as in the Persian Gulf; contributions by member states working together under UN resolutions but without a unified UN command.
Madam Speaker, the reaction is beginning to come in from across the country. I have here a letter which was faxed to my office two days ago, and I quote:

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Suggesting that we should agree to link withdrawal to the discussion of other regional issues is nothing short of agreeing to negotiate with terrorists and hostage takers-no matter how "legitimate" these grievances may be.
Even more unhappily, the thought of allowing the deadline to pass without following it with speedy and decisive action would lead us to contemplate an even more horrific problem-
While we all wish there were another outcome, it seems evident that the only action that could avoid the current confrontation is our own capitulation which would most certainly only delay an even more horrible future outcome. Those who blame Mr. Bush and the western nations for these circumstances are like those who blame the victim of rape and burglary for the crime perpetrated by the real guilty party.
I know this went on a bit long, but I wanted you to know that there are thoughtful people who support what you are trying to achieve and we do not always show up on the evening news.
I will quote a second fax which came into my office yesterday.
Ibo many Canadians have died in wars in history to have this country turn its back on the need for a co-operative United Nations effort in the Middle East, lb not fulfil the obligations and initiatives of the United Nations would reduce Canada to a less than mediocre entity in the world community. Canadians have died for civility, for justice, for individual rights and the United Nations is the manifestation of the ideals for which they gave their lives.
I said that I wanted to talk briefly about a 19-year old wounded in the trenches. This happened in Sanctuary Wood on June 2, 1916. It was a story which I did not hear until almost 75 years later when the man who was wounded in those trenches attended a reunion of his regiment in Calgary and for the first time told his family the story of the bloody experiences, the mindlessness, the banality and the horror of war.
I am very grateful I was with him that particular day because as as a child I had begged him to tell me of the glory of war and he had always refused to say anything about it. But my father who was hit by a shell in Sanctuary Wood on June 2, 1916 taught me what no movie or history book could tell me about the absolute horror and the stupidity of war. War he said, is sometimes the only course of action when you are dealing with a bully and someone who abuses the rights of others.
I also would like to mention a 24-year old Palestinian whom I met in 1959 while travelling on a train from Gaza to Cairo and who became a close friend. This man of Palestinian origin, Salah el-Dim Subaih, was a teacher who was being resettled in Kuwait, where he served for many years. After he settled he invited me to his
wedding. I was not able to go, but I sent a gift and we became fast friends by correspondence.
Later in the 1967 war I served as the post office for his family in Gaza who were sending letters to relatives in Cairo. There was no mail going back and forth until the Red Crescent and the Red Cross set it up.
From that came waves of gratuity and friendship which I think is really the only basis on which the new world order, of which many have spoken in this House, can be based.
There is something to be said about Arab Canadians. The Prime Minister referred in Question Period to their situation today in response to a question, as he did in his speech the other day.
It is perhaps not a well known fact that in my city of Edmonton, approximately 10 per cent of the Canadian Arab population resides. It is a slightly different profile from the general profile in the fact that generally speaking, Christian Arabs outnumber those of Muslim and Druse origin by three to one in our country, but the majority in Edmonton are of Muslim or Druse origin, although there are substantial numbers of Christian Arabs as well.
We have, as well, a growing Jewish community in Edmonton, largely due to immigration from the Soviet Union. I salute those leaders of the Jewish community in my city, along with the Arab community, led by the example of Professor Baha Abou-Laban, who have engaged in dialogue from the beginning of the time of the intifadah. They have tried to establish, and successfully I believe, the practice and the belief that we here in Canada wish to separate ourselves as much as we can from the quarrels abroad. But that can never entirely be done.
In the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who spoke in this House on August 19, 1914, when this House was debating the question of the first World War, and in a reference to fellow citizens of German origin at that time, he said at page 10 of Hansard:
They are certainty among our best citizens. They are proud of the land of their adoption, which to many of them is the land of their birth, and they have shown more than once their devotion to British institutions. But, Sir, they would not be men if they had not in their hearts a deep feeling of affection for the land of their ancestors, and nobody would blame them for that.
January 17, 1991

Madam Speaker, those words can apply to Arab Canadians today.
In the words of the Prime Minister speaking on Tuesday, January 15,1991, on the subject, he said at page 16990 of Hansard:
On this point, I want to reassure Iraqi-Canadians that they will not
be subject in any way to illegal surveillance or unwarranted detention,
as was the case in regard to other citizens during World War II. That
lesson fortunately has been learned in this country.
I wish to associate myself with the words of the Prime Minister and to pledge on behalf of the Government of Canada that that pledge and that undertaking will be upheld, and that restraint will be the order of the day. We will not repeat the mistakes that were made during the Second World War when groups of Canadians of various origins were isolated and were dealt with unfairly-
These are turbulent times, but those who have lived through times of war and times of the formation of history tell us that this is the stuff of history. How do we sort our way through the confusion?
The best way is to commit to the rule of law and to the rule of order, and so therefore I proudly associate myself with the resolution before this House, which I strongly support, and with the conduct of Canada's foreign policy in supporting the work of the United Nations in the Persian Gulf, and I pray, humbly, along with I am sure all members of this House, that the conflict will come to a swift and final end and that a way can be found to establish a permanent and lasting peace based on the principles of the three great monotheistic religions throughout the Middle East and throughout the world.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, my question to the hon. member concerns the situation in the Middle East.
I wonder what his position would be on an international peace conference on the Middle East once hostilities have terminated; whether he would support a homeland for the Palestinians and the resolution of that difficult situation for those people; and whether he would sup-
Govemment Orders
port the re-establishment of an independent, not occupied Lebanon.

Madam Speaker, it is a rare privilege, and I mean that sincerely, to have the opportunity in this House to engage in dialogue with the hon. member.
I do indeed support the principle, once peace has been established in the Middle East, of whatever effort can be made toward finding a lasting peace, as I said in the conclusion of my remarks.
If detente between the two superpowers can be preserved and if indeed the cold war has ended, many of the objections to convening such a conference will have been removed. I think that President Bush has recognized that in some of his statements over the past 12 to 18 months and indeed, such a conference would be appropriate.
With reference to a homeland for the Palestinian people, it is my belief that the UN resolutions, not the series that we are debating here today, but the earlier resolutions on Palestine and the preservation of the state of Israel, which is a condition precedent in my mind to an establishment of a Palestinian homeland, ought to be followed. The answer is a qualified but strong yes to the hon. member.
With reference to the Lebanese question, yes, I believe that as soon as possible and as soon as security can be established the occupation of Lebanon ought to cease, and that wonderful country which, when I knew it over three decades ago, was referred to as the Switzerland of the Middle East, can once more find some serenity and peace within itself and security from its neighbours.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my friend across the way for his comments and afford him the opportunity to add his comments on the following review prepared by the United Nations children's organization, UNICEF, which, in a gulf crisis advisory on January 15, wrote: "The situation of Children: In the event of war in the gulf region a number of factors, apart from damage and destruction to buildings and infrastructure, will affect the welfare of children and women in the region. There will be serious shortages, particularly of food, water,

Government Orders
medicines and energy supplies. Services will be severely curtailed due to diversion for emergency and military needs. Prices will spiral upward and the economic situation could be complicated by the devaluation of local currencies, especially in the majority of the countries of the region which import about half of their essential needs. Widespread environmental degradation resulting from war-related pollution and climatic changes will have unpredictable effects on the local population. The situation will be worsened by the possibility of breakdowns in water and sanitation facilities, especially in urban areas."
I know the member will want to respond with concern for those innocent victims of this conflict and I welcome his comments on that analysis by UNICEF.

Madam Speaker, I know that the time is limited and I will try to respond as well as I can. I agree that that assessment is probably very accurate. I have not seen it. I thank my hon. friend for mentioning it.
I wish Saddam Hussein could have been listening to the hon. member this morning. I wish he would realize that this is what he has put in train. It is in train and at some point it will come to an end. After it comes to an end, then the world, probably financed by petrodollars because they are available in that area, must commit itself to a rehabilitation program for the entire area. This is not only for men, women and children but to restore the infrastructure of the area which will be severely damaged for the entire Middle East. Perhaps it will be time for a Marshall plan for the entire mid-east with participation and collaboration by all parties, perhaps hand in hand or perhaps following a peace conference and a settlement.
There has to be change, and there has to be removed from the scene in the Middle East the sources of discontent that give fuel to the engines of madmen like Saddam Hussein.

Madam Speaker, the world is a much sadder place since January 16, 1991, because the demons of war have been unleashed and absolutely no one knows where this war will lead. Absolutely no one knows what problems, if any, will be resolved.
I think that point was captured very well by William Johnson in an article in The Gazette today entitled: "War's initial success-". Will it boost the government's chances?
It is really extremely sad when one believes that a military action that will destroy literally thousands of lives could in fact do that.
The most pertinent points are the following, but can peace be won? "Will the military victory be followed by a political and diplomatic triumph?" He goes on to point out that it may have some effects in that direction, but he also asks the following. "It could also usher in an era of renewed terrorism, of deepened Arab sullenness, of a growing rift between the nations of Islam and the heirs of Christendom". Therein lies one of the critical issues.

When I was elected on November 21, 1988, I had anticipated a number of issues I felt I would have to come to terms with. I had done a lot of reading and research on the trade agreement with the United States and I had forseen the negative impact on working men and women throughout Canada in various industries.
I had realized also that the tax reforms which the government was contemplating would cause serious hardships to Canadians, especially those in the low and middle income brackets.
Those were major issues. I had throroughly anticipated them. But never had I foreseen that, as a member of this house, I would have to deal, as today, with a war. Neither this war or any other war.
As an idealist, I thought we had established a new world order whereby new peacefull solutions could be developed to such problems as poverty, hunger and sickness in the world without.
Unfortunately, I was wrong. Unfortunately also, technological progress exceeds by far the mechanisms which have been developed to implement peaceful solutions.

I say not at all in a partisan sense that it is unfortunate the Prime Minister had not recalled us earlier so that we could have had this debate, hopefully before hostilities began so that everyone's positions could have been put on the table.

Again, I think in a non-partisan way that while the Prime Minister would like us to believe that he is in close and significant contact with President Bush, it is a grossly exaggerated claim.
For example, why would President Bush, knowing full well that the Canadian Parliament was in the process of discussing this question, not withhold hostilities for a few days? Why could he have not respected our democratic process? Surely, if he had come to the same conclusion, he could have reached that two or three days later.
I must add that I am extremely proud of my party's position and of my leader's position on this issue. We condemn Saddam Hussein. We condemn what he was doing in Kuwait to his people and what he did last night to Israel. Let there be no doubt about that. We condemn him and all people who act as he does.
But there is a double standard. There are people who have committed as great an atrocity, and we have simply verbalized our discontent. That is unfortunate. We too applaud the great, great patience that Israel has shown and the restraint it has demonstrated. I was pleased to hear today that the same comment was made with respect to a number of Arab nations, because they too have shown restraint, and a number of Arabs throughout the world have done the same. I pray that this will continue.
My party supported sanctions, an embargo and diplomacy. We provided proof that those were working in spite of what was said. We had an array of credible individuals from the political scene, the military scene, and a number of other sectors who showed unequivocally that sanctions were working, not only affecting the civilian population but getting at that military infrastructure.
We brought forward evidence that has never been refuted. There is no way under any circumstances that any member of government has ever provided even a slight percentage of the evidence that we put forward.
We had little doubt that if we had been more patient we could have come up with different kinds of solutions. We requested additional time. Perhaps the best indication of how we went about it was the addition of the amendment to the current motion which has been debated, asking whether or not we support the United Nations.
Government Orders
Of course we support the United Nations, but it does not mean we have to follow it blindly. It does not mean that we cannot bring some precision to its position. We offer the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by adding-"through the continued
use of economic sanctions, such support to exclude offensive military
action by Canada at this time."
We felt that more time could have given us an opportunity to explore the effects of sanctions, greater diplomacy, and perhaps solutions that we had not thought about.
Our party's first option in case of hostilities was to withdraw our troops from the theatre of war. That did not mean we could not be supportive in other ways. Quite to the contrary. We lost the decision, as the House well knows, when the Prime Minister and his government decided to go to war.
Our support of the United Nations has been unequivocal. Member after member has mentioned it. We believe so much in the UN that we wanted this multinational force under its command and control.
Canada is now at war. What are we as a party doing in this situation? Are we for or against this war? Clearly, unequivocally we are against it. We have said it time and time again. Is it a necessary war? We consider it an unnecessary war at this time. Are we united with the government? In terms of providing the adequate support for our troops to ensure their safety and security, yes, absolutely. We want them to have the best in order to protect themselves against possible death and injury. Are we united with the government on the suppose^ need for war at this time? No, we are not.
As a result of the Prime Minister's decision to go to war, as some members have mentioned, Canada has now lost its innocence. Whether or not we like it, we have, according to many people in the world, become an aggressor.
People will say: "Are there times when we need to go to war?" Yes. Absolutely. Unfortunately! When our people are at risk, there is no doubt in my mind. When our country is at risk, there is no equivocation. But is it not sad that, in today's society, we have not developed mechanisms that would permit other alternatives than mass destruction?

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
We are at war. What do we do now? We must stop the war as soon as possible. There will be massive destruction of the infrastructure, of buildings, of roads, of bridges, of hospitals, and of schools. But what about the massive destruction of people? It is not only soldiers who are being killed in Iraq. There are little girls, who are not terribly different from little Canadian girls. There are young men in their teens, who are very similar to young men here. There are moms and dads. Whether you are a mother or a father here or a mother or a father in another country, surely it has the same kind of significance. There are grandparents and other relatives.
We need to seek a peaceful solution as quickly as possible. Surely this continued brutality is not the ultimate solution. We need to anticipate the "fallout" that will have been created by this war, the problems that will be there that were not there before. We all know that by supposedly resolving something we often create a series of unanticipated other problems.
What might some of those be? There will be emotional trauma not only felt by the civilians, by the boys and girls, by the moms and dads, by the seniors and by other citizens as well, but by our own servicemen and women, by our own soldiers. There will be massive economic and social instability for Iraq and for other nations.
What do we do now in terms of trying to respond to that particular difficulty? And what about the environmental impact? Have we thought of that? Have we thought of the difficulties in any significant kind of way? Are we starting to identify those now so that we can react, hopefully tomorrow or very shortly, to those particular challenges? What about the difficulties in bringing about a just solution?
We have talked of linkage. We have talked of peace conferences. We have talked of a number of other alternatives, but we need to put those on the table so that they are ready when the time comes. We need a just solution. As I pointed out before, a military conquest will not resolve those problems.
What are we going to do in terms of attempting to avert war in other troubled areas of the world? Or, having been "successful" in a military way, do we continue to operate this way, or do we come forward with
different kinds of solutions or mechanisms other than war that might work?
What about potential additional conflicts because of this war? As was pointed out, this is a massive war where there will be massive destruction and loss of lives, but there will be additional conflicts. Will other countries, for example, that feel as if they have not been treated fairly by Iraq want to seize a particular opportunity? Will Iraq, assuming that it has been devastated and conquered, carry away this feeling that it must get even? And who will be the victims of that kind of behaviour, that kind of attitude?
I suggest that as a first step in responding to those problems we need to bring the conflict under UN command.
I want to point out another major concern that I have, and that is the managing of information during conflict. It would appear thus far, if one has looked at what has occurred, that it has been open; but I wonder how true that is. Has it been "managed" rather than "open"?
Do we know the truth about what has occurred? What are the implications of that management, assuming that it has occurred, on news information for us as Canadians in the future? Not only in theatres of war, not only during conflicts, but what questions does that raise? I think there is no one here, if we want to be fair about it, who would not suggest that the military is trying to put the best light on what has occurred thus far. Why all the coverage, and why those particular scenes as opposed to others? What are the implications of that? Are we being made to think in a particular way in order to support a decision that has been made? I think so.
There is great sadness because we have not developed other mechanisms but those of war in order to resolve problems and because we have made massive and intriguing technological advances, not only with war machines but throughout society, and juxtaposed against those technological advances it seems that we have not moved forward at all on other fronts.
Let us look at our country very briefly. Poverty affects almost five million Canadians, most of whom are women. Many of them are single parents, but there are over one million children affected. We have two million people on welfare today. Over one and a quarter people are unemployed, and about 500,000 people are going to food banks. Those are the critical problems.

January 17, 1991

Government Orders
If we are having those difficulties in a country that is as rich and powerful as ours, what about those other countries in the world who have less? What about countries devastated by war or affected in a very serious way?
It is sad that our technological advances far outstrip our ability to work out problems such as poverty, employment, appropriate distribution of wealth and responding to the unemployed and those in great need.

In our society, war spells failure. It is not a solution. Of course, there will be a "winner". But this "victory" will cause in turn many new unknown problems which simply cannot be anticipated.
What is being done today, if anything, to address the serious problems which will affect not only Iraq, but other countries of the world?
As Liberals, we were prepared to go to war if we necessarily had to, for instance to protect our country and our people. But we strongly believe that war should only be considered as a last resort. Nobody should go to war without having exhausted all possible avenues.

The path of war is much travelled. We know that. Whether we talk of large wars or small ones, it is still war. It is still destruction, the loss of lives, and the maiming of men, women and children. The path of peace is much, much less travelled. It is time that we explored and started to travel the path of peace much more frequently than we have in the past.
I would hope, whatever our religious sides, we are still believers and-

-that we will all pray in our own way for peace, a new world order where problems can be solved without war, where our own children and those of the rest of the world can feel secure, where men and women will accept to work together to build a new society based on friendship, love and co-operation.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to the closing remarks of my colleague. I agree with his last remarks to the effect that all of us must work together for peace, love, friendship, and harmony between nations. I would simply ask him, considering the seriousness of the situation and the fact that war has broken out and that the House is debating a resolution concerning our support for the United Nations, the former leader of the Liberal Party clearly stated, and I quote:

This is a crucial test for the United Nations and Canada must support it. This is a crucial test for collective security and Canada must support it. Does he agree with that declaration?

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague for her comments and her question.
She quoted the former leader, and that is precisely the case-a former leader. But now we have a new leader. I clearly explained the position of my new leader. As a former deputy minister, I am not one to go and tell people with whom I used to work how to handle their own affairs. We have a new leader and a policy which has been fully explained not only by the leader but also by my colleagues and myself.
The debate does not relate to the fact that Mr. Hussein has committed unacceptable acts, not al all. The fact is that war engenders war. Perhaps the war will end in a military victory, but it will create other problems.
I agree with my colleague that the problem is very serious. The diverging views have to do with the fact that we would have waited a little longer to see if sanctions might not produce the same results, or if other much more creative solutions might not have been found. That is the difference. I am not being mean when I say that. You are the government, you have the right to do what you are doing and I respect the fact that you have that authority.
But you know, Madam Speaker, and I said so at the beginning of my remarks, we had offered evidence from a wide variety of very credible people that the sanctions did affect the people and were also beginning to undermine the military infrastructure of Mr. Saddam Hussein. The government did not disprove these facts.

Government Orders
I even have a quotation from Mr. Clark dated December 28, if memory serves me right, when he wrote to his colleague to convey the same point of view. Today is January 18, which means he said that three weeks ago. Thank you for your comments and question.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened to the hon. member from Saint-Boniface with great interest and I would have a question for him.
We are presently debating a motion which reads:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
One thing is not clear in my mind. Did he say he was going to vote for or against this motion?
My hon. colleague knows full well that I said nothing on that subject. What I did say, and I will repeat to refresh his memory, is that we Liberals support the United Nations.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: And this motion?

Now, wait a moment. I am getting to it. You sometimes take a little time to get to the point. I want the same privilege. I said that we Liberals support the United Nations. Indeed, I said that one can support an organization, whether the United Nations or any other, and not agree with every proposal it puts forward. I did not say whether I supported it or not. That is a surprise. I did say, though, that we had moved the following amendment:
That the motion be amended by adding immediately after the
word "Kuwait" the following:
"through the continued use of economic sanctions, such support to exclude offensive military action by Canada at this time."
If my hon. colleague wants to know if I support the United Nations, the answer is unequivocally yes. As regards my support to the proposal, I will think about it.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am extremely concerned that my colleague made a speech without having an opinion on this motion. I want to go back to this point.
Today, we have a few thousand servicemen and women out there who cannot afford to pussyfoot about like he seems to want to do.
Does he, as a Canadian and as a member of this House which collectively sent thousands of our fellow countrymen and women up to the front, have as much guts as these people or does he plan on pussyfooting much longer?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question. I don't dance. I don't waltz. Am I as brave as the troops? I don't know. I am not a military man, and quite frankly, I don't envy their position at all.
Sure, theoretically, you can say we sent them, but I didn't send them. You may have sent them, but I certainly didn't. Certainly not.
Am I evading the issue? I said I wanted more time to think. If you ask me what I would do if I had to say yes or no today, I would say no, without adding the amendment. I made that clear.
Do I support the United Nations? Yes, without reservations. I don't understand what the hon. member is trying to do. It seems to me his questions are not very logical. Surely, he cannot be serious.
In fact, I am rather disappointed, because I used to have a pretty good opinion of him. He is often quite fair and quite charitable. He tries to be rational and objective. I suppose like all of us, he has his ups and downs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a political party that intends to run the country some day must show what side it is on. Its members must have guts and be able to say: When there are serious decisions to be made, I will set aside my party affiliation and make the decision that is appropriate in the circumstances.
What we are asking the hon. member for St. Boniface, who, by the way, is extraordinarily fluent in both official languages, is whether or not he will vote in favour of supporting the United Nations in its efforts to get Iraq out of Kuwait.
The question is straightforward: Yes or no?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for her question. We do not see ourselves as a party in waiting that may come to power some day. We shall come to power, and very shortly. I just wanted to make that clear.
January 17, 1991

What about guts? I suggest the hon. member ask the people with whom I have worked whether I have guts. You want to know how I intend to vote? Wait until the vote is taken. I will cross that bridge when I come to it.
With respect, I think it is too bad the hon. member is trying to suggest things that are just not so. I thought that, especially on an issue as serious as this one, she and her colleagues on the other side of the House would have been fairer in their comments.
But don't worry, we will come to power. Don't worry, we have the guts. And above all, don't worry because I intend to vote the right way, and I know what the right way is. Just wait and see.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is obviously with deep sorrow that I rise today in this House. As a member, I had never thought that I would see the day where I had to speak to a motion dealing indirectly with a declaration of a war which is already under way.
Madam Speaker, if I may as a posthumous tribute I would like to talk about my father. In 1939, at only 23 years of age, he was already a member of the Royal 22nd Regiment. My grandfather died the same year my father was called to duty. My grandmother was left with 18 kids and since my father was single, he became head of the family. Consequently he was exempted from active duty. During my childhood, after the war was over, my father always said he would have liked, even after becamimg head of the family, to contribute to the war effort and, as a Canadian and fellow countryman, to go up to the front line to fight for the fundamental rights of Canada during the 1939-1945 war.
Madam Speaker, I believe most Canadians do not understand the origins of this conflict. Since the outbreak of hostilities, I have been carefully watching the news and I would like to take this opportunity to commend the many reporters still in that region who have been doing everything they can to accurately report on the events in the Gulf. I would like to wish them the best, and my thoughts go to their families. Several citizens have called "open lines" to express their views,
Government Orders
and the vast majority of them have admitted not understanding the very nature of the conflict dividing that region of the Middle East. I think as Canadians we should try harder to understand what is going on elsewhere in the world, because those events do affect us. We have the evidence right here: there is a war and some of our fellowmen and women are in the theatre of operations ready to fight for our values and a world order.
Not only about the Middle East but also about other regions of the world, I would urge my constituents to widen their horizons by examining what is going on elsewhere so as to appreciate the motives and the historical reasons at the root of dissidence between Arab nations. As for Israel, I did go there as a member of a delegation with the Canada-Israel committee, like most other members. Those who have not yet been invited should soon be, or if they were invited perhaps they could not go. Anyway, I went there and I think it is a beautiful region. I would like to visit other countries, I have Arab friends whom I have not seen for some time and who often come to Montreal. I know them very well. I have a lot of affection for those people. I met them quite often. We stand to gain by understanding and getting to know their culture and traditions. Once I even smoked that famous water pipe which Arabs enjoy after a meal.
Madam Speaker, utterly unbelievable as well is the fact that we are watching the war on television, wondering whether it is real, whether it is a dream, or whether it is a movie. But it is reality, there are bombings, people are scared, anxiety prevails. Just imagine that you are a citizen of Jordan, of the West Bank, or of Saudi Arabia, and asking yourself whether the missile aimed at a base is not going to hit your area or your house. We can only feel very deeply for all these men, women and children who have to live under such incredible conditions.
Another thing that is different in 1991 is that women are now on the front line. Women did their share during the 1939-45 war, but they worked in hospitals looking after the sick and wounded.
But now there are 67 Canadian women involved in this war as members of the Canadian Armed Forces. It was felt that women should avoid at all costs being involved in a war, because they had to look after their husbands

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
during World War n, but today, some men are watching in front of their television sets perfectly aware that there wives are serving in the gulf area. It is unbelievable. I wish to pay tribute to the 8,000 women who are members of the Canadian Armed Forces and tell them how proud I am of their colleagues who are over there involved in all sorts of operations, handling military equipment, to defend values which are dear to our hearts, Madam Speaker.
