Should the fact that Israel has chosen not to launch a counterattack be interpreted as evidence of weakness or of strength? Madam Speaker, I suggest it is unquestionably evidence of strength. By refusing to retaliate is kind for the sake of this vast land and for the sake of their fellow citizens. Israeli leaders are showing extraordinary and remarkable composure, and I hope they will show the necessary fortitude and good sense in telling their fellow citizens to be patient. In short, having visited this region and having met Mr. Shamir personally, I plead with him-I am sure he is not listening to what I, the lowly member for Argenteuil-Papineau, may have to say to him who is involved in such a serious conflict-not to do anything which could endanger an already explosive situation.
Madam Speaker, I am sure some of my constituents are wondering today: "What could I do personally to take part in this war effort? How can I help? Can I send money? Can I send food?" I wish to tell them that they can use my county office. I wish they would phone me to say: "I wish to send this or that". I promise to do everything I can to send their offerings directly through the various organizations which will look after the serious problems which will arise following this war. I feel we do not insist enough on the fact that the minute this conflict is over, tomorrow or the day after, we will find that houses have been destroyed, that there are women and	children-families-without shelters,
wounded and handicapped people with all sorts of horrors which I refuse to contemplate today, Madam Speaker.
So, if my constituents want to do something concrete, they can communicate with my office and I promise to look after this personally. For instance, if a person asked me what he or she could do personally back home, I would say: "If you are a smoker, do not smoke a package of cigarettes for two days; or if you eat sometimes in restaurants, stay home and keep the money in order to use it for the war effort." Canadian men and women
have shown over the years that they are extremely generous, not only in time of war, by also in time of peace helping hungry people in developing countries deal with their problems.
I will certainly support this motion, in spite of the fact that, like many honourable members from both sides, I feel that war is a failure. I suggest it is above all the failure of a man who decided that he would control the world. It is also the failure of international leaders who did not realize that this man was stockpiling weapons and arms. I am sure I speak for all Canadian men and women when I ask: Should we continue watching people earning a living by manufacturing war equipment which someday can be turned against us?
Madam Speaker, these are very difficult choices which the government had to make under the circumstances. But as I was saying earlier to my friend the hon. member for Saint-Boniface, making this type of decision required a lot of guts. We made this decision. I am in perfect agreement with the motions which support the United Nations and their efforts to bring this dictator to his knees.
Madam Speaker, I hope that the war will end soon, I offer my best wishes to our fighting men and women over there and their families, as well as to the journalists. They can count on my prayers.
Madam Deputy Speaker. The hon. member for York South-Weston requests the floor. After the unfortunate exchanges we had about an hour ago, I think some gesture on his part would be appropriate before I recognize the hon. member for debate.
I will therefore give him a chance to make that gesture, and I hope he will do so. Otherwise I will have to recognize someone else.

Madam Speaker, in the circumstance I would ask the opportunity to meet with you in your chambers to discuss that matter. In the interim, I would ask that you recognize me on legitimate points of order and privilege.
But at your earliest convenience, I am prepared to meet with you in your chambers to discuss the matter and then to return to the House and indicate my position on the record.
January 17, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I will be replaced in the chair some time in the next hour. As I have been the occupant of the chair since 10 o'clock this morning, I think everyone will understand that I will need to refresh myself and maybe have a little bit of food.
At that time I will certainly meet with the hon. member. In the meantime I think that it would be right for me to recognize other members. Once we have spoken, we will settle the matter. I appreciate the hon. member coming forward with the suggestion at this time.

The hon. member for Saint-Denis, for questions and comments on the speech by the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau.

Madam Speaker, I hope that the exchange that will take place later today will be held according to the best parliamentary traditions that bring us together today.
I would like to thank the hon. member for Argenteuil-Papineau for her comments, to which I listened with great interest. I particularly appreciated the fact that she really thought about the issue, saying that she found this war difficult to accept, and explained why. That is a rarity in our parliamentary system.
She told us it was hard for her to vote on this kind of motion because there were other reasons she would have liked to include, but that in the circumstances, she would vote in favour of the motion if we ever voted on this issue. This is not a confession but it is an almost embarrassing expression of honesty.
As I said before, she really thought about the matter. She said she didn't know what could be done. There were so many people suffering. I heard all the statements that have been made since yesterday. As you know, and the hon. member said as much, she was a guest of the Canada-Israel committee. She saw part of the what the Canada-Israel committee wanted to show her. However, she is aware there is always another side to these issues. There are millions of people in the Palestinian territories that have been waiting 45 years for people like her to get up and say: It seems to me something has to be done. And that is why I want to act as a witness to what she just said, as a witness who
Government Orders
listened very carefully. I feel she has a good heart and is prepared to think about what will have to be done later on. What are we going to say once, this terrible war is over. We can go off to the crusades, to war, but meanwhile, parliamentarians have to do their job. If we don't take the trouble to think about these things, what are we doing here while the war is going on?
I will not talk about the essence of the issue, since that would be making a speech. But I want to say there must be parliamentarians. If we, as parliamentarians of the world, of the western democracies, limit ourselves to reflecting on what could be done-In that, I thank her for shaking me up, but not too roughly-people must understand that terrible tragedies will follow, not only in a small part of the world, but everywhere in the Middle East, horrible tragedies. Did we try to picture these two or three million refugees who are leaving because they are afraid, or because they are kicked out? They are living in tents, waiting for people like her try something, to find a solution or suggest something. I greatly appreciated her speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
If you don't mind I will first answer. I wish to thank my hon. colleague for his good words. Clearly, it is because I know people from that area that I might have a more open mind. What I was pointing out is that Canada should open itself to the world. There is war in the Middle East, but there might be wars elsewhere in the future, and if we are ignorant of traditions in those countries, it will be difficult for us to judge the reasons for those wars.
The hon. member raises an important issue and I congratulate the Canada-Israel committee for the way in which they showed us the country. I went to Bethlehem and in the occupied territories. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we should do the same with other countries in the Persian Gulf area, that is visit them to try to understand them and find solutions to this problem.

Mr. Speaker, we were recalled to the House of Commons last week to debate a resolution to reaffirm Canada's commitment to the United Nations resolution 678 which authorized member nations to use all necessary means to bring the crisis to a successful conclusion.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Needless to say, all of us here have taken this responsibility very seriously. This is an emotionally charged issue for all Canadians, and for me personally I can honestly say that I have never before been called upon to take part in such a difficult decision for all members of Parliament.
In the name of peace, a brick was thrown through my constituency office window. In the name of peace, I have been told that we should bomb Iraq. In the name of peace, I wish we could all lay down our arms and use this energy to help the homeless and the underprivileged.
In the name of peace, I wish Saddam Hussein agreed with me. He can still join the forces for peace.
Since the United Nations inception some 40 years ago, I do not believe it has ever had to face such a difficult crisis. Throughout its histoiy, the United Nations has been instrumental in resolving conflicts in restoring and keeping peace in many regions. However, the effectiveness of the United Nations as an international body of dialogue is now being put to a test where its future effectiveness may rest on the outcome of this war.
I believe that everybody wants peace. I do not know of a single member of Parliament who is in favour of war. What we are really debating is the most effective method by which we can achieve a lasting peace. Of course, we should try to avoid war. I believe that is what we have tried to do since Iraq invaded Kuwait in August.
Sometimes war cannot be avoided. That was one of the lessons we learned from the Second World War. World War II also taught us that we can wait too long before we move to stop an aggressor. Chamberlain's politics of appeasement did not work in 1939.
What I feared most is that in our quest for peace we would allow Saddam Hussein to develop his arsenal of war to such a level that in a few months or a few years we would be facing an even more dangerous aggressor. How would that serve the international community and the cause of peace more effectively? I have trouble with that concept.
Before the outbreak of war I heard that at the first sign of fighting Canadian troops should pull out. But in all good conscience, how can we? What do we tell our allies,
"Get on with the job. Pm 4,000 miles behind you"? If we do, how will our commitment to upholding world order ever be valued again? How moral is it to cut and run?
Canada has earned the respect and the trust of all nations because of the effectiveness of our Armed Forces, not only in battle during the First World War, the Second World War, and the Korean War, but also because we have been an effective member of the United Nations peacekeeping forces. Our history is not one of following the United States into battle.
After the First World War, Canada has always made these decisions at home and that is the tradition we are still following today. Canada has always stood for freedom and Canada has always stood firmly with her allies wherever freedom has been threatened. We have never run away and left our allies to do our fighting for us and we are not going to do that today.
The United Nations was formed to provide a forum for resolving international conflicts. Our presence in the gulf is in response to the collective voices of 28 member nations calling for a solution to end the conflict initiated by Saddam Hussein when he used his military might to invade and occupy Kuwait.
Until Januaiy 15 we were there to monitor the sanctions imposed by the United Nations. I was always hopeful that a last-minute diplomatic effort might bring a peace, but all diplomatic efforts failed. Saddam Hussein is not interested in dialogue or negotiating and I do not think he shares our concern for peace, justice, and human life.
To those that feel we should wait a little longer for sanctions to work, all I can say is that if Canada had been invaded I think we would all be praying for freedom-loving nations to come to our aid. We would be hoping that others would send their sons and daughters to liberate us. I hope the United Nations would respond to our cries for help, as we have responded to the cries for help from Kuwait.
This is not a time for our allies to have to question our support for the United Nations coalition but, more importantly, it is a time for our young men and women in the Armed Forces to know that we are with them 100 per cent. Their families must also know that we do not take their commitment to world order lightly.
January 17, 1991

If ever there was a time to show a united front, it is now under the leadership of the United Nations. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe that we must follow through on our resolve and support the government decision to stand with our allies and take whatever action the United Nations forces determine necessary.
We know that our forces are engaged in a war. I say this with a heavy heart and much sadness. I have lived through war and I do not wish the experience on anyone.
I pray for peace and I pray that this war is over quickly.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the hon. member's speech with great interest. However, I noticed that she said if Canada was invaded from other countries, we would not cry to our allies.
The question I have for the hon. member is: Where was Canada when other smaller countries were subjected to aggression? Where was Canada when other smaller countries were being trampled upon by invaders? Where was Canada when Cyprus was invaded by Thrkey? Or is that another story because there is no oil there? There is no interest. We were not invited by President Bush.
Why does Canada only speak out against other aggression but do nothing? Why the double standard? Why should we not form a unique policy and stick to it? Or is it that this time we have particular interests? Or is it that at this time we have to heed what President Bush says?
Let me not be misunderstood. I am with our forces 100 per cent. But I question the double standard of the government and the party which she represents.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his question. I would like to say that the United Nations was formed 45 years ago to unite countries and to assist in keeping peace in the world.
We went through quite a period of time with the cold war. The cold war kept the actions of the United Nations suppressed. It was not able to carry on and protect many of these countries. Now, with the cold war diminished, we had every hope that this body of nations would work.
I must admit at the time that Cyprus has been helped by our peacekeeping forces and that was under a Liberal government. However, I think that the United Nations is
Government Orders
still the body to work with for peace and international law and order.

Mr. Speaker, earlier today an hon. member stated, and I quote: "Too many Canadians have died in wars in history to have this country turn its back on the need for a co-operative United Nations in the Middle East. To not fulfil the obligations and initiatives of the United Nations, it would reduce Canada to a less than mediocre entity in the world community. Canadians have died for liberty, for justice, and for individual rights and the United Nations in the manifestation of the ideals for which they gave their lives."
Excuse me. Is the hon. member on a question or debate?
It is a question.
Well, would you please ask the question?

Mr. Speaker, in reliving some of the things that happened pre-World War II, I would like to ask my colleague if she sees a parallel between what happened in pre-World War II and what has happened over the last year in Iraq.

Mr. Speaker, the situation that led up to the present situation is very similar to what happened before World War II. There were a lot of people who were frightened of war. They did not understand what we were getting into. I can understand that fear. It is not an easy thing to address to oneself.
However, we stood behind our soldiers and we helped them by standing behind them. It was so very important for them to be assured that we were for them, thinking of them, and praying for them. I think this is behind every situation like this.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with what a tremendous hope this country entered 1990 and with what a shattered hope we are now entering 1991.
This is a war that was to be swift and definitive. Yesterday, on one channel that I watched as I joined other Canadians in trying to keep up with the news, Mr. Bush was reported to say last night that this war will not be short, nor will it be easy.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
I join every member of the House in feeling tremendous support for and tremendous pride in the young men and women who are representing us in the Persian Gulf. I also join with those in the House who believe they are heroes already because they are there, prepared to do what their country asks of them. But I do not agree with the role that their country is asking of them.
That does not mean, for a moment, that those of us who do not agree with the role, do not support the men and women on the front. But I am terribly concerned. In 24 hours, we have gone from President Bush pumping up the world, preparing it for a war that would be short and "clean", to saying now that we are facing a war that will not be short and will not be easy.
This war is a mistake. Like most Canadians in the last three days, I have left meetings and I have left the House, and I have gone home and been glued to the television set. That, in itself, is different for us as Canadians, when it comes to war. I have been glued to the television set hoping that I would get the news and that the next little piece of the story would tell me more about what is happening.
Like other Canadians, I have sat riveted to the television set late into the night for the last three nights and two things have struck me. First, because we are getting live reports as events unfold, we are operating on unverified information that changes from minute to minute. The whole country and the whole world is on a roller-coaster. As we saw last night as the bombs were dropping in Israel, there were all kinds of rumours about what was happening. That struck me as being the new way in which we will view the war. We will all be there with a picture window on the theatre of war every night.
But the other thing that struck me was when I was watching CNN at around six o'clock last night, was a caption that said "authorized footage from the American military". That made me think and it struck me that every night on television we see footage very quickly of other skirmishes around the world in other wars around the world. We have seen some pretty horror-filled stuff, starting with the Vietnam war, through the eyes of television.
But when I started to think about that, I had a sense that I was watching pictures of pilots getting into planes, pictures of pilots getting out of planes, pictures of troops being moved one way and the other across the desert. I was seeing a lot of file footage. I was on the roller-coaster because there is a voice background about what people think is happening. Yet, I felt that I was not being shown the truth about the impact of what had happened. I think Canadians are starting to feel that, and are going to increasingly feel that.
It is true that in the first three days we have not seen the impact, but we cannot be protected forever from that impact. If we have the technology to be there, then why should we start censoring what Canadians are going to see?
I am very concerned about the kind of sense that that is going to leave Canadians with. Today on CBC radio, when I was driving in this morning, there was a psychologist talking about how we as Canadians are responding to what is happening in the gulf.
In talking to some people I have found that they were made to feel embarrassed about feeling anxiety about this war because there are those who say: "If you think we've got it bad, think about those in the gulf."
It is normal for people faced hourly and continually with an unknown quantity like this war to feel anxiety. It is important for us as Canadians to talk about that and also to think it through to come to a conclusion about what we as Canadians believe we should be doing about this great and horrific unknown.
What troubles me about many pieces of this debate in the House is that there are references to only talking about half the story. If somebody is talking about the humanitarian side, somebody gets up and says: "You're only talking about half the story," or "You're only talking about the people in Iraq. Why aren't you talking about the people in Saudi Arabia? Why aren't you talking about the innocent victims in Saudi Arabia? How can you just talk about innocent victims in Iraq?"
In the time we have nobody can cover the whole blanket. But we do all have concerns and we are trying to cover the whole blanket collectively. If one speaker talks about innocent women and children dying in Iraq, it does not mean they do not care about the innocent women and children in Saudi Arabia. If one person speaks without mentioning Israel, that does not mean we are not terribly concerned about people in Israel.
A good point.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not have the opportunity in Question Period, for example, to expand our argument to be all-inclusive. We have to focus to one area. Yet we have responses, both from ministers and members on the other side of the House, suggesting that when we are trying to deal with one issue, somehow we are excluding all the others. That I think is a tragedy. It is a tragedy that the Canadian people will soon start to figure out. It is mischievous and it is deceitful. It is an example of how the government with its disdain is starting to show itself to Canadian people. It is with disdain that the government in fact has shown itself to hold Canadian people.
I would hope that as we continue this debate, late into the night to ensure that we all have an opportunity to speak, people will believe that there is not one parliamentarian in Canada who does not feel a tremendous level of patriotism and that we all are terribly concerned. We may not agree. I may profoundly disagree with the government's position on this very important issue. But because we raise issues of concern, we are not somehow less patriotic or somehow less committed to our young men and women in the gulf.
One of the things that has been missing in this debate is input from Canadian people.
The hon. member on the government side of the House who spoke before me mentioned that she was doing things in her constituency to ensure that people could make contributions to the war effort. I had hoped I would have had an opportunity under questions and comments to question her because, while it is very laudable that she is encouraging people in her constituency to bring donations and so on- and that is another piece dealing with the whole question of the war and its impact- I had wanted to ask her if she in fact believed that at this point a pause for peace would not have made a tremendous impact.
Today, the hon. member for Victoria during Question Period indicated to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that U.S. commanders had said the air raids which involved more than 1,000 sorties by American, British, French, Saudi and Kuwaiti aircraft had broken
Government Orders
the back of Saddam Hussein's air defence system, command control, and communications organization. He said to the minister that he would urge the Prime Minister to urge the United States to consider a pause for peace.
The howls from some members on the government side were shocking. Even more shocking was when the Secretary of State for External Affairs said: "We are not going to reward Saddam Hussein with a cease-fire."
Well, a pause for peace is not a reward that anybody is asking for, for Saddam Hussein. A pause for peace is a reward to the allies. It is a reward to the victims, the women, and the children in Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, and Israel. It is a reward for the families and friends of those who are serving Canada in the gulf, and it is a reward for the world if it ends the war.
The suggestion that a pause for peace was suggested to reward Saddam Hussein I think is shocking and despicable. It was meant only to discredit somehow what was said in a genuine way by an hon. member of the House.
I said that I was concerned and sad that Canadians have not had the opportunity to input to the government their true feelings. Indeed, many Canadians have not determined yet what their true feelings are about this war.
I was very fortunate, as we were being recalled to the House of Commons, to be at a meeting where there were a number of my constituents. I quickly took out a pen and some paper and asked them to tell me as I came back to Ottawa what in fact their feelings are about the war. These letters are a week old and many events have unfolded since then, but I do not think the sentiments of these constituents have changed.
The letters begin: "I have asked Joy Langan to tell Brian Mulroney my feelings about the Middle East crisis." That is all it says. I did not try to guide their thoughts. These are a couple of them and I would like to put them on record.
The first one, from a woman named Bernice Gehring from Maple Ridge, states:
My aunt, Dogney Anderson of Craigmile, Alberta was named the
first mother of the year because she lost her three sons to the
Second World War, all within three weeks.

Government Orders
She died in her eighties believing that Canada would never again enter into or be supporting war.
You have a responsibility to her and to all of us.
Respect our belief in peace.
Bernice Gehring
I have one from a gentleman in my riding which states:
Mr. Mulroney, I, Lou Schillaci, am a naturalized Canadian citizen. My former nationality is a United States citizen. I served in that country's armed forces from July of 1967 to October of 1971 when I received an honourable discharge from the U.S. Air Force. I moved to Canada in search of employment, having married a Canadian citizen in 1971. In August 1980,1 chose to become a Canadian. I live here proudly and one of the reasons I have stated as a reason for my decision to adopt Canada as my country is that Canada is a peaceful nation. Their army is used for peacekeeping services, not war. The problems in the Persian Gulf should be negotiated, not solved by intimidation and threats of war and Canada must lead the way to peace. Your government's position in this situation is not reflective of my own and I beseech the Members of Parliament to withdraw Canada's support for the war in an offensive manner in the Persian Gulf.
I have a lot of these. I will not try to read them into the record. I will, as I promised these people and as I promised the students who wrote letters and came to my office, have them delivered to the Prime Minister because I believe those Canadians have a right to be heard.
The night action began in the Persian Gulf, I listened to the news late into the night. About the time I went to bed, I think they were estimating that about 150,000 people had died. Later we heard it was 350,000. Some people said that was right and some said it was wrong. It is not relevant; I could not imagine the horror and the carnage that would kill 150,000 or 350,000 people. I could not conceive how horrid that slaughter must have been. I do not for a moment defend Saddam Hussein but I do believe that if there were ever a dream and if there is a dream now, that one moment of peace for negotiation or for reconsideration or resolution of this problem is worth our egos, whether it be the President of the United States or the allied forces, who stop this from continuing.
I noticed another thing on television and I am quite concerned about it and it is not the kind of thing that grabs the headlines. I noted when I was watching the air raid on Israel last night, pictures of children putting on
gas masks with gaping holes because they do not fit properly and mothers putting plastic bags over and around the gas masks and pictures of a child in a crib with ordinary plastic over the frame.
We have the technology and the money to spend a million dollars on a cruise missile. I am absolutely flabbergasted that we do not have gas masks to fit children. Maybe we have run out, I do not know. I am asking the question. Maybe the government will be able to tell us. I was just astonished by the tragedy of children having gas masks placed on them that do not fit, using plastic bags to hold it together and the trust on the faces of parents thinking that would protect them.
This war, I think, is the biggest heart-break for all of us. For every mother and father who has a child in the Middle East and for every mother and father living in the Middle East with children; for every one of us who believed and dreamed a year ago that we were, in fact, entering a new world order, that it was going to be a world in which we could talk to each other and resolve our differences, a world that could grow up and get away from the school yard style scrapping and the egotistical, "I am bigger than you" or "might is right" or all the things that were part of the old world order. For many, many of us that dream is shattered.
I will ask one more time, as I am sure my colleagues will before this debate is through, please, Government of Canada, ask the President of the United States to pause for peace, to give this war an opportunity to end before the horror continues.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very carefully and thoughtfully to the words of the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam. I have two very specific questions to ask her, but I wanted to say a word or two before asking them.
I do not think any of us in this House could possibly fathom the horrors of war. We all share the feelings, fears and frustrations of the families and of the victims of the present hostilities in the Persian Gulf region.
January 17, 1991

While I was listening to the hon. member, I was going through my signature book and I, too, came across a letter from one of my constituents, a Mr. Raymond Dewar of Richmond, British Columbia.
I would just like to read the very short words of Mr. Dewar. He says:
Today's Vancouver Sun reported the campaign being launched by a large number of groups under the general caption of "Peace Organizations".
Similar "Peace Organizations" in Britain during the 1930s were able to intimidate the government of the day. The result was a failure to take action when action was possible. They helped to make Hitler's early conquests possible and made it certain that World War II would occur.
Certainly the United States has made mistakes in previously supplying Iraq, and certainly there are economic considerations involved in preventing the control of oil. But it is also clear that unless Iraq is stopped there will eventually be a Middle East war, probably with Jordan joining Iraq and invading Saudi Arabia and the other small states. They would then turn to exterminating Israel, and Israel would use its atomic weapons and all other means. The time to take action is now.
Please, stay firm in the resolve of the Government.
This leads me to my three simple questions. I hope the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam would take note of these, because they are quite fundamental, practical questions.
My first question is: Why were the people in Tel Aviv last night wearing gas masks? Which nation upon this earth has chosen to use poison gases and perhaps biological weapons in an attempt to exterminate another neighbouring country?
Second, while I appreciate this is a hypothetical question, I would ask the hon. member and all members opposite: Had Kuwait not happened, had the war not been started by Saddam Hussein last August 2, had the first hostilities been an attack by ballistic missiles on Tel Aviv last night, what would the position of the New Democratic Party be in such case?
Shall we sit back and wait for more missiles to fall? Would Canada stand idly by? Would we have a pause for peace today? That is a very good question that I think the New Democratic Party should answer.
Third, had the counteroffensive against Kuwait been launched unilaterally on August 3 or 4 by the United States, or had a counteroffensive been launched last night by Israel against Iraq today, what would be the plight of Israel?
Government Orders
If the counteroffensive had been launched by the United States without the support of the United Nations and this country, if the counteroffensive had been launched last night by Israel, how much greater would the possibilities have been of a huge conflagration in the Middle East, one which would be surely stopped because of the combined efforts for peace by the United Nations coalition of which Canada is proud to be a member?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I have to say to the hon. minister that try as I might to write down those three questions so I could give him a response-and I am not going to invite him to repeat them again-he said three questions, the last question was about five questions in itself.
I would point out to the minister that I made a very serious speech. I asked some questions in my speech, questions about fact and they were answered by the minister by asking me rhetorical "what if" questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: This is the time for you to answer questions.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That is right. I am trying to answer but the hon. minister wants to argue with me, Mr. Speaker.
But I will stand here and I will address as best I can this long list of questions. The minister said, "Why were the people wearing gas masks last night?"
Right now.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
That is fine. I am in the House. I am sorry, I am not watching a television monitor. I am in the House and I am dealing with my knowledge when I came in the House.
The question is, why were they wearing gas masks last night. My response to that rhetorical question is, we all know why they were wearing gas masks last night. That is a silly question. The question is: Why are there not gas masks to fit children? Why are we standing here asking questions about why are they wearing gas masks instead of saying, would it, could it be possible that there could be dialogue for peace?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Six months.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The hon. minister said "six months". We had six months and nothing happened. We have struck a very, very horrific blow against the people of Iraq as well as Saddam Hussein. Nobody in this room is defending Saddam Hussein. We are saying, let us talk, let us think, let us see if we cannot at least among ourselves talk about a way to start toward peace.

Government Orders
The second question was also speculative: Had Kuwait not happened, what would the position in the New Democratic Party be? First of all, when we take positions we are dealing with positions based on what did happen, not "but if this did not happen our position would have been". Really, I think the minister is just a little bit confused in his questioning.
I appreciate that the minister sat in the House and listened to my speech. I would appreciate it very much if he would think about what was said in my speech. Rather than trying to trap and trip each other up, we should look at ways to resolve the crisis in the Middle East.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I think the last point the member made was exceptional. That is the point to be taken. We say we are going to be non-partisan but we still get into one-upmanship, or the feminine gender of that, and "we are more moral than you". It was very evident today in Question Period. Let us try to outdo one another and let us try to insult colleagues and try to make restitution or perhaps an apology later, but not likely.
In any event, I want to say that the member brought a human face, a very poignant message, so I do not think anybody should try to trip her up and say, "What about this, what about that" and what about a hypothetical question.
My question to the member is a serious one concerning the cost of war. We can look at it in two ways. First, the cost in human lives. She mentioned the numbers 150,000, 350,000, one million. Where will it end? We have no idea of the human cost as of yet. Second is the monetary cost. Some people say in the prelude to this war, in 1990, it has already cost $30 billion. The Globe and Mail cites today the Congress of the United States saying it may go to $86 billion, a $2 billion a day war. At what cost do we continue this war? Why did we start it and at what human cost, what monetary cost? Could we not spend money in a more beneficial way in this world in this present day?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague's question almost begs the answer. Of course, the cost is
incalculable, both in this war and in a continued way, both to the Middle East, to the world, to the environment, to the people, to our parents in Canada who have children in the war, and to children in Canada who are watching television and who are frightened. The cost is incalculable. We can go all over the world and we can find places where this war is taking its toll, whether it is monetary or emotionally.
Mr. Speaker, just one last word, because I was trying to answer the three specific questions of the minister earlier. I neglected to answer his comment about peace organizations in England intimidating the government from taking action in the Second World War. He referred to his constituent's opinion. I would like to remind Canadian women today that women in Canada are taking action for peace today and we should not be frightened.

Mr. Speaker, I think, like most members this week, we have entered into this debate with a very heavy heart, and obviously, as far as I am concerned, with a very troubled mind. It is not easy. Frankly, I have gone through a mental miosis this week as to just where I was going to come down.
I have to say that on Tbesday when this debate started, and this may surprise some members, I thought the Prime Minister gave one of the best and strongest speeches that he has given since he has been leader of the Conservative Party and certainly since he became Prime Minister.
Certainly during Question Period that day the Secretary of State for External Affairs, much to my surprise, because I have often differed from him from time to time, I thought again showed a grasp of the situation, and in his contribution to the debate it helped, believe it or not, affect my thinking.
Earlier in November I voted against the government motion and supported the amendments against the government motion because I honestly believed then that there was more time for these sanctions. Having heard the Prime Minister and the debate here in the House from other conscientious colleagues, I started to shift. I still wondered, but the wonderment and confusion was gradually being erased from my mind.

I am not going to go over all the horrors and cost of the war. There is a cost of war in bodies. There is a cost of war in dollars. For most of us in this House, the only reason we know about war is watching television and the Vietnam war. We have read books and we know it is not good. That is what makes it so difficult. The public out there is for peace. We are all for peace, too, and against war, every member in this House.
Obviously, as we listen to different members, we have different ways to approach those two fundamental basic issues. But to tiy to cloud the word and try to trick other people and pretend to the public that there is not a member against war and not a member for peace, that does a disservice to the member who is trying that.
Having said all that, I think the Prime Minister was correct. His speech was powerful. I slowly shifted. I said in November that I did not want my two sons to go to fight in the shifting sands of the Persian Gulf, where the sands themselves are symbolic of the shifting alliances and the shifting allies that have been there for hundreds of years and/or even in recent years. But, I started to come to the conclusion that one must look at what happened in Manchuria, Ethiopia, and Spain was not mentioned earlier, Austria, Czechoslovakia, and finally the line was drawn at Poland. After all the periods when the so-called free world in the thirties did not move, in my own mind on Tuesday I thought that "Well, Patrick, you have to face up to this, you cannot hide behind a party label because you are an independent member now''. Frankly, I thought at one time it was going to be easier if I could have hid behind a party label, but I knew I could not. I was slowly coming to the conclusion that, boy, the chips are getting pretty close. You have to support the reality that there have been mistakes. I am going to review some of the mistakes, but we do not have too much time in this debate. Quite frankly, I wasn't even going to speak.
My first point is that I have come to be embarrassed that this House is still debating this motion. What would I do if I were in the Persian Gulf serving with the forces that we have been so laudatory about. We are supporting them so well. We are all with them and the allies, and we are all against Saddam Hussein. If I were a little Canadian over there in the Sinai Desert, in Arabia, in Qatar or in any such interesting place, if I turned on the old CBC international before the government cuts it off-but that is a digression-and I heard that the
Government Orders
Canadian Parliament was in the fourth day of debate to approve a resolution to support military action and the action of the United Nations in getting Saddam Hussein, if I heard that members were still debating this mission, I would say that is the whole reason the public thinks this Parliament of Canada is full of hypocrites and out of touch with reality; especially if I found out that the United States of America, from talking to the GI Joe over there, took up the debate in its Congress, with 435 congressmen and 100 senators, for two days. Fundamentally they are the ones who are the most involved in this matter with some 400,000 troops, let alone all the dollars involved.
They came to a decision in a very divided House because their country is divided. We know what the debate was. I was amazed that the Senate, run by the Democrats, did not vote against the President and/or the House of Representatives, almost two to one Democratic. It voted very solidly for the President.
There I am a Canadian with this GI Joe, and he is saying: "What is your country doing debating the resolution? You have 2,000 people around here and three ships out in the sea". Then I find out that Great Britain voted in one day. Of course it has different parliamentary procedures but it voted very fundamentally in one day. It had its debate-and we know there are different rules over there-but with a heavy, very definite socialist Labour opposition the vote was 534 to 57.
Then we come to President Mitterrand of France which has troops in the Middle East. They in their Parliament in a day voted 523 to 43 to support the United Nations. Then we have the socialist government in Australia and the Government of Netherlands which has a lot of socialist members. Again they supported-and I do not know the numbers- the United Nations. Yet we are still debating this resolution.
Let me deal with the last part of the Prime Minister's speech. Frankly, I give the member for Vancouver Quadra full credit, as I give full credit to my former colleague, the member for Fraser Valley, for speaking from the heart. Even though they took different positions, I empathize with the member from Fraser Valley because I said some of the same things in the debate in November. I know we had anguish in that debate in November because he wanted to speak, but there were different suggestions that perhaps he did not speak then, and he had the guts to speak on this debate.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
We then had the former leader of the Liberal Party, the member for Vancouver Quadra, come into this House in a most dramatic way and make his presentation. After all the years I have been in this House it was one of the more dramatic moments I can remember, other than the Munsinger affair in the second year I was a member here in 1966. One of my colleagues was here. His name was Mr. Justice Cardin. He was standing over there and throwing out the name Monsignor affair, when he meant the bishop in Quebec. That got everyone involved in a two-day vote of privilege. That was one of the more dramatic moments that I can remember when the member for Vancouver Quadra made his presentation on such a large issue.
What are the guts of it when we shake it all down regardless of the mistakes that have happened before? George Bush and I have not agreed with all the moves of the government that have got us here. Let me turn to the speeches of the leaders on Tbesday. I listened to the leader of the Liberal Party. Frankly I respect him and like him as a person, but I got totally confused in terms of the policy of the Liberals on this motion, having known a little about Mr. Pearson and a little about the history of this country. It was listening to the leaders that day that started to switch me, but, if I had any doubt, it is when the bombs started to move and the fighter planes took off that night. That is the time when I think you have to put up or shut up.
With all the reservations, this is not the first time that there has been a multinational force in the Middle East. Good gracious, as far back as 1,000 years ago, under the cross of Jesus, the Crusades came into the Middle East and they did not solve much. In fact, one could perhaps argue that what happened then, in terms of trust and mistrust, has left behind some of the fundamental problems we find in the Middle East today.
If we have to worry about that, let us talk to that romantic character called Lawrence of Arabia and all the promises he gave to the Arabs in the First World War to try to inculcate and make sure that the Arabs fought against the Thrks and, in so doing, against the Germans. Those promises were not kept and we know other things
were done after the First World War, with the creation of the State of Israel.
All of these things are part of history and we are in a very real quicksand in this situation, with all of that history. That is why I have had the fundamental concern about going to a war in the Middle East and not exhausting all the problems of sanctions.
Then, we get into the presidential policies and/or the policies that have now been supported by all the members of the coalition, the deadline of the United Nations and no discussion until there is a full withdrawal. These are the sort of elements from the Second World War of unconditional surrender. And all historians say that it was the policy of the allies of unconditional surrender, which seemed so good at the time, that prolonged the Second World War for anywhere from two to three years, with all the consequent loss of lives and loss of dollars.
We were getting into that position. I could not understand, from reading the papers and listening, especially to CNN and other broadcasts, as we headed into the United Nations debate and on the days afterward, up until January 15, why the west, the allies, the coalition of which we were part, which is bigger by millions than the country of Kuwait which has a population of 17 million, had to worry about saving face. It is an irony that hit me. Good gracious we get into this situation of ultimatums, withdrawals, no negotiations, the charade that there is no linkage, and here we have the 17 million against all the other millions in the coalition and the irony that here that part of the world believes so much in face and we believe more in lives.
As this debate began at the first of this week, I was certainly ready to opt for the lives, forget about face, and make sure we had a conference. And whether there was a blink or a wink, to come up and say that, as I guess people tried to do in the last two or three days, after Tbesday when the bombs and planes started to fly. I could not believe it because what concerns me, regardless of the history that I have recounted and the shifting sands of the Middle East which are completely symbolic with the shifting allies you have in that country, is that with all the history I am not seduced at all. I am very concerned about the slogans about the surgical strike.
January 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, you and I may be mild historians, but in the Civil War the slogan was "One week to Richmond". In the First World War it was "Three weeks to a victory parade in Paris" and in the Second World War it was "A Month in Normandy and Berlin by Christmas". All these things we do not even have to think about, but we should and I hope leaders thought about the situation when the United Nations last acted to get itself involved in military action, i.e. Korea. Korea moved like a piece of cake until we got to the Yalu River and started to make a fundamental miscalculation, which involved the whole Republic of China and all the consequent loss of life there that was needless and unnecessary and perhaps would not have happened, if there had not been some miscalculations. Perhaps, for different reasons, Israel, that we all looked at last night with such anguish, may be the Yalu River. Who knows? For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am most concerned indeed. I believe we have the power and the American technology for this war. There is no doubt about it.
In watching CNN this morning, the laser bombs going down air vents, tremendous, but horrible. Yet, all that technology could not even keep out radar bugs and a fellow called Noriega when the Americans visited little Panama. I hear Noriega is going to be in the Supreme Court for the next two or three years, hopefully long before this crisis is over.
We have all these things. Sometimes technology does not do it, and I am concerned. I do not believe this war is going to be over in two or three weeks. I think it is going to be much longer.
I do believe, as a lot of the experts I have listened to have said, power versus patience. What concerned me from the start in this thing-and it has not been touched much-is that it has not really been examined again in the United States, and perhaps it would be unpatriotic to do it.
The biggest problem I have with this is the American ambassador to Iraq, eight days before the invasion when she, April Glaspie, had an audience with President Saddam Hussein. Among other things, he said: "You people are weak. You cannot sustain 10,000 bodies in a battle". That shows you where patience is going to be against power and that is what we have in this crisis.
Government Orders
But the worst thing that was said is that when he, the president asked her: "What is the position of the United States with Kuwait?" She replied-and she was echoing American middle eastern policy that was examined by the subcommittee on middle eastern affairs, chaired by Lee Hamilton three weeks earlier-"that is a longstanding boundary problem between your country and Kuwait. It is an Arab conflict, and you do not have to worry about the United States on that".
That was the worst signal to send because it was eight days later on August 2, that the invasion occurred. After all of that we now are where we are today. I do agree that we should have called Parliament earlier and had a debate in a more general atmosphere when we were not in battle. There is no doubt about that. When President Bush escalated the whole equation the day after his American election by 150,000 troops, not being a great military genius, but starting to realize that this was going to be more than just a smouldering problem, I knew in my mind that we were on a one-way street. But I still thought the leaders of the alliance, for example the President and/or Saddam Hussein with others trying to influence him, would not get everyone boxed into a position so those planes had to fly.
Having said all that, what I could not understand about the Liberal position without getting too political was that in effect once hostilities were brought out, they were going to bring the people home. If it was a UN flag, it was fine; but if it was not an UN flag it was not very good.
I can tell you that long before the member for Vancouver Quadra spoke, but after I heard the Leader of the Opposition speak Thesday, I thought of Mr. Pearson. I honestly thought Mr. Pearson, who had such a contribution to make for peacekeeping and his interest in the United Nations, would be rolling over in his grave.
I know my time is moving very quickly, Mr. Speaker, but I just could not believe this: they were there to do a good job, but if hostilities break out we have to run for home.
Without going into a lot more history, some members may remember, although I will bet you that the majority does not remember, that in the Second World War when I was a little cadet I went to camp. On the first weekend pass, I ran home and told my father that I had met some of the finest men in the world. They were soldiers up in camp. It was pretty full; it was wartime. My father asked me who they were. I am not going to say the regiment, but I did give him the name of the regiment. I was a kid

Government Orders
then, 16 years old. I should not have been in cadets because I was two years too young, but I was six inches too high and got in. My father said: "Oh, son, they are very good people, but these are zombies". I said: "What do you mean, zombies?"
"Oh, those zombies. They are fighting for Canada. They enlist, but they are not to be sent overseas." That was the condition without getting into all the internal and domestic politics then.
That was the Second World War. I did not believe, until I heard the leader of the Opposition yesterday or the day he spoke, that in effect his position on the troops retreating if hostilities broke out, the Canadian forces were going to be international zombies and the laughing stock of the world.
Mr. Speaker, you are telling me that my time is almost up. I have not really got started, but I know time is precious here.
I just want to say that when the chips are down, the planes start to fly and the fighting breaks out-coming back to where I started-I cannot believe that, if I were a soldier over there hearing that we were still debating this, I would think that debate was in my interest.
Saddam Hussein may be listening to a little of this. He has heard some funny things in this Chamber, but it certainly has not upset him.
In conclusion, I want to say that I agree-because of those two speeches-with the member from Fraser Valley and, obviously, the member for Vancouver Quadra. I repeat what the NDP tried to get here. I think it would be interesting. I think we should, as a public duty, have Opposition members and other members take out their spleen on the government, because it is not in good repute.
I really think if the Gallup polls were not reflecting some of the things that they do reflect-that is reality- that this debate may not have continued as long.
Let's have the vote. Let's have it a free vote and just see where everyone stands on this.
I think I am going to conclude with what really shifted my thinking before the bombs and planes started to move because, then, I certainly did believe that we have to stand united. Otherwise, at the least, we are really going to be misunderstood.
I want to quote a sentence from the historic debate in the United States last week by Senator Danforth and by those who have watched the debate. Evidently, Senator Nunn and Senator Danforth gave the real classic contributions on both sides of the issue, and they were very close.
I came down, and I wish members would come down on this as I read it. It pertains to the United States. It is a very short quote, and this is what switched my mind before I heard the Prime Minister and the bombs:
The key to peace is-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. Your time is over. It is question and comment period.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Annapolis Valley whether he could give us some quotes that might have taken place in the debate in the U.S. Congress that he feels might further elaborate upon the position that he was getting to.
I am wondering whether the hon. member would have any notes.

Mr. Speaker, naturally, I am very appreciative of the perception of the hon. member for throwing that question to me.
I would just like to read the quote of Senator Danforth. I think it is fundamental:
The key to peace is maintaining a credible military threat, and this is precisely the point our pending votes will address. I cannot vote to deprive the president of the credible threat of force. It is indeed a supreme irony that it is only through the threat of force that a stable world can be maintained. But that is an irony that we have recognized ever since World War II.
In conclusion, to supplement that quote-I do have a minute or so on the answer-this is what has happened this whole year with the walls coming down and eastern Europe opening up. It was because there was a credible military force- NATO and the allies-that these things happened.

Some of the same people who are wanting to take a pause now and who always want to talk about peace, and not of military deterrent, were taking that same position in some of those times.
What really boggles my mind is that I understand the importance of the UN flag, but this position of some people and perhaps the Liberal position at the moment-I do not know what its position is-is to take the exception and say: "Oh well, if the coalition under the UN resolution was under the blue UN flag, that would make it all right."
Since the UN flag is not there, they can stand back and talk about more time for sanctions. This, to me, is not very logical. The last time the UN flag was used, it was a blue flag. There was an American commander, General McArthur.
I bet you some people in the House, if we debated that, would perhaps have been against the punitive UN commander whom we knew was going to be the commander: General McArthur.
Here, we have many UN resolutions. The allies under that UN resolution had many problems in coming to that, with all the dangers in that area. I do not believe that this war is going to solve the problems. I think we are going to be left with all those historic problems unless we do have that conference and we do admit the linkage.
But to try to hide behind a vote, to delay a vote, and to hide behind the argument, "Oh well, more sanctions", when bombs are flying, and not to come up with a vote to support our troops there now, and by this interesting specious argument of UN resolution, yes, but no UN flag, no, when in effect we now have an American commander in the Middle East without the blue flag but UN resolution, I just cannot understand it.

Mr. Speaker, I will give a chance to others in a minute. I would just like to say I listened with great attention to the good speech made by my hon. friend. Historically it is never bad to say that I had the honour of knowing and sitting with his hon. father in this House so many years ago. I can recognize a great talent when I see one. The member has delivered quite an effective speech I must say. I would just like to be on record to say that I am delighted to see that some members, I may vote differently I do not know yet, agree that linkage and an
Government Orders
international conference are the types of things that we should have looked into a hell of a long time before we reached the very sad time we are going through.
I will read again his speech. He went from I would say almost around the clock in his emotion on that debate from one position to another. To me, this is what Parliament is all about. This is what independency should be all about, regardless of how we will vote on this issue. I appreciate very much what I just heard.

I appreciate those words coming from the dean of the House who also served here when my father was here. I know we do differ from time to time on specific votes, but we do not differ in the respect that we both have for this institution and for the respect that you can have for members even though you can violently disagree with their positions.
If I may, I forgot to get this on the record, Mr. Speaker, because, again, I have gone on a roller coaster this week, as a lot of other members have. If it were not President Bush, it was President F.D.R. where polls are so fundamental, television is so real and there, that it makes it even more difficult perhaps for trying to pull together a coalition and all the things that are necessary when you get involved. I know we have to admit that those are things in the past now. We are in this battle.
I am all for the new order but unfortunately we have new orders but we have old dictators. That is perhaps part of the historic problem.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to congratulate the member from Annapolis on his speech, not because we are seat mates but because, as the member from Montreal indicated, it was an excellent speech.
The resolution we are debating is:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
I agree fully with the member that it would be almost preposterous for us to have a vote on this. Which member in this House could find himself or herself voting against a resolution like that. I may be wrong but I think a lot of members who were for sanctions before would find now, since we are in the thick of the fray, that to vote against it now would seem to be a knife between the ribs for the men and women who are serving on behalf of Canada in that part of the world.

Government Orders
I wonder though, and this is the question to the member, whether there may be an unintended benefit to this debate, which is that it gives the chance for members to make points as time goes by. Had we adjourned yesterday, and we did not, thanks I believe to the member for Calgary Northeast, the House would have been out of session. I think it is important that the House stay in session, even if members get up every day and give speeches on some aspect of the war or on latest developments. I wonder if the member might not agree that is the reason why this debate might reasonably continue practically indefinitely so that members from all comers of the House may speak. It seems nonsensical now to have a vote on it.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of my hon. seat mate here. I know he shares many of the thoughts all members have this week.
I agree. I think if the House were to adjourn, the public would say the members are out for another holiday, even though we have come back before February 18. There is a real problem here. At the moment there is no business on the Order Paper. Realistically, I do not know what this House of Commons is going to be doing legislatively. But, yes, it does afford an opportunity for Questions Periods. The big point is this debate. I do not know if I agree with my hon. friend that all members will be voting for this resolution. I think the resolution should be put and the debate should be over with so that the Canadian in the Middle East is not embarrassed by other nationals asking what their Parliament is doing. "Is it still debating? You have a great bunch of wierdos. They cannot get together. They all preach United Nations support. They all say they are against Saddam Hussein. They all say they are for peace and against war. What the hell are they talking about?" Get the debate over, have the votes and then I do agree that between House Leaders there has to be an opportunity for the public to be involved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too think that this House should vote on this motion. We are three days into this war and I think that once all hon. members have had an opportunity to express their opinion that the question should come to a vote.
As the previous speaker mentioned, I think our Canadian soldiers and I am sure the international community will be looking for a signal as to just where the Canadian Parliament stands on this important issue.
There are some important principles involved in this debate and this whole question. They began with the invasion of Kuwait in August last year. That was an unprovoked attack. All members of this House, I am sure, agreed with the Canadian government when it condemned that invasion. At the same time, I am sure many members of this House did not believe that the condemnation by Canada or, indeed, other peace loving countries would be enough to reverse the flow of events in the Middle East. Condemnation alone was not going to work.
I believe it was very proper, therefore, that Canada in conjunction with many other countries of the United Nations invoked sanctions. Sanctions can do a number of things. I can tell you that at the time Canada invoked those sanctions, I had some doubts as to whether they were going to drive Iraq out of Kuwait, but I did believe it would put pressure on Iraq and hopefully that pressure, along with pressure from other countries in the world would convince them to pull out of Kuwait. At the time I did not think this would reverse the course of events. I am not making a categorical statement that sanctions can never work or should never be tried again. Of course they should be. Just as a condemnation by Canada the day after the invasion of Kuwait should be tried, so should sanctions.
The only question now is whether we should move beyond sanctions and support our soldiers and, indeed, all those fighting pursuant to the United Nations resolution. Should we give them our support now in forcibly expelling Iraq out of Kuwait? Obviously, we have different opinions and they have been heard in this House. There have been a number of reasons put forward, usually several in one argument as to why we should forcibly try to expel Iraq from Kuwait.
In a number of those arguments, I have seen individuals make the point again and again about the boundaries of Kuwait. I quote from one newspaper article which said that "the boundaries of Kuwait were arbitrarily set by a colonial power," as if that somehow lessens the legitimacy of a particular country.

I would be very hard pressed to come up with more than a handful of countries whose boundaries were not either set, influenced, or in some way shaped by colonial powers. Indeed, Canada's boundaries were shaped and set by a colonial power. That gives no other country in this world justification to invade Canada. That does not call into question the legitimacy of this country, nor should it for the State of Kuwait.
As well, I have had a number of people say to me that this is all about oil. I have had letters on that. Indeed, I was approached in church one day by someone who said that this was just about oil.
From my point of view, I do not support the United Nations resolution, nor have I supported the actions of this country involved with this because of oil, nor should anyone ever commit Canada or ever suggest that is the reason why Canada would go to war, because of oil.
While the lack of oil causes some discomfort for Canadians in terms of higher prices and I know that it has a very bad effect on the Third World in increasing prices, that should never be the justification for war.
There are those who continuously hammer and make the point about United States' leadership and the position of President Bush and the American Congress and that somehow this calls into question the legitimacy of trying to force Iraq out of Kuwait. I disagree with those individuals completely. Their dislike of either the American administration or the United States should not in any way cloud their opinion as to what is right and what is wrong. That has nothing to do with it.
I appreciate the fact that the United States is supportive of this. I appreciate the fact that the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and others are supportive of this. But, regardless, this does not change the principle as to whether or not Iraq should be in Kuwait.
Hon. members have made the point again that, if Canada is so worried about Kuwait, how about other examples? To that extent, I guess I agree with them. I believe the world did fail Ethiopia in 1936. We failed Ethiopia and we failed Czechoslovakia a couple of years later. I agree with those individuals who recognize and
Government Orders
understand the fact that the cold war for almost all of my lifetime paralyzed the world and the United Nations into doing what is right. I would only suggest to them that, yes, we have made mistakes in the past. It does not mean that we have to make mistakes in the future.
One of the critical things as to whether or not we should go beyond words and sanctions was contained in a report that was released by Amnesty International a few days before Christmas. I believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs tabled that report in the House of Commons within the last couple of days. I will refer to a news release which I would be happy to table because I intend to refer to it. It contains comments by Amnesty International, which I believe has no particular axe to grind other than to get at the truth, and it helped to convince me that we are dealing with a country that will not listen to sanctions, words, or condemnation by the United Nations or any of its members.
This is the news release that was released one week before Christmas, December 18, 1990. According to the investigations of Amnesty International, they detail how "Iraqi forces have tortured and killed many hundreds of victims, taken several thousand prisoners and left more than 300 premature babies to die after looting incubators from at least three of Kuwait City's hospitals. The report catalogues 38 methods of torture used by the Iraqi military, including cutting off people's tongues and ears, shooting them in the limbs, applying electric shocks to their bodies and raping them." It goes on to state: "Time and again we were told that the most common way soldiers killed people was to take the victim to his family's door-step, have his relatives identify him and then shoot him in the back of the head."
What is interesting about this is the Iraqi government never denied it. I was waiting for some sort of indication that this was not true or that they disputed this. I never saw that.
Any country that is prepared to invade another and start looting incubators and indiscriminately killing people is one that should be met with the force of Canada and every other peace-loving country in the world.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I agree with others who have spoken in the House that war is ugly, hideous, and horrible. Many people lose their lives.
At this point, the war in the Persian Gulf is but a few days old and the full extent of the damage is not known. I am not speaking of physical damage. We know that there will be considerable physical damage done to Iraq, now Israel, and perhaps other countries in the Middle East.
Does the hon. member recognize that there are hundreds of thousands of people who could lose their lives? I am talking about innocent Iraqi civilians, Israeli civilians, and civilians in other countries in the Persian Gulf who may lose their lives. Indeed, we know now that a significant number have lost their lives because of an international principle; that principle being that an aggressor should not be rewarded.
Has the member approached this very serious matter from a human perspective to understand what it may have felt like for innocent Iraqi civilians living in Baghdad, just as the innocent Israeli civilians living in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, when the bombardment started and as the bombardment continues? Does the hon. member feel that these hundreds of thousands of people who will lose their lives-and we do not know the full extent of the human damage that will be done until the war is over- really care about international principles?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the hon. member. He began by asking if I realized that, in pursuance of this international principle of the United Nations, that one country cannot arbitrarily invade another, and do I understand that people will be killed.
If we take that comment of his to its logical conclusion, then we are hamstrung, because we could never act. We could not have acted in 1939 because the same question could be posed. He could have said to me: "Mr. Nicholson, don't you know that if you try and stop Adolf Hitler now that individuals would be killed?"
I guess I would say to the people of Iraq that they should have been putting pressure on their government for these last six months to change course.
The hon. member is asking me from a human perspective. I guess I put myself in the position of those parents whose children have been violated in Kuwait, through no fault of the Kuwaitis. Kuwaitis were not at war. They did not provoke the war. They had done nothing to have this inflicted upon them. I guess I look at it from their point of view, the indiscriminate killing that has been taking place in Kuwait, and I say that should be condemned. It should be stopped. The international community should come together as one to drive those invaders out of that country.
That is the human perspective that I bring to this and I would ask the hon. member about the position of his party, that we should get out of there now. This is a bad one, a very bad one, and I hope that he would rethink that and say: "Look, we are here. We could get this job done. Let's get it done as expeditiously ask possible." That is possible. If this coalition sticks together, we can get this job done and I think that Israelis, Kuwaitis, and I am sure people of that part of the world will say: "This world is a better place to live in if Saddam Hussein is not a threat to this region."

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask a question about the orders of the House.
The member who just asked a question earlier today used some very unparliamentary language and processes in the House. Madam Deputy Speaker was in the Chair and she indicated he would not be recognized until such time as he had done the parliamentary thing.
My question to you is: Does the position of the Speaker apply, or is it the position of the individual Speaker in the chair who is going to decide whether the member is going to issue an apology to the House for the manner and methods in which he spoke to the Chair?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I have to admit that I am not aware of any such ruling on the part of the Deputy Speaker. I will inquire.
The member for York South-Weston was the only member who stood up for questions and comments and, since I was not aware of the incident just pointed out to me, I had to apply the rules and recognize the member.
January 17, 1991

That being said, I appreciate the comment and will inquire as to what should be done. If need be, I will follow up on this. I know the member in question met with the Deputy Speaker.
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Hamilton East.

Mr. Speaker, like many other members of the House and like many other Canadians, I have watched the events of the last 72 hours with the range of emotions, with the heart-pounding, with the adrenalin coursing, and with the sense of fear and foreboding about what this war might have in store for us as Canadians, and also what it might have in store for the world.
I had a prepared speech, Mr. Speaker, and I had a clear position prepared in advance of the decision of the United States to attack Iraq. The events of the last 72 hours have rendered that speech and, in fact, this resolution redundant. They have rendered it redundant because, like it or not-

Canada is at war.
While I am sure during this extremely emotional and difficult period for all of us it would be pretty easy for some of the government members to poke holes in the positions that have been taken by opposition members over the last number of days, I, speaking as an opposition member, personally. Have gone through the range of emotions and I have to tell you that whatever the outcome of this war, and I fear the outcome will be felt for many years to come, it was the wrong time. It was the wrong time because, in the emerging of a new world order, we did not give the opportunity for economic strangulation and for economic sanctions to work. Yes, it was the wrong war. And yes, last weekend I marched in my own community, side by side with members of the human race, representing Canada, Israel, Iraq and Kuwait, none of whom wanted this war.
Government Orders
The member for Niagara Falls spoke earlier about the atrocity of taking a baby from an incubator. Who, in his right mind, could ever condone such atrocity? But the atrocities that we are potentially about to witness will be wrought upon innocent victims. I do not speak only of women and children; there are innocent men, women and children on all sides of this conflict who will die as a result of the decisions of men to take us to war. I marched on the weekend with an Iraqi constituent in my riding who said to me that Saddam Hussein is crazy. That is why this person left that country. He could not have the input into direct foreign policy that he would like to have in a democratic country. But he has brothers there who have children and he has cousins, all of whom are under potential threat of imminent and innocent, individual death. In a war, there are no winners and no losers.
I think about the First World War when my grandfather watched his own father die on the field of battle not knowing it was his father and what that did to him. He was given six hours to live, his body was riddled with shrapnel; that was in the First World War. There is no war in which you have long-term winners and losers and one of the emerging truths of the 1990s was that we were supposed to be entering a new world order, where civilized countries would find civilized ways to deal with human nature.
