We are seeing that civilization break down, not only in Kuwait but also in Lithuania, Latvia, in the Baltic States, and in many other parts of the world, where the international recourse has not been, at this stage, to war.
All those arguments can be made and they can be made in a very direct way. But the fact of the matter is that the Canadian government has committed Canadian men and women to the battlefield. My sister-in-law may be called up. As a former air force doctor, who retired from active duty last year, she is still on the list of recall and may be called over. I know how frightened she is and how she dares not pick up the phone when it rings, in case she is called up. I know as we speak how powerless we are in this House to affect the nature of this war. There are thousands of Canadian families who are looking to us, as members of Parliament, for support for their loved ones.
How abhorrent war is, how much I have opposed this government's and, indeed, the American government's early use of force when, in fact, the avenue of sanctions

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
had not been exhausted. I cannot in good conscience turn my back on the Canadian men and women who have been sent over there to represent our country in a conflict that could have unlimited and continuing implications.
While government members may probably experience the same doubts, fears and forebodings that we feel on this issue, it seems to me that this particular resolution at this stage is redundant. Indeed, under the circumstances, perhaps the wisest course of action would be a withdrawal of this resolution I agree that we cannot send a message to our women and men in the Armed Forces that in any way equivocates our support for their actions.
Whatever we as individual members and indeed as parliamentarians thought about the reasons-some legitimate, some illegitimate-that conceived this call to war at this stage we must send a message of full and unequivocal support to those women and men whose lives are at risk; to those families; children the age of my daughter, watching their mothers and fathers go off to war; and also to those children on all sides of the conflict who will undoubtedly lose their lives as a result of this war.
I cannot give any lecture on the military nature of what our actions should be from this point forward. I am no military expert. Perhaps one of the greatest feelings that we have felt in this Parliament is a sense of powerlessness. International events are unfolding so quickly that we in this chamber or in the other place really have virtually no influence on the agenda that may unfold.
We huddled around our television sets last night as the retaliatory bombs came forward and we saw the fear ingrained in the eyes of that CNN reporter in Saudi Arabia who feared the possibility of a nerve gas attack. We saw the fear gripping a nation, the nation of Israel which has used, I believe, calm reasoning in deciding not to retaliate. I am not sure that under the circumstances I would have been as calm and as reasoned.
But there are ways that we in our own way can influence this agenda. I think it is important in the context of the House of Commons that we continue to press the government with its allies to try and find a peaceful solution. We must press on the issue-as I did this morning-that not only are there Israeli children who could very likely be killed in this conflict, but there are Palestinian children in the West Bank, in the Gaza.
There are Iranian children; Iraqi children and Kuwaiti children. Perhaps in an as non-partisan way as we are able, we can continue to keep the government agenda and an agenda for strength through peace.
In the longer term, Mr. Speaker, our objectives have to be to re-examine the notion of civilization in the context of the new world order because as the bombs drop-and so they will on Iraq-we are seeing not only destruction of Iraqi installations, but also the destruction of one of the world's most ancient civilizations.
The very notion of statehood when in the Middle Ages the people agreed to the state of serfdom, they did so because their lords were to provide protection. The very notion of civilization and statehood has been developed so that we could, in fact, protect ourselves.

But in the national context, Mr. Speaker, we were able to do that, if we look at Europe, for instance. Until 1945, Europe had always been at war, 2000 years of war. But after 1945, after experiencing the horrors of war, as they were experienced in Japan, from that moment onwarde they realized that a civilization's real progress is not predicated on war but on peace. And that may be why, Mr. Speaker, we are seeing a new order in Germany, because they realize the Berlin wall was useless.

I think it is about time that, in the over-all context we examine what we mean by "new world order". Why is it that in national and individual contexts we have been able to develop for ourselves, by which people can solve problems in a legitimate, non-aggressive way, that very formula that has escaped us once again in the international arena?
The First World War was supposed to be the war to end all wars. Yet, within a very few short decades we moved into another war.

Mr. Speaker, who would have thought that we, in Canada's 34th Parliament, would be here to vote on war? I could never have imagined that. Who would have thought that my three year old daughter, when I was feeling really down and disappointed yesterday, would say: Mom, is the war making you so sad? She is not yet four, Mr. Speaker. But what can we give our children?
January 17, 1991



In the long term, we have to look for new solutions of diplomacy and economic sanctions that justly recognize that the problem of the Middle East is not going to be solved merely by eliminating Saddam Hussein.
There will be other Saddam Husseins. With the coalition as fragile as it is, if it splits apart, the potential for international disorder is even greater as a result of actions that have been taken in the context of the United Nations.
How do we look to this new world order?
I would like to speak for a moment to what I perceive to be, not only in this House but across the country, the so-called gender gap of war. It has never been my intention as a person in politics who happens to be a woman to suggest that, as women or men, we have the divine right to see the world differently.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if you discussed with the women members on all sides of this House you would find, as you would if you spoke with women across this country, that there is a radically different way with which we approach this issue of war.
I do not think a woman leader would claim that we were going to go in and "kick ass". I think that is the kind of terminology that belies a misunderstanding of the need to exercise all avenues of diplomacy before moving to war. In that context, I truly believe that women and men who are out there on the battlefield and also those here in Canada must begin to share more our collective wisdom and feelings.
I think you will see, Mr. Speaker, over the course of this debate that women in this House have risen perhaps more emotionally than many of the men.
Yesterday we heard the hon. member for Mount Royal and the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands speaking with eloquence and from the heart, but in a way that brought a particularly individual perspective to the issue. I happen to believe that for all the emotions we share, for all the feelings we have and for all the reasons that we have to be together on this one, it is so critical that in
Government Orders
the arena of war we take a step back and reflect upon the real meaning of war. Some will criticize me for this, but I would like to think that perhaps the nurturing and creation of life which is unique to womanhood has given us a perspective which makes us much less likely to send our sons and daughters to war.

I say that, Mr. Speaker, not because I think the feminine perspective is better than the male perspective.
I say that because of the way women have been socialized, with their ability to create life, they are far less inclined to take a life.
I think that in the new world order, whatever the outcome of this war-and it is expected to be short with as little loss of life as possible-we must learn from this perspective. We must learn from this ability to create life that a new order, a new civilization cannot call itself civilized if killings and wars are the way we solve our problems.
Mr. Speaker, that is the duty of this Parliament, because obviously-a few members in this House are not going to affect the course of events taking place in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf.
Mr. Speaker, if we as parliamentarians, if Canada and the rest of the world want to recreate some of the hope we had at the end of the Cold War in 1990, we should have chosen new instruments to improve our ability to settle our international problems, whatever they may be.
Mr. Speaker, that is why, although I hate war, as I hate the fact that innocent people will be killed on all sides, I believe that despite the fact that I deplore this government's decision to involve us in this war, we are in it, nevertheless.
We must be prepared to give our full support to our men and women who are over there, and who are working for us all.
But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, in this House we must focus on the most important question of all which is the creation of a new order that shares the responsibilities, aspirations and hopes of all citizens of this world.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have probably heard more speeches from that hon. member than any other member in this House. I say that because of course I think most members will know that I have known the hon. member probably longer than any other of our colleagues here. I have to tell her that whether she realizes it or not, she has probably given the best speech she ever has given. I think that the tone of the House listening to her is a testimony to that. The House, as all members will know, but Hansard does not record, was dead silent listening to the member's remarks, and with good reason.
I want to tell her as well that when she spoke of the powerlessness that we feel as members, that if her discourse today is rewarded, as it should, that it should have an influence on members of this House in terms of what their position is on this issue. I say that from the bottom of my heart.
I want to raise with her this whole business of the powerlessness that we feel as legislators on this issue. It is one that I share, and I raised it in my speech yesterday. We are debating a motion which basically asks us if we are in favour of United Nations' motions which have already been placed into effect and have already been caused to happen; in other words, the motion is redundant. Even if it were not redundant, the motion was structured in such a way and presented at such a time that if you voted for it, you were voting in fact for war and if you voted against it, you were voting against the UN.
I find it deplorable that this issue, as gut-wrenching as it is, was presented to this Parliament in that way. Instead, we should have been presented a motion that asked us point blank, before the hostilities began: Do we or do we not, as a country, want to participate in those hostilities when they do begin and if they do begin? I would have still voted no to the proposition. But I think I had a right to hear the proper question, as opposed to the one that we did hear.
Second, now that the hostilities have begun, I do believe that what we should be asking, notwithstanding the fact that I disagree with what has been done, is
whether or not we support our forces which have already gone over there, not whether or not we should be voting on a motion which is redundant and which was wrong even before it was redundant.

Mr. Speaker, I will take the member's compliments as intended. It is true that the member and I have spent a lot of years together and we have fought a lot of wars, but none of them have been of the nature of this war. They have all been political wars.
I would have to say that notwithstanding the member's comments and notwithstanding the nature of the resolution when it was first presented, I think the responsibility is upon all of us right now to put our political battles behind us, to cease and desist from the natural temptation to score political points on this particular issue. I think in that light it is important that this resolution be withdrawn because I think it is a redundant resolution which, whatever the vote, is going to send potentially the wrong signal to our armed forces.
In the light of the delicate nature of the situation right now, I think we would be far better off to speak to a resolution upon which we could all unanimously agree to give our full 100 per cent support to those Canadian women and men who have been asked by their country to serve in our interest in the Persian Gulf. That is why I hope that this resolution will be withdrawn and we vrill be able to bring forward a resolution that will meet the test of unanimity of this House which is obviously going to be very crucial for the morale of those soldiers who are over there fighting on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, I thank and commend our colleague from Hamilton East. I would like to make a comment and ask her a question, if I may.
The member for Hamilton East said that, in war, there are no winners and no losers. I suggest, referring back to what is being taught in our administration schools, you are either in a win-win situation or in a win-loose situation, and in the latter case, there are always loosers. Unless both sides win, they both end up loosing. I thought I had heard the hon. member for Hamilton East say that there were no winners and no loosers. She may wish to take this opportunity to make a correction.
January 17, 1991

My second comment, which is also a question, deals more directly with her position on the issue. We know where she stands as a woman. It is indeed pretty unusual-and she mentioned the risk of giving rise to criticism-to talk about the value, and more particularly about the fundamental difference between male and female. So that everything is clear, I wish she would use the time she has left to reaffirm the fact that recognizing individual differences does much more for personal growth as well as that of nations than playing on similarities and that relying too heavily on the concept of similarity involves a notion of levelling the base. So, by recognizing individual differences, we do not necessarily address what must be something else than levelling the base.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton East has one minute and a half to answer.

Briefly, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was quite right when he said that there is an exception to every rule. For instance, when comparing men's and women's different attitudes, a colleague mentioned Mrs. Thatcher. It is clear that to a certain extent, Mrs. Thatcher was not typical of the sensitive individuals I was referring to earlier. Having said that, I suggest it is important to recognize our differences. I have always insisted on the differences between Francophones and Anglophones, men and women.
As far as winners and losers are concerned, it is true that we may win in the short-term if Saddam Hussein, confronted with the forces of the United States and their allies should withdraw. It would be a short-term victory. But what about the long term? I mentioned my grandfather because I saw how his life changed following World War I. We had come out the winners, but my grandfather remained a loser. He could never find a job because he was unable to work, as a result of the injuries he had received in the service of his country. Mr. Speaker, there were also losers on both sides following the Vietnam War: traumatized Vietnam veterans, broken families, dead children. In such a context, in the long run, there are neither losers nor winners in a war, just a forum from which to start a new war. That is what I am concerned about: If we succeed in destabilizing the Middle East, there might be winners in the short run, but in the long run, what will happen to that international forum which
Government Orders
was already shaky before Saddam Hussein started this war?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Outremont has the floor for the next ten minutes.

If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to use some of my time to reflect on the comments made by the hon. member for Hamilton East. Of course, there is never a winner and a loser in a win-win situation where the adversaries must either both win or both loose.
Mr. Speaker, I did not think I would have to take the floor. My position was known. I had other means to keep in touch with the people of Outremont.
Recent events force me to speak. I want to address my remarks to the Jewish community of Outremont, Quebec and Canada to offer them my sympathy and my prayers.
Hon. members know that the riding I have the honour to represent is home to people from various ancestries and that multiculturalism is thriving in that small microcosm. But as I said, I think it is important and necessary for me to rise and offer these people my sympathy and my prayers. Very humbly as well, Mr. Speaker, I would extend my sympathy to the people of Israel.
If I may I should like to comment on the dynamism of the situation we are experiencing. From the onset I felt-and I still feel-that there was no hesitation and that the position had to be clear. The Prime Minister made this statement in the House on January 16, and I quote:
The Time has regrettably come therefore to act in the interests of preserving world order and in safeguarding the effectiveness of the United Nations. A failure by the world community to act would have undermined the United Nations, turned a blind eye to naked aggression, condoned violations of international law and encouraged other potential aggressors to defy world opinion in the pursuit of their own criminal ambitions.
Allow me to quote him:

"The time has regrettably come therefore to act in the interests of preserving world order and in safeguarding the effectiveness of the United Nations. A failure by the world community to act would have undermined the United Nations, turned a blind eye to naked aggression, condoned violations of international law and encourage, other potential aggressors to defy world opinion in the pursuit of their

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
own primitive ambitions. If Canada had stood aside, we would have
betrayed our own national interests, repudiated our own
responsibilities and dishonoured our own traditions."

Mr. Speaker, this is why I thought there would be no need for me to rise and that my position was known as a stong supporter of the motion now before the House.

Entering a war is never easy, at least not for Canadians. We are by nature a passive people and we have a long history of promoting the peaceful settlement of disputes, both at home and abroad. Why do we value stability? Why are we recognized internationally as people who cherish peace? It is partly due, in good part, to our multicultural landscape. Canada was founded by immigrants and new immigrants continued to inject new ideas and new vitality into our society. But we learned long ago that we had to be sensitive to each other's needs in order that Canadians of different origins could live peacefully and side by side. We had to be willing to listen and talk, negotiate and compromise, and as a result we have become "experts" in resolving conflicts with a minimum of violence.
We have another principle which has allowed us to be seen as a peace-loving nation. It is our unfailing support for the United Nations, an organization that stands for peace. Canadians have to create a United Nations as we know and we have continued to support it financially, materially and militarily at a level which far exceeds our relative strength in the world.
Although the United Nations is a peace organization, it recognizes that sometimes force must be used against the most blatant acts of aggression. This is perhaps not easy for many of us to accept since the cold war prevented the UN from exercising its peace and security function for so long. But the principle of collective security against aggression is at the core of the United Nations charter. To deny this fact is to reject the very raison d'etre of the UN and to accept the law of the jungle in international affairs.

Mr. Speaker, life is not what it used to be. Everybody says so, or at least that is what we hear practically everywhere we go.
Older members of society like to talk about the good old days, when everything was so much better. According to them, there were no wars, no murders, no thieves. Not exactly, but there was a lot less.
In any case, the facts say otherwise. It seems this is not true at all. There have always been wars, there have always been murders, there have always been thefts and storms and people dying.
We have every reason to believe that today, life is more satisfying and more enriching than it has been for many centuries.
The leisure society appeared a few decades ago, because we had attained a more acceptable standard of living. If the leisure society could have appeared earlier, it would have done so, and earlier generations would have benefited.
As this leisure society evolved, society became more compassionate as our social conscience became more sophisticated.
Mr. Speaker, in a family there are all kinds of personalities. Some are more aggressive, others are more passive, while others are more creative.
Many families, especially Quebec families which tended to be large, had what was commonly referred to as a black sheep. This was a child that often just did what it felt like doing, unlike its brothers and sisters.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is running out, and I want to thank you for letting me know. I will have to conclude. What I meant is that the child that was considered the black sheep would get special attention from the other children. Often, one of the smarter siblings was able to discipline this child.
I use this particular example because the present situation is actually just that: one of the children of our international community has asked the other children of the family to take care of what is considered to be a black sheep.
January 17,1991	COMMONS
And since you asked me to conclude, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that I support this motion without any hesitation, and I do so with my knowledge of personal and group psychology and with the honesty I also found among my fellow members.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Five minutes for questions and comments. The hon. member for Saint-Denis.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the last words said by the hon. member for Outremont. He said: "I give my full and entire support and I do so knowingly as a psychologist and expert on human issues".
As you see, I am quietly preparing part of the speech I will probably make, I am not sure. But that is the main aspect I intend to discuss in my speech.
As an expert on human issues-and I agree-would Dr. Hogue be so kind as to tell me, while these military operations are going on against the unacceptable invasion of Kuwait by Saddam Hussein, at a time when a number of nations have decided to start a military operation, and I will not comment on that in my question to the hon. member-
However, doesn't he think it is time to send some messages as soon as this conflict is resolved militarily, it is obvious that the people who are now trying to get Saddam Hussein to surrender or withdraw will win, I think that is pretty clear. Isn't it time for Canadian to send a message? To, all those people who are in desperate straits in that part of the world? I am thinking of our friends in Jordan, because I remember what our Prime Minister said when His Majesty King Hussein came here to address the House.
I remember what was said by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada when President Herzog of Israel came and also addressed the House on that very spot.

And we will have to do that before these people become so desperate they get involved in disastrous schemes-I am thinking of those 1.5 million Jordanians of Palestinian origin, 60 or 70 per cent of the population of Jordan, where hatred now looms so large that every solution is doomed. And the same applies to the people in the northwest territories and Gaza, who say there is no hope left.
Would it not be time for Canada, while the government does its thing, and I will not pass judgment on that-to send messages that Canada is determined to get

this over with as soon as possible but we then have to take care of all these loose ends?
The hon. member who is an expert on human psychology is aware that these loose ends have been around for quite some time in the Middle East.

I want to thank the hon. member for Saint-Denis, in the riding next door to mine, for a question that is intriguing but difficult to answer.
I will try to marshall all the intellectual honesty I possess, and of course this includes my deeper feelings on the subject.
Generally speaking, the answer is yes. To do so, however, we will all have to do more than just tolerate each other. We have to accept each other, and I am sure you realize I have no illusions about this. The notion of belonging is fundamental. At the same time, there is also the notion of trust which is just as fundamental. No one in this House, starting with yourself, would believe that the Prime Minister or the Minister of External Affairs take a position because they feel like it. They do so because they have what they feel is the best possible reading on the matter, and of course I don't have to speak on their behalf. The best possible reading required that the decision be made but, on the other hand, perhaps we should go through a specific exercise before getting that far, and the exercise that we are seeing here in the House is not one that stresses our weakness.
I feel it shows our strength and our ability to take a position and at the same time not only address the people of Israel but also the Palestinians and peoples all over the world to tell them that the Parliament of Canada, on whatever side we happen to be in this Chamber, is a responsible body and that at the same time we try to be fully aware that there is a fine line between peace and war-
Resuming debate. The hon. member for Drummond.

Mr. Speaker, by invading Kuwait on August 2, Iraq provoked the worst international crisis in recent years, in a region that for a long time has been know as particularly explosive, with profound enmities exacerbated by poverty and economic disparity, muffled hostility between religions and countries and the resulting extremism and blind hatred. This is a region scarred by eight years of war between Iran and Iraq, an unending civil war in Lebanon, repeated con-

Government Orders
frontations between Arabs and Israelis and violent disputes between Israelis and Palestinians.
The act of aggression committed by Iraq was a direct challenge to the international community, at a time when the end of the old adversarial relationship between the superpowers had opened the way to legal recourse, dialogue and co-operation to deal with international problems and safeguard peace and security.
We are going through a time of extraordinary change in the world. In eastern Europe, people are throwing out communist ideology and embracing the freedom and responsibility of democracy and a free market economy. In Western Europe, the process of political and economic integration is accelerating. In 1991, 340 million Europeans will finally form a single market.
The invasion and annexation of Kuwait by Iraq has destabilized the world order, disrupted development projects in the Third World, upset the transition towards a market economy in central and eastern Europe and will continue to affect political and economic systems throughout the world.
Since the beginning of the crisis, the international community has spoken clearly, with an unprecedented consensus. Now that the cold war is over, the United Nations organization could build a lasting international order. It is therefore very important, Mr. Speaker, to remind Canadians of the fundamental reasons behind the government's position in the Persian Gulf crisis and its involvement in the war.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to recall briefly the events that have taken place since August 2. On that day, the Iraqi army invaded Kuwait with a major and impressive military force consisting of more than 150,000 men, 1,200 tanks and 1,000 armoured cars, shocking the Arab world as well as the rest of the international community, which immediately condemned this invasion.
This invasion, which came without provocation, went well beyond any resistance that Kuwait could have offered. The Iraqi forces quickly took over the capital, plundering the country's resources without the slightest restraint and persecuting its inhabitants. After six days of
unequal and bloody combat, Saddam Hussein declared that Kuwait had been annexed to Iraq.
The UN Security Council, of which Canada is a member, demanded the immediate withdrawal of Iraqi troops. An economic, financial and military embargo was also ordered in the Persian Gulf against Iraq and Kuwait, an embargo observed by Canada which agreed to become part of the international strike force.
As I said earlier, the reaction of the international community was fast and clear. The UN Security Council adopted 12 resolutions to put an end to the unwarranted occupation of Kuwait by Iraq.
More than 30 countries took part in this multinational action, including the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Austria, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Syria, Pakistan, Bangladesh and the U.S.S.R.
The action also included African countries like Niger and Senegal, and new democracies in Central Europe like Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Poland.
After the period of grace granted Saddam Hussein by the UN Security Council, there was no indication, unfortunately, that Saddam Hussein was prepared to withdraw his troops from Kuwait. In fact, his position seemed to harden from day to day, supported by the Iraqi Parliament.
A meeting between Secretary of State James Baker and Iraqi Minister of Foreign Affairs Tariq Aziz, as well as conciliation efforts attempted twice by UN Secretary General Mr. Perez de Cuellar, failed to advance the cause of peace and a diplomatic solution to the problem. Armed conflict became a possibility.
Mr. Speaker, we must review the reasons that caused the Government of Canada to provide military aid. We must not forget that our military participation is consequent on a series of resolutions adopted by the vast majority of members of the UN Security Council.
Our membership in this organization is above all an act of faith in all the ways in which we can possibly guarantee peace in this world. Many people who condemn the use of force included in resolution 678 fail to understand that the UN charter contains not only statements of principle in favour of peace but also provisions respecting to collective security.

Drafted following the atrocities of World War II, the Charter provides for the measures needed to enforce its provisions, should these be ignored by a given nation.
Everyone, including myself, hopes that international conflicts are resolved peacefully. All Canadians share that hope, I am sure.
However, when a situation may worsen to the point of being the threat to international security, and when all persuasive arguments seem to have failed, what then?
Wait until an entire nation is massacred and decimated? Stand by while human rights and the rights of a nation are violated unrestrainedly, without any reactions from the rest of the world? That is the crux of the problem.
What made this situation intolerable for the international community, Mr. Speaker?
We knew that Iraq had upgraded its military forces and that it continued to reinforce its facilities in Kuwait.
Mr. Speaker, Canada must fully support the position of the UN. If we were to dissociate ourselves in any way from this agency whose first mission is universal peace it would be tantamount to suspending our belief in humanity.
If at a given time, a group of human beings no longer believes in understanding, tolerance and trust among nations, should we in the name of a precarious peace, let them go ahead and destroy their neighbours?
It is regrettable that the Persian Gulf crisis led to war rather than a peaceful settlement. There is no such thing as a good war. War is humanity's least noble invention. We all want to avoid it. Saddam Hussein remained deaf to the pleas for peace until the last minute and, by refusing to withdraw from Kuwait pursuant to the UN ultimatum, he opened the door to war. The main thing to remember is that if we want peace we must uphold the principles enshrined in the United Nations charter. We must be prepared to defend what we perceive as being the good cause. By acting otherwise we would be telling Saddam Hussein and other potential aggressors that the UN is unable to respond efficiently to aggression.
Government Orders
On January 16, unfortunately, the time had come to take the measures required to restore world order and maintain the efficiency of the United Nations.
In the United Nations charter, the peoples declare their solemn resolve to live in peace and unite their strengths to maintain international peace and security.
Under the terms of the charter the Security Council is primarily responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security, and for the peaceful settlement of conflicts.
Since their inception the United Nations has often been called upon to prevent a dangerous situation from degenerating into real war, to convince adversaries to use the conference table rather than resort to arms, and facilitate the return to peace, or at least end the fighting when hostilities do break out.
Despite failures and setbacks the UN remains ever more prepared to restore and maintain peace in the world.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I hope the war will be short so that our fellow citizens who are defending freedom and the cause of enduring peace will soon return home.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments, five minutes. Resuming debate. The hon. member for Scarborough-Agincourt.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a very important motion put forward by the government. Basically, we are debating whether we should go to war or not go to war. It is redundant. We already engaged in war two or three nights ago when my colleague from Dartmouth came rushing in to let the House know that we had engaged in war.
Calling the House back to debate it is redundant, because we have already engaged in war. However, I want to put on record not only some of my feelings and thoughts, but also those of my constituents.
We called over 2,000 constituents over the last weekend and Monday and asked them whether they felt Canada should participate in the gulf situation in an offensive role or whether the sanctions should be given more time. The results of this poll were overwhelmingly that more than 70 per cent of my constituents were opposed to an offensive role being played by the Canadian forces. I would like to read for the record some of the comments of my constituents.

Government Orders
Mr. Goldthorpe said, "I hate war and senseless killing of our young people. It is just terrible, and I think they should try and negotiate peace".
Mr. Jaffray said: "My understanding was that the Canadian troops were only supposed to be a defensive force and not supposed to take any part in the attacking of Hussein. I would rather see the Canadian troops operating under the flag of the United Nations".
Mrs. Beath said: "Canada's stand should be to support the United Nations' position of sanctions, but should take the initiative on the Palestinian issue and call for the United Nations to continue with sanctions until such a time as they have proven not to be working".
Mrs. Akers said: "I think sanctions should be given more time. You cannot back someone into a comer; it has got to stop. There cannot be a war; it is going to affect us over here. Please, no war! The sanctions need more time".
Mrs. Bloemink said: "I don't think this war is a thing that is desirable. I think we have been led into it. Our boys should not be sacrificed to greed and profit, which is what the whole thing is about. It's a hypocritical situation". Mr. Guildys states:
The economic blockade which the Government of Canada and the
rest of the world has been pursuing in the Middle East, is probably
the right way to go.
As far as war is concerned, I have always been against war because
innocent lives will be threatened.
I listened very carefully to what my constituents were telling me. I met with my constituents and I listened very carefully to what the Canadian people are saying. The constituents of Scarborough-Agincourt could be wrong. I could be wrong. However, they are not in favour of war.
If the Canadian people are saying no to war, how can we as parliamentarians say to the Canadian people: "We are deaf and we are not going to hear you. We are not going to pay attention to you. We are going to put you in a situation where we are going to engage in war". If we look at the history of how the Canadians forces were sent there, if we look at the events that led to our young men and women being engaged in war, we would see that at no time were we clear with the Canadian public. We
would see that at no time did we come forward and say, "Canadian public, this is what we are going to do".
Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2. The House was not recalled immediately in order to debate the very important question: Should we send Canadian troops? Should we commit Canadian military equipment into the gulf? Should we commit young men and women of our Canadian forces into the theatre of war?
The Prime Minister made the decision. The Minister of National Defence went off to Halifax to see the three ships go out. There was a big hoopla and a big hurrah, and they thought, "Maybe we will go up in the polls for taking the same stand as Maggie Thatcher in the Falklands". Then the House came back.
Of course, this House was led to believe that we are there enforcing sanctions under the United Nations resolution. We can clearly see how even that great body, the United Nations Security Council, was arm-twisted and taken out of context and forced so that the vote happened when it did. It is very important to know when the vote did occur. The vote occurred in the United Nations the last week that the United States was the chairperson. Everybody there had an interest again. The Russians voted with the United States.
Let us examine for a minute why they voted with the United States for the deadline in order for war to take place. Because right now the Russians are in chaos in their country and the United States has promised them food and aid. The Chinese abstained from the vote. Why did they abstain from the vote? It is important to note that. They wanted to be on the side of right for a change, and not the wrong side as they were in 1989 when the tanks rolled in Tiananmen Square. All of the other countries supported the U.S. because they had a lot to gain. It is my opinion that sanctions, if they had been given a little bit more time, would have worked.
We must first of all take a hard look at why this debate is Necessary. Iraq under the leadership of a madman, Saddam Hussein, invaded its southern neighbour Kuwait. While this is a major concern to the world community, it must be taken in the context of recent world history. There have been instances of a larger country taking over a smaller country, some of which attracted the attention of the United Nations and resulted in punitive action to the aggressor country.

One example of that was Cyprus, in 1974 on an August morning.
Millions and millions of people all over the world were watching an aggressor, not less powerful than Saddam Hussein, not less crazy than Saddam Hussein, and not less militarily viable than Saddam Hussein, invade a smaller country, a country where three nations were supposed to be protectors; Thrkey, Greece and England.
Yet one of those countries that was to be the protector invaded the Island of Cyprus. What did the Cypriots have to fight off the Tbrks? They had an army which was made up of a minimum number of forces, guns and hand grenades that dated back to World War II. They had no oilfields. They had no money. Because they had no oilfields and no money, they had no friends.
Yet, if we were to parallel the two countries, the population of Kuwait is about the same. They occupy about the same place in the Middle East. They have about the same temperature. There is one difference between the two countries. One country is rich in oilfields. The other country is not.
Yet the rest of the world, although it condemned the occupation of Cyprus, and although the defence minister said that valiant efforts were put forward by Canadian troops acting as peacekeeping forces, we did not see the Americans send 450,000 men over there. We did not see the French come to their aid. We did not see the British react. We did not see anybody take any action. We did not see Canada send three ships and 2,000 men. Why not? I go back to my original calculation and conclusion. There was no oil. Maybe it served their particular interest to have that island divided. I question why the double standard.
There are reasons we should have given sanctions more time to work. We must first of all take a hard look at why the sanctions would have worked. History shows us that if you put enough pressure on somebody, he will react one way or another. Maybe what happened to Benito Mussolini, another madman in World War II will happen to Saddam Hussein and maybe the world will be at peace. The Italian dictator told his good friend- another dictator, Adolf Hitler-that if oil had been included in the economic sanctions imposed by the
Government Orders
League of Nations in 1935-36, he would have been forced to remove his troops from occupying Ethiopia.
There have been other instances, Madam Speaker, when sanctions have been applied with extreme effectiveness. I would like to explore a few for the members of this House who say that sanctions would have not worked.
American sanctions applied in the early 1980s were instrumental in forcing the Polish government to free political prisoners. The Indians' partial blockade of Nepal in 1989 to 1990 caused widespread disruption in that country which resulted in a change of government that was sympathetic to India.
When I was growing up, I remember a little country called Biafra. In the late 1960s the world watched with great interest sanctions applied by Nigeria which had a devastating effect on the economy and the social infrastructure of Biafra. If we are to learn anything from the past in regard to sanctions, it is that for them to be effective, they must be applied as strongly as possible and must be given enough time for the effects of them to be felt.
I noticed the other day that the Secretary of State for External Affairs said our sanctions are not working. Things were getting through. When he was challenged, he could not back that up.
The first part of this has, without a doubt, been achieved. The world community at large had acted as one of the most effective trade blockades ever seen. The only part missing in these sanctions was time. History has shown that sanctions of a few months are not effective, but given a reasonable amount of time would likely have resulted in the crippling of Iraq. It is indeed unfortunate that the Americans did not have the will to give sanctions a chance.
There is an old song sung by the Beatles of the 1960s that says: Give peace a chance. Had we given sanctions a chance to work, maybe we would not have seen what happened. Maybe there would have been no casualties. Maybe the madman would have moved back. As we speak today, maybe there would not have been Scud missiles fired into a third neutral country that has nothing to do with this war. However, Saddam Hussein

National Defence and say that we are going to pull our troops out. And where are we going to take them? That is a very important question. We are probably going to send them to the gulf. Why? Because there is oil there and because Bush got on the phone and said: "Send us your forces".
It is interesting to note, for the record, when the first strike was made. Out of the almost 30 countries of the multinational force, which were the countries that actually led the first strike? Let me put this on the record. They were the United States, Britain, the Saudis, Kuwait, and Canada.
I know that I only have a few minutes but I want to analyse this. The United States, why? Because it has interests in oil. The same thing applies to Britain. The Saudis were protecting themselves from aggression. In the case of Kuwait, it was because their country was overrun and Canada because we have a Prime Minister who does not know the words "foreign policy". We have a Prime Minister who does not know what Canadian foreign policy is. When the President of the United States picks up the phone, it is: "Yes, Sir, we will do it. Yes, Sir, we are going to send the 24 planes to the gulf. Yes, Sir, we are going to send our three ships".
You are going to say three ships and 24 planes make a hot lot of difference to the multinational force that is there. It is the aspect that we are there so the Americans do not raise the flag as in an American war. They say: "Oh, we had Canada with us".
Well, I would say it is about time we look at a foreign policy which is made in Canada. I say that it is time we look into other aggressions such as in Latvia, Lithuania, Sri Lanka, and throughout the world. Through the years of Mr. Pearson Canada was truly and honestly a United Nations peacekeeping force. Aggression, yes, when it is needed. Fighting, yes, when it is needed. But first and foremost sanctions must be given a chance to work. They have proven time and time again that they work. Therefore sanctions should come first and foremost before we pick up and push the button on the doomsday machine. That is what is happening. We are pushing the button.
We are not any better than Saddam Hussein. He is a madman who killed millions of children and women. He pillaged. One can say that we are killing. One can say
Government Orders
that had we given time, maybe another two months, that would not have been done.
I am going to close by saying that I am supportive of our troops 100 per cent and I join with other members of this House from both sides in praying and wishing them the best so that they will rejoin their families. No-one can stand up and listen to the cries of a six-year old when he says: "My daddy might die".
