speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I understood the member correctly he indicated that Canadian forces were part of the first strike. In light of the fact that that is not my understanding, I would ask him if he could provide me with any supporting evidence he has.

Madam Speaker, when war broke out the minister of state for defence was speaking and my colleague from Dartmouth came into the House and asked if the minister could explain the role the Canadian forces were engaged in at that time. She used a particular term "sweep and escort". Those were her words. Maybe "sweep and escort" is not the right meaning-I am not a military man-but from my reading of the newspaper I understand that they would escort or sweep in front of the bombers. They would be flying in protective cover. So if you are up and you are flying when the others are attacking what are you doing? I might have misunderstood, Madam Speaker, but when the Prime Minister came in and said that we were at war I clearly understood that.

Madam Speaker, needless to say I am pleased that a new member of this House has raised the question of Cyprus.
I have raised that question for years and years, but I did understand that the world was such that Ihrkey, a great allied military power in NATO was our strongest wing in NATO against the Warsaw Pact. I understood that, even though I disagreed that because of that we should do nothing.
Now we have what we call a new international order where we ask everybody to respect the decision of the United Nations. And we see that our friend Ihrkey is with us today in this new adventure. I asked once, I asked twice, I begged privately: Are you now saying that there is a new international order whispering at least to the ears of the Ihrkish, saying "the time has now come to get out of Cyprus." I was in Cyprus, I know Cyprus as well as I know Lebanon. I call it honey on earth.

Government Orders

The honey of the world-Cyprus and Lebanon. But because they were denied help from the beginning the situation gets worse.

Cyprus has a population of 600,000 people with 200,000 refugees. Who cares about Cyprus? Who cared about Lebanon at the very beginning? Who cares about the Palestinians? I do not agree with the invasion of Iraq and Kuwait.-I do not support Iraq attacking Israel last night, destroying a few houses. It could have been a monstrosity. But do you see the same paranoia on CNN television when every day people in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are being humiliated, deprived of school, university and college, deprived of water and deprived of freedom? Oh, we will solve it. Read the speech made by my Prime Minister to his Royal Highness King Hussein of Jordan when he spoke here. Read the speech of His Royal Highness begging us to understand. Read the speech of the President of Israel who spoke right there. I listened like a gentleman, as I should, to his speech. There were promises and more promises. There was no action during that time. People got desperate and more desperate. Hate is building. Who knows now if King Hussein, who we used to call our friend, will not be the next victim because of people who have no more hope.
I am asking that government and I am asking my colleague to make a comment. The time has not come to make war, but it is a fact of life so I have to support my Canadians soldiers. Do you think we are a bunch of kooks? We pray for our Canadian boys and girls who are there now. We are not going to deprive them of money or anything they need to come back healthy. I beg of my country, Canada, and at the same time send signals around the world that we will look after all these injustices that have been going on. Is it asking too much from a Canadian?

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Saint-Denis for giving me a chance to express maybe something that is called hatred, maybe something that members of this House have not been alluding to. Greece was under Ottoman occupation for 400 years, until 1821, when they rose and kicked the conqueror out. Since 1821 to this day, children in Greece
are taught to hate the Tbrks. The children of Turkey are taught to hate the Greeks. I was part of that growing up. My children are also part of that and their children, because of their heritage, will also be part of that. This hatred gets passed on. The hatred in the Middle East gets passed on. With the children of Cyprus the same thing gets passed on. Let's stop discussing war and start discussing peace.
Some of my colleagues in the opposition are saying that war has started.
With the discussion we have here, we are the only Parliament in the world that is still discussing war or peace, or this or that.
I say to my colleagues that it is very important that we are here continuing this discussion even if it has to sit 24 hours.
If my colleague from B.C. disagrees with me, I say to him-
I did not say anything.

I am sorry if I misunderstood you.
It is important that we sit here and discuss the machinery that can be unleashed upon human beings. How many of you have seen people killed in war? Children?
I was in Cyprus, and I have seen the work that our Canadian forces can do. I know what they are capable of. I am proud of them. I say to you, Madam Speaker, that we should supporting our Canadian forces in peacekeeping roles, not in acts of aggression.
Acts of aggression must be stopped once and for all here, today.

Madam Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to address the motion by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and seconded by the Deputy Prime Minister.
Since the debate began, the circumstances have regrettably deteriorated to hostilities in the Middle East. I believed at the outset that this would be the most difficult decision I will make in this Chamber. It is more difficult than others because of the consequences of any war.

I cannot claim experience in war except as the son and nephew of a World War II veteran. As many considerations are involved in every decision by members of Parliament, I have tried to view this from numerous perspectives.
The motion is straight forward:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
I wish, first, to address the motion from an international perspective and not so much from a war analysis. As the world continues to undergo rapid change, including a move towards a more global community, I believe it is important to protect our only instrument capable of international order and peace: the United Nations.
As other colleagues in this Chamber have indicated, four to six years ago, the nations of the world formed an organization: the UN. The UN's primary purpose was to be the maintenance of international peace and security.
The charter would give the world the right and the capacity to deter aggression and to reverse it by force if necessary when it occurred. It was organized for the circumstances we are faced with today.
As the former Opposition Leader said: "This is the crucial test for the United Nations." The UN has adopted a total of 12 Security Council resolutions since Iraq attacked Kuwait on August 2. As a member of that Council, what does Canada now do in view of its disregard by Saddam Hussein?
As a founding member of the UN, does Canada now withdraw because the situation is becoming tense?
Second, I had planned to speak as well from a national perspective, because we all have to answer the question: What course is right for Canada and the cause of peace?
Having been in touch with various leaders in my constituency to debate and assist me in determining my position in response, I had to resolve this very personally. I have always said in other conflicts that I do not advocate violence and that I value life.
Government Orders
Some constituents have stated their opposition to the war. My 7 year-old daughter cried because of her own fears of war. These made it more painful for me to come to a conclusion on this motion.
Because I have been involved, although in a small way, with the United Nations, I had to reflect on my own personal beliefs. I recall the day, as a Canadian delegate to the General Assembly of the UN in New York when resolution 678 was being discussed.
It was then that the sudden chill and realization of the real potential of war was made upon me for the first time. Since then, I spent much time in thought, in agonizing about what was to be my position if the circumstances that face us today were to occur.
Throughout, one view did not change, and that is my position in support of the United Nations. As one who has been to both Geneva and New York at the UN on several occasions, I had come to believe that the UN could do very great things for human beings; things like the establishment, the confirmation, and the protection of rights of all peoples.
Now the question comes at a time when its very role is challenged by Saddam Hussein. Do I abandon support? Or do I reaffirm the support as the motion calls for in continuing support for its purpose.
Having considered arguments on both sides of this very difficult issue, there are still those all over the world who rely on the UN for the protection of their rights.
Madam Speaker, allow me to digress for a moment on another, but related, concern. What do we do now? What should we do for the future? What positive considerations had to be given for post-war initiatives? I humbly suggest two recommendations for consideration by this House. First, pass this motion at the earliest opportunity to reaffirm our support for the United Nations. Second, and as important, establish a peace mission immediately, perhaps either through UN Security Council meetings or through Middle East peace talks under UN observation.
I believe as many other colleagues have mentioned earlier, even a few minutes ago, that now is the time to address peace with every effort possible.
I believe also in the defence and construction of a durable structure of international order. I will be voting in favour of this motion because I support our troops. I support Canada, and I support the United Nations.

Government Orders

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for Edmonton Southeast.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member and I are from the same province. We both have training as lawyers, although I know that that is an unpopular profession. Next to a politician, perhaps the most unpopular.
I wonder, though, if the member has not very much oversimplified the matter. Is he, for example, aware of the article that was written by a highly respected economist, Mr. Gary C. Hufbauer, and co-authored by him, pointing out in part that if ever there was a place where sanctions would be likely to work, for geographic and reasons, Iraq is it, given the fact that half of Iraq's GNP is involved with oil. Had we given sanctions another few months, according to the article, by the summer or fall there was an excellent probability that Mr. Hussein would have left Kuwait.
While he is answering that, perhaps he could also deal with my second point which is that it is estimated that half of the people who are going to die in this war are going to be Iraqi children. Because of the war with Iran, Iraq's population consists of about 45 per cent children under the age of 15.
I wonder if he might also tell us whether he thinks it is really good for the United Nations, when it could have used this model of isolating and embargoing with truly effective sanctions, for it now to become part of the Pax Americana which seems to be evolving because of the problems in the Soviet Union. I realize those are three questions, but maybe he would deal with any one he cares to.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the very difficult question.
First of all, I am not thoroughly familiar with the article he mentioned, but the information I am aware of is by the allied forces and the United Nations on whether or not sanctions in this case are working. It is my understanding that they were working on the wrong people. Sanctions in this case, were working against the poor people and the children in Iraq, but not against the
military. I think the collective information and the collective decision of allied members of the United Nations certainly must be better than the information I have. It was their decision that sanctions were not working and I support that.
With respect to the number of Iraqi children who will die, that is one of the reasons I said in my presentation that it was a difficult decision for me to make. In my opinion, no war is good because of the impact on innocent lives.
In terms of other situations around the world, I can only call on this House to consider any kind of peaceful resolution or mechanism to deal with existing conflicts anywhere in the world with respect to children. Any contemplated use of economic sanctions should not be necessary to begin with.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak to one of the most important issues in Canadian history. Canada's commitment to the United Nations during the Gulf Crisis will undoutedly be recorded among the most significant aspects of our history.
This debate is a discussion about war and peace, a debate about right and wrong. This debate is about standing up for what is right, about taking a stand and fighting against evil. Canadians from sea to sea know that now is the time to reflect on Canadian history, Canadian traditions and Canada's ongoing commitment to peace.
Canadians from coast to coast also know that now is the time to contemplate and decide our future as part of the international community. From an international perspective this debate is about Canada's commitment to peace and peaceful nations. From a national perspective this debate is clearly about leadership.
There are those who say the aggressor must forcefully be dealt with. Others say wait until Saddam Hussein is struck with a feeling of peace. What can peace mean for Saddam Hussein? Does it mean more time to prepare for war? Peace is, indeed, an elusive, valuable and oftentimes fragile treasure. In recent history, world peace has been to a large measure attained by the United Nations, an organization founded specifically to pave a path to peace. For decades the UN has been successful as a team of peaceful nations joined together
January 17,1991	COMMONS
to protect the weakest among its members from aggressive bullies like Saddam Hussein.
Saddam Hussein has continuously demonstrated, by his words and by his deeds, that he rejects peace. The evidence against Saddam Hussein tells a fearsome story: use of poison gas on his own citizens, wake of death and destruction when Iraq invaded Kuwait, development of biological and chemical weapons. It tells of attempts to develop nuclear weapons, and other weapons of mass destruction, associations with terrorist groups and of the recent missile attacks on Israel. On August 2, Saddam Hussein started a war with the international community. His actions and statements have continuously demonstrated a disregard for human life, international law, property, and his own personal integrity.
To ensure the continued success of the United Nations, it is extremely important for Canada to honour our commitment to the international family, within the United Nations, and stand together against the evil of Saddam Hussein. Canada cannot accept the benefits of the United Nations and then, when times are tough, reject its responsibilities. Canada must play a prominent role in the United Nations, not only when times are easy but, more important, when the situation becomes more difficult, as it is now in the gulf. Canada must continue its commitment to paving the path of peace, now in the gulf and also in the future. Through the United Nations, Canada must continue its efforts to expel Saddam Hussein from Kuwait and ensure the enforcement of international law.
As in the case of some others, my age limits my experience with war. I, of course, remember television reports of the Vietnam war and I remember hearing stories of other wars. In my family, my grandfathers had committed part of their lives to military service and, during the Second World War, my father served overseas as a member of Canada's Armed Forces in the Signal Corps. I recall, as a small boy, becoming focused on war every year, during the Remembrance Day ceremonies. In our home, the ritual every November 11 was a memorable one. Early in the morning, my mother would busy herself by assisting my father, shining and preparing his war and military service medals and, while they discussed memories of the war years and Dad fitted and adjusted his navy blue Royal Canadian Legion beret, I am sure they reflected on the years during the 1940s when, as

Government Orders
newly weds, they found themselves thousands of miles apart and, although hopeful, they were somewhat uncertain about their future. After the small town parade, religious service and gathering of veterans, my father would return home to respond to questions from my brother and me.
Year after year, as a boy, I asked about war seeking, perhaps, a comment about heroism or glory. Year after year, I received the same lecture. War, I was told, was horrible. War, he told me, meant fear and terror. War was dirty. War meant unbelievable destruction. War, he described, was an awful experience to be avoided whenever and wherever possible. But he also lectured me about responsibility and commitment and about duty to Canada. Although the concepts of responsibility and commitment were less difficult to comprehend, I only began to understand the meaning of duty when I learned that, even though an old leg injury of his offered him an easy escape from conscription, my father enlisted as a volunteer to serve the interests of our country because he believed that it was his duty. Canada has a duty to support the efforts of the United Nations in the Gulf. Canadians from coast to coast must all join together to express our strong support to those who are on active duty in the Persian Gulf as members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Madam Speaker, at the outset I would like to say a few words about my constituency which rarely has the opportunity of being in the news that is now on everybody's mind during this current situation. I have the honour of representing Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca which includes the largest Pacific coast naval base of the Canadian Armed Forces, as well as other contingents of our armed forces and of course, represented by the only armed force anywhere in the world that has won a Nobel Peace Price. TTiis price for peacekeeping was awarded to the Princess Patricia Light Canadian Infantry based in Victoria.
I was struck by the reference to one's parents. Since this is probably one of the few speeches I make toward the twilight of my career, I will do something I have never done in my 25 years in public life and respond similarly for a few minutes.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
My father was bom in this country, raised in Winnipeg, Manitoba and in his first year of university volunteered to go overseas in the First World War. My father spent 10 months in the trenches, was wounded twice and suffered through a gas attack, and finally and ultimately lost his eyesight permanently in the fifties as a consequence of his service to this country.
My mother was a peace activist. My mother was responsible in her day for having me swaddled in bandages in 1936 as a victim of the Spanish Civil War protesting the rise of Fascism at that particular time. So the bona fides that all of us Canadians have of similar histories are important to reflect upon.
My father also talked to me about duty and devotion, as the other member spoke, but my mother and father also spoke to me about responsibility of conscience. I am Jewish, but I had the great opportunity of having two wonderful parents, and then attending two Catholic universities. I spent six years with the Jesuits and was exposed to Christian philosophy. I majored in Thomastic philosophy. A strange combination, a Jewish Thomist but nonetheless, here is the product.
The consequences of that amalgan in my background heightened the awareness that flag-waving and jingoism are indeed important for all of us at any given time in our life. But the most important thing for any one of us is to understand that we, as individuals, are responsible for our own actions. We serve a nation and we are proud to be Canadians, but this country is not great on the basis of some symbol or jingoism; it is great on the basis of individuals being responsible to their own conscience and then expressing that through the democratic process that we have, ultimately leading to this Chamber.
So there will be differences of opinion and no one must be diminished regardless of party on the basis of that difference of opinion. So far, this debate has been marked by a minimum amount of partisan activity, except that it has broken out regrettably from the government front benches in a way that has dismayed me, and today was a bit of an example of that. I hope it is the end of that, but it has broken out and I need to mention that.
This problem is presented as if it was an either/or situation. But we have to reflect just a little bit of how we reach this point.
Who sold the technology to Iraq? Did the Iraqi scientists spend Gross National Product of their country in developing surface-to-air missiles? Where did the Scuds come from? Where did the mirage airplanes come from?
The very panoply of a ray of arms against Iraq is a reflection of the arms they were able to buy from the Soviet Union, France, the United States and anyone else who wanted to sell it. We talk about the missiles zooming through the air, the Iraqis having this, that and everything else. Who sold it to them?
What was available on the market? To castigate members of the Liberal Party or my party for not following an absolute ginglism demands we examine whose hand has been behind the scene in preparing the material available for Iraq. The Soviet Union's hands are dirty. The United States' hands are dirty. Yes, this country, too: Its hands are dirty.
Not one western nation stood up during the time of all of these sales or in the great debates during the League of Nations, was against arms and arms embargoes. It was necessary for the Prime Minister of this country to sell his point and to be selective about his comments on history, and he has not done this House a service.
I thought it dismaying that he did not mention those people from this country who fought for freedom who have still to be recognized by Canada officially. Those are the brave young men of the Mackenzie-Papineau brigade who volunteered from Canada, served in Spain and gave their lives there against Fascism. Still, they have not been recognized by this country because there is a political division.
Nobody's hands are clean nor am I a saint, but I do read history. Who sold the guns to El Salvador that killed those six Jesuit priests and murdered those two innocent women? Who made the arms available for Salvador Allende to be murdered in his presidential office after he was democratically elected? Who was it who invaded Panama or Grenada for that matter, or Afghanistan?
While we talk about this new co-operation at the United Nations-God help me. I hope it is a reformation in the minds of those international leaders who now sit at the Security Council, including China with its hands at Tiananmen Square. Remember, they sit and deliberate without a clean background.

We are human beings, and we do make mistakes. Alas, I think we have made another mistake. This is a great testing time for the United Nations, but what a terrible test. We should have given more time for the embargo to work.
I find it ironic that I quote a former head of the CIA. To give strength to my argument, it was nonetheless the former head of the CIA in the United States' hearings who gave the evidence that Sanctions would work had we waited a bit longer.
The speech of the Leader of the Liberal Party and that of my own party clearly made that point. They represent, combined, a higher percentage of vote reflected in the general population than the government's.
We have a legitimate point of view that we have to present without the partisanship. I wanted to comment about the force of international law. The Prime Minister says-we all agree-that international law must be regarded. The court in The Hague was appealed to just within the last 10 years by the Government of Nicaragua to stop it from violating the sovereignty of that nation by placing mines in the Managua harbour.
When the Government of the United States was faced with the possibility of losing the case in the court in The Hague, it announced that it would ignore the decision in the court.
It is not good enough. I am hoping now that all the words, jingoism and statements by the big five and the Security Council means that never again will they be selective of when they decide the rule of law should apply to them as a nation. I hope out of this experience the Soviet Union will never again move in and crush the people of Lithuania. I am thankful that they have agreed to a referendum. I hope that imperialism of the extreme left will never show its hand again and the imperialism of the right will begin to stay its hand based on the rhetoric that is now being applied to this current situation.
I have some personal comments about this current situation. Five years ago, with the advent of Mikhail Gorbachev I spoke to a Catholic priest who is a very good friend of mine and I said: "Explain to me how this phenomena happens." He said: "Dave, the only answer I can give is that it is a gift from God." Being a bit of an
Government Orders
agnostic, I was willing to accept that explanation because I was pleased with what I thought was happening. We saw the beginning of the end of the cold war. We saw the alliances, both in the Warsaw Pact and in NATO, being forced to question the necessity of their continued interests. The military and Soviet Union and some of the military in the west felt threatened by the thaw of the cold war. Certainly the militaiy industrial complex that General Eisenhower warned us about also got very frightened.
With the cold war ending, we have to look at our parts of the economy, as the Soviets looked at their parts of the economy that were essentially built on the arms trade. The only way the arms trade can be sustained is by having a war. We have got one now. It is too simple to say that this war was arranged to sustain the arms race but it is pretty convenient. We have moved now from the cold war to the new crusades. Why do I say the new crusades? Because the magic trigger words used in the cold war were anti-communism or anti-capitalism. Those two trigger words have now become passe in world history and we have reduced ourselves to finding new trigger words; anti-Arab, anti-Jew, anti-Christian.
The fundamentalist Muslims have been appealed to in this debate to rise up against the infidel. Saddam Hussein has defined this aggression, that he initiated, as being a jihad. He is the one who added the dimension at this point of a religious war and there is fertile ground for what he is saying. On our side, we have witnessed in the Middle East serious attempts by serious people, both in the Palestinian community and in the Israeli community to get an international peace conference going, only to see it scuttled time and time again.
If nothing else comes out of this series of tragic events whose catalogues of loss of life have been described far more adequately and passionately than I can, by hon. members in this House, I want to believe and understand that this government will be in the forefront demanding an international conference on all that regions problems and everybody at the table.
Not only is the first casualty the truth in a war, but reason and logic and a perspective that is necessary for picking up the pieces afterward. I wanted the embargo to work. Now that we have a war. I hope to God it is over as quickly as possible with a minimum loss of life.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
This is not a football game. This is not the NHL on television. You don't just turn off the channel and think that it is over. Unbelievable human, economic, and social carnage will be left there. What have we got to put in place when Saddam Hussein is gone, with a population that is full of hate and anger against the Christian infidel and the west? Do we think that some benevolent person is going to come in and rule Kuwait with an understanding hand? He or she will be murdered within one month. We are going to be in a quagmire there and anybody who thinks we will not have to put peacekeeping forces inside Iraq and Kuwait perhaps, but certainly in Iraq, is right out of their mind.
The peace and tranquillity of that nation as it goes through a major transformation will require that. I hear commentators on television saying that: "oh, no, it is surgical and, bang, it is over". Do not kid yourself.
Not only must we be ready to participate in a peace conference but we must also be prepared to understand that part of our budgets must go to playing a role in that peacekeeping force.
We talk about this war being over. I mention Iraq. Then we look at Syria. Assad today could have been yesterday's Saddam Hussein. He is in the same situation. It is ironic and I do not say this with humour but General Noriega and Saddam Hussein were very close friends of George Bush when he was the head of the CIA. I want to warn any would-be dictator who is heading out into the future to avoid a friendship with the President of the United States because within a few years look what history has shown us.
Hussein is Syria. What are his hands clean with? Nothing. What are they dirty with? Take a look at Lebanon. Jake a look at his vision now of his opportunities and our worry that he may break in this fragile coalition-and he may break. Thank goodness Israel has had the common sense not to retaliate in the last 24 hours. Thank goodness for that.
Hear, hear.

We look at Mr. Mubarak in Egypt struggling to hang on to power, graciously forgiving a $7 billion debt by the Americans. Some cynics would suggest that they bought his support for his role in this. Not me, because I am too young to be a cynic. But when I look at his position and know that the population in his country is ready to hear the siren call of a jihad then I worry.
Then we look at the Soviet Union above Turkey, Azerbaijan, and right across the southern part of the Soviet Union, fundamentalist Islam has become the rallying cry against Moscow domination and we have seen visuals of people being murdered because of religion inside the Soviet Union. Again an example of the new crusades.
Fundamental Christianity, fundamental Islam, fundamental Hebrew, fundamental Judaism, fundamental anything, all have the problems of being absolutely right with no vision that perhaps someone else has a point of view as well. If we allow ourselves to be tied in continuously in this war on the basis of the new crusades, then the Soviet Union is in for turmoil, we are in for turmoil, and international terrorism will be based on "remember Iraq; throw another bomb".
I do not think that has been thought out over there. I came to this Chamber surprised that deputies never even sit next to the cabinet ministers. Where are the experts? Where are the people who advise this government? Even in Question Period, sure it is the opposition's role to make questions available that might jab the government, but it is not the government's role to be facetious in response. It requires statespersonship over there. I do not see much of it and it worries me. Lester Pearson did not act that way. Louis St. Laurent did not, and John Diefenbaker did not.
I have a few more things to say but perhaps I will get to say those in response to questions and answers. But I want to conclude my formal remarks by quoting the Pope's statement of three days ago. He said it in a framework that there are no winners and no losers. He said: "The whole world has lost over what has happened this last week".
Madam Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member might have a few more comments to elaborate on the information that he was giving this House.

Madam Speaker, I have not said anything that is uniquely mine. I have only reflected wiser heads who do not have a political base which requires them to be more confined. The only thing original in what I have said is my perception that we are really in the new crusades. Everything I have spoken about has led me to believe that.
January 17, 1991

If there ever was a time for the religious community leaders of this world to provide alternate leadership, this is it. It is a time for the Chief Rabbi of Israel, the head Muslim mullahs and the Christian leaders of the world to call their own special inquiry or their own special World Council of Churches meeting, because we all pray to the same God, and we had better make that sure to all our relative adherents. We all pray to the same God, and I hope she understands our wavering when we do this. The reality is that it would be a good alternative and it is also extremely important for salving the egos of males who are involved in this kind of thing to understand that there is a higher course to deal with. I suggest the Canadian government be the first to appeal to the world's religious community leaders on an ecumenical basis to perhaps provide new leadership in problems that are fraught with religious differences above everything else.
This debate is important. How we vote is not important. I do not want anybody to go out of here believing the jingoism that we have to vote for being in the war. We are already in the war. What I had to say before the war started is a heck of a lot different than what I have to say now in dealing with that reality. The Liberal Party understands that and so do we. Our position is clear.
We are opposed to any aggressive role by Canadian forces. But, we must be there to offer humanitarian alternatives. We must be there so that we never again see the visuals of refugees in the water looking for ships. Do you remember those visuals from Vietnam of kids and mothers, regardless of race, creed or colour, looking for a boat or a haven, and how it took the world quite a while to respond? We must never let that happen again.
We have to help Jordan pay a little bit of the bill for those refugees even though they are having an internal fight about whose side they are on. We have a lot of work to do. Let Canada begin to work. Let this government understand the reflections, the desires and the demands of the average man and woman in this country who do not give a fig about Tories, Liberals or Conservatives, but want peace and leadership from this country to deal with the very real human problems that have been created by this disaster and a warning to all those nations who led us to this. Your hands are not clean. You want clean action now, you had better, never behave the way you did in Afghanistan or Vietnam or Panama or elsewhere again.
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Esquimalt- Juan de Fuca had started to explain the many layers of casualties that occur in a war situation, the layers of casualties with regard to truth and our attempts to try to grip the situation by reverting to simplistic arguments to think that we have some control over this. One of those simplistic arguments that is put forth against our party is that we are anti-military. Well, nothing could be further from the truth.
I would like the member who represents the riding wherein the largest naval base and the Princess Pat Light Infantry, the recipients of a peace prize are located, a neighbouring riding to my own, to talk about the role of the military, the distinguished role of the military throughout Canadian history, and how we can now go on from here with that reputation for Canadian military action. Our position is not criticism of the military. I would like him to expound on that.

Madam Speaker, within the last two weeks I had, in my responsibility as a member of Parliament, to be on one of our naval ships, as we saw the crew leaving for the east coast. I was participating in the military ceremony. The captain on the ship was incredible. He allowed us to talk to crew and go wherever we wanted.
The debate among the crew is the same as the debate here in this House. It is no different. They had Liberals, Tories, and New Democrats in uniform. They all had similar opinions. But, the one basic condition and foundation they had in dealing with each other was the genuine desire to be a different kind of service in the Canadian military, based on the traditions my colleague mentioned.
Let no one believe that our men and women who are in uniform for this country are jingoists or rambos. We have the most responsible military force ever in our history. They are well educated, well trained, philosophically based, and understand their traditional role as peacekeepers. They will do what is asked of them. They are doing what is asked of them. We are proud of the fact that they will do what is asked of them. But they will also do the work that we have them for in Cyprus, in Israel, in Lebanon, and in other areas. They are trusted, believed in, and respected.

Government Orders
When this is over, let us understand that Canada is ready for an extension of our role internationally to continue using our military forces for peace.
