speechtext:
Madam Speaker, much has been said throughout this debate about the role that Canada has played in the past, what we as a nation should be doing now, and what our role will be in the future.
Canadian forces were actively involved in both World Wars and Korea. As a nation we have paid a high price for freedom and I think sometimes that we have come to take it for granted. Over 100,000 Canadian lives were lost in those wars. How much different history might have been today if our allied forces had not made that ultimate sacrifice to fight and die in a senseless war. I think we have all agreed that all wars are senseless.
We are reminded of this every November 11 when each of us, as members of Parliament, attend the services and see that diminishing line of veterans who appear each year, those who have served their countries in the
past. There are very few from the First World War, if any, and some from the Second World War and Korea.
With those reminders to all of us of the role that Canada has played in past wars, it has given us the opportunity to enjoy some of the freedoms that we have: the freedom each of us has to run for elected office and to speak out freely whether it be in the House of Commons, on the street, or in the media.
A lot of people gave the ultimate so that those of us who enjoy the benefits are able to live the lives we do in Canada. Sometimes I think we take too much of that for granted. We see perhaps at times fewer and fewer people at Remembrance Day services. We dust off our memories once in a while to remember those who have contributed to Canada's role as a nation and the respect we have earned throughout the world, both in serving in active duty and the peacekeeping role that has been talked about so often during the debate in the House.
As a young child growing up during the latter years of the war, my most vivid memories are from the small prairie town of Medicine Hat, which at that time had a population of about 10,000. We had a prisoner of war camp on one side of the town and a military training base for the air force on the other. Young men from countries all over the world came and trained there. We also had young men in that prison camp, many of whom were little more than teenagers. They had probably fought in a war wondering why, as many young people do, they were in it; what cause they were fighting for; and if they were going to get back home and see their loved ones. At the end of the war there were more prisoners in that camp than there were people living in the city.
Young men came over from the British Isles and Europe to train and fly planes and then went back home, not blowing whether or not they would ever be coming back to Canada again. Some of them did, and that has been a remarkable part of our community. People from both sides have come back: those who served in the war and others who were prisoners. They have made their homes, raised their families, and somehow between themselves resolved some of the differences they had.
January 17, 1991

It certainly is not easy for any of us in this House to discuss the situation we are now into, knowing that almost by the minute that it is changing. Television is running almost 24 hours a day now. It is an experience that none of us has had to go through. It has been distanced in the past, but this focuses it very closely on what is happening in today's world.
The Canadian Council of Veterans, in commenting on the present situation, remarked that Canada's veterans have worked long and hard for peace but that there comes a time when the principles and ideals for which we fought in previous wars must once again be defended. This is such a time.
I believe that Parliament has a duty to support the United Nations resolution as it is written, and therefore the resolution that is before this House. That we must use this terrible method of attempting to secure peace and stability throughout the world is a sad reflection on the ability of mankind to resolve our differences.
At the San Francisco conference that gave birth to the United Nations there was a vision of keeping the peace and collective security. This vision was strongly endorsed by Canada and resulted in articles being written into the United Nations charter, enabling member states to aid one another and repulse aggression if necessary by military means. Canada was there at the beginning, upholding the principle of collective security. The Persian Gulf is a crucial test for the United Nations and Canada must support it. With the benefits and security that hopefully go with membership to an organization such as this one also must go the responsibilities.
It was the failure of the League of Nations to respond effectively to aggression that led to its demise.
When Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait on August 2, the war in the gulf had effectively started. Reason and diplomacy were apparently not options that he was ever to consider seriously.
I think every effort was made. The United Nations, through its leadership, attempted every avenue open to it. There was diplomacy used here which gave Saddam Hussein every opportunity to stand back from the position he had taken and give the pause for peace we had so much hoped would occur. There was no indication that he would end the aggression and every indication that it was just a matter of time until it escalated.
Government Orders
While sanctions may have had an impact if applied rigidly and long enough, there was no guarantee that economic weakness would get Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. He appeared willing to let thousands of Iraqis and those in occupied Kuwait suffer before any effect would have been felt by the military.
I know there have been untold accounts of what may or may not have happened to improve the situation, to extend the deadline that was set. I have read a number of articles. I will quote from The Gazette of Montreal for Thursday, January 17, 1991:
Those in Canada and elsewhere who suggest that the world faced a choice between war and peace missed an important consideration: peace now-if it did not include Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait- probably would not have meant peace forever, or even for very long. It would have meant complicity in Iraq's aggression, and the setting of a precedent that would encourage new aggression elsewhere. It would have meant acceptance of Saddam Hussein's evident plan to dominate the Middle East, regardless of the wishes of its inhabitants. Israel and Saudi Arabia had reason to fear his intentions. But Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, whose major sin, it seems, was to have lent Iraq a large sum for its war effort against Iran, shows that even Iraq's friends were not safe.
Indeed, the choice probably was between war now and war later-against a stronger Iraq that could well be equipped with nuclear weapons. Economic sanctions have not worked, despite the fact that they succeeded in cutting off Iraq's oil exports, nor is there convincing reason to believe they would have worked quickly enough.
The United Nations is about peace. But it is also about collective security. Canada would have been wrong to shirk its responsibilities.
Margaret Thatcher commented the other day that dictators never surrender but must be defeated. There will no doubt be continuing disputes between nations long after the events of the Middle East have come to pass, if they ever do. I think we must weigh in our own conscience our values and our love of this country. We must hope and pray we can resolve a difficult situation which has been made much more difficult by the fact that war has taken place.
Setting that aside, the UN with all of its imperfections is our last best hope for the security of the world.
Canadians everywhere have a right to express their feelings. I know that all of us, in our hearts and our wishes, hope for the same result, whether it is those of us in the House, people throughout the country or, I am sure, in other nations, that we can conclude what has taken place. War is probably the result of human frailty. Perhaps all of us have failed to a large degree, and some in smaller ways. But I guess all of us show that this is a result of failures by those of us in various levels of

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
government, right across the scope of countries from one end of the world to the other.
I only hope and pray that soon all of us can look back on this and realize that there has to be a better way of conducting the affairs of the world. My sincere hope is that the United Nations is the avenue open to all of us.

Madam Speaker, I would ask the member who has just spoken, for whom I have a lot of respect, if he wishes to make any comments to the House about about how those nations, which form part of the allied force, will speak to the Arab world, the world of Islam, after the war.
While he is at it, I wanted to ask the Prime Minister today about an incident that took place this morning on a bus in Ottawa. A young person who is, I believe, of Arab origin, possibly Iraqi, got a bloody nose. Somebody who was on the bus says it was a very nasty incident. I wonder if he has constituents of Iraqi origin or other parts of the Arab world. Does he have any thoughts for them today as well?

Madam Speaker, I would like to say to my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast, that certainly I do believe we have some. There is not a large community of Arab people within the constituency, although I know of a number. Certainly incidents such as he mentioned are the types of things that all of us deplore.
I mentioned earlier about the prison camp and the people who are serving the military on the other side. I guess I have reason to feel that at that point in the hostilities, feelings perhaps were running as high as they are now. Yet I have seen a coming together or a melding of those societies. Young men who were prisoners of war came back to live in that community, and others who had served in the forces have come back and have learned to live and work together.
The scars are going to be deep; there is no question about it. I think if the situation remains as it is, with Arab forces on either side, there may be some hope for resolution afterwards. I think the more it goes on, the more we escalate the war that is going on. Should those forces become involved, it is going to make it much more
difficult. I am sure right now for those people, the Arabs on either side, it is going to be very difficult. I do not know if there is ever a healing process. I guess there is not a healing process from the Second World War.
If one talks to the people in Lebanon, their views on what happened there, I am sure, will go on for generations. I am sure, as the hon. member has indicated, what is taking place today will probably remain. The views of those people regarding the way they view the rest of the world and perhaps the way they view us will probably be changed indelibly.
As for incidents such as the hon. member mentioned, it is my hope that we could rise above that kind of thing. I think we are Canadians first. We all come from different backgrounds and different walks of life. The fact that we came from somewhere else that is involved in a situation like this is, I think, something that any Canadian should be able to overlook at this time. I do thank the hon. member for his question.

Madam Speaker, this debate is fundamental, it is significant, and it may have consequences that none of us can foresee now. We are discussing a decision on Canada's support for UN resolution 678 and, most particularly, the involvement of our Canadian Armed Forces personnel in a military conflict. We are discussing a war that, like all wars, means death and destruction.
The decision was a perplexingly difficult one because it was so far removed from the usual Canadian sphere of experience. Today I believe you could count on the fingers of one hand the number of MPs in this present House of Commons who have served in wartime in Canada's Armed Forces, during either the Second World War or the Korean conflict, which ended more than 37 years ago.
This in itself says a great deal about our country, its role and attitude in world affairs. Our knowledge of war is either as a very distant memory or as history. By tradition, Canadians are not a militaristic or warlike people. Traditionally our peacetime armed forces are small in number and too often neglected, but also extremely professional, as they are once again showing at present.
January 17, 1991

I do not consider myself a hawk or to be in any way hawkish in my approach to international affairs; quite the contrary in fact. During my brief two years in the House, I have had the honour of representing Canada at discussions in Japan, which led up to the United Nations Agreement for Verification of Disarmament and Arms Reductions. I have made statements in this Chamber commending initiatives towards disarmament and for the reduction of nuclear weaponry. Recently, I was one of the country's representatives at the meeting of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization's parliamentary group in Britain.
The role of NATO has often been misunderstood. While it is essentially a military organization, it was never intended to be an aggressive force. NATO was founded, with Canada's renowned peacemaker Lester Pearson playing a leading role, as a means of guaranteeing peace through co-operative security agreements between the member nations. In that respect, NATO provided an unqualified success through the 40 years of the cold war. Though it is not recognized as such, perhaps Canada's greatest contribution as a world peacekeeper may well have been in helping to create and maintain the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
Canada's reputation as a world peacekeeper goes back as far as the aftermath of the Suez crisis in 1956. We developed an enviable record in that regard in the Middle East and elsewhere in the succeeding years. Many have questions on whether we now might jeopardize all that through our present role in the Persian Gulf.
Here it is significant to look back to another important aspect of our nation's history. Though I have stated that by tradition we are neither warlike nor militaristic, Canada has been faced with the necessity of war and has been ever ready to do all or more than we were expected to do.
This was true particularly in the two world wars during the first half of this century. More than 600,000 Canadians participated in the First World War and one in 10 did not return. Our role in 1939 to 1945 was such that at its conclusion Canada had for the first and, we hope, the last time in our history a complete, full-scale army in Europe.
Government Orders
We had what probably was the world's third largest air force and fourth largest navy. This was no small commitment of achievement on our part because at that time we had approximately 12 million people. I do not speak boastingly of this, of course, though it should be a source of pride for Canadians.
My point is that Canada does have a proud tradition in peacekeeping and also of rising when necessary to join other nations in resisting aggression. I believe a similar necessity now faces us today.
I have listened especially to the arguments of those who claim that economic sanctions should have been given more time to prove their effectiveness against Saddam Hussein's regime in Iraq. I wish I could agree with that view but, in my view, reality shows it to be different.
There are those who say that we should have attempted further negotiations with the Iraqi leader. Again, I personally and most sincerely wish that this was possible. But how can there be negotiations when he refuses to even discuss the basic demand of those arrayed against him that he leave Kuwait and restore it to its sovereignty? In recent days, he has rejected or ignored all the reasoned appeals from world leaders pleading with him to avoid an armed confrontation. Last night's unprovoked attack on Israel is a clear indication that peace and negotiations are not on his agenda.
This is not a crisis of blood for oil, as some would have us believe. "Blood for oil" is a catchy but dangerously simplistic slogan, an attempt to reduce the gulf crisis to a ridiculous common denominator. While the value of Kuwait's oil undoubtedly was a reason for the Iraqi invasion, that oil is of minimal importance to us in Canada. World oil prices have been affected, but no responsible world leader, and certainly not the United Nations, would confront Saddam Hussein just for that.
One disturbing effect of the whole discussion on the crisis in this chamber and elsewhere is the claim that our government is marching to war in some sort of lock-step with the United States administration in Washington. Sadly, I am coming to believe that there are those in Canada who, for whatever reason, so dislike our next-door neighbour that, when considering foreign policies, they first determine the U.S. position and then take the opposite. To such minds, if you agree with the U.S., you are therefore automatically wrong and are a lackey of Washington.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
In the current situation, of course, this totally ignores the fact that the U.S. is one of 28 nations, as is Canada, supporting the United Nations in acting to thwart an act of naked aggression. As the largest and most powerful nation in the present world, the U.S. consequently has accepted a leading role in the gulf. The United States is not the villain; let us be clear about it. Nor is it the author of the current crisis in the gulf region. To suggest otherwise is to play into the hands of Saddam Hussein and his skilled propagandists.
Personally, I think we should be grateful that the United States has been willing to accept such a large portion of the responsibility and, as a democracy, has the ability to do so. I also personally think that we in Canada might be grateful that we have such a nation as our neighbour. Canadians would be thinking quite differently if we lived beside a regime such as that now governing Iraq.
I am sure that no one in this government or in this Parliament is at all comfortable with a decision such as this one committing our Canadian Armed Forces personnel to service in the region under armed combat. However, there comes a time when such decisions are necessary. If we are to fulfil our responsibilities and our obligations as a member of the United Nations, this is such a time.
It is a sad time, particularly when you think back to the sudden optimism we shared just one year ago. That was when the Berlin wall and the Iron Curtain came down. Nations of eastern Europe were emerging to enjoy new-found liberty. There were some who even wondered if there would be any future role for our armed forces. There is and it is that which we are now discussing.
Through the history of this country there have been many ifs, like haunting sign posts along the road as aggressors march to their rise in notoriety. What if Hitler had been blocked when he marched into the Rhineland or when he later demanded Czechoslovakia? What if Mussolini had been stopped from seizing Ethiopia?
Today we have the unique situation in which through the United Nations countries of the world are confronting and seek to turn back another such aggressor.
Canada has a clear role and as parliamentarians we have no honest choice but to accept it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to say I listened to my hon. colleague's comments and I know that he was speaking from his heart when he said on behalf of all of us we hope for a swift and veiy complete end to these hostilities.
He mentioned in his presentation that there are 28 countries involved in the American-led forces, or in the coalition in opposition to Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait, Canada being one of them. At the beginning of the combat there were four countries involved and now we are seeing others come in. I think the latest involvement includes perhaps nine different countries out of the 28. Right from the very beginning Canada had indicated its support militarily for the United States-led initiative and, of course, we have now seen in the last number of hours the commitment to CF-18s in terms of flying with the American B-52s in their carpet bombing of parts of Iraq.
My question is actually very straightforward to my friend and that is: Does he understand or perhaps what is his opinion why Canada was so quick off the mark as one of the handful of countries out of the coalition of 28 to get involved in a military commitment with the American forces?

Madam Speaker, at a briefing this morning, it was indicated that Canadian aircraft still have not taken part in any new role in the Middle East. They are still flying escort, if you will, for the shipping in the northern Persian Gulf. At the briefing today there was no request for Canadian aircraft to change their role. It is not clear at this point whether they will be asked to change their role.
I think it is significant that under the direction of the government and the Prime Minister the Canadian aircraft were obviously requested to stay out of the first waves of bombing that went over Iraq.
But we cannot back away from the fact that Canada has played a significant role in the United Nations for many years. We have fought in Korea along with other nations in an aggressive stance. We have taken on many occasions, as the member well knows, the peacekeeping role in other assignments in other parts of the world.
January 17, 1991

This is one further such assignment. Canada continues to play its role in the United Nations to support resolutions that were passed by all its members.
I trust that Canada will continue to do the same. I see no reason why Canada cannot, in the future, play a significant peacekeeping role in the situation after this war is over, and certainly in other future situations around the world.
This, in my opinion, will not change Canada's significant position in the United Nations currently or in the future.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his contribution in this particular debate.
I believe it essential that members of Parliament indicate their feelings and express to their constituents their particular perspective in this most serious situation.
We are, however, debating a resolution that reads as follows:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
The resolution itself, it seems to me, is not relevant because hostilities have indeed broken out. This particular resolution, of course, was put on the Order Paper before hostilities broke out a few days ago.
I would like to ask the hon. member whether he agrees that the resolution is academic at this point? Would he not agree that, at some point soon, this House should pass a resolution-hopefully unanimously-indicating its support for the troops that are presently in the Persian Gulf?

Madam Speaker, of course as the member says, we are reasserting the motion in front of us. We are reasserting support for motions that have been passed in this House on previous occasions.
We had discussions along the same lines in November. In fact, this Parliament was one of the first seats of government to pass such a resolution, and this is here now only to allow us as individual members to again express our views should we wish to.
Government Orders
This is not taking any particularly new position as far as this House is concerned. Certainly, I think most members here in their discussions have stated their support for our armed service personnel currently in the gulf.

Madam Speaker, in July of 1990, I went to the Middle East.
I was rather uneasy but very consumed by anticipation and curiosity. I was going to the Holy Land. Little did I know that this was to be the journey of journeys. Little did I know the experience I would have, the emotions that would stay with me and, most of all, the people I would meet and the knowledge I would gain.
We all know that the Middle East question is one that is composed of a multiplicity of complex circumstances and factors some of which are so fundamentally ingrained and inextricably intertwined that even close examination is not sufficient to truly appreciate and understand the whole question.
I really did undergo a major political metamorphosis as I sat there that morning on the Mount of Olives overlooking the city of Jerusalem. I felt a great sense of personal peace and appreciation for the countryside.
I thought-as I stated earlier-as I stared over the landscape and spoke to the people with me on this day that I had come to a land of beginnings, enormous history and culture, never knowing that I would be facing a day like today when the city is filled with fear, anxiety, confusion and chaos. I was at a loss for words to describe my feelings as I was travelling throughout Israel. I met many people and went to many places; Beitzhour, to Ramallah to Beirzhit, the universities that were shut down for 36 months, to Jerusalem, to Bethlehem and to Jabalayia, to the heart of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip to the refugee camps where 1.7 million people live in the most over-populated conditions.
It was to be a journey I would never forget. If I read about it or heard about it, or maybe if I had spoken to someone about it I might have doubts about what I saw, but from what I was already told, I had pictures floating by my eyes as we travelled through the refugee camps. When you see those things for yourself, when you see those conditions, and when you talk to those people, and break bread with those people, and you open your mind not only to your sense of history but to the present circumstances and conditions and the future expecta-

Government Orders
tions of those people, all of those diverse groups, it really is quite a different story.
You feel the sense of alienation. You feel the sense of frustration. You feel the sense that these people have a struggle, that each and every one of them is involved, from the youngest child who can walk to the oldest person who can carry something, they are all involved in the human struggle for survival.
And I wonder as I stand here today, Madam Speaker, why all the bravado? Why all the rhetoric about power and about war? Why all the euphoric mesmerization with war? Why is it that we look at the science of destruction and see it as something to be admired, when leaders who have had experience with war and who have probed the questions of how to obtain peace have questions remaining and have lived their lives without answers to questions like places in the Middle East?
Madam Speaker, there are many people involved in this war, including us who have been thrown into this situation. There are people there now who are Canadian citizens and my caring thoughts are with those people and their families. I have a press release here from the Grand Chief of the Mohawks, Chief Joe Norton and he says the Mohawks of Kahnawake have approximately 22 men presently in Kuwait fighting with the United States Armed Forces against Saddam Hussein's Kuwaiti army. These men were among the first to be sent to the American lines before Christmas. As well there are a number of Mohawk men in the Persian Gulf with the United States Marines.
He goes on to say that the United States Army initiated a huge recruiting drive to persuade Mohawk men to join the U.S. Army in 1990. Mohawk men, according to the U.S. Army recruiting officers are sought by the Americans because they are known for their fearlessness, fighting capabilities, and bravery.
There are many such Canadians and other people over there who have been thrown into this war, who have had put before them some very difficult questions.
I guess I should say that those Canadians are watching this debate in Parliament with anxiety and fear as we have watched the events unfold in the gulf. I guess it is good to say we are involved in a debate that few of us
have experience with because we have no experience with the previous world wars. Many of us have no experience in understanding the goings on of military activities and the strategies thereof.
But we have an appreciation for two things perhaps. One, we have an appreciation for the fact that we live in a peaceful country, that we have peace in Canada. We live in a democratic country. We have people out there. It is not just the military and the families that are out there, we also have journalists. There is always the friendly battle between journalists and politicians; we have people like Eric Rankin. We have people like Jim O'Connell and Brian Stewart. These people, in doing their jobs, risk their lives. They go out there to bring us the message and to bring us the news. I know journalists. Their oath is to the truth and to bring the facts to us. Those people are also out there.
Here we are debating the crisis in the Persian Gulf, but I feel that we are a bit late. I also feel that this particular motion is redundant. I believe that we should have been here within the last 10 days, not within the last three days. I believe that many of the things we have wanted to say have been cast aside because circumstances have so drastically changed.
I believe that Parliament must be given explicit right to debate a governmental action to commit Canandians to a potential war zone "before"-and I underline and underscore-"before they are dispatched". I believe that Canada has more to offer to peacekeeping than to war. Perhaps it is my fault. Perhaps it is the way I perceive things that will not allow me to accept anything other than a true struggle for peace. In my heart I believe that peace has to be our objective.
Canada's longstanding commitment to multilateralism and support for international institutions has given Canada a level of credibility matched by few countries. That is what we have to offer this arena.
You heard the Prime Minister today, Madam Speaker, say, "We are not a superpower. We are not a major deterrent". That is what the Prime Minister stated today.
Just look at the lead role taken by Pierre Trudeau and his peace initiative in 1983 to 1984. Let me quote Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
Trudeau. "If our future depended on Canadians alone, we could be confident that it was safe and sound. But no nation today holds its future securely in its own hands. We share this planet with about 160 other nations, all of whom interact with us in a global system, embracing our security, our economy, the health of our environment and the quality of our lives."
I do not want to focus on hindsight at this point but the question is on many of our minds. Did we really put enough effort into diplomacy? Will we ever know? We never had a report from the United Nations telling us that we had exhausted all possibilities.
Those statistics were not released to us or to our Canadian citizens. We will not know. How can we disprove what the government side has to say? How can they disprove what we hold as our position that perhaps we should have held out for more negotiations and for diplomacy to work and for sanctions to work. We will never know. That is the sad situation we are in today.
Only a year ago, citizens throughout the world had high expectations for peace. I had phone calls from Germany the night before the Berlin wall came down. We were at the German embassy, having supper, discussing the possibility of the reunification of Germany. What an exciting debate that was. The next day the wall came down. The cold war was coming to an end.
Today we are faced with a crisis in the new and short lived international order. The Berlin wall is down and the cold war is ended, but just a short year later on August 2, within three hours the situation was quite different. Iraqi troops accomplished their objectives. The Government of Kuwait was overthrown and Iraq was in control.
During the Vietnam War it took a considerable period of time for the American public to come forward in peace rallies to really wrap their minds around what they wanted and what they did not want with the Vietnam war. We had numerous peace rallies across Canada. It did not take that long. We had one that I hold dear to my heart because 10 students in my riding got together and organized a peace rally. We had 400 people in Yellowknife at minus 40 degrees Celsius in support of peace and many calls and letters from my constituents. My
Government Orders
constituents believe that war was not the only option left to us in the Persian Gulf. That is a belief. That is not something that I am using to hurt anybody or to insult anybody. It is something that people believe in. They believe as I do, that sanctions and diplomacy could have achieved our objectives.
Are we so short on leadership, hope and ideals that we have forever rendered the use of sanctions and diplomacy useless? Can we ever expect them to work? Will there ever be the credibility to try and force them in the future? That is a huge question. We have run the risk of losing that particular tool in a crisis in the future. It is interesting to note that today there are numerous peace rallies being held all over the place and people have questions. I ask myself, what will this movement be like if the war becomes unmanageable or has it become unmanageable?
What we have seen in the initial operation is that this war in the Persian Gulf will be like no other war. It will be unparallelled with its intensity and furore. We saw the television clippings of Baghdad lit up like a Christmas tree. There is no joy in that. American power will be unrestrained this time. This time I believe there are no limits. We know that there have been at least 100 bombing runs. This is the beginning of the air portion of the campaign. There has yet to be a ground operation which I feel could be much more devastating in terms of casualties. I believe this is only the beginning and that we have sadly underestimated the capacity that is there for the destruction of human life and for the destruction of a civilization and for the impact that it has on the world psyche in terms of peace.
Canada needs to provide a humanitarian role. Today, there are thousands of refugees running from Iraq. They are fleeing to Iran, of all places. After an eight-year war between Iran and Iraq those refugees are fleeing to Iran. War does not make sense. Refugees need our assistance. Canada must also provide food aid.
I want to take a few minutes to look at the issue. It is not black and white like many have portrayed. I believe that the Secretary of State learned when he travelled to the Middle East that there are some legitimate concerns within the region, such as Iraq's access to the sea. On the other hand, we are dealing with Saddam Hussein.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Saddam Hussein, as everyone knows, has gone to war twice in the past 10 years. He is a man who has grown up with the mentality of a revolutionist and he still is. That is the approach he has endorsed. That is the thinking of this man. In the countryside of the Middle East there has always been the opportunity for violence, and there still is, even when I was in the Middle East last summer.
When Hussein was a young teenager he joined the revolution and I believe that he has stayed there ever since. We have seen Iraqi TV showing pictures of him as a defiant person the day after rallying his troops. He is a Third World leader who wants his hands on the economic jugular of the entire world. He is determined to dominate the Middle East. We knew about his greed for money and for power. That is why the world united in supporting economic sanctions and very eloquently so. I cannot believe that we have done such a fast turnaround. I simply cannot believe the words that were expressed by a number of people, especially leaders in the States, who first endorsed economic sanctions and who-including Senator Edward Kennedy-said to Canadians that we had to give sanctions a chance. The President and Mr. Baker were people who sincerely endorsed sanctions and appealed to everyone involved to give sanctions a chance. Well, we have gone beyond that. We know it. But I believe in my heart that we will never know for sure because we have taken that pre-emptive step in aligning ourselves with our neighbours.
Although you will not hear it from those who wanted to proceed immdiately with military force, the economic sanctions were working to minimize Hussein's power. His exports were all gone; 90 per cent of his imports had been stopped and Hussein was quickly running our of revenue and currency.
We also need to understand that there will be thousands of casualties, maybe tens of thousands. Canada must provide medical and support services to those victims.
We also need to understand the ecological impact of this war. There are over 1,000 oil wells in Kuwait, 350 of which are pressurized, which means if they cannot be blown out and capped they will cause very intense fire storms; 10 million gallons of oil will bum daily; 500,000 tonnes of ash will move to the upper skies adding to the the carbon dioxide buildup, creating holes in the ozone, obstructing sunlight which will force the temperature down.
Canada has the technology and must help to manage these environmental disasters.
It is certain that the financial cost of war will be billions and billions of dollars. The quote I was given is that it costs $3 billion a day.
In conclusion, I would like to end my speech by reading a quotation I think is quite effective.
Canadians know that our security cannot be achieved in isolation or the security of any country, but we have the responsibility to ensure that all our global problems are tackled, not in a combative mode, but through co-operation.
War is the science of destruction and it cannot be stated better than this. A great world leader once said:
When people speak to you about a preventative war, you tell them
to go and fight it. After my experience, I have come to hate war. War
settles nothing.
Dwight D. Eisenhower.

Madam Speaker, I appreciated very much the speech by the hon. member. I do agree with her that war does not solve any problems. I think we should have let sanctions take their place and work. It may have taken about six months and at that point Mr. Hussein would have probably given up.
I would like to ask the member a question. Does she think the Americans gave the wrong signal to Iraq, when the American Ambassador, April Glaspie, said to Mr. Hussein, and I quote:
We have no opinion on the Arab conflict, like your border
disagreement with Kuwait.
This is what the Abassador of the United States said to Mr. Hussein on July 25. Did she think this was a signal to Mr. Hussein that he could invade Kuwait and is there a responsibility on the part of the United States that this happened?

Madam Speaker, I must admit that I would be one who would be the last to ever be able to understand how the Americans make their decisions and how perhaps someone like Saddam Hussein would respond and would have motive to respond. I must say that I have a lot of questions of my own that are similar. I do not know if the wrong signal was given but I feel in my heart that if we are going to talk about what we might term motives, then from the very onset of this whole conflict American involvement is something that I fail to understand. I have failed to fully appreciate it, if I might put it that way.
January 17, 1991

I always felt the Americans would strike first. I felt particularly sad because I felt for countries like Jordan that are compromised or countries like Israel that would become targets.
That is why I felt so strongly that perhaps we have underestimated the capacity to have prolonged peace instead of starting wars by not allowing diplomacy, the full range of whatever leadership capabilities there are, to take on an effective role and for sanctions to have worked to have allowed that. If that was not happening, why were we not told specifically and explicitly that it was not working and the reasons why?
In terms of this specific question, I cannot pretend to guess at what the motives of the Americans are. I can only look at what has happened. I cannot look back to even the Iraq-Iran war. My colleague, Mr. Barrett, who was here over half an hour ago-
An hon. member. Who made a fantastic speech.

-talked about the Iraq-Iran war and motives not just of the Americans, but of the Soviet Union, in a number of places throughout the world. I cannot say that I fully appreciate. I cannot say that that was the reason why, but people do have questions about why there is involvement. People do have questions about how many perpetrators there are in a war. There is not just one. There are many. How many fingers are on the trigger of the gun? There are many.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciated the remarks of my hon. friend. They were timely and very thoughtful. I was particularly moved by her comments on how this whole horrible mistake was a reflection of missed diplomatic initiatives and her concern that perhaps enough attention had not been given to sanctions, but also a wide range of other diplomatic initiatives that hopefully could have convinced Saddam Hussein to remove his forces from Kuwait.
I think that she will share with me a feeling that the United Nations has missed an opportunity. We were relieved at the end of the cold war and felt that the United Nations hopefully could play a different role in terms of really seriously solving these international disputes when they came up.
Government Orders
I wonder if she would share her views. Does she feel, as many of us I think do, that the United States in a sense uses influence to such an extent that resolutions are moved in the United Nations that some feel are not only inappropriate but go against the charter of the United Nations. Further, that really we missed an opportunity by simply going to war, by mobilizing allied forces to go in and crush in such a brutal way the Iraqi military and that we raced in as we have done in the past. We know that we do not solve the problems. We perhaps even make greater problems for the future by doing that. Yet we have missed an opportunity with a revitalized and more meaningful United Nations because of this particular action.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the very poignant questions and comments that my colleague has made and I must say that there is an uneasiness about the role in which key players have engaged in this whole crisis. The United States is one of them, but Canada is another. We are thrown into a situation where I really believe we will never know for sure the opportunity that was missed, but I guess you can say that we live to fight another day and to see other opportunities.
The United Nations and our government have the responsibility to encourage member nations to engage in activities that would perhaps reprofile the activities that the United Nations engages in for the security and freedom of countries and the maintenance thereof. I think that is something for which we would hope. Perhaps it is time for a conference as one of my colleagues stated. I have believed, since I went to the Middle East, that the United Nations could spearhead a conference on the Middle East that would deal with very difficult questions. They are not simple, they are very, very difficult questions. The Palestinian question, I believe, is not just a problem for the Palestinians; it is a problem for the world, for all of us to try to work at and with which we can deal.
In this particular crisis, we have indeed missed an opportunity and I believe there was ambiguity. I believe that many people have very many doubts about why that ambiguity existed, whether it was self-serving on the part of one member state.

Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I am grateful to the member who was on the government side who did not stand up just now although it was the government's turn to debate and to the Liberal member from York South-Weston who was to speak and who let me go ahead because I have some ill children at home.
Despite its very imprecise wording, most Canadians probably think that we are here debating whether our Armed Forces should be an active part of the invasion against Iraq. Given that some of the 1850 of our fellow citizens present in the gulf are already taking an active part in the war that is fully under way, we all pray that it is almost over. We saw last night in the case of the missiles sent to Israel that anything can happen and we all pray that anything will not happen.
I think that many Canadians must think that this debate has become so superseded by events as to have become irrelevant, redundant and ludicrous. The reason that the debate continues, I believe, is that enough of us here feel that somehow as the debate winds and turns and twists with changing events in the war,-and I think we are all very grateful to the hon. member for Calgary Northeast because I believe it was only he who prevented the House from adjourning last night,-but somehow as the debate carries on and turns and rolls, it gives us a chance to keep sitting here as legislators and elected people from all across Canada to continue to debate the dominant issue of our time.
I think many of us feel that we should be here rather than home. We should be here sitting every day, questioning the government during Question Period and somehow try to address our minds to the issue that is dominating Canadians from sea to sea to sea.
Under a House order, I understand that when nobody else gets up in this debate whether tonight, tomorrow morning, Sunday morning or whenever, the debate is over. A vote is to be held only if all three party leaders agree sometime next week.
Whenever it will happen that the three party leaders agree, of course, remains to be seen. On the issue of the vote, I am one of those who thinks that it would not be useful to have a vote on the matter, but it is not my decision to make.
I might put on the record my understanding of what some legislators elsewhere have done since war began among the members of the coalition. I only have a few to bring information on, but the House might be interested to know that the United States Senate voted, as I am sure most members know, 52 to 47 in favour of authorizing the President to go to war before the war began.
A vote held in the last few days-I believe it was yesterday-was 98 to zero in favour of going to war. The House of Commons in Britain remains in session as the war proceeds, and I think that is of interest to all of us. I hope ours will, too, one way or another.
The House of Commons in Britain voted 600 in favour of war and 57 against. I am told that Italy and France have done the same sort of thing with the same sort of numbers, but I do not have the figures. Italy voted yesterday. France also voted.
You may say: "What about Japan and Germany?" Those countries have no forces on duty there, and neither of those Parliaments have held a vote on the issue.
People wonder how Parliament gets involved in the requirements of the National Defence Act and our new Emergencies Act. I am told and I believe that the declaration of a state of war must be done by a proclamation of the Governor-General of Canada. Similarly, the invoking of emergency powers is legally done by cabinet order.
It appears that the cabinet intends to do neither of those. The Solicitor General indicated today he did not foresee, at this point, the Emergencies Act. Is it not all academic now that up to 2,000 planes a day are flying over Iraq? What about the lives of those 1,850 fellow Canadians who are exposed there?
Now that hostilities have begun and we are fully involved, how can any of us vote against this motion if it comes to a vote in the very vague, ambiguous language it is in. Maybe that is a good reason for not having a vote. I know there is a strong difference of opinion on that.
Every member of this House from every seat and every comer of the country wishes all the members of our Armed Forces a safe return to their families and homes in this country. They will have our full and unanimous support now, I hope. If a withdrawal of Canadian personnel were to create greater risk for personnel from the other countries involved, I think they should now stay.

It may be of interest for you to know, Madam Speaker, that opinion against Canada taking an active part in the war was running strongly against in Southeast Edmonton. My calls were about eight to one against having Canada participate actively in the war.
An estimated 2,000 Edmontonians attended a rally near Edmonton City Hall against the war over the last weekend. Thousands of others have demonstrated across the country, including Ottawa.
There was an audience of almost 200 at a conference on children at the University of Alberta last weekend. I asked if they would indicate by a hand vote how many of them favoured Canada participating in this war actively, and not a single person raised his or her hand.
Presumably, one of the reasons why the people at that conference were opposed to it was the sentiment by the Canadian Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War that more children than soldiers will die if war breaks out as, of course, it has. I understand that almost half of Iraq's population, because of the Iran-Iraq war and other factors, is now under the age of 15 years and it would appear that the physicians are correct, far more children will die than soldiers.
Those of us in this Chamber who were opposed to the adoption of the unamended motion, before war broke out-I took the motion to read in the context before the multilateral forces could begin war in Iraq-should not fudge on the horrors since August 2 in Saddam Hussein's self-declared 19th province of Kuwait. Tb the best of my knowledge, the consequences for Kuwaiti citizens and other residents have included more than 500,000 of them fleeing the country. Amnesty International says that Iraqi soldiers have murdered hundreds of unarmed residents and hundreds more have vanished in detention. There are 38 different methods of torture used by the Iraqi occupiers according to Amnesty International. More than 300 premature babies, and I think this has probably bothered Canadians more than anything, are believed to have died when the invaders seized their incubators for shipment to Baghdad. In short, the military followers of Saddam Hussein, in recent months, have forfeited sympathy from people of good-will everywhere. They have violated every principle for which Canada, the United Nations, and public international law have struggled for decades.
Government Orders
Why then was I not able to bring myself to support the use of force against such a madman a few days ago? First, because I think war should come only after there is no further reasonable hope that sanctions will work. Until war began, we could still hope that a full economic embargo and blockade would force Hussein to leave Kuwait completely. I would cite here some of the conclusions in a recent article, co-authored by the highly respected Gary Hufbauer. He writes: "The available evidence indicates that UN sanctions will begin to bite by this coming spring or early summer with a 'high probability of forcing Iraq from Kuwait, as early as the fall'. War might prove quicker but the costs of an attack include the costs probably of thousands of lives", mostly Iraqis, I suspect. Hufbauer went on to say: "Iraq is highly vulnerable to sanctions because of its geography, the nature of its economy and the full, unprecedented co-operation of the sanctioning nations. Specifically, Iraq's only export, as we all know, is oil and that product constitutes nearly half of its GNP. Despite Hussein's exceptionally brutal and complete control of his people, therefore the probability of success of a complete embargo over time", in Hufbauer's view remains over 85 per cent.
Contrary to the view which we have heard much of here, Madam Speaker, that sanctions do not move tyrants, they have been used successfully against ones of many different strips. In the early 1980s, American sanctions contributed to General Jaruzelski's decision to release political prisons and ease regression in Poland. Economic sanctions have also contributed, at least to a limited degree, to the downfalls during the 1960s of Trujillo in the Dominican Republic, Ngo Diem in Vietnam and, during the 1970s, to the fall of Idi Amin in Uganda and Anastasio Samoza in Nicaragua. Mussolini is believed to have confided to Hitler that, had the League of Nations included oil in its sanctions against Italy in 1935-36, he would have been forced to withdraw from Ethiopia within a week.
Finally, a very important issue is that of the United Nations institution and its role in the world today. I believe too many people in the world think that this is a United Nations war; it is not. It is true that the United Nations charter allows the use of force but only as a last resort. In this case, I believe that the Security Council resolution 678 of November 29, 1990, should not have

Government Orders
been passed unless and until the sanctions had been given a reasonable chance to work. Geoffrey Grenville-Wood, the National President of the UN Association in Canada, put it very well, the other day when he said: "It was a bad resolution, bad for the United Nations and bad for world peace".
There are so many possible consequences to the position in which the United Nations now finds itself. For one, instead of using the situation for the United Nations as an opportunity to bring in a permanent policy of isolating and embargoing tyrants and invaders, this will become a precedent for the United Nations using violence, killing children and all kinds of horrors that go with war. As somebody who believes strongly in the United Nations, I am profoundly unahappy that that is what is likely to happen.
I might, Madam Chairman, point out here that the United Nations Association in Canada, which ironically enough seems to be the most vocal critic of the United Nations role in this matter, is an organization to promote the UN. In our country, it is strongly felt that it has become a very effective critic of the United Nations, particularly of the Security Council resolution I just referred to.
This association wrote yesterday to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not know if it is proper for me to quote from the letter. It is addressed to him. He is not here to speak to the matter himself, but let me say in fairness, that the United Nations Association in Canada is profoundly unhappy with what is happening, how it is happening and how the United Nations performed in this matter.
I do not know that there is much more that I wish to say. In conclusion, we are now in a war. I know that my friends in the New Democratic Party think that you can draw a distinction between the less than 10 nations who have already participated in the air attacks on Iraq. They and others in this House, I suspect, do not want Canada to be involved with air attacks on Iraq.
As I indicated in my talk, I am afraid that now that we are into it, as much as many of us in this House-at least on this side-did not want to see war break out, I salute
the Leader of the Liberal Party for having withdrawn his position that the Canadian troops should withdraw if an act of war broke out. I do not think now, as much as I said in my speech, it is going to be children and civilians that are going to die in the greatest numbers because of this war.
Mr. Hussein said that they are going to fight to the last child. I understand that as of today his wife and children have been moved out of Iraq. I am sure that the last child to die in Iraq will not be one of his. It is always one of the tragedies of dealing with tyrants of this nature.
I think what it comes to is that if a vote is held on this matter, I will vote for it but subject to the points I already have made.

Madam Speaker, I guess it is a comment and a question.
I am interested in the hon. member's conclusion. I do respect the sincerity of the member's comments, but obviously the nation of Iraq under the control of the madman we have all heard and seen, Saddam Hussein, has inflicted untold misery on his people over the years. In fact, they tell us that during the eight and a half year struggle with Iran-a war that he inflicted on his own people in a sense-cost the two countries something in the order of one million lives. They tell me that it has been ongoing torture for his own people since 1968 when he took control of that country.
My question is simply this. How do we as an international group, and citizens of the world, like the right hon. member of Quadra said the other day react with to madmen such as this, if it is not through a united effort and indeed, Madam Speaker, through the United Nations?
Mr. Kilgoun Madam Speaker, I thank the member for his question and I know from television last night that he has a son who is engaged in the war and so his position is all the more significant than those of us who do not have children in the war. If I had a son or daughter in the war I guess I would be all the more tormented than I am sure he is. I respect very much the sincerity with which he holds his view.
January 17, 1991

One point that is probably worth making is that if the west, and there are a number of countries which I do not need to name, had not provided arms, the latest weapons, the uniforms, the jets, the fighters, the bombs, to both sides-as the member I am sure knows, some countries were providing it equally to both sides-during that horrible war, maybe that war would have been suffocated. Some countries in the west have a very direct involvement in that because, in effect, they were stoking the fires.
We should be ashamed of that. I knew a man-he is dead now-who was a Muslim who said to me one day that if the west wanted it could stop that war in three weeks. But we did not, we did nothing as far as I can see. For every one of those people who died in the war some countries in the west have a direct responsibility for that.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague for his very candid remarks. It is a very difficult deliberation that we endure in dealing with this issue.
I would like to ask him, with his experience as a parliamentarian, how much latitude he feels Canada will have in engaging in peace initiatives and engaging in a role as peacemaker and mediator if need be in the whole crisis or perhaps in a post-war scenario. What role will Canada be able to perform or be welcome to perform if we do not cease the kind of rhetorical bravado we engage in in our condemnations? Is that the role that we should continue to play? Should we continue to make our pronouncements so provocative and so inflammatoiy that it would limit perhaps our opportunity to resume our traditional role of peacemaker and mediator?

That is an excellent question, Madam Speaker. Another way of saying it is if we win, we lose. What is going to happen to Canada in the region? Assuming that Iraq is beaten quickly there is going to be a turmoil, instability, enormous nationalism, enormous animus against the countries that participated in this coalition. Is Israel going to be better off after this? Is Syria going to take over part of Iraq? Who knows what genii are going to come out of what bottles after this happens, after Mr. Hussein is removed.
I agree that we should tone down the rhetoric. I mentioned before, and I do not know if the hon. member was here, the young person who was beaten on a bus in Ottawa. I have constituents from Iraq and I am sure that most of them came to Canada to get away from Saddam Hussein.
Government Orders
Canada's role is going to be diminished by this in terms of being a peacemaker. Our stature is going to fall in the world. There is no doubt about it. We are going to be seen as being simply the little brother or the little sister of pax Americarma. We cannot tell our men and women there now to get out, leave your tents and get on the next plane back to Canada. We would be the laughing stock of the 28 countries in the coalition and of the world if we did that. I guess I can be permitted to mention that the words inscribed on the stone out there by John McCrae from In Flanders Field. He happens to be my grandmother's brother and our family hero. He is our biggest family hero, I think. Those words "if you break faith with us who die, we shall not sleep though poppies grow in Flanders Field". How can we live up to John McCrae's wish for Canada if we tell our people now they have to get out?
On the question of whether we can tell them not to take an active part in the raids over Baghdad, and I am inclined as the member knows to think we should not be taking an active part with the CF-18s and that kind of thing. We would be accused of cutting and running now and I am glad the hon. member for Saint-Denis seems to agree.

Madam Speaker, I have the greatest admiration for my colleague from Edmonton Southeast who has just spoken. I particularly listened to the philosophic point of view that he is able to bring with his wonderful background and knowledge. Frankly, it is Friday night, the Sabbath has fallen and normally I would be with my family having cooked a Sabbath meal and lit the Sabbath candles and said our prayers. I really cannot go today and my family, my husband, my mom and dad will have to manage with their own soup and matzo balls, regretfully is all I can say.
I really feel that this in a sense is where we should be trying to find what the next step, the next move is going to be for the hon. member for Saint-Denis and myself, the hon. member for Mount Royal, into some discussions that are not going to be easy, but hopefully will be fruitful. I certainly say to you in this House and to you, the hon. member for Saint-Denis, that I appreciate and I understand the role and support you give to your Palestinian perspective. I know you will accord me the same right and I think we both respect the rights of all peoples, Israeli and Palestinian, to live in peace and harmony together. I know that he has spoken in that respect in the international arena. As I was standing here and thinking about this, I was wondering-

January 17, 1991
Government Orders

The honourable lady said I understand the feeling of the hon. member for Saint-Denis for the Palestinian. That is a debate. You must understand my feeling for Israel, too, because if I let an hour go by people will say there is one sided Prud'homme versus one-sided lady, and you know I will not accept that. I am a Canadian. I believe in peace and justice for all and in the Middle East peace and justice for all means all! She was with me internationally when I made sure Canadians try with 1,000 international people to vote you know how. If you accept this, you should be complete. Members voting against Iraq for having used gas, I am the one who did that. It is not other members. Be complete but do not put me in this debate with you.

how. I cannot stop it and it is of great concern and I wonder if he feels as powerless as I do?
