Madam Speaker, I do. The terrible thing is that it is a high holiday today. Knowing the person who is pushing the buttons to send the missiles, if he has any more mobile Scud missiles, what is he going to do tonight? Is he going to send chemical missiles, if he has any left? It is hard to contemplate that these kinds of things could be going on at the end of the 20th Century.
May I just add before I am cut off that I personally was delighted to see that the member for Saint-Denis, was reaching out, perhaps not in a gentle way, but to try to show that he was not in dispute with the member for Mount Royal. I hope that as time goes by those members will continue to reach out to each other. I salute both of them for doing it. I hope it continues in the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to begin by saying that I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate, although I wish, as other members do, to be very frank, that this debate was not necessary.
It has been a very difficult and very disturbing week for all citizens of the world, for Canadians and certainly for members of Parliament.
I would like to begin by reassuring all Canadians, particularly those from Brandon-Souris whom I have the honour to represent that the decision on this motion is not one which any member of this Parliament, irrespective of party, takes lightly.
I am certain there is no one in this country who wants a war. The reality that as of the other evening that we are again at war, is one which has spawned an obvious sense of mental fatigue and mental depression here on the Hill and elsewhere in the country.
The coming down of the Berlin wall occurred so quickly it was almost an unbelievable achievement. That

led many to conclude and to hope that the type of hostilities which had characterized the earlier parts of the century, the 1930s and the 1940s and since then the cold war, Korea, would not again be necessary. The despair that has resulted from the fact that we are now at war is evident in the House. I think it has been evident today because we have not had our finest moments in this House today, I am sorry to say. It is evident in the faces of members in the House. I sense it in the employees of the Hill when I talk to members of the maintenance staff. I sense it in the faces of the young people who serve the House as Pages.
I would like to note categorically the fact that much of the world is again at war is evidence of failure. It is evidence of our failure as nations and as people to resolve our differences by other means. I think this is a particularly difficult failure for many people to understand, and particularly for young people to understand. TVvice during the course of the week there were large groups who came to visit my constituency office. I wanted to say to them that I understand their apprehension with what was then the possibility of war and with the reality of war that is here now.
One of the things I guess that troubles me a little bit about this debate is the fact that to a significant degree those of us who are participating in this debate are perhaps older than we would wish to be, and perhaps we are conscious of our age at a time like this because we are conscious of the fact that chronologically we are not able to represent in a physical sense, particularly those young Canadians who are so concerned.
To them I would say I believe I understand their fears and apprehensions and maybe try to say that I believe that because I too was once young. I remember being very young during World War II, watching with nervousness the events there, even though I was only a child who was well aware of the fact that my uncle was there; he had been wounded and had malaria; and the immense excitement when I found out he was coming home. I remember following the Korean war with a great degree of detail, even though we did not have the communication devices available to us then as we have now.
I think I can understand in that sense the feelings of youth. I would also say that when I approach this debate I am very conscious of the fact that I speak as a father. I
Government Orders
am very proud to be able to say that my two daughters are in the gallery watching as I speak.
So to my youthful constituents, I am very sincere when I say that I understand their concerns and I hope that we can prove that we understand their concerns even though we may not always agree.
There is something particularly numbing about this war, due to the fact that it is so vivid before our eyes. As I sat in the lobby this afternoon, I watched live television from Tel Aviv and from Jerusalem, two communities I have had the opportunity to visit. I watched the journalists live as they listened to the sirens, sirens that they could hear and I could hear, thanks to television. I watched them put on the gas masks and then with relief remove them again because the alarms tonight so far at least have proven to be false.
Live television certainly brings us closer to the war than we, as Canadians, would otherwise be. I think we have to be conscious of the fact that, however, while the war seems to be taking place in our living room, we are still distant from it. Fortunately for us we are distant from the grossness that is war and may we always have that privilege of being distant from it.
I am conscious, however, that there are residents of my constituency somewhere in the Middle East, somewhere in the Persian Gulf. Some have been there and came back, having volunteered to go. I am conscious of the fact that I have a constituent in Brandon who has family in Baghdad as of this moment. He, who is from that city, watches with a special fear and awareness as to what the reality of the war may be.
I am also conscious of the fact that although we are devoured by this particular crisis, and indeed it is a crisis of immense proportion, there are other wars occuring in the global community today that we should not forget, even though we tend to do so. I had plans now changed because of the crisis in the Gulf to be visiting part of the horn of Africa next week. There are civil wars in Ethiopia, in Somalia, in Sudan, to name but three as well as famines in those areas which may take many, many lives. In our resolve to deal with the crisis in the Persian Gulf I hope we are reminded of the fact that there are other ongoing conflicts which need our attention, even though we are not inclined to be as conscious of them.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
We must also pay some attention to the question, why is this struggle and debate taking place and how should we be responding to it. The key point on which we all agree is that we wish there was no need for war. However, the war to which we refer really began on August 2. The question in many countries of the world, despite what the newspapers may have been telling us these last few days, was not whether or not some nation would commence a war but is how we would respond to a war that began some five or so months ago. That war began for a variety of reasons when the Iraqi forces led by Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait.
I firmly believe that the real key to world security and peace lies in the principle of collective security. I believe-and I know there are differences on this point within this House-that the principle of collective security has been tested these last few weeks and days. The principle of collective security, as I understand it, requires that all members of that community who are part of that pact respond to those who are in need and to those who are the victims of aggression.
One of our difficulties in Canada these last few days has been the fact that Kuwait is a long way away, that most of us know nothing of this nation which was invaded last summer. I suspect many people had almost forgotten about the invasion, forgotten about the occupation and forgotten about the aggression. The principle of collective security to me suggests that we, as members of the United Nations, or as members of the global community, have a moral responsibility, as well as a military and political responsibility, to respond to those who are the victims of aggression. If we turn the other cheek and ignore this invasion, as some of my constituents have suggested we should, not only do we fail those who live in Kuwait and those who are victims of this aggression, but we would fail the very principle of collective security, we would fail part of the undertakings which we accepted when we joined the United Nations.
As I think about the events which have been unfolding these last few days, I am reminded of my own historical studies. I spent a fair amount of time studying European diplomatic history. Curiously, my masters thesis at the University of Oregon was on British pacifism which was so closely interrelated to the appeasement policies of 1930s. In my mind it was directly related to the outbreak
of war in 1939. As I look at this part of history, I cannot help but remember the great future which so many people felt existed for the League of Nations at the end of World War I. They dreamed that we could put together a new world community to help ensure that the holocaust that was World War I would never have to be relived again.
One of the great difficulties of a world organization such as the League of Nations or the United Nations, is the fact that it places upon its members obligations to come to the assistance of others who may be distant or not well understood.
To some degree, it requires a willingness on the part of those nations to give up part of their sovereign decision making powers. When the League was tested, as it was on several different occasions in the 1930s, and when the world community was tested by the aggressions which occurred then, the world community failed to respond.
In our failure to respond to the invasion of Manchuria in 1931, in our inability to respond adequately to the invasion by Mussolini of Abyssinia or Ethiopia in 1935, in our failure to deal with the Hitler of 1936 at the time of the occupation of the Rhineland, or later when he invaded Czechoslovakia in 1938, a serious mistake was made. Not only did those who were making decisions at that time, in my mind, fail their brother nations elsewhere in the world, not only did they fail to respond adequately to the aggression which was occurring, they also failed the very principle of collective security. In doing so, they helped destroy whatever hope remained for the League of Nations.
The tragedy of those several failures was that those aggressor nations clearly were encouraged by the failures of others to respond to their aggression. They concluded in that lack of response that those who would oppose them were weak, and they were encouraged to continue with their aggressive policies. Tragically, the end result was that at a later time and at a much greater cost, the nations of the world had to respond to a Japan, to an Italy and to a Germany.
The cost in human life was immensely greater in the period from 1939 to 1945 than it would have been if the nations of the world had joined together in 1931, 1935, 1936 or even in 1938. I draw a parallel between the
January 17, 1991

diplomatic challenges of the 1930s and the challenge which faces the world in 1991. In doing so, I am not trying to equate Saddam Hussein, the individual, with the evil that was Adolf Hitler. I am not in the position to draw that parallel, to know whether it is an adequate, accurate or appropriate one.
I think, however, there is a very definite parallel in the challenge facing the members of the United Nations today as there was to the League of Nations in the 1930s. I share the views of others who have suggested there is something bizarre about us here in Parliament debating an issue that has now been out-distanced by events.
I do believe that the issue before us, to a very large degree, is whether or not we are going to provide support to those members of the United Nations-in this case, Kuwait-that have asked for it. Are we going to fulfil what I consider to be our moral obligations to assist a member state in a time of difficulty?
I would prefer, for all sorts of obvious political reasons, that the United Nations flag was flying there in the company of the Canadian flag, but I understand why that is not possible at this time. I would urge members of this House not to dwell on that unduly. Resolution 678 of the United Nations, in which members of the Security Council freely participated, clearly gives us the mandate to proceed as we have. I am satisfied that we are there as part of the United Nations community. I have no difficulty with the question of who is in command.
I am sad, however, that the debate is necessary. I am sad and depressed that there continue to be the Saddam Husseins of this world who, for whatever reason, are determined to make their mark in history at the expense of others. I am sad that they, in their Machiavellian and diabolical manner have concluded that their best military defence is an attempt to bring Israel into a war by the unprovoked attacks which occurred last night.
As others have done, I would like to commend the Israeli government and the Israeli people for the immense discipline and self-restraint which they have demonstrated since then. I do not know, if I were responsible for such a decision, that I would have the will to restrain myself under those circumstances.
Government Orders
I am saddened by the fact that the diplomatic community, the world community, has once again failed. But I believe that there are times in our history, and this is one of them, when we must, given this scenario which has unfolded, respond to certain individuals and to certain communities with force because they seem to know no other language. I had hoped that the massive build-up which has occurred in the Persian Gulf would act as a deterrent to Saddam Hussein. Perhaps it would have to any individual who is more rational than he.
Now that we are there, now that we are at war, my concluding message, and I would hope the message of this Parliament, would be to all who are participating in the Canadian forces, to all who are participating in the forces of the coalition, that we are proud of them. They are willing to serve on our behalf, they are willing to put their lives at risk in support of the traditions and beliefs which are theirs and which are ours. I would hope also that this Parliament would send a very clear message, even though we may disagree on how they got to be there, that we are with them in spirit and in fact. We hope the war which is now taking place will prove to be a very short one and that the cost to human life will be as minimal as it possibly can be. That is my hope, that is my wish.

Madam Speaker, I listened with attention to the hon. member's speech and I was distressed by parts of it. He is trained as an historian and has worked as an historian and it is perhaps the lack of a sense of history that is one of the great burdens most of us carry today. If I heard him correctly, he made a number of comparisons between Mr. Hussein and Mr. Hitler and then, at the end of about four minutes of his speech, said something to the effect that he was not in a position to say whether the one is like the other. Where I come from, with respect, that is called sophistry. If he is going to make a case that one is indistinguishable from the other, he should have the courage at the end of his arguments to draw that conclusion.
I would ask him if he has read the article that was published widely by Gary Hufbauer and Kimberly Elliott on the question of sanctions. It includes the quote that I referred to in my talk about Benito Mussolini having confided to Hitler that, if the League of Nations had included oil in its sanctions against Italy, he would have been forced to withdraw from Ethiopia in a week.

Government Orders
Lastly, I would ask him why it is that the United Nations Association of Canada, Douglas Roche, our former ambassador for disarmament, and many other people, I think it is fair to say, are quite distressed-a mild word-as to what has been done in terms of sanctions, and what is being done by the United Nations?
Why is it that he thinks that the United Nations Association of Canada, headed by its president, Jeffrey Grenfell Wood, is so concerned about what is happening? I would ask if he would speak to those matters?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have two or three points in response.
What I suggested during the course of my remarks was that I saw a very real parallel between the diplomatic challenges that faced the League of Nations in the 1930s and what faces the United Nations and member states in 1990-91.
I said I did not believe I was in a position to determine whether Saddam Hussein had the same type of destructive personality as did Adolf Hitler. The hon. member seemed to be disturbed by that, but perhaps he has a greater knowledge of those two individuals than I do.
I think I understand Adolf Hitler fairly well, having read most of the biographies. I have not read biographies with respect to Saddam Hussein.
With respect to the question of sanctions, as the hon. member knows, sanctions have been employed as a first step in many instances. Sometimes they have been employed as a final step. Their record of success is not as great as we would wish. I see no evidence that sanctions employed to date with respect to Iraq have had an effective impact on the military capacity of the Iraqi government.
Without doubt, there has been a very substantial impact on the citizens of Iraq. If, indeed, that were a democracy, where there was some form of opportunity for expression of public opinion, then the impact of those sanctions on the citizens of Iraq might have been able to have made itself felt through the political system on the Government of Iraq.
But in a society where there is no such democracy, where cabinet ministers have been removed with apparently no evidence whatsoever and executed at the will of Saddam Hussein; where chemical warfare has been used on the citizens of the country, I think there is no opportunity whatsoever for an expression of popular discontent as a result of sanctions to have any kind of political and/or military effect.
I see no evidence that they have succeeded. I see the Iraqi Force, having invaded a sovereign state, having no inclination to withdraw whatsoever.
I see an immense amount of injustice that has been done to a nation and to its people. I am aware, however, of the historical differences which exist in the Middle East with respect to the difficulties of drawing boundaries, et cetera, but irrespective of the fact that there is a history of outstanding difficulties. There is nothing in those difficulties; nothing in my understanding of how nations and people should respond to each other that in any way justifies the actions of the Iraqi government in the invasion of Kuwait.
There is nothing in those difficulties and in the historical problems which have existed that in any way in my mind absolves us as Canadian people, or absolves us as a Canadian government, or absolves us as a Canadian Parliament from accepting what I consider to be our moral obligations; to come to the assistance of that same country-Kuwait.

Madam Speaker, I am very impressed with the parallels and with the sense of history that the hon. member for Brandon- Souris has, and with his ability to bring that out in his course of debate. I think his credentials speak for themselves in that area of history. It is most interesting to note that his thesis was on the appeasement policy of Britain during previous wars. It was very, very impressive.
One of the things on which I want to question is the point he made that we have been outdistanced by events in this war in relation to the debate that is taking place this evening. Some hon. members yesterday, for example, pointed out that the question is perhaps academic or moot in the sense that we are engaged in war, and why are we debating it?

I feel personally that it is very, very important that we as a Parliament show the same sort of solidarity that has been shown in Britain. I would simply like the member to comment on that sense of solidarity and us being behind the world community in this effort to rid itself of a demon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, I want to make it very clear that I accept the fact that there have been and continue to be important differences of opinion on this matter. I impugn no motives whatsoever to those who would differ from the positions which I have expressed.
I believe it is important to make certain that those who are fighting abroad and are prepared to fight abroad, understand very clearly that they are doing something which has the support of the people back home, because if they do not have that support, the most logical question in the world which they will ask themselves is: "why am I here?"
If I may say so, and perhaps I am entering into an area that I should not, I am aware of the fact that the hon. member who has just asked me the question has a son in the military within 80 miles of the Kuwaiti border. I would think that the hon. member's son and those who are there with him need that kind of inner contentment that comes from believing, not only that they are doing something which is right, but that other people believe they are doing something that is right.
On behalf of myself and my colleagues, I would like in a very personal sense to ask if you would convey our message of support to your son.

Madam Speaker, I could not agree more with the hon. member when he says that we have to convey to our troops in the Middle East our unanimous support for their efforts in what they are doing there.
Can I ask the member how that is achieved by a resolution that says that this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations and ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait? Would he not agree with me that it would be far more beneficial and far more direct, if his intention is to express support for the troops in the Middle East, to adopt a motion unanimously in this House stating in clear language that that in fact is the case?
Are you asking the troops who are putting their lives on the line in the Middle East to interpret from this
Government Orders
particular motion, this redundant motion that was put on the Order Paper before hostilities broke out, to read into this particular motion, a motion that says that we support the United Nations, support for them?
Would he not agree that it would be far more prudent, far more reasonable, if he wants to achieve his objective, to withdraw this particular motion and to replace it with a motion that will have the entire House unanimously show its support for the Canadian troops in the Middle East?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you will recall, there was a similar motion placed before this House in November which passed the House but did not have the support of all members and/or all political parties. Those who are there serving in the Canadian forces know why they are there and they in my mind, interpret the failure of this House to support this resolution as a lack of support for their commitment. Having dealt with this motion, other members of the House I am sure, under House rules, are certainly in a position to introduce motions which they would wish to present.
The item before the House which we have been debating for three days and may debate all night is clearly that this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending aggression by Iraq against Kuwait. That is the motion which is before the House as you know well, Madam Speaker, and that is the motion on which hon. members will have to decide whether they will vote yea or nay.

Madam Speaker, I am very glad to rise in opposition to Government Order 27 which is:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
The NDP caucus and in fact the party through its executive after good discussion has opposed this war and this motion since all of us in the House and outside the House know the motion means authorization of this war and the motion was entered before the war began. Now that Canada is in this war we still oppose it and in fact what is happening deepens our reason for opposing it even more.
This war is already doing serious damage far beyond Baghdad and Iraq through creation of refugees and other disruptions of the economy. There was an attempt last night by Saddam to extend the war further by another unprovoked attack on another nation not partic-

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
ipating in the war by a missile bombing of Israel. His goal of course was to bring more Arab nations to his side.
So far, thanks to the truly heroic self-control of the government and the people of Israel that move by Saddam has not succeeded. I salute Israel for its courageous patience and I salute the 3,000-year history of its ancestors up until this time in its struggle to live in peace.
There is still a danger that this war can become a renewal of wars that have lasted for centuries; wars between the Arabs and the Muslims on one hand, and between the peoples of European origin on the other, the new crusades as my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has put it. All the more reason then to negotiate an end to this war now; to bring together a conference on peace in the Middle East which the United Nations asked for, particularly to resolve the Arab-Israeli dispute. Canada's struggle is different than Israel's because of its place in the world. However, I believe the same principle of restraint must apply to Canada. I believe that by pursuing this war it is most likely to cause much more harm than good to the people of Kuwait, the people of the Middle East, and to the whole natural world.
Saddam was certainly wrong to invade Kuwait, entirely wrong. Even if he had a legal dispute with Kuwait, which he may, he should have negotiated it or gone to the world court, not start a war.
The U.S.S.R. was also wrong to arm its ally or colleague, Saddam. The U.S.A. was also wrong to sell him arms, to make him its protege against Iran. France was also wrong to sell him arms. Canada was also wrong to sell components for the U.S. helicopters that were sold to Saddam. President Bush was wrong to signal to Saddam a week before the invasion and, more than that, was wrong to not concern itself, right up to the time of the invasion, with a so-called Arab-Arab border dispute. He was wrong to refuse his congressional committee's recommendation at that time in July for sanctions to be imposed to stop Saddam.
However, our nations have contributed to the creating of Saddam, the brutal invader. There was an attempt to use sanctions to deprive Saddam of the revenue and the
material means to maintain his war. Sanctions were starting to do that, cutting off 97 per cent of his revenue. After the U.S. election, the U.S. doubled its military in the gulf and carried on some commercial deals with some of the other countries concerned. The momentum for war became unstoppable. Now the war is on. Many Canadians still oppose this war, many of all ages, who are not in this House.
Yesterday, the major churches of Canada issued statements on this war. For example, the Most Reverend Michael Peers, leader of Canada's Anglicans, has rejected the notion that war in the gulf is justified. He said yesterday:
It is beyond dispute that Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait, in flagrant violation of international law and with its foul atrocities against the Kuwaiti people, is unacceptable and contemptible. Nevertheless, the decision of the Canadian government to commit our forces to war and the call today from Canadian politicians to close ranks and support the war effort is deeply problematic. There are issues here upon which religious leaders have a duty to comment.
He proceeds then to list the traditional Christian criteria, the six principles of a just war, and to measure the present war by their standards. He concludes:
This war in the Persian Gulf does not meet the tests provided by Christian tradition for a morally justifiable engagement at this stage. The Prime Minister has commented that Canadian participation in combat roles in this conflict is both reasonable and moral. I reject his sentiments and his reasoning-. I call upon all Canadians of good will to pursue all efforts to bring about peace and the cessation of this destruction.
Madam Speaker, he has found the war lacking on those grounds.
So does the General Secretary of the Canadian Council of Churches, Dr. Stuart E. Brown, in a statement endorsed by the heads of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Canada and the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Primate of the Anglican Church of Canada, the Moderator of the United Church of Canada and the Moderator of the Presbyterian Church in Canada. The statement says in part:
War cannot resolve the Gulf Crisis. We call on Canada to work urgently at the United Nations to dissuade the Security Council from authorizing the use of force, either to try to expel Iraq from Kuwait, or to depose Saddam Hussein's government in Iraq. We urge Canada to work through the United Nations in support of economic and diplomatic measures toward peace and justice for all people in the Middle East-.

The most effective instrument with which to register the unacceptable character of this invasion of Kuwait is economic sanctions-.
This is not the time for ultimata; rather it is the time to search for non-military solutions, even if that means compromise and a less-than-ideal resolution. War will most certainly not produce an ideal solution.
I quote also from a letter today sent to the Prime Minister from Monsignor Robert Lebel, Bishop of Valley-field and President of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, with copies to the leader of the Liberal Party and the leader of the New Democratic Party. Referring to the bombing of Israel by Iraq last night, he says in part:
This latest act of Iraqi aggression is not sufficient justification for Canada to escalate its participation in the military conflict.
He said he had heard it was being considered in the cabinet.
He continues:
We maintain that this is a war that should never have been started. Economic sanctions coupled with diplomatic efforts by the international community were simply not given the time required to be effective.
He calls on the Prime Minister and the Canadian government to do three things:
(a)	refrain from any further military involvement by Canada in the Persian Gulf War;
(b)	urge the UN Security Council to initiate steps for a cease-fire and a resumption of negotiations for a peaceful settlement;
(c)	concentrate energies in developing an international plan of action for humanitarian aid and assistance regarding all affected countries in the Middle East.
Here is a statement by the Right Reverend Dr. Walter Farquharson, Moderator of the United Church of Canada:
We deplore the bombing of Baghdad and the claim that it was a success. It is, in fact, a tragic failure, even as the invasion of Kuwait by the Iraqi forces was a failure-.
We reject the claims of our leaders that there were no alternatives. We remain committed to the principles of a just world order and to the United Nations, but in light of modem warfare and the technological changes in weaponry, we are convinced that ultimately world order is only effectively pursued by non-military means.
Government Orders
Human beings are capable of creating terrible weapons and of wreaking unthinkable destruction. They are also capable of resolving their conflicts, reconciling with enemies, and healing wounds. They must take responsibility for the good or evil effects of their actions.
In the wake of these terrible events, we implore the leaders of all countries to draw back from inflicting even greater destruction on the people of the Gulf region and from placing our own relatives serving in the Gulf in greater danger-.
We commit ourselves before God to the dreadful but sacred task of laying on healing hands for all who have been wounded in these terrible events. We have no other choice because we believe God's intention for all of us is the lowering of every clenched fist and the healing of every wounded nation.
We of the NDP opposed this war before the bombing of Baghdad, and we oppose it now. We say to pull back our troops out of the theatre of war and find better peacemaking roles for them; to plan with the United Nations members for a peace conference, including an Arab-Israeli one; and to start now helping to provide urgent medical, food and other help to the refugees and displaced persons of this war.
As my final comment, Madam Speaker, some have suggested that a stand such as my party's is too partisan and partisan at an inappropriate time. I say no, it is not partisan.
I have been working for peace since the late 1940s. It was the result of my experience in World War II, in which I had to ask myself how we got into the fix in which Christians considered it their duty to God as well as to the king to kill Christians. How did we get ourselves into that fix? I came to the conclusion that it arose principally from the economic conflicts between countries, which need to be moderated before they break out in war.
I was active in the peace movement for 10 years before I joined the CCF-NDR I would not have joined if I did not judge it to be a parliamentary party committed to peace. I continued active in the peace movement.
I was very happy to represent my party yesterday afternoon at a rally of about 2,000 people in downtown Toronto opposing the war. I believe the movement is growing.
We are not taking this stand against the war to distance ourselves from the government, with the idea of advantage in the next election. We are taking this stand as

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Canadians. Many of us are taking this stand on the basis of our religious convictions, which I, for one, held before I became a socialist and continue to hold and continue to practise. We are taking this stand as loyal Canadians trying to serve the best interests of the Canadian people and as citizens of the world, believing that in the best interests of all the peoples of the world, now and in the future, the thing to do is to end this war. We are saying to stop the war now and do all that is possible and necessary, along with other countries, to build peace now.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I have listened to the comments from our colleague and I have had many occasions to speak with him in the past about his feelings on such issues. I can understand his feelings and sympathize with them a lot. I know that our colleague is a man of the cloth and he has very strong feelings on issues involving peace. I congratulate him for those. I do not always agree with him on his views, but I think Parliament needs someone who has that kind of a view to constantly remind us of the importance of peace. I want to tell him that even on those occasions, albeit rare, when I do not totally agree with him, he is nevertheless a conscience for this House in those issues. Again, I congratulate him.
I want to get to a specific point with regard to what is happening today. In my opinion, we are discussing a motion that I believe was wrong when it was presented to this House. It is not what the government wanted as an answer. The government really recalled Parliament to find out whether or not Parliament would agree to a Canadian participation in a war effort, should there be one.
I would have disagreed with that proposition; I would have voted against it. I still think it is the question that should have been put. Nevertheless, that being said, it would be redundant now anyway. Would our colleague not agree with me that the motion we have before us was the wrong motion to put to start with? Even if he does not agree with that proposition-although I think he does-it is redundant in any case. There is absolutely no meaning in discussing today whether or not we agree or disagree with resolution 678 of the United Nations, once it has been placed into full force, including the military component of it. This is just slightly worse than redundant. Could he comment on that, please?

I thank the hon. member for his encouraging remarks and for a very pertinent question. Yes, the resolution was a wrong resolution because it was clearly asking for an answer to a question it does not state. It stated a motherhood question: whether we want to support the UN in stopping aggression. Of course we do. But this was not the issue. As the member has quite rightly said, the issue was whether we support war as the means chosen by the United States and others within the United Nations.
It reflects the point that has been made by some previous speakers as to the methods used by the United States to win certain allies to its cause, including the fact that Canada-or rather the Prime Minister-as a reward for loyal support in war, now seems assured of a seat in the Mexico trade talks.
There are other deals with other countries.
On the question of withdrawing the resolution to find a better one, I would say by all means the government should withdraw it. If it wants to put one in that would ask for support in the war, I would oppose that.
If it wants to put one in that divides the questions and says whether we support the war, the decision of the politicians to make war, or whether we oppose the decision of the politicians to make war, we still give all support we can to those individual men and women who under orders, having trained and become competent in their work, are risking their lives to carry out this government's orders. I would certainly continue to support those men and women, but I do not support the war to which this government has sent them.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully and attentively to my colleague's speech and I want to tell him that I too put a great deal of faith in peace and do not like, and indeed dislike, war and states of war.
Every now and then, he mentioned that his speech was not partisan and that his decision was dictated much more by his conscience. I respect that, because I think that it should be taken for granted that each of us has to live with his or her conscience and is allowed, in this country, to make decisions according to it.
January 17, 1991

Government Orders
Unfortunately, Madam Speaker, when responding to my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, he could not refrain from playing politics and showing his anti-American bias. I did not expect that from him and it clashed with the general tone of his speech.
I cannot help but wonder why, after making an excellent speech, and convincing at that, my colleague apparently was unable to set aside his partisanship while dealing with the critical situation presently facing Canada and particularly the people who are in the gulf.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member may be right. In fact, I have rewritten my speech several times, or replanned it and rewritten it entirely once in order to make the point that I made in the speech.
Speaking more extemporary, yes, I did take a swipe at the activities of the President of the United States. I entirely believe in what I have said, but if the hon. member feels that I have spoiled a good effect of my earlier speech, then it is quite possible that he was right.

Madam Speaker, I am amazed when some of the opposition members and members of the New Democratic Party refer to the resolution and the motion in question. It reads:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
If they were to read the motion, it would be clearly understood. The member knows full well that this House voted on the original motion on November 29. That vote was won, with two to one in favour of the motion. It is simply reaffirming our support for the United Nations.
If we are indeed a citizen of the world, what does he expect us to do? Are we to back away from the United Nations or not act collectively with the rest of the world against Saddam Hussein, which basically is what it comes down to? It is the rest of the world, with the exception of a few, versus Saddam Hussein. Do we remove ourselves from international responsibility? Do we remove ourselves from a sense of collective responsibility? That is the question that I ask of the member.

Madam Speaker, I must say that the member who questioned me appears to be confused about the meaning of the resolution. Paragraph 2 of the demands says that the United Nations authorizes member states co-operating with the Government of Kuwait to use all necessary means to uphold and implement resolution 666 and all subsequent relevant resolutions and restore international peace and security in the area.
It does not say that we have to go to war to do that. It does not say that. It is this government, of which the hon. member is a supporter, that interprets that as saying we go to war.
There are two major faults with that use-or abuse, I would say-of the UN resolution. First of all, the UN resolution did not say that it is time now-
Oh, oh.

Madam Speaker, I did not interrupt the hon. member. They did not give any report. There was no report from the monitoring committee on sanctions. They did not resolve the question of the effectiveness of sanctions; they simply left it vague. That was a veiy faulty resolution. But as it stands, it does not order us, or even ask us, to go to war.
Second, if it did intend, without saying it, that we should go to war, it did not provide any democratically controlled United Nations command. There was no authority of the United Nations. It is not a matter of whether there is a blue flag. It is not a matter of whether the American general is to be called the United Nations general. It is a matter of whether the action is under the authority of the United Nations and under the control of the United Nations. It is a matter of when the United Nations will say when to stop. What this does is to encourage any member who says he is co-operating with Kuwait to do anything that he thinks he might do and claim the United Nations justification.
That is a fraud, Madam Speaker.

Thursday, January 17, 1991
[Editor's Note: Continuation of proceedings from Volume
B.]

Madam Speaker, I have been a member of this House for approximately six and a half years, and by far this is the most important and most serious matter that has been considered, in my view, in this House in the last six and a half years.
As I speak here tonight, my country, your country- our country-is at war. I do not believe that Canadians fully comprehend and have come to grips with what it means to be at war today.
We are not debating a resolution; we are discussing the fact that Canada is at war. The resolution before this House-and I would like to read it for the record-reads:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
This particular resolution was put on the Order Paper before war broke out. A lot has happened in the last few days. It has been a most remarkable week, a week that many people will never forget in all their lives.
This Parliament was reconvened on Monday because Tuesday happened to be January 15, the artificial deadline that was imposed, after which the United States and other member states of the United Nations had the authority to use whatever means necessary.
There was a meeting a few days before between Secretary of State of the United States, James Baker, and Foreign Minister Tariq Aziz of Iraq. As we know, those talks did not produce a peace, and a few days later the Secretary-General of the United Nations tried one last time to convince Saddam Hussein to quit Kuwait. It is academic now, the whole question of whether we should have been called back earlier. This House started its discussion on Tuesday. We debated throughout the day. The deadline came and went on midnight a few days ago, January 15. On Wednesday night this House was in
session and debating this particular resolution, and the bombs started to fall on Baghdad, the bombs started to fall in Kuwait and Iraq.
Following that initial bombardment the night of January 16, the stock market went up and the price of oil went down. All the economic indicators went in the complete opposite direction than the experts predicted. There was a sense of satisfaction in the United States of America, and indeed throughout the world, that somehow that particular bombardment, that particular military operation at the beginning of the war, was successful. People were talking about a quick resolution, a quick ending to this particular war.
But just last night, once again there was horror in the Middle East, this time in Israel. Scud missiles were launched from Iraq, an unprovoked attack on a non-participating country in the Middle East. It was clear what Saddam Hussein was trying to do, but the Israelis-the people of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa-had to suffer through the unspeakable horror of the possibility of a chemical attack, chemical warheads on those Scud missiles. We thank the Lord that chemical warheads were not used. We thank the Lord that casualties were not more severe.
Those people who were so positive on the night of January 16 became a little more pessimistic on the night of January 17 because the so-called dogs of war were unleashed. We went to bed last night not knowing whether there would be a Middle East today. We did not know whether Israel would retaliate as a result of the unprovoked attack. We are grateful that Israel has shown so much restraint so far in this particular case that it has not embroiled itself in the conflict as well.
As we speak in the comfort of the House of Commons in Ottawa at almost eight o'clock in the evening, I must make the point that there are millions of people in Israel and in Iraq who are absolutely, utterly, and completely terrified. Picture for a moment the many Canadians who are sitting tonight in the comfort of their own homes or

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
in safe places somewhere in Canada, but think of the millions of people in Israel, in Iraq, in Jordan, in Saudi Arabia, and in Kuwait who do not know what is happening. The people in Iraq are hearing the bombs. They are hearing anti-aircraft fire being returned. Think of our children. Think of all the children who are listening to what is happening. This unspeakable horror that is taking place will be forever etched on their minds.
On Monday we saw the deadline. On Tuesday we saw the bombing of Baghdad. On Thursday night we saw the bombing of Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, and Haifa. What is happening tonight in the Middle East? What is going to happen tomorrow night? When will this war end?
I think it important that we step back for a moment and ask ourselves why.
Hon. members opposite say there is a good reason why our country and other countries are involved in this brutal, hideous war. They say there is an international principle, that an aggressor must not be rewarded.
Madam Speaker, do you really believe that the thousands upon thousands of people who have already lost their lives as a result of the bombardment really care about any international principle concerning aggression? Do you think the millions of people who are suffering and will suffer really care? Members opposite and others argue that war was necessary in order to stop what Saddam Hussein was doing in Kuwait. He was plundering and raping the country. Civil rights were being denied and people were being brutalized. Yes, they were. We know they were. Cases have been documented.
What could be worse than the constant bombardment? Tune in to CNN and watch the satisfaction when the briefings are given at the Pentagon that there are 1,000 or 2,000 sorties a day. What does it mean? What does a sortie mean? It is not a pleasant walk in some pleasant park under pleasant sunshine. A sortie means a bomber, whether it is an F-14 or an F-17 or an F-18 with hundreds of pounds of explosives that are being dropped. Yes, on military targets or strategic targets. Knock out command and control, knock out the Scud missiles, the mobile launchers. Only 80 per cent are successful. What effect is it having on human lives? What scars are being left on those who will survive this particular war?
All too often over the last number of days during this particular debate and before, people seemed to have almost forgotten the cost of war in human terms and what it all means. They have not asked themselves why Americans, Canadians and British are involved in this particular war. Why are we on the eve of destruction? The implications of what is happening are far-reaching because the Americans say that Saddam Hussein must not be rewarded. The aggressor cannot be rewarded and he must be removed from Kuwait.
I understand why millions of lives were lost in World War I, the war to end all wars. Unfortunately, it did not. Many millions of lives were lost in World War II and Hitler came close to defeating the British.
I had the opportunity during the summer to travel through France and to visit some of the sites of some major battles of World Wars I and II. I walked for hours along the beaches at Dunkirk. I walked for hours along the beaches at Dover and I was reminded of what happened there 45 years before. The principle they were fighting for was democracy and freedom. It was something people could understand. They knew why people were fighting. But try to explain to your children that Canada is at war because there is some international principle which says an aggressor must not be rewarded.
I agree an aggressor should not be rewarded. But is war the answer? Is it the answer to send out 1,000 or 2,000 sorties every day, constant bombardment? Is the answer Scud missiles landing in Israel? Is the answer the fall of King Hussein of Jordan? Is the answer Syria joining forces with the Iraqis? War is the answer Iran joining forces with the Iraqis? War is not the answer, but we are involved in the war. We are there whether we like it or not. Canadian troops are there and we pray to God that it will not be necessary for Canadian troops to be involved in a direct way in hostilities there. We pray to God that the war will end as quickly as possible, but in my view, it was so unnecessary.
In the Second World War those who were alive then, and those like myself who were not but who read about it, knew who the enemy was. We knew; they spoke about the enemy. As I was preparing for my remarks, I was asking myself who is the enemy in this particular war? As I was brought up, I was taught that usually there is an enemy that you shoot at in order to kill and destroy. Are the Iraqi people the enemy in this war? Of course they
January 17, 1991

are not, but Canada is at war with Iraq. The enemy is not the people of Iraq, the innocent men and women. Perhaps the military and the army-the roughly 500,000 troops-are not the enemy. The enemy is Saddam Hussein. He is the person, the one individual who has caused all this. Should we be involved in a war that might take the lives of millions of people, that will scar the psychology, the psyche of millions of others around the world? Should we be at war? I think not, Madam Speaker. We ought not to be involved in this war.
The United States is the main combatant on the part of the allies. We know the reason why the world is at war tonight. It is not to remove Saddam Hussein from Kuwait. The reason that the world is at war is to remove Saddam Hussein period, to eliminate, to destroy Saddam Hussein in order that he no longer can be the leader of Iraq. The reason why the world is at war is to eliminate the threat that Saddam Hussein, the Iraqi threat. What are the consequences as a result? Who are the casualties? What are the casualties? We know what the devastating economic impact will be. We know that human suffering and human destruction will be immense. What about in the long term once this war is over, whether it is over in the next few days, weeks, months or the next few years? What will the world be like after the shooting stops? Will the entire problem be resolved? Will the world be safe and peaceful afterwards? Will the world be safe from other Saddam Husseins? Will there be others? I think there will be. Once the shooting stops the problems will only begin as a result of the war that we find ourselves embroiled in.
War was not the answer. Economic sanctions were not given the opportunity. Economic sanctions were working. It was not proven to us, it was not proven to the world that economic sanctions were not working. The onus was on those who wanted war to prove that economic sanctions were not working. The fact is that the evidence is overwhelming; whereas diplomacy may not have been working over the last number of weeks, over the last number of months, sanctions were in fact working.
I would like to cite a speech that was given by Senator George Mitchell just last week when the United States was debating in Congress whether or not George Bush should be given the authority to go to war. We all know that the vote was close both in the Senate and in the
Government Orders
House of Representatives. Senator Mitchell said, and I quote:
War carries with it great costs and high risk. An unknown number of casualties and deaths; billions of dollars spent; a greatly disrupted oil supply and oil price increases; a war possibly widened to include Israel, -
We know that he was right.
-Tlirkey or other allies; the possible long-term American occupation of Iraq; increased instability in the Persian Gulf region; long-lasting Arab enmity against the United States; a possible return to isolationism at home.
The grave decision for war is being made prematurely.
These words were spoken before the United States embarked on its campaign, as it referred to it. He went on to document what went on in the United States in the weeks preceding the decision to go to war when Mr. Bush said these sanctions were working. Secretary of State Baker said these sanctions were working. The head of the CIA director William Webster said that sanctions were working. He pointed out that more than 90 per cent of Iraq's imports and 97 per cent of its exports had been stopped. He documented in very clear terms how sanctions were working yet they were not given an opportunity. Instead, the United States decided that war was necessary.
We do not know where this will all end. We do not know what the final result will be. I note that my time is nearly expired. I had much more to say but let me conclude by saying that and I my party support the Canadian troops that are there in the Middle East. We hope and pray that this war will end as quickly as possible and that our troops can come home to their families in a safe fashion. We also hope and pray that Canada will play a major and leading role in developing and working toward a long and lasting peace, as difficult as that will be, after the hostilities stop. We hope that our country will still be in a position to work toward a long and lasting peace in the Middle East, a recognition that there are many people who have differences there, that the Palestinians are entitled to a homeland of their own, and a recognition of their rights, that Israelis have a right as well to be safe in their nation. Answers must be found, and I am convinced that Canada can play that role in the future.
