speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my friend who just finished says that we should withdraw the present motion supporting the UN resolution and then goes on to say: "But we support our troops". What he is saying is that we do not support what is happening in the

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Middle East, that the troops should not be there, but we support them in what he would term an illegal or an unwanted act, one with which he would not agree.
I would point out that his leader said we should support the United Nations up to a certain point, but when they fire a shot then we should pull out. These people on the other side have to make up their minds; they must support the sanctions of the United Nations, of the multinational force of which our troops are a part, because if they do not support that, how can they support the troops in an action that they do not support? It does not make sense.

Madam Speaker, there is no sense in what the hon. member said and it is very difficult to make any sense for him. The hon. member has just displayed the pettiness that we have seen day in and day out coming from that side of the House of Commons and, in particular, from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Of course, we support the troops.
Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
for International Trade): I know that that member many times breaks the rules of this House. He just accused me of motives that I do not have and I did not have when I rose in this House and asked my question. I asked a question, I asked a very clear question; I asked him if he could explain that. He then impugned the motives that I was using to do this and that is against all regulations in this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would be appreciated if nobody would impugn motives and we would answer questions and debate this very serious question without getting into unpleasant situations again. The hon. member for York South-Weston.

The hon. member suggests that it is inconsistent to be opposed to Canada participating in the war taking place and to support the troops after war has broken out. We know that in the United States the vote was very close in the U.S. Congress. It was very close, but once the decision was taken, once that country went to
war, the entire Congress fell behind the American troops in the Middle East.
I believe that here as well in the House of Commons we had our differences in principle as to whether or not Canada should participate, whether or not war was the answer or war is the answer, but surely every last member in this House, indeed every last Canadian, should show support for the men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces who are putting their lives on the line in the Middle East as we speak here tonight. I do not believe there is anything inconsistent in those positions.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving us this account of the Middle East issue and demontrating that we are indeed-of course, that goes without saying-supportive of our troops in the present circumstances.
However, to say at the same time that if we do not approve of the sanctions, it means that we do not support our troops, that is absolutely ridiculous.
Considering that almost half of the United States Senate-and they are involved-recommended that the sanctions be exhausted before taking military action, I put this question to the hon. member: Had sanctions been workable up to the last minute, does he believe that the risk of loss of lives would have existed anyway?

With all the certainty I can command, I believe that if sanctions were given a chance, sanctions ultimately would work. Members of the Senate in the United States and of the House of Representatives made the case very clearly. I would like to quote just very briefly from the speech of Senator Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts. He said, before hostilities broke out on Tuesday evening, before the United States went to war, and I quote: "Sanctions have not failed and no one can prove they have. They still have a good chance of achieving our objectives in the Gulf. Saddam Hussein is paying a heavy price for his aggression: 95 per cent to 90 per cent of his oil exports have been shut down. Iraq's

economy has been cut nearly in half. Saddam has no foreign exchange to prime his war machine. A trickle of consumer goods may be slipping through, but Saddam cannot run his country or his war machine on that."
The evidence was overwhelming that if given the opportunity, sanctions would have worked. Hundreds of thousands of lives could have been saved if the United States showed the restraint that it is asking Israel today to show in order to try to contain the conflict there. If the Americans showed restraint and allowed sanctions to work, hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of lives could have been saved.

Madam Speaker, I quote from Hansard January 16, 1991, page 17133:
Nobody pushes the United Nations around, not even the United States. No one nation, especially not the United States, is able to impose marching orders on that institution.
No, this is not an American adventure. It is a United Nations action in collective security, one of the greatest historic developments of our time-
I am quoting the former leader of his party, the former Prime Minister of Canada, the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. It is amazing to me that an individual can fly in the face of a former Prime Minister, whom he supported and for whom he has all kinds of respect. It is simply amazing.
Before I finish, I do want the member to respond to that comment. There is a very important distinction between what happened in the United States House of Representatives and what is happening here. Certainly there is disagreement in this House and there is disagreement in the U.S. Congress. No one questions it because this is what this forum is all about. None of us questions it; in all sincerity, none of us.
The difference is simply this. The hon. member mentions that he is behind our troops, despite the differences we have had over this particular issue and the motion before us. He is behind the troops. The difference between that party and the individual senators and congressmen in the United States who had differing opinions is simply this: not only are they behind their troops, but also they are behind their President.
This is something on which I would like a clear distinction. I think they have a responsibility to be behind
Government Orders
the Prime Minister, the minister of defence and the Government of Canada. That is a very clear distinction. They can hide all they wish behind that sentence or that little phrase they like to use that they are behind the troops.
I think, they have to be behind the Canadian people, the Government of Canada and, indeed, our Prime Minister.

Madam Speaker, the member is asking the impossible. He is asking me to join the 12 per cent of Canadians who are behind the Prime Minister of Canada. It is ludicrous to suggest we ought to get behind the Prime Minister and thereby show support for our troops.
When I say showing support, I do not mean by some vague resolution that says this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait. That is not showing support.
If the hon. member wanted to show support for the Canadian troops in the Middle East, then why does he not convince his House leader and his Prime Minister to bring forward a resolution that says very specifically, "therefore be it resolved that this House of Commons fully supports the Canadian men and women in the armed services who are currently serving in the Middle East"? We would be more than happy to lend our complete and unanimous endorsation to that particular resolution.
We are not simply using rhetoric when we talk about supporting our troops. The troops should be supported in every way possible, whether it is with military equipment or whatever. What is important in our view is that there be a clear and unequivocal resolution coming from this House indicating support for them. I know he agrees with me, so he should start talking to his House leader to put forward an honest resolution in this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In resuming debate, I will be recognizing the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk. I would like to make sure that the hon. gentleman is still sharing his time with the member for Ottawa-Vanier.

I, like many others in this House, had prepared myself for days to speak in this Chamber on behalf of the Canadians I was elected to represent, the people of Haldimand-Norfolk, on the reasons why Canada should not resort to war at this time.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
But many things have changed in the last 48 hours. The allied armies have sent thousands of bombs into Iraq. Saddam Hussein has bombed Israel. Israel has shown courage and goodness in its restraint.
Our nation is now actively involved in war against Iraq. Canadians are torn between a war they did not want and a desire, now that this country has gone to war, to support our soldiers and our allies.
The decision has been made to commit Canada force, and we now know it was made long before many of the members in this House were given an opportunity to address and vote on the issue. In fact, it is safe to say that fewer than one-tenth of the members in this House were given any influence whatsoever on Canada's decision to abandon sanctions and go to war.
We in Canada are, of course, proud of our democratic traditions. We know that these democratic traditions must be respected if we are to survive. Yet this government declared war, bit by bit, although more than 90 per cent of the members of this House, and thus Canadians, had been left completely in the dark.
Canadians are alienated from the political process, and their mistrust and cynicism grow unabated. If we continue to disapprove of Saddam Hussein, the dictator, as he is so often called, then we had better remember quickly where the power comes from in our country. It comes from the people; not just the war cabinet, not just the top bureaucrats, but the people.
I spent the last several months talking with people in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk. I have received many calls throughout the last few weeks. One was from Leon and Susan Hudecki, who are totally against troops in the gulf. They asked, "Sanctions were working, so why is war necessary?"
There was another one from Sue Stevenson of Waterford, who said, "Sanctions should be extended. Peacekeeping is okay. We do not want war. We need further negotiations. Keep negotiating, please".
Here is another one from Ron Machelli of Tillsonburg who says: yes to war. He is concerned because Hussein is dose to having nuclear power.
Madam Speaker, as you can see, there are differences of opinion across this country on this issue. Among these
people, there were generally three camps. There were those who felt that Saddam Hussein was a madman impervious to the reason of economic sanctions. He had rolled into the sovereign state of Kuwait. His soldiers had raped, maimed and murdered. We as Canadians had a moral obligation to join with other countries to get him out of there, and the quicker the better.
There were those who said that no circumstances justify Canadian involvement in war. I respect their view and I am saddened to have to tell them that we, the politicians of this world, have failed. We have failed to engage this new world order. The optimism that sprang from the destruction of the Berlin wall has faltered.
There were those, the greatest in number, who said that sanctions are still working. They asked why this government had done an about-face; it now has no support for sanctions and instead wants to support war.
That was a question I could not answer, because the government has yet to provide a reasonable explanation of its contention that sanctions were not good enough and that force could not wait. In fact, the evidence is to the contrary.
It may seem to some as a little too late to express regret and concern over the abandonment of sanctions and the resort to force. But I believe it is important to take a few moments and attempt to give a voice to the struggle Canadians face as to whether or not Canada should be at war.
In September, U.S. President Bush told a joint session of Congress:
These sanctions are working. Iraq is feeling the heat. . .Iraq's
leaders. . .are cut off from the world, unable to sell their oil, and
only a tiny fraction of goods are getting through.
In October, U.S. Secretary of State Baker said that sanctions are fulfilling the role as planned. Just one month later, CIA Director William Webster said:
All sectors of the Iraqi economy are feeling the pinch of
sanctions, and many industries have shut down.
Figures put the loss to Iraqi imports at 90 per cent and the loss to Iraqi exports at 97 per cent. Sanctions have shut them down. The flow of spare parts and military supplies from the Soviet Union and France, Iraq's major suppliers, has stopped. Iraq's foreign exchange reserves
January 17, 1991

have diminished drastically, rendering it virtually impossible to purchase foreign goods in defying these sanctions.
Let the government make no mistake: the Canadian public has major reservations about this war. Canadians want to be heard on this issue, and they want their elected officials to represent them in any decision of our forces in the gulf. This government has an obligation to the people of this country to consult them throughout this matter.
For eight weeks following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, this government refused to recall Parliament. It showed no interest in consulting the opposition on the formulation of an all-party position in this matter. Many people in Haldimand-Norfolk have expressed great concern and loyalty to the United Nations. I therefore think it is important that I try to correct some of the confusion surrounding its role.
I found it somewhat ironic that, despite this government's contention that it had United Nations sanction, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Javier Perez de Cuellar, knew nothing of the attack on January 16. We should remember that this is a U.S.-sanctioned war. The distinction may on surface seem to be academic, but it is not. None of the forces currently engaged in the Middle East are taking their orders from the United Nations Council, but instead from a U.S. general.
Canadians mourn the abandonment of Canada's role as a peacekeeper. Our belief in the supremacy of dialogue and our confidence in the potential for negotiation have earned us not only international respect, which far outweighs our size or our economic power, but also has given us national pride and national identity.
Now Canadians are asking themselves: Who are we? What is our role in the world and what role do we play in this conflict? Has our resort to force compromised our peacekeeping role. May it still be needed?
Many of those with whom I have spoken in my riding are now torn. I feel confident that I speak for most of them when I say that we cannot turn our backs on our troops, no matter how much we regret the order to send them to war. Our soldiers must know that we respect their dedication and loyalty, that we pray for their safety, that we will provide necessary equipment for them to
Government Orders
fulfil their duties, and that their families have our support and our gratitude.
We must commit ourselves here in this Chamber to doing the greatest thing we can for our soldiers, which is to pursue peace, to using our international prestige to find a solution, and to rediscovering national traits we once used well in the name of peace: tolerance, the desire to listen, the ability to communicate and respect for human dignity.
The end to this war may well come from the military, but the solution can come only from diplomacy. Canada must put itself in the front lines in finding the solution.
[Translation}

Madam Speaker, there are numerous references to dialogue and negotiation in my hon. colleague's speech. He feels Canada should have perservered along that line.
I want to remind him, first, that it takes at least two sides to have a dialogue and that, way back then, Saddam Hussein refused to take part in a dialogue.
Second, negotiation also calls for two sides who are willing to negotiate. Now, Saddam Hussein refused to negotiate until the last minute. He even came very close to refusing to see the Secretary-General of the United Nations.
How can he say that Canada should not have got involved in such action, that it should withdraw its support to the UN and keep negotiating, when it has been established that Saddam Hussein did not want to negociate any more?

Madam Speaker, what I said in my speech here tonight was that I felt, and that people on this side of the House felt, not only that negotiations were not carried on enough, but that sanctions were not given enough time to work.
I think I showed, by giving the hon. member figures in my speech tonight that sanctions were working, that Saddam Hussein was cut off, and that, in fact, if we look at the circumstances, Saddam Hussein, more than likely, did not know the resolve of the United Nations prior to making his move into Kuwait.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
If we look at the history of the story, if we read what has gone on in the past, that the Americans themselves failed diplomatically, failed in all ways to inform Saddam Hussein before he went into Kuwait, we see that they would not stand for it.
The fact that the international world community formed together was a wonderful thing. It was good that Canada got involved in the forefront and sent members of the force over there to enforce these sanctions. That is the way to get people to negotiate.
I only regret that this government and these allies did not give sanctions enough time to work.

The hon. gentleman talks about sanctions. I would just like to ask his opinion on sanctions that were discussed in a Liberal release on the Persian Gulf crisis on December 21.
I know the gentleman must be familiar with it because it is the Liberal policy. It says here: "The Liberal position is that Canada should promote sanctions, rather than the threat of war". It reads on later: "On the one hand, this would involve imposing a threat of new sanctions such as a drastic reduction in Iraq's water supply, controlled by Turkish dams, if Saddam refuses to reconsider his position. Alternatively, a refusal to consider speedy resumption of food aid to Iraq".
I am not familiar with international law, but if the hon. gentleman is promoting sanctions that would limit water and food to an opposing country, I would be shocked. Yet it is clear in this policy. I would like the hon. member to discuss it when he is indeed walking down the main street in Hagersville, talking to his constituents.

Madam Speaker, it was his government that chose to go to war. It was his government that said sanctions were not working. It was his government that refused to give this House any proof whatsoever that sanctions were not working.
It's his obligation to do it.

Whether or not this war is a long war or a short war, people will die. They will die whether or not we get this over quickly or whether or not it is dragged out forever and ever.
This government made the decision for Canada to go to war. What our party wants to do now that that
decision has been made, is to support our men and women over there, and to have this House debate openly and freely the issues involved around Canada's role there.
I would hope that the hon. member will take charge of his caucus and his government and make sure they present to this House a resolution that shows that this House supports our men and women who are in the Persian Gulf now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a difficult and serious debate. It may well be one of the most disturbing debates in this House since I first became a member. I don't have much time, but I would like to make a few comments.
The government tabled a motion in the House last Tuesday which reads as follows:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
I was here in Ottawa last August when the government made its decision to send Canadian troops, resources, equipment, and Canadian ships. I spoke in our party caucus, and, we supported the government's initiative, an initiative that had been launched by the United Nations to apply economic sanctions in order to convince Saddam Hussein he should free Kuwait.
Our mission then was the same mission we have today. We are still convinced Saddam Hussein should free Kuwait.
The motion before the House today is defective. It is entirely obsolete, because it ignores the fact that there have been changes in the world.
We can hardly say the Liberals were part of the decision to go to war. We were against that decision. We said many times that now was not the time to proceed with military action.
We supported the sanctions. We were convinced that over time those sanctions would have the desired effect, which would be to persuade Saddam Hussein to free Kuwait.
January 17, 1991

We didn't change the ways and means. This was done by forces independent of this caucus, of the group to which I belong, the Liberal Party.
In an amendment to the government motion that we tabled last Tuesday, we said that for the time being, we should not resort to military action. We said that for the time being, economic sanctions and diplomatic efforts should be continued, so that no one could say we had failed in our task to maintain peace in the world.
The decision was made by others. No one can blame us today and say that the Liberals changed their minds. We did not change our minds. The mission remains the same. The mission is to free Kuwait and to convince the aggressor, Saddam Hussein that he should leave Kuwait.
I listened to a number of the speeches made in this House. I listened especially to speeches by ministers to find out whether they contained a message that would have been reassuring with respect to the efforts made by this government internationally to convince the aggressor, Saddam Hussein, to give up his plans to occupy territories that are not his.
On the contrary, for months we saw no constructive action by this government. All of a sudden we were told: "We are going to war. Canada is taking part in a coalition."
And today, we are asked to approve a motion that does not say that we are going to war but that we support the United Nations in its efforts to liberate Kuwait from Iraqi oppression.
I repeat, this motion is defective and poorly drafted, so much so that I fail to understand how the government can possibly want us to believe that this motion, which is in fact obsolete, could be voted on today by this House and that we are actually taking a vote in the House on the decision to go to war and support our troops.
I do not have much time but I will one thing: we support the Canadian troops. We support the mission aimed at liberating Kuwait and, now that the decision has been made, for we have always been consistent on this issue,-we have said that we support the mission to liberate Kuwait,- we support the sanctions. Now that without consultation and without telling us first the government has decided to go to war, I think it is clear
Government Orders
that the mission remains unchanged: to liberate Kuwait, but not to put the world and that important region of the world on a war footing, a terribly dangerous escalating process which might begin in the next few hours and likely compromise world peace for years to come.
I listened closely to the speeches of my colleagues. A moment earlier a question was directed to one of my friends, one of my colleagues, about the sanctions. It is not up to us to show that the sanctions were not working.
We think that the sanctions were working. If we are to believe the American authorities, the sanctions were working before the election. What happened all of a sudden that they no longer work?
The onus of proof rests with the government. We did not get a satisfactory response to our questions about that.
I do not have much time but there is another point I want to raise. The situation has changed over the last 24 hours. The current situation in the Middle East, with the state of war between the coalition and the Iraqis, has changed the minds of a lot of people.
A few days ago, the American Congress voted 47 to 52:47 American senators voted against the participation of American troops in the Middle East war. Yesterday, Madam Speaker, now that war has broken out, 98 American senators supported their country at war. It is a heart-felt sentiment.
I cannot stand here today and say that I do not support the men and women of our armed forces who are there to defend-in my name and under my flag, under the command of my country-the cause espoused by my government, whether I like it or not.
I do not support this government. Everybody knows that, but it made the decision. As a Canadian therefore, I have to support the decision that was made and support the Armed Forces.
The decision we will have to make, the vote we will have to take in a few days, I hope, will be an intelligent vote. I swear to you, Madam Speaker, that we will gladly rise for that vote because all of us here-Muslims, Jews, Christians-pray to the same God for peace. I hope she is listening to us!

January 17, 1991
Government Orders

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend said that this debate is a most difficult one. Indeed it is, definitely. Not only is it difficult, but its complexity is such that we have lost sight of our objective.
During the few minutes he has left, could my hon. friend elaborate on this and put the debate back in perspective by emphasizing the real meaning of the vote we may be called upon to take, defining what is at stake and restating what is exactly Canada's position.
The Canadian position is clear: Although we would have supported the use of four military forces to enforce the sanctions, we are opposed to their participation in direct military action. Now we are faced with a war.
Could my hon. colleague tell the House once more that we just cannot tell our fighting men and women that we cannot support them, for they are just a bunch of terrorists? It is inconceivable that the government should hope to convince the Canadian people of that. It is an absolute aberration. Would my hon. friend care to elaborate on that point?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my good friend, the hon. member for Saint-Denis, a man who knows how to put issues in their proper perspective, for his question which is quite relevant.
First of all, may I say that there is no shame in seeking peace. I should be delighted, as I am sure the hon. member would be, if our forces could help bring back peace.
Only God knows when a vote will be held within the next few days; I certainly do not. What I know, however, is that the three parliamentary leaders will have to agree on the proper time for this vote, for the motion or order of the House dealing with this issue grants them in this particular instance the right to decide when the vote will be held. I do not know when it will be taken. I really do not know.
What I can say, however, is the vote on this motion. It may be that the significance of the wording may have been lost for, as I said, the motion is now redundant, obsolete. We just could not put the true question before the Canadian people which would read: In view of the
fact that our military forces are already fighting side by side with other armed forces in the Persian Gulf, do you support them, yes or no? That is the question.
I support our military forces. I hope and pray that they will return home as soon as possible before this confrontation escalades into a war of which everybody understands the importance and significance. Should there be a shift in the Arab coalition tomorrow, we would be faced with a very difficult situation. All we are asking, is for Mr. Saddam Hussein to regain his senses and withdraw his forces from Kuwait. We have nothing to gain in bringing him to his knees or in destroying Iraq. We have no territorial ambition or vested interest in that region, but we want to re-establish international order.
Madam Speaker, I suggest it is in Canada's interest to work for peace and, as I said earlier, there is no shame in seeking peace. In fact, that is the very objective of our military forces.

I want to compliment my hon. colleague from Ottawa-Vanier for elucidating government members their consternation regarding how people can feel about the circumstances in which Canada finds itself, in the face of a war that no one wanted and yet a war in which we are participants.
When members of my party, had the choice not that long ago between peace and war we chose peace. Who would choose otherwise? When we had the opportunity to choose between sanctions and war, we chose sanctions. We defended the opportunity that sanctions would afford peace. We defended the opportunities that sanctions would afford level-headedness, rationality and a peaceful mode to a conflict resolution.
We continued to do that, right up until that very last moment, not 48 hours ago. We understood the risks of waiting our time, of biding our time. We took the government to task on the fact that it was beginning to act unilaterally without consulting with this Parliament, without consulting the people of Canada. It acted unilaterally and changed the usual role, the normal role that Canada had played on the world stage as a peacekeeper that the minister identified as one that co-ordinated conflict. We changed from peacekeeping to peacemaking. Overnight, without consultation in Parliament, we
January 17, 1991	COMMONS DEBATES	17377
became policemen of societies throughout the world. In the minister's words, we have become the policemen of the new democratic order.
We found ourselves in a position where we were objecting to a government that had unilaterally decided to involve Canada in an adventure. Such as it was, this last summer, an adventure in the Middle East, an adventure which threatened to destabilize the very precarious stability, the very fragile balance of power that existed prior to August 2. We could find absolutely no reasons other than supporting sanctions, for doing anything other than looking for the vehicle that we were participants in establishing in the United Nations as a focus point in a medium for seeking solutions.
As of the other day the choice is no longer between sanctions and war. It is between war and war. It is not a choice that we would like. It is not a choice that Canadians want. It is not a choice that any rational human being would relish making. It is difficult for all Canadians to be faced with such a choice. Other colleagues before this House have pointed to the difficulties, the attrocities and the sacrifices in humankind, in material, in resources, in lost opportunities, in genius and human talent that go wasted because of this type of conflict resolution.
But we face it, Madam Speaker, and because we face it, all Canadians now have a choice of a long war or a war which is to be completed as expeditiously as possible with minimum damage to our own international reputation, to our domestic reputation, and most importantly to the men and women we have sent into a theatre of war without seeking the consent of Parliament. We are in war and so it is not illogic that those of us who represent the will of the people throughout this land would seek to indicate to each and every one of them that it is not theirs, the responsibility for waging this war without the approval of Canada is not theirs. That responsibility lies with the government opposite.
We, on this side of the House, support our men and women. The objectives they have to achieve are objectives which we can identify despite the government's obfuscation of them. We have entered into a theatre of war without knowing the reasons why. The government
Government Orders
and through its members over the course of this debate has sought to depict the situation as one in which the world order is pitted against the machinations of one evil, diabolical individual. I would buy that. I do not think there is anyone in Canada-perhaps no one in the Western World-who has not been convinced that we are dealing with a type of individual who should not be the leader of Iraq, let alone any other country in the world. We have an obligation to deal with the threats that Saddam Hussein poses not only to the Middle East, but to us on an international basis. We find ourselves being unwilling combatants in a war that no one wants. But, as combatants and as representatives of the public we have the obligation to ask this government for what purposes these combatants sacrifice themselves and about the emotions and the contributions of all Canadians.
Is it simply to remove the dictator from Kuwait? I remind government members opposite that the road to Kuwait taken by the allied forces runs through Baghdad. I remind government members that allied war machinery is raining havoc, death, and destruction on millions of people in Baghdad. I remind government members opposite that those same tools of death and destruction are going to be aimed at our own men and women, just as they have been aimed at victims in the Middle East.
We witnessed yesterday, much to the shock and horror of all people around the world, a senseless attack on Israel, but a Machiavellian one nonetheless. Although I do not know whether as a peace loving Canadian I would be able to resist this kind of provocation, we are asking Israel to ignore the infractions of its national interests, its national security, and the menace of death to its citizens in order to allow the allied forces to secure the kind of peace that we could all participate in.
When we take a look at the objectives for which we are engaged in war, can we stop simply at ousting the dictator from Kuwait? The answer to that has to be a resounding no.
How can we do it most effectively? How can we do it most efficiently? How can we do it so that we produce the most long-lasting result?

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Hon. colleagues, at least on this side of the House, recognize the moment that we entered the theatre of war we were committed to doing a variety of things. One of them was the liberation of Kuwait, not necessarily to replace its feudal government with another feudal government, but perhaps to give another system of government a greater opportunity to exist.
We recognize as well that in order to maintain stability, we have to make some commitments to ensuring that the integrity of Kuwait outlives the withdrawal of the allied forces from the theatre of war as surely as it witnessed their entry.
I have been listening to the debate from the government side as to how this is going to be accomplished or whether in fact this is an objective. I have heard not one indication so far that we will have to destroy the military threat that Iraq poses to all of its neighbours.
We have witnessed it in the past. We have seen it in operation against Iran for eight years. We have seen it recently in operation against Kuwait. We saw if just yesterday in operation against the State of Israel, which is not a belligerent nor a combatant nor a participant in any of the conflict. We saw it just recently used against other ethnic minorities in the State of Iraq, the Kurds and others on the Turkish border.
An objective has to be the destruction of that military machine. Another objective has to be the re-establishment of some stability.
Is it the government's intention to destroy Iraq and then to leave a power vacuum that will be filled willy-nilly by other powers in the area that have demonstrated a predatory bent in the past?
We know already of Syria's history into Lebanon. We know already of Saudi Arabia's movements in the area. We know in that that Saudi Arabia increased its military potential with the purchases of $22 billion worth of arms only last August.
Can anyone on that side of the House reasonably expect that that increase in armament potential is going to re-establish a very fragile balance of power in the Middle East? Can we forget the national security interests of Israel? I think not. All members in this House
have indicated that that has to be crucial to any kind of balance of power.
In addition, what are we going to do once we have destroyed the leadership of Iraq, once we have destroyed the internal domestic political structure? Are we prepared to leave a large peacekeeping contingent in order to restore domestic order? Are we willing or are we being asked by the government to put in place an authority to have an allied army of occupation and administration not only in Iraq, not only in Kuwait, but also in Saudi Arabia?
The government is very short in some of the questions and objectives that it says in which we will participate, but the government has already committed Canada to involvement in the war without declaring war. Surely, as in 1918 when we participated in the First World War, our presence in the conflict would give us an opportunity to sit at the peace table and to work out part of a peace plan that should be long lasting.
What are those objectives? What are those plans? Does not the Canadian public deserve the right now to know for what we are committing enormous political military potential, for which we are committing, as well, domestic national strife? We are pitting Canadian public opinion against Canadian public opinion on the question of war and war in the Middle East.
If we are to be true and serious participants in this activity for collective security, we will have to define what we mean in terms of collective security and longterm peace. As I said at the outset, the question is no longer one simply of sanctions versus war. We are never going to be able to resolve that argument. We have not given ourselves the opportunity to find out whether sanctions will work. We are never going to be able to afford ourselves the opportunity to see whether any other peace mechanisms would have produced the desired result.
Keep in mind, government members as well as opposition members, that we had the same objectives whether through sanctions or through war: the ousting of a dictator, the liberation of an occupied territory, the destruction of a war material, and the re-establishment of a fragile balance of power in the Middle East. The fragility of such a balance of power is to be seen in the kind of threats that a friend of Canada is witnessing on a
January 17, 1991

day-to-day basis. As we speak, we know that the Israelis whose a nation is about the size of Prince Edward Island are facing imminent dangers of missile attack and armed invasion. We are asking them, and we should ask ourselves as well, if they are to make the sacrifice for peace what will be our sacrifice. Well, we are not going to make very many and I hope not, but at least truth should not be one of them.
Canadians can make a contribution in the Middle East. One of my colleagues, an expert in military matters, said that there is a variety of contributions. There are naval contributions, aviation, land troops, support contribution, and the humanitarian side.
Members from my caucus-and I see it has been replicated in the NDP caucus as well-feel that the humanitarian support that Canada can provide would be of long-term value, not only for the people in the area, but for Canada's reputation world-wide.
We have already seen the enormous dislocation and difficulties that the conflict has created. We saw it at the very beginning when over 60,000 refugees fled through Jordan. We are seeing it again. We know, through the bombardments that are taking place on both sides, that we are going to have in access of 750,000 more refugees. Some estimates point the number of refugees at 1.5 million. How will we restore order if we cannot take advantage of the opportunity to provide humanitarian needs at a time of great crisis. That would be in keeping with many of our roles in the UN.
George F. Kennan, a former U.S. ambassador to Moscow, dean of American foreign policy and the author of the containment policy, said just shortly after World War II when Europe was witnessing or living through the experience of post World War II economic, political and social destruction: "Against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos, governments would seek to perpetuate human misery in order to profit from it politically or otherwise would encounter the opposition of-" and I could add there the United Nations and Canadians everywhere.
To do something less would be to shame the objectives which we say we applaud when we involve ourselves in this conflict. Our government owes it to all Canadians to indicate to what extent we are participating in a long-
Govemment Orders
term peace plan, much as the allied powers in World War II at Quebec, Casablanca and Yalta already began to prepare for peace. We have not been given an indication of that, other than to say that we will establish a military might beyond any contest in the Middle East.
But that is going to be very short lived, and we cannot cast forward surreptitious suggestions about peace. We have already made efforts to sacrifice virtually everything on behalf of peace. For example, I know my colleagues to my left have often alluded to an international peace conference with a set agenda and objectives to ensure a set end of results.
When we got to the point where we were willing to sacrifice national security interests of Israel in order to secure peace and were not able to obtain it, we knew that vehicle was no longer a viable option for us. But we must to have something in place.
Will the government come forward to tell the Canadian people what that plan is? It cannot be that we are simply going to leave our troops in the Middle East. It cannot be that we will give to them the policing authority in a land where co-operation and harmony has been disrupted over the course of the last 50 years by the economic dislocations of rationality that oil brings, both with its wealth and with its jealousies.
In closing, I can only add the ominous words of a letter sent to me by the Canadian Arab Federation just recently: "There is no such thing as a military solution to the Middle East conflict. War would only poison relations between the west and 200 million Arabs and one billion Muslims for decades. An international disaster would result. Indeed the new world order we speak of and hope for would likely be lost".
Our search for peace has to be one that is rooted in long-lasting profound initiatives. Our party on this side of the House is asking the government through this resolution to stop hiding behind obfuscation and to come forward with a peace plan that all of us can vote one.
I know that all Canadians following this debate would agree that no one wants war. Now that our government has put us in a war, we want a plan for eliminating the need for war as quickly as possible. If there is war, I know all members here on our side of the House, all members of the Liberal caucus, would say to our friends and to our sons and daughters in battle right now that we would be

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
the first to volunteer in order to be with them and to bring them back home safely.

Madam Speaker, I will be sharing my time with the member for Timmins-Cha-pleau.
Madam Speaker, we are here tonight to discuss a moot question and an irrelevant resolution. We are talking about a war that is proceeding as we speak in the House of Commons, and some Members will be speaking until three or four o'clock this morning.

Thank you very much Mr. Speaker. As I was saying this debate is about war. We are talking until three or four o'clock in the morning because the government did not call us back at the appropriate time. The Congress of the United States saw fit to get the job done and passed a resolution. Spoke to a resolution that was appropriate. We are not doing that. We were brought back nearly on the eve of war to discuss a resolution that was already nearly outdated. I am not an historian nor have I ever been in the Middle East, so I think that is a disadvantage for those of us who have not experienced the actual setting or the theatre of war. Some of my constituents have told me that just, maybe, if George Bush and the Prime Minister of Canada and more politicians were in the theatre of war, there would be less war declared.
The Prime Minister has quoted Lester B. Pearson on several occasions. I suggest that it has been selective quoting and I would also like to quote that the right hon. Prime Minister. In 1957, when he received the Nobel Peace Prize he said: "We prepare for war like precocious giants but for peace like retarded pygmies". I think that quote more aptly raps up what the Prime Minister meant at that time and what our party also stands for we are really treading on a tight rope between utopia and cremation. Just six months ago, the Berlin Wall was brought down, the cold war was over, the satellite countries of the U.S.S.R. were seeking independence, there was detente between the United States and the U.S.S.R. Now we have problems in Lithuania and the other satellite countries. We have this conflagration in the Middle East. The turn of events has been so
Government Orders
dramatic, going from the very positive to the very negative. Indeed, we are on a tight rope and we could go either way.
We have been consistent in saying that this war is unnecessary and unjust. It is a war about power, about money and about oil. A journalist, and I think a wise journalist, said that if Kuwait were full of coconut palms or date palms, certainly we would not be trying to drive Saddam Hussein out of that country. We invaded Kuwait. We would like to get him.
The young people and the senior citizens of this country, the young people who have not experienced war, who have not been sullied by war, in one united voice say no, war is not the solution. At the opposite end of the spectrum, visiting the legion in my community, the veterans who have experienced war said war is no solution. It will not solve anything. And just this evening, it was very timely, dated January 15, One Voice, the Seniors Network spoke against this war. "We want to see Canada playing a more active and independent peacekeeping role in its support of the United Nations. We can enforce sanctions and take part in diplomatic negotiations but we must not be aggressors in this conflict", say the seniors, the veterans who have experienced war and the young people of this country. I had occasion to receive some letters from students in a school in my community and, to a person, to an individual, they say war will not solve anything.
If we can cure so many of the diseases, surely we can resolve our differences. One student said if he could go to Iraq, he is sure if he spoke to Saddam Hussein, he could convince him that this war is wrong. It is ironic that just several years ago, the United States was propping up Saddam Hussein in Iraq. It was giving him arms. He was a hero at that time. Now, all of a sudden he is a diabolical murderer. He is a jackal. He is a barbarian. Has he changed: No, he has not changed. He is the same individual. He was a barbarian then and he is a barbarian now.
Everyone says in their speeches that Saddam Hussein is evil incarnate! Yes, of course, he is an evil individual, but we are wreaking havoc upon millions of people. Have we declared war as well on the Iraqi children, the Arab countries of this world, the Israelis? That has been the domino effect, the spillover. The war, as we have said,

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
will not solve the problem. It will merely be a conflagration of all sorts of nations. There is no solution in war.
I read an article by Richard Gwynne and I think we have given it short shrift. Saddam Hussein wanted a war. We are going to create a martyr. If he is martyred, what will be the end result of that? It will not solve any of our problems. It will create myriad more problems that probably will be unsolvable. While we are unable to solve those problems, how many hundreds of thousands of people will be killed?
Turning to the concept of sanctions, do they work or do they not work? Would they work or would they not work? We get conflicting stories as to whether they were or were not. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said there were undetected products getting through and that is a paradox if I ever heard one. If they are undetected, how do they know they were getting through? Some say sanctions are effective and some say they are not.
This time, we cannot wait. Saddam Hussein will take the food from the children and the women and give it to his soldiers. We are saying that is not acceptable to us. Our alternative is a bomb. Send a thousand sorties a day and decimate the country.
I am sure if the young children in this country had the choice between being hungry and facing the devastation of these bombings, the choice would be obvious. Sanctions should have been given more and more and more time to work. Saddam Hussein wanted this war and we gave it to him. We played into his hands and the solution will not be there. This country, as long as this leader was present, would be a pariah state and other countries would not deal with him.
As I speak Jordan is perhaps to become involved. We knew Hussein would attack Israel, he said so. The Israelis expected it, so it is no surprise, but that does not make it good. This could be genocide. This could wipe out an entire nation.
The cost will be $2 billion a day. It could cost $86 billion. You say: "well money is insignificant, it is irrelevant," but surely in this day and age, with people starving, dying of malnutrition, that money is important. The money could be put to a much better use than this war.
The question is: why are we at war? Can we answer that question? That question that will have to be answered later on when the war is over. Why did we go? To get the aggressor out of Kuwait? To protect our life-style? The President of the United States said to protect our way of life, to protect jobs. That is farfetched. It did not work.
Finally we said we had to get rid of the aggressor. Yes, we must get rid of the aggressor, but is this the way? It is the least desired of ways or alternatives that we should have followed. But now we are into it, and once we have it started, how will we be able to get out of it? Who will be there to pick up the pieces when this is all over?
As for negotiations, negotiations took place, we think. At just about the last negotiation James Baker said: "We are going to try a new spin on an old approach. The carrot is that if they pull out of Kuwait we will not use the big stick". That is negotiating, to use the big stick. Indeed, we are using the big stick. There is bomb after bomb after bomb after bomb.
Winston Churchill, who got much of his fame while being involved in conflict, said: "Jaw, jaw, jaw is better than war, war, war". We accept that and we are against this war. We are consistently speaking out against it. We rally around our troops, and our motives are constantly questioned regarding whether or not we support the troops. That is almost dishonourable. It is despicable to even to suggest that we do not. These people would rather see us rally around the guns.
I will close by asking whether it is the right thing to do, if you are bearing arms and attempting to be a part of an aggression. I cannot help but think of the medics and the padres during wartime. Who could be considered braver than these individuals who went into the front, for the most part totally weaponless?
Please let us not get into saying we do not support our troops. Nothing could be further from the truth. We are against this war. We are against aggression. We believe, unfortunately, that it is now out of hand and that there is no turning back. In view of the way it is escalating, what will it be tomorrow and the next day and two weeks from now? Let us hope it ends as soon as possible.
January 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the conviction with which the hon. member spoke. I have just a few comments and possibly a question.
No one questions the distaste for war; none of us does that. It is certainly an option that no one would prefer. I think one of the issues that was brought forward by the member is somewhat confusing in the minds of the Canadian people; something I guess he did not bring out. It is simply the fact that Saddam Hussein has inflicted severe punishment upon his own people, for hundreds of thousands of his own people have died over the years. In fact, thousands of his own people have died this year. Hundreds of thousands reportedly have died in the country of Kuwait, which he has taken over, and continue to die at this very moment.
The unanswered question of this whole equation is: How many of those people would have continued to die at his hands if the United Nations had not acted as decisively as it has and collectively on behalf of the world to rid the country of Iraq of this individual? Peace at what price? This is really the question I am asking the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the sincerity of the question.
My answer is that violence indeed begets violence. Yes, I suggested that Hussein is a barbarian, a jackal and all those terms that people have defined him as being. Anybody who would turn upon his own people and use poison gases and all these deadly weapons upon his own kind is all those things. I have also read the horrors in Kuwait, unspeakable horrors, things that when you read them you say are just unbelievable and repulsive.
The government's answer appears to be: "Well, our solution is to go in there and decimate. And rather than allowing maybe 10,000, 15,000 or 20,000 to die abominable deaths, torturous deaths, let us do it quickly. Let us get in there. Let us bomb. Let us have a blitzkrieg. Let us see how many and how fast we can get in there to do the job." I understand from the very graphic pictures on television that these weapons are so technical they can actually pinpoint and hit a bunker. These are the kinds of weapons we are using.
Government Orders
The answer cannot be to wipe out a nation although that is possible. We have heard of 150,000, we have heard of 350,000 people killed. I do not know. Nothing has been verified. One wonders what will happen. In a small incident like Panama it was suggested that very few people were killed. It was later evidenced, however, that hundreds were killed. Hundreds of thousands of people, perhaps a million people, if the conflagration continues, will die. That is not the solution.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Portneuf, very briefly please.

Certainly, Mr. Speaker,
I shall be brief. I have a question for my hon. colleague. He sides with those who claim that we should have continued to negotiate with Mr. Hussein, a man who had just ended an eight-year war with his neighbour. We had assumed, he and I together with most world leaders, that the war was over in the Middle East and that there would be peace. Hardly a few months later, this same Mr. Hussein invaded a small country. The collective realization of world leaders of countries that are UN members was that Mr. Hussein had not abandoned his military ambitions, but that he wanted an extension of the war in the Middle East in an attempt to take over a number of countries. He certainly did not prove world leaders wrong yesterday when he attacked Israel, a country which so far had not been directly involved in this war against Iraq. I wish the hon. member could explain to me how much further the United Nations could negotiate with this man, when admittedly every possible effort had been made. In other words, to use the hon. member's own words, at one point should one decide to use the big stick to make someone understand that enough is enough?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question and I also accept the fact that it is a difficult question. It is like sanctions. How long do you negotiate, how long do you allow sanctions to work? I do not know. I do not have the answer. I do know, however, that this solution is wrong. It is not a solution to have a travesty upon the world. It will reverberate across the world next month, next year, next decade, and perhaps next century. We may never recover from this.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
To answer as to what time, I have no concept. Sanctions may have taken a year and a half. They say that it is too expensive. It is too slow. Compare that cost with the $86 billion to $100 billion cost and the million lives or whatever. I do not think there is any comparison.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to take part in debate on this very serious issue we have before us. I think one of the things that should be made very clear at the onset is that I firmly believe there is no one in this House, no one, who supports war. We made it very clear that we all oppose war, but the way in which we try to express ourselves in that opposition differs.
The main thing that we are discussing is the motion we have before us. When I read it, I was a little confused.
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
I support that. But what I do not support is the fact that the United Nations, as a peacekeeper, as a body of nations that supports peace, has decided to go to war in its Resolution 678.
If my understanding is correct, under section 42 of the United Nations charter, there must be evidence and there must be proof that all other methods have been exhausted prior to going to and calling for war.
I am not convinced, and I have not been convinced in this House by the members on the other side-that all options have been exhausted. I do not think that sanctions were given enough time to work. I know it has been said, many times: "How long? When do you call a stop to this? When is enough enough?" I do not think that losing one's life is worth all the oil and all the money that is going to be spent in this war.
On the question of sanctions, I would like to quote the rt. hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs on January 16, 1991 on page 17112 of Hansard. In response to a question put to him by our leader, He said:
What I am telling here is that we have the most airtight system of sanctions the world has known and yet even with the most effective network of sanctions we have known, there are strategic imports getting into Iraq.
It seems to me that if we have the most airtight form of sanctions in the world, we have a bushel basket that does not hold water. That is not, in my opinion, a sanction that is functioning.
So what does it mean? It means that we do not have the most airtight sanctions in the world, in my opinion. I find this statement rather silly, quite frankly.
If there were chemicals and machinery coming through the back door or coming into the country somehow, we should have stepped up our patrols, we should have stepped up our sanctions.
There is no evidence I have heard in this House that tells me sanctions did work. I think we jumped the gun so to speak. I think we acted too quickly. I think if we, as parliamentarians, and it has already been said, but it is worth repeating, if we were made to enter the field of battle we would not be so quick to say: "let's go to war". We say that Saddam Hussein is a maniac, he is not too stable, we do not know what he is going to do next, that he is willing to kill his own people to achieve his goal.
When we drop those bombs on Iraq, we are killing civilians. We are not killing the military. I have a letter from the Canadian Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War. They were the Nobel Peace Prize winners in 1985. In the fifth paragraph of this letter it says: "The vast majority of casualties and deaths would be suffered by the civilian population. In wars since 1980, 84 per cent of all war dead have been civilians. Forty-five per cent of the population of Iraq and Kuwait are children under the age of 15. Medical facilities there are inadequate even for peace time. But they would be paralysed by war".
I have numerous letters from students in my riding who have written to me saying that this war is stupid. "We do not want war; we want peace. There has to be another way. When you fight with somebody else, that is violence and violence does not create anything but more violence." These are 10, 11, 12 year old kids telling us this. And here we have the Nobel Peace Prize winners
January 17, 1991

Government Orders
saying we value the lives of our Canadian men and women serving in the Persian Gulf to enforce United Nations sanctions on Iraq. We join with their families in praying for a resolution, through the United Nations without war. That is the same thing as the kids are saying.
It does not take a genius to figure out that this war is wrong. It was wrong from the beginning. We did not support it and we do not support it now.
I have a communique from the staff of the Enterprise, a local newspaper in my riding in Iroquais Falls and it says: "Dear Cid, give peace a chance. Please act on our behalf here in Iroquais Falls to do whatever you can to avert a war in the gulf area that could mean the loss of many lives and a world-wide tragedy."
Nobody wanted this war. It is a war that is based on greed not need. It is based on the need for money. Why does Saddam Hussein need Kuwait? He needs it because he is broke. He just came out of a an eight-year war with Iran. He needed the money and this is what this is all about. He wants the oil. He wants the money.
"What is the price of peace", we were asked a little earlier. What is the price of a life? Is a life worth all this? Would losing one life-what if it was yours-be worth it? I do not think so.
There are many things that can be said here this evening. There are many things that have already been said. Our troops are in the gulf. My position and my Party's position is very clear. Our troops are there. There is no question about that. What are they going to do there? Are they going to become part of the aggressive forces? In my opinion they should be used in the role that was designed through the United Nations, that is to pursue the role as peacekeepers. We should be assisting with medical needs, humanitarian needs. We should be offering escorts to the hospital ships. Our CF-18s should be offering protection for those hospital ships. They have a role to play, but that role should not be an aggressive role. It is to be a humanitarian role for the protection and the continuation and pursuit of peace. Once we become aggressors, we are on the same level as Saddam Hussein. We are not above him; we are below him, because we have now become the aggressors.
In the pursuit of peace, our troops do have a role to play. I do not suggest for a moment that they should withdraw and come home and forget all about it. I think they should be there. I think they should be serving the needs of the civilians, of the refugees and not become the aggressors. On that note, I will end my comments.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau on a remarkable speech and I sincerely believe him when he says that each and every member of this House wants for peace.
On Remembrance Day less than two years ago, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and I were in Normandy where we visited the huge cemeteries covered with thousands upon thousands of crosses and tombstones with inscriptions listing the ages of the people buried there: 17, 18, 19, 20 and 22. As we left these cemeteries, we could not help but appreciate the beautiful landscape and the happy people and reflect that such was the price these young heroes had to pay to secure this peace.
In the various villages where memorials were being erected to honour Canadian war dead, we spoke to young people, young parents, who said: "We are doing this today because we want for our children to remember those who years ago paid this peace with their lives." Canada remembers. For nearly 45 years-I am sure my hon. friend will agree-it has expended a lot of effort working for the cause of peace.
Yet, there comes a time, once war has been declared, when it is necessary to stand up and be counted. As a union leader, he certainly realizes that people can negotiate for a year or two. Then out of frustration, the parties will start hurling verbal abuse at each other which may turn very quickly into physical confrontations. Society, however, has developed laws and rules of behaviour: The parties may go to court and ask for a ruling.
On the other hand, when the leader of a country decides not to resort to diplomacy and negotiations and even the occasional slap on the wrist, but rather to chemical weapons, tanks and aircrafts to destroy entire areas, how do we stop him? I should like the hon. member to explain to me tonight how, at the international level a judge could enforce international law? Here it is always possible to call the police and say: "Listen, you

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
have to enforce the law". It is possible to put people away in jail, but it is not possible to put a whole country behind bars. Therefore I would like him to explain to me how in the future, we could find a way out of these dead end situations; is not by waging war.

First I want to thank my colleague for his question, a very serious and sincere question, I believe.
It is true that we spent some time in Normandy about two years ago, and it is true as well that as I walked around the tombstones I was heartbroken to realize that all these young people had died because of the war. This is why today I speak so strongly in favour of successful peace negotiations. I also believe that it is not good enough to say that a time comes when war is the only option. In this instance the negotiating process was not carried through to the end, all avenues were not explored.
As to the sanctions, I feel that they were not given sufficient time to give results. I should like to quote from a statement I have here, but unfortunately I have only the English version.

Retired U.S. Admiral, William J. Crow, former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, stated in testimony before the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee:
If in fact the sanctions will work in 12 to 18 months, instead of 6
months, the trade-off of avoiding war with its attendant sacrifices
and uncertainties would in my view be worth it.

I quite agree with that statement. I do not think and I was never convinced that enough time was given for the sanctions to take effect.
Specifically concerning the question of my friend, I am tempted to quote a letter, also in English.

We ask that all governments work to make the sanctions even more effective and that every effort be made by the Secretary-General of the United Nations to negotiate the withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait. We
are convinced that this is the turning point in world history when we can choose to act as an international community to develop a world order that does not rely on war to settle conflicts.

Mr. Speaker. I participate in this debate tonight with a definite sense of futility in view of the unfolding events in the Arabian Gulf beyond the control of this House and even well beyond the control of Canada. The debate has become futile in the sense that it does not lead to any meaningful or effective decision by this Parliament, since war is already under way and Canada is there. Many members of this House, including myself, regret this very deeply and would like to have had the opportunity before war started to make some of the arguments that are now moot.
In the present circumstances, I rather regret the extent to which this debate has gone and the fact that it continues to be partisan. I do not believe that this is an appropriate time nor an appropriate issue for the scoring of what may be regarded by our people as somewhat petty political points since Canada is now involved in a war and we are all first and foremost Canadians. I believe that we in this House enjoy substantial agreement on many points. I want to emphasize these points of agreement before I explain, for the benefit of the people of Canada why I believe this matter could and should have been conducted differently.
The resolution before the House would affirm the support of this House for the "United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait". The objective of the UN in this matter is something on which I believe we all are in agreement, that is the removal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the restoration of the legitimate Government of Kuwait. Where we have differed in this House is on the question of the appropriate means for the world community to pursue in order to achieve this objective. We on this side believe that economic sanctions should have been given adequate time to effect this objective in parallel with ongoing diplomatic efforts. The government believed that the time for war had arrived. It and the Prime Minister bear a heavy responsibility for the consequences of this decision.
January 17, 1991

While I deplore the fact that we are at war, I support whole-heartedly the objectives which our forces are pursuing. In that sense, I now find myself in support of the resolution before the House.
The holiday season this year was made gloomier by anxiety and haunted by fear. The world was at a crossroads, but we could tell that the situation was bound to worsen. For sure, the over-all Canadian agenda was not rosy. I was particularly struck by the televised messages from our troops to their families and friends here in Canada. The Canadian soldiers on foreign soil or cruising over distant waters were not posted abroad as peacekeepers, but indeed they were very close to getting involved in deadly combat.
[English)
How could so much have gone wrong so fast? How could it be that we were contemplating the imminent engagement of Canadian forces in battle, not in Europe but in a far-off desert? I suppose all of us wonder why we are really there. Is this really about oil? Is it really a case of the United States somehow co-opting the world community to assist it in its first post-cold war effort to assert its influence in a new and threatening way? If there were no oil in Kuwait, would we even care about the subjugation of this small nation by the Iraqis? Would we have objected if the Iraqis had succeeded in defeating Khomeini and had perhaps occupied the Iranian oil fields?
These questions are to me very unsettling and very disturbing as I contemplate the situation that confronts the world in the gulf. But they do little to help address the issues that have confronted Canada as a member of the world community and that may perplex the world for years to come. There remains little room for debate now that the President of the United States has taken and acted upon the decision to attack Iraq. That decision was made in Washington alone, and this is not the way the world should work in 1991.
I speak in this House of Commons to appeal to our government not to abandon the pursuit of peace even in the face of war. Despite the commitment our nation has made to engage in this action, we must not fail to search for avenues of peace to stop the destruction as soon as
Government Orders
possible. Even in war, let us counsel restraint in the world community.
There should be no dispute about why we are in this situation. The massive, unprovoked and brutal assault launched on August 2 by Iraq against the nation of Kuwait and the subsequent purported annexation of Kuwait as a province of Iraq cannot be tolerated by any civilized nation. Iraq openly and defiantly violated international law and ignored the charter of the United Nations. The world community reacted with remarkable speed and consensus. Canada was right to support the UN resolutions condemning Iraq and demanding its withdrawal from Kuwait, as well as imposing economic sanctions.
There have been some who have equivocated, either because they claim to see some legitimacy in Iraq's alleged grievances, or by citing a double standard lurking in the world reaction to past wrongs of a similar nature. I do not agree with these objections.

The matter of the Iraqi's grievance concerning the artificial boundaries imposed by Britain, their claim to part of Kuwait's territory or their recriminations about the Kuwaitian leaders are nothing more than a smokescreen to throw everybody off balance. Frontiers may well have been cavalierly delineated, but they were accepted by the states of the region and in fact became legitimate. No other state in that region went to war over a boundary issue. Besides, Saddam Hussein was as happy as could be to acknowledge the legitimacy of the Kuwaitian leaders when he sought billions of dollars for his war with Iran.

It is true that there is a strong odour of hypocrisy in the air as the world community unites to condemn Iraq. So many times the world community has stood by and failed to condemn, let alone take meaningful action against, aggressors. Even now the Soviet Union seeks to intimidate the people of Lithuania through brutal means while the world does little more than gush empty rhetoric.
This is an argument that should be turned inside out. If a double standard has been practised, it surely means that the world community needs more experience in collective action. I suppose that if clean hands and a single standard were necessary prerequisites for world community action, there could never be such action at all.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Frankly I am less troubled by the supposed hypocrisy of the United States than I am by the logical conclusion of the argument upon which it is based, namely that the world community cannot act in accordance with the United Nations charter pursuant to resolutions of the Security Council, if the force required to implement these resolutions is primarily provided by the United States. To conclude thus is to ensure that the United Nations will become totally irrelevant and, further, that the United States will act unilaterally in future, when it believes its interests are threatened.
Then there is the cynical belief, to which I alluded previously, that all of this is motivated only by oil. Of course, it is indisputable that had this aggression occurred in some resource-poor region not so strategically located, the response would have been much different. I suppose this is part of the harsh reality of international politics, but it is surely not an argument against international action.
Of course we should not sacrifice human life for oil, but I fail to understand why the powerful economic reasons for ensuring access to important oil reserves should be the basis for undermining the legitimacy of international co-operation against aggression. Oil, whether we like it or not, is vital to the world economy. While this is especially true of the industrialized economies, it is also true that oil is vital to the struggling developing economies. The fact that oil is at stake in this crisis makes its outcome crucially important to the world economy, but it cannot be said that this fact should somehow impede the moral legitimacy of world action against Saddam Hussein.
It is almost too much to contemplate the potential disaster for the world economy and the human suffering that would ensue if Saddam were able to interrupt the supply of oil from the gulf region. I am convinced that none of the hand-wringing and equivocation I have heard is sufficient argument against an international effort, based upon economic sanctions, to turn back Saddam Hussein.
While the cold war period was one of unrelenting tension, it must be said that it was a period free from major international conflict. Regional conflicts were not permitted to get out of hand because of the threat of
escalation to a superpower confrontation and all that such confrontation could mean.
In the post-cold war world, peace will no longer be built on mutual deterrents, and the balance of power will be replaced by the preponderance of power. If the United States and the Soviet Union no longer see their interests as being in contradiction, or if the Soviet Union is in fact in the process of decline as a superpower, then some new and very important questions must be asked. Examples are: What counterweight or other external limitation will there be to U.S. power? What protection does the world have against violations of international law if there are no international policemen? What mechanisms can exist at a multilateral level to ensure that international law is applied even-handedly in situations where force is required?
In the absence of mutual deterrents of superpowers to impose restraint on international aggression, it seems to me that the emerging post-cold war order can follow one of two patterns. Either the international community evolves an effective method of responding to breaches of international law, or there will develop an ad hoc unilateral response to situations deemed by one or another superpower or indeed lesser power to be vital to its interests, probably with little or no consultation with international organizations.
The invasion of Kuwait by Iraq provided the international community with its first clear post-cold war test. It is a clear test, because there is no justification in international law for Iraq's action against Kuwait. After August 2, there were not many choices available to the world community. I could think of three.
The invasion could have been ignored or treated as an Arab problem in need of an Arab solution. This overlooks the fact that no Arab state possessed the military strength to enforce an Arab solution against Saddam Hussein.
Second, the international response could have been to move into the gulf to prevent further aggression but, perhaps after a period of sanctions, to accept reluctantly his annexation of Kuwait as one of those unfortunate things that happen in the world. This option makes the statement that observance of international law is strictly
January 17, 1991

Government Orders
voluntary and acknowledges the inability of the international community to enforce observance of norms, which are surely essential to long-term peace and security.
The final choice, one would have hoped, was to apply the provisions of chapter VII of the United Nations charter, which in itself includes the use of force "as requested by the Security Council of the United Nations". Unfortunately, in this first test of the post-cold war period, the Security Council was not used to bring the pressure of the world community to bear on Saddam Hussein through genuine collective action. Rather, it was used to rubber stamp unilateral superpower intervention in a manner that seemed to meet none of the tests of prudence and sobriety that ought to accompany the decision to destroy the lives and property of hundreds of thousands of people.
