I want to take pains to ensure that my remarks are not misinterpreted. I wish in no way to appear to sanction, accept or condone the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait. We must not forget the fear and loss suffered by many innocent individuals, including Canadians, who were held hostage by the Iraqis in strategic locations, in complete violation of international law and all norms of human rights. The hostage taking was made even more outrageous by the introduction on August 25 of the death penalty for Kuwaitis found to be harbouring foreign nationals.
In addition to the plight of the hostages, the occupation of Kuwait by the Iraqi forces will doubtless be remembered as one of the most brutal and vicious events of modern history. The 82-page report issued by Amnesty International verifies this completely. If the territorial imperialism of Iraq were not enough, the report of Amnesty International, which other members have referred to, would compel me to the conclusion that international action against Iraq was necessary.
But this is not the essential question. The question rather is: What action is appropriate? By whom should it be taken? The further question we should be asking is: What should Canada's role have been?
I believe that the taking of offensive action by the international force in the gulf against Iraq was the wrong action at the wrong time by the wrong force.

Although force is never rejected outright and might eventually become necessary, it would be a tragic mistake to resort to that option now. We did not give the sanctions enough time for them to be effective.

It does need to be said that the decision to abandon economic sanctions in favour of offensive action will result in unknown but quite possibly horrific consequences. Not only is the conflict certain to result in massive numbers of dead and widespread destruction, but the outcome can never be certain. For that matter, if the alliance of forces does prevail, what then? There is the potential that Saddam will achieve martyrdom, that his defeat will further inflame the Arab dislike for the west and will undermine the governments of Arab states that have supported the alliance and been friendly to the west.
There is the potential need to send occupation forces into Iraq after the war. There is the possibility that neighbouring states will attempt to take advantage of Iraq's defeat by seeking to take Iraqi territory. Perhaps Iran from the east, Syria from the west, and possibly Turkey from the north. There is further the possibility that the spread of the war to Israel will split the alliance against Iraq and possibly bring other Arab nations into the conflict.
But by no means the least importance, there is the risk of a serious ecological catastrophe.
Finally, what should Canada's role be in this terrible situation? Canada has built itself a marvellous reputation in international affairs. Canada's influence has greatly exceeded its might for half this century. With that history in mind, it is all the more embarrassing that in this crisis our government could find nothing innovative or original to contribute until the Prime Minister sent a letter to the Secretary-General of the United Nations last week.
I know, that my time is nearly over. I would like to conclude by saying that I believe, the failure to follow the steps outlined in the charter of the United Nations, chapter VII, establishes a very worrisome precedent.
The end of the cold war does not mean the end of the need for collective security based upon international co-operation. However, just as Neville Chamberlain gave appeasement a bad name and thereby influenced

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
countless foreign policy decisions since, this precipitous action in the Gulf may give collective or co-operative security a bad name as well.
We have all watched our television screens during the last days and witnessed the horrors of war. It struck me how capricious life is. Why is it that I was born in Canada and can witness these horrible events safe in the knowledge that the bombs will not fall on me while someone just like me is hiding in a shelter, his family clutched to him in another country wondering why fate has dealt him this card?
Until the leaders of this world find a means of ending the madness of war, we must not rest. We must never tire for working for peace among all peoples.
May God protect our men and women serving for us in the Gulf. May God protect the people, both civilian and military, from all countries who face such grave danger at this time, and may God forgive us all.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the hon. member, It was for the most part, a very thoughtful argument through the course of debate. But there are a couple of points that I wanted to make to which the member could possibly respond.
I think I will begin by quoting our former Prime Minister and leader the right hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, when on Wednesday, January 16, 1991, he pointed out so clearly:
No, this is not an American Adventure. It is a United Nations
action in collective security, one of the greatest historic
developments of our time,
He went on to say: "certainly in my lifetime".
I mention that only in the sense that I think we are disillusioning the Canadian people when we think that the UN Security Council members rubberstamp the views of any member. Is he telling us, for example, that the U.S.S.R., France, Great Britain and China have rubber stamped the actions of the United Nations?
Further, I think that he has to look beyond articles 41 and 42 of chapter VII and take a very strong look at chapter VII. If he does, I think he would again understand the reasoning so behind this and that the UN was
clearly living within its original charter and certainly within chapter VII. I think, again, that he has to look beyond sections 41 and 42 exclusively.

I appreciate the question, Mr. Speaker, because it does give me an opportunity to explain that point which I unfortunately had to omit for lack of time.
I believe that the United Nations was not asked to fulfil its mandate under chapter VII. In lieu thereof, it was asked to write a blank cheque to the United States to launch offensive military action against Iraq. I regret that Canada went along for the ride without even so much as questioning the timing as far as we know.
Chapter VII, as the hon. member knows, of the UN Charter provides a clear framework for international collective action in the face of a renegade state. Chapter VII includes the establishment of a military staff committee and requires, in article 42, a determination by the Security Council whether economic sanctions "have proved to be inadequate".
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, whom I think is veiy familiar with the problems of former leaders standing up and contradicting current leaders, as Mr. Diefenbaker often liked to do, perhaps rhetorically asked the opposition in this Parliament to prove that sanctions were working. What a ridiculous proposition for him to make.
First, this is a matter which the Security Council must decide. It never applied its collective judgment to the issue of whether economic sanctions were working. That procedure was totally short-circuited.
Second, surely the burden of proof must be on those who say the economic sanctions are inadequate. Is this not the argument that the Prime Minister of Canada has been so proud of making in the context of the G-7 nations to Margaret Thatcher? When she argued that sanctions were not going to work against South Africa our Prime Minister said: "Yes, sanctions are the way to go". Yet he seems to be willing to accept on very little evidence, as far as we can see, that sanctions were not working.
My concern is not that this is a question of approving the United Nations engagement in the battle in the Persian Gulf: Rather it is a matter of saying Canada should have stood back and said that the procedures in chapter VII are vitally important. They have only worked
January 17, 1991

once in the history of the United Nations and that was because the Soviet Union chose to absent itself on Korea. Now we have an historic opportunity to see whether genuine, collective and co-operative action can work to enforce peace and security throughout the world. Why not use those procedures? Why short-circuit them and turn that right over to a superpower to make the sole determination of whether it is time to take military action.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for this second opportunity to respond.
Just one point that I want to emphasize clearly is the fact that, again under artcile VII, there is no sequence of events, or there are no specific steps that have to be followed with regard to sanctions. There is no pronouncement that has to be made with regard to whether or not sanctions are effective.
If we go beyond the very narrow interpretation of Articles 41 and 42, and look at chapter VII, with the clearness and the intensity of chapter VII, I believe the member would find that we have clearly operated and performed as required under chapter VII.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that this is merely a matter for legal interpretation. For what it is worth-and I am not an international lawyer-I read the provisions of article 42, which say: "should the Security Council consider that measures provided for in article 41, namely the sanctions, would be inadequate or have proved to be inadequate, then it may take such action", and so on. It seems to me that in the absence of such a determination being made, the following provisions of article 42 should not have been taken. That is the legal argument.
I think the more important argument is this: As we move on into the post cold-war era, as I tried to say in my original speech, we really have two choices in terms of how international peace and security is enforced in the world. Either we have a collective security approach, which engages the determination of multiple nations, preferably the United Nations, or we relegate it to an enforcement by a superpower or even medium power in a regional dispute, that can enforce the peace or the action that it seems to think is desirable.
Government Orders
What I think is lacking in this case is an evident desire on the part of the nations that sat and made this decision to carry through to its logical conclusion the collective security concept, which would have engaged the minds of all those members of the Security Council in the decision to take offensive military action against the renegade country Iraq.
Rather than doing that, the procedure was short-circuited and simply delegated to the President of the United States to make on his own. As I said in my speech, I do not think that is the way the world should work in 1991. If we are going to ensure that we do have continuing peace and security and are not subject simply to the whims of a superpower, we must hope that the world determines mechanisms that can ensure, first, that action is taken when it is necessary; but, second, by doing that we establish, a series of precedents to demonstrate that there should not be a double standard and to prevent the need for collective security from arising. That can only happen when we really do have a clear system in international law that has proven to be effective and workable. And I think we have lost that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
During the time that I have been in this House, I have felt uneasy about being a Canadian on a number of occasions, particularly with the passing of the free trade agreement, uneasy about Canada's loss of its independent economic objectives, with the slashing of social programs, with what that has done to the caring and compassionate society that Canada has a reputation for. But never have I felt so uneasy about being a Canadian as I have over these last few days at witnessing the outbreak of war against Iraq and this government's actions. I know that many Canadians share that unease. I will mention the extent to which my constituents have voiced their concerns to me in a moment.
Canadians know that this House is debating whether or not going to war against Iraq in pursuit of efforts to get Iraqi troops out of Kuwait was right or wrong. It has taken place, but that is what we are debating now, as to whether or not it was right or wrong.
Let me at the outset make my position perfectly clear. Along with millions of Canadians, I am firmly opposed to this government's decision to support war. I am opposed

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
to this government's decision to deploy Canada's young men and women in an offensive military role. I am opposed to this government's decision to involve Canada in an unnecessary and deadly war.
The decision to attack Iraq was and remains a morally unacceptable one. War in all its forms is madness. It seems incredible that the lessons of the past have not been learned. Have we learned nothing over the years? What will it take for this government and for President Bush to realize that the military offensive will solve nothing?
We all have a moral responsibility to stop this madness, to stop the carnage, to stop the killing of tens of thousands of people who just happen to have been born in Iraq, people who have no responsibility for the actions of Saddam Hussein. This war will have and is having severe political, economic, environmental and human costs, costs that could have been avoided if this government, the U.S. government and other governments had been as committed to peace as they have been to war.
This war is madness. Church groups the world over have pointed out that the unspeakable loss of innocent civilian lives is unacceptable on moral grounds. There can be no getting away from that. Those who support this military offensive have no choice but to accept some responsibility for the so many innocent people who have been killed and who will be killed as a result of this military offensive against Iraq. That is my position and that is as clearly as I can state it. But let me also make it clear that I share the world's revulsion at the actions of Saddam Hussein. It is reprehensible and immoral, and there can be no getting away from that.
Let me also say that I wish for all Canadians involved in this war a safe and speedy return home.
I have wondered why over time this government appears to forget that people actually suffer from its practices, principles and legislation, from its attack, for example, on this country's social policies; that children actually go hungry because of its policies and by its refusal to put justice ahead of big business interests; that over 40,000 children die every day on this planet because Canada and other so-called civilized countries pursue the international policies they pursue, such as selling
Iraq and other dictators around the world the arms that they use to destroy innocent women, men and children.
As has been so clear over the last few days, war cannot resolve long-standing conflicts. It will only explode them wider and deeper. This war will not stop aggression but rather will accelerate the cycle of violence and revenge, and this may not be restricted just to the Middle East.
After this madness is over, then what? The killing of thousands of innocent Iraqis, Israelis, Saudis, Kuwaitis, and soldiers of the so-called allies, and injuring so many more, could well make it impossible for post-war diplomatic efforts to overcome. This massive attack on Iraq is no basis on which to build a new stable order in the region or in the world. Most likely, it will lead to years, if not decades, of vengeance and make it impossible to bring about reconciliation.
The NDP has a long and distinguished record in arguing that peaceful solutions must be sought to resolve disputes. That has not always made the New Democratic Party popular. But we and many before us have maintained these positions because we have been confident that they were, are and will remain morally right. Nothing made me so proud than to stand with my colleagues in the NDP in this House earlier this week when we alone of all members of this House voted for peace against war.
That resolution read that we support the sanctions and other activities of the United Nations, but that such support should exclude the involvement by Canada in a military attack on Iraq or Iraqi forces in Kuwait. Only the members of the New Democratic Party supported that resolution. Only the members of the New Democratic Party chose peace over war.
We alone among Canada's political parties stood with the majority of Canadians who demanded an end to the violence as a means of resolving disputes, who called for an end to the build-up to war, who called for an end to the madness, who called for peace.
We lost that point, but so did Canada and Canadians. In spite of their opposition to war and their call for peace, Canadians were dragged into war by this government. We in this House had the opportunity to speak out against Canadian forces being used to attack Iraq, and only the New Democratic Party stood with Canadians in voting for peace and against a military attack on Iraq.
January 17, 1991

While we have been urged by this government to fight for freedom and democracy in the Persian Gulf, we must remember that war is the very negation of both freedom and democracy.
The U.S. and its allies, including Canada, might win this war but only by adopting the self same tactics which we all condemn in Iraq. Canadians are appealing to this government to stop this resort to brute force and to work constructively for peace. The people of Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing, the part of Canada which I am proud to represent in this House, have been telling me to speak out against military intervention. They have told me about their conception that this war is madness, and how sad and betrayed they feel as Canadians at having their government commit our young men and women in the gulf to attack Iraq.
The people of Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing have spoken out with only a few exceptions against this war. My riding has a significant population of Canadians of Mennonite heritage. They have a fine tradition of not only speaking for peace but of acting for peace, and acting in a peaceable manner. Their ancestors suffered because of their commitment to non-violent dispute resolution and I have heard from a large number of them. They have spoken out for peace and with disappointment at this government's decision to take Canada into a war.
I am reminded of the Cuban missile crisis when then Prime Minister Diefenbaker refused to be drawn into a potential war with Cuba, which the U.S. threatened to do. And that was in our own backyard, so to speak. Mr. Diefenbaker stood for an independent military role for Canada and we all were, and are, thankful for that. This government had the opportunity to stand for the same thing and refused.
As many experts point out, it seems that a so-called victory against Iraq will only lead to greater instability, greater hostility and greater conflict in the Middle East. It will not, it cannot solve anything. There will still need to be diplomacy and peacekeeping efforts after this war is all over.
Where once Canada would have had the international credibility to participate actively in these critical and creative activities it has, by its declaration of war against Iraq, forfeited any credibility in this dispute and perhaps in disputes to come. Canada cannot expect to be an
Government Orders
enemy one minute and an impartial arbitrator the next. For many Canadians this is the saddest part of this whole episode. Canada's reputation as a peaceable, peaceful and peacekeeping country has been seriously compromised. It is tragic indeed that one of the first results of the end of the cold war is a war. Have we really learned nothing?
Let us not forget the advice of so many experts, including the head of the CIA, William Webster, and United States Admiral Crowe, former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, that sanctions were working and, given enough time, would have worked to get Iraq out of Kuwait. Impatience and suffering do not justify war and even greater suffering.
In terms of support for the United Nations, we in the New Democratic Party and I personally, have supported every United Nations resolution which advocated a peaceful resolution to the crisis. We supported 11 out of the 12 Security Council resolutions. However, we did not support UN Security Council resolution 678 which imposed the January 15 deadline for Iraqi withdrawal and which authorized the use of force after this date. We oppose that resolution and we will continue to oppose that resolution. The United Nations Association in Canada is also concerned about the role that the United Nations played in this conflict.
I think that we will find over time that the United Nations has been irretrievably harmed by its actions over the last few months. Canada still has a role in resolving and stopping this war. Canada should work with all its energies towards diplomatic efforts to stop this war. It should press for an international conference aimed at resolving the situation in the whole Middle East region. It should argue for effective measures to resolve conflicts in the region, including solutions to border disputes. It should provide any and all humanitarian aid it can.
It should work as hard for peace as some have worked for war. Canada can offer so much, could have done so much, and can continue to do so much for world peace. It really is tragic for all of us that instead Canada chose war.
In closing, if the Prime Minister wants a fight, if there is a fight, I will fight with him. If there is a war, I will fight with him the war against poverty in this country and around the world, the war against hunger, the war
Government Orders

January 17, 1991

against homelessness, the war against violence and racism, the war against unemployment and the abuse of women and children, the war against illiteracy, a war in favour of saving our planet and protecting our environment, and a war in favour of ensuring dignity for all Canadians. I will fight that war with him, but he needs to get his priorities straightened out. Money was available for war but not available for hungry children.

Mr. Speaker, when you unleash the dogs of war, you never know on whom they will turn.

That is my message to the aggressors of this world. [English]
On August 2, Saddam Hussein invaded a smaller neighbouring country. At that point, our government did not see fit to recall Parliament. However, the United Nations Security Council deplored this act and unanimously imposed economic sanctions on August 6. Still, no recall of Parliament, until the very end of September.
During the fall session, little information was given to Parliament. Sanctions were not given enough time. No report was given to Parliament regarding sanctions. The government decided that it would be best just to meet in cabinet-

*. .secretly, never providing any information. The government always kept Parliament in the dark.

The government refused to have Parliament meet at the end of December and waited until January 15, a very infamous date. Prior to the Christmas season and after, it preferred committing our military to the gulf without proper debate and without giving sanctions the proper amount of time. That I deplore greatly, because it does not inform the full Parliament, it does not provide for unity in Canada when we are faced with a major horrific catastrophe in the world.
Did the sanctions work? Never has the committee of the United Nations ever reported on it. Our government did not report to Parliament. We have heard that it was
40 per cent effective and becoming more and more effective. This is what we understood.

But it was always information received indirectly, from outside sources.
Was enough time allowed for the sanctions to work? We don't know. Our party was in favour of negotiations and peace. Our party wanted sanctions but at the same time insisted on peace negotiations. That is the whole philosophy of the Liberal Party.
I heard the Prime Minister and members of cabinet mention Mr. Pearson's name several times. It was Pearson here and Pearson there, but always to justify their position, their philosophy, their approach. I noticed they always took what Mr. Pearson said out of context, to justify their own decisions. What I find really sickening is the way they suddenly changed Canada. This country used to be a proponent of peacekeeping.

Canada used to be a world renoun peacekeeper until our present government changed this.
How will we ever become neutral peacekeepers from now on? This is really a vety important question. This is really a turnaround in Canadian policy. We did not give sanctions, in my estimation, enough time.
If the government finds that this is incorrect, then I would add that it did not give Parliament enough information to know whether or not sanctions had been given enough time. All this time the Prime Minister made arbitrary decisions.
I made a survey in Carleton-Gloucester prior to the infamous date of January 15. We discovered that people wanted a negotiated peace and preferred sanctions.

On January 15,1 met a group of students from a school in Orleans, the Ecole elementaire Reine-des-Bois, accompanied by their school principal, Mr. Ouellet. The students arrived with a huge sign, a petition signed by all the students and asking the government and Parliament to discuss peace and only peace.
Phone calls and letters I received from my constituents in Carleton-Gloucester were about peace, not war. Parliament was not reconvened until January 15. I was here every day during the holidays, except for Christmas, and I noticed several members of the opposition were
January 17, 1991

here as well. We still hoped the government would be called back. Unfortunately, our Prime Minister preferred to act as though the British parliamentary system did not exist. Under this system, Parliament must sit so there can be dialogue and debate and the opinions of all parties can be heard. That did not happen. The only thing we saw was the Prime Minister acting like a company director.

-the Board of Directors to make decisions and then only to inform the shareholders.

In the motion that was presented and which I will quote in my speech, the government moved, on January 15 of all days:

That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.

My conclusion is that this kind of motion is fuzzy, unspecific, and full of interpretations.

The Liberal amendment moved that day was worded as follows:

That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression of Iraq against Kuwait through the continued use of economic sanctions, such support to exclude offensive military action by Canada at this time.
That is le quinze janvier. There was no military offensive, autre mots, at this time. This was voted on, may I point out, prior to the 6.45 p.m. announcement of war; the hostilities had taken place.
The NDP amendment read:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait through the continued use of economic sanctions, such support to exclude the involvement by Canada in a military attack on Iraq or Iraqi forces in Kuwait.
Government Orders
That meant, autre mots, no military offensive ever. [Translation]
And that is still the NDP's policy: Never defend yourself. However, at 6.45 p.m. on that fateful day after the motion was presented, the attack started and war was effectively declared.
At this point I would like to quote a letter sent to the Prime Minister by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops on January 18, 1991. I will quote only the most important part-and this is from the Canadian bishops- which reads as follows: "We maintain this war should never have started. Economic sanctions and diplomatic mechanisms were not given enough time to be successful". The letter was signed by Robert Lebel, Bishop of Valleyfield, President of the Conference.
Hostilities started at 6.45 p.m. on January 16.

The motion by the government then became in my mind absolutely redundant. The government agenda is really the question here. What was its political agenda? Was it double-tracking with military the agenda of another country or countries? What did our government know?

What did it not share with all members of Parliament? I say the Prime Minister did not share that information. We all heard on television about the President of the U.S.S.R.

The President of U.S.S.R. apparently was informed one hour prior to the invasion. It is a well-known fact that when hostilities of this nature occur, especially when the United Nations is involved, the major country involved informs colleagues, friends, especially allies, and most especially those with whom it is going to fight shoulder to shoulder.
I suspect strongly that the Prime Minister knew before 6.45 p.m.-and he knew when he tabled that motion- that war was to take place the very same day he convened Parliament. He knew and did not inform Parliament. I do not find that proper in a parliamentaiy system.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
The government motion, in my mind, is now irrelevant; it is redundant.
Saddam Hussein then decided the next day, January 16, to attack Israel.

I think Saddam Hussein is a devil and a madman. We should put in his place right away. We now have another ally to defend, in this case Israel.

I must congratulate Israel for the restraint it has presented to date.

It has been attacked constantly. It knows how to defend themselves, and I admire Israel for holding back now. I condemn Saddam Hussein for attacking a country that was at peace, a country that did not attack first. We must protect our allies. We must protect the other countries.
We know that 6.45 p.m. is now history. Hostilities have started. There is a war on. I think this whole debate has become redundant. I fail to understand why the government is so anxious to have members debating all day and all night, non-stop. We should take advantage of this moment to unite.
Look at Israel, for instance. Are the parties in Israel's Parliament at each other's throats, launching accusations, making stupid remarks and contradicting each other? No, they are united. That is what we should be today. Now that hostilities have started, now that a war is on and Israel, a country that was at peace, is being attacked, we must realize everything has changed. The Parliament of Canada, the government, the opposition and independent members should stand together, because our common objective is peace.

We must stand together. We must support our Armed Forces in the gulf. Presently their activities are in sweep and escort operations que j'appuis. I have one compliment to give to our government, and that is its decision to provide a field hospital.

I am sure that all Canadians will agree, whatever their political affiliation, that providing a field hospital is a positive gesture, entirely in line with the philosophy of Lester B. Pearson.

That was a proper decision, if there was one. This country must support the United Nations. This country must be united. Parliament must be united. The allies must be united. We must be united in all our actions to secure peace.

I have to say this, and I am not ashamed, that every night before I go to sleep, I pray for our forces and for peace. I would urge everyone who is not actively involved in activities in the gulf, other than talking, dialoguing and trying to find a way to bring peace, to find time during the day to say a prayer for peace, for mankind, for the men and women involved, whether they are on active duty in the Persian Gulf or happen to be parents in Canada, the United States or Europe, throughout the world. Our main purpose in life should always be peace and happiness for ourselves and others during our short lives on this earth.

Mr. Speaker, I have an observation, a comment on the member's speech. One of the things that I wanted to clear up for the record is the fact that the Secretary' of State for External Affairs did report to the Standing Committee of External Affairs and International Trade on December 10. On that day he went through the use of sanctions and the effects of sanctions on Iraq. I just wanted to bring that to the member's attention.
In summation on December 10, 1990, the minister said that sanctions were necessary but not sufficient to meet our declared objectives: the withdrawal of Iraq from Kuwait and the restoration of its sovereignty and legitimate government.
I wanted to bring that to the member's attention. I do not think it is a whole lot different from the conclusion of his former leader on Wednesday in this House. The member handed out a compliment to our government. I

will hand out a compliment to the member in exchange. Although the member disagreed with his former leader on Wednesday, I do give him credit for sitting here, on camera, throughout that speech. I think that tells us something about the member in question.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Carleton-Charlotte for his compliments. I always admired his sincerity.
I want to tell my colleague who made these comments in response to my speech, if I may, that it is in fact up to cabinet to give proof of the effect of the sanctions, whether they worked or not. We should not have to play guessing games and government backbenchers should not have to make comments. I suggest the burden of the proof lies with the ministers.
Before closing, I must remind the hon. member that a UN committee was to report on the sanctions. As far as I know, there has been no such report yet, unless the hon. member or the Prime Minister are once more withholding information from members of this House.

Mr. Speaker, as you have probably noticed, today the focus of the debate is rapidly shifting, if not by the hour, certainly by the day. When we started debating the deadline for the sanctions, diplomatic initiatives came to mind. There was still hope and still some time left. We have gradually moved from that analysis in our debate to a discussion of the role of the armed forces on escalation, to bringing hostilities to an end, and to rebuilding peace on the ruins caused by this war.
Parliament was recalled when the clock was almost striking midnight. It was at the very last minute that Parliament was recalled and it certainly did not give parliamentarians a sense that our debate and our vote was meaningful in relations to the events outside this building and away from the Hill. Unfortunately, that was not an isolated case. There is a pattern.
I would like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that in August of last year Canadian ships were committed by the Prime Minister after he met President Bush and two
Government Orders
weeks before the United Nations Security Council approved the sanctions on August 25.
In September, Canadian CF-18 aircraft were committed 10 days before the recall of Parliament.
I must also bring to your attention the fact that Canadian ships had to delay their arrival in Suez in September in order to circumvent the legal requirements that Parliament be recalled within 10 days of a warship going on active service.
I do not need to remind you that in November, when the Security Council set the deadline of January 15, the Secretary of State for External Affairs downplayed the deadline by calling it artificial. Well, events have shown us how artificial that deadline was.
In January, Parliament was given 13 hours this week before the deadline came into effect to start the debate. When the bombs began to fall on Baghdad, we found ourselves in the midst of this debate.
Evidently, there is something wrong in the consultation process on the part of the Prime Minister with his own Cabinet and on the part of the Prime Minister with his own Parliament.
The people of Canada, of whom Parliament is a reflection, have not had much to say in this debate. Canada went to war before Parliament could complete this debate. The decision of course was made some time ago, long before Canadian CF-18 pilots would escort bombing runs over Iraq and Kuwait, and long before KC-135 tanker planes would refuel U.S. bombers in the gulf region. This lack of participation on the part of the Canadian people through its parliamentary system is only one of several disturbing facets of what has happened in recent weeks and months.
At this stage, as we are concluding this debate tonight, we realize that the demands of the war machine are virtually insatiable. There will be demands for more Canadian participation. There will be demands for ground troops, for combat troops and the like. We do not really know where Canadians stand on this matter. Maybe it would be fair to assume that the Canadian public is as divided on this matter as this Parliament is. It is legitimate to ask whether Canadians want war to resolve the Kuwait problem. Do Canadians want to see Canada participate in a U.S.-led war, mandated by a Security Council consisting of only 15 nations, albeit very

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
powerful ones? Do we, as parliamentarians, really know what lies ahead?
There are several dangers that must be outlined and put on record, as we can see them today, on behalf of the Canadian people who expect us to make a decision and cast a vote with the best of our ability to look into the future.
The first danger that might face us very soon is that this war might become a confrontation between the West and the Muslim world. It is an horrendous prospect. If this were to happen, it would turn the clock back, not a decade, or a century, but several centuries. It is something that must not happen, but it is a very possible danger.
Another danger that comes to mind is that of a complete dissipation of Canada's international reputation as a referee, as a peacemaker, and as a nation that does not take sides in a war, but does attempt to resolve conflict and has the confidence of the parties involved. This is a role that Canada has increasingly enjoyed in the world. This is an asset that is very important abroad because it has an enormous amount of positive benefits.
This dissipation, is something that is of profound concern to many of us. It is a dissipation on the international scene which we are witnessing at home in a more tangible manner. We see it in institutions that bind east with west and north with south, institutions such as the CBC or Via Rail. Dissipation has also taken place in the last six years in federal-provincial relations.
A third area of danger has to do with the environment. This is not the time to go into greater depth in this matter. Scientists have elaborated and made some rather disturbing forecasts as to what could be the damage to the environment by the production of dangerous gases should an oil field take fire as a result of war activities.
Fourth, there is danger in the presence in Muslin countries of foreign aid projects which are run by western volunteers. Those initiatives have a profound significance in a variety of ways, particularly in Asia and in some parts of Africa, and they might be in danger if there were a serious backlash on the part of Muslin communities to the presence of western volunteers.
What must we do? We cannot stop at outlining dangers. We we also have to look at the future and explore, where we can, what Canada's role could be during these hostilities and after the conclusion of the war. I will just dwell on one of these two topics very briefly. That is the role of our Armed Forces which my colleague from Ottawa South has touched upon. It has a particular significance and could be of importance to our future.
I refer to the fact that we have fewer than 2,000 men and women involved in these hostilities less. In relation to the 500,000 Armed Forces personnel involved in that theatre as members of the U.S. led force, our participation is marginal. It represents probably less than 1 per cent of the total forces.
Our participation during this war, of course, can be of two kinds, one offensive and the other defensive, and we have a choice. We can make a choice between either of these two roles. We can make a decision and make a shift because the numbers involved are not so large.
I submit that instead of being involved in offensive exercises, such as air raids, fighting on the ground, attacking installations, and any other offensive activities of a military nature, we could expand and reinforce and become fully involved in medical services, support services in field hospitals, in the care of the wounded, in the protection of those involved in the provision of these services, and the like, in other words, in a humanitarian defensive role within a military context. I think that Canada would have enormous respect if it were to perform such a role. It would then not be seen as being part of an attacking offensive contingent with destructive motivations.
As I said, our forces are small and therefore it should be reasonably easy to shift our presence from the offensive to the defensive. It would also be a role that would be readily identifiable and permit us to build confidence in Canada in the Muslim regions of the world where these events are being watched very carefully and very closely.
When the war is over, hopefully very soon, the building of peace in the Middle East will have to start. We will be looking at the ruins and devastation, both in human and material terms. Confidence will have to be restored and it will have to replace confrontation. We will have to build confidence and we will have to build on
January 17, 1991

confidence. It is during these hostilities that Canada can lay the foundation for confidence building for the period following the war.
Therefore, the role of Canada's Armed Forces is of great importance from the point of view of Canada's particular interest and Canada's particular role internationally. There is an interest that we might look for.
We are a middle power. We will want to develop we will have to develop, new relations in this part of the world which by then will be war torn and in shambles.
In conclusion, at the same time we will have to look at a United Nations, its role, and the way it functions. In so doing, we will have to look at the charter under which it operates and at the Security Council which is its main engine and executive centre.
At this point in history, the charter is 45 years old. Obviously it needs to be re-examined and reshaped. It needs to reflect the new face of the world community, the family of nations, because today it has over 150 member nations, compared to the 60 or 70 it had in San Francisco in 1945.
If we do that-and I would urge that we should do that-the question of the veto power has to be examined. The veto power is given to the five most powerful nations, and they can determine the direction of the world at times by just saying no. We should be asking some difficult questions, including: Why should any of these five nations be given the power to say no? Is this power still relevant? Does it serve the interest of the world community? If it does not, then we should ask ourselves whether this power, which may have had historical meaning and been a necessity in 1945, ought to be removed so as to place all members of the Security Council on a equal footing.
This concept has emerged in recent decades in many other institutions where fewer and fewer privilege powers are assigned to a limited number of individuals. That concept has also to reach within the walls of the United Nations Security Council, I submit.
These and other questions must be tackled soon if the world community is to be truly reflected and represented through the decisions of the Security Council. As the charter is written now, I doubt that it is the case. I do not need to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the decision of
Government Orders
setting the deadline for the sanctions made by the Security Council has set history in a direction which we, on this side of the House believe to be the wrong direction for humanity to take.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a short comment on some of the opening remarks of the hon. member in relation to public opinion and whether or not we are doing the right thing.
It is up to the people of Canada to determine whether the government in fact is doing the right thing, but I would like to quote some numbers. I know it depends on whose figures you are looking at and whether they are right or wrong. They are from January 17.
The majority of Canadians, 71 per cent, approve of Canada's actions to date in the gulf. This represents a change from January 15 when it was about 58 per cent. The majority of Canadians, 77 per cent, favour maintaining or increasing our military commitment. An interesting statistic is that only 11 per cent favour withdrawing all forces from the region. Of course, withdrawing all forces from the region was a position that the Leader of the Opposition took just four short days ago.
In response to public opinion, no one knows whether they are right or wrong, and I don't think any politician should put his faith in public opinions. For what it is worth, I just wanted to pass that on to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that implicit in that information on the part of the member is the question of whether or not I concur with his findings. As he quite rightly pointed out, it is a well-known fact that one selects statistics very carefully in order to make one's point, and I am sure the hon. member has chosen those statistics very carefully.
The hon. member also knows that Gallup polls change considerably and that the very' same data could dramatically change almost overnight if casualties were to begin to happen. That was demonstrated by a poll taken in the United States where the support of American public opinion would decline very rapidly as the number of possible casualties increased. In a way, that is a sad statement because it would seem that we assign a price to life that depends on the number of victims and it determines whether or not we are in favour of the use of

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
force, depending on the number of lives that would be lost as a result of that activity.
I would point out to the hon. member that according to him 11 per cent of Canadians were in favour of withdrawing from the region. Withdrawing from the region is not such a bad idea if we start with the premise that we do not believe in using force in resolving the situation in Kuwait.
For Canada to perform a role as a peacemaker or referee in this matter, maintaining its reputation, would not have been such a bad idea, withdrawing once the hostilities had started. It would have shown a high degree of sensitivity on our part for the solution for which we are all searching, a solution other than the use of war.
I would not be surprised if, in the weeks and months ahead, Canadian public opinion were to shift in a direction much less supportive of the war initiative than it is now. That process of declining support is already in place, in my understanding of the polls.

Briefly, Mr. Speaker. I have a question for the hon. member for Davenport. The member and most of his colleagues referred to various types of sanctions and suggested the sanctions against Iraq should have been intensified.
I would like to know if he agrees with the official position taken by his party on December 21, 1980. On page 4 of this statement, we read that it is the position of the Liberal Party that Canada should ask Turkey to cut off water supply and to restrict food supply. In other words, should we starve and deprive of water the civilian population of Iraq to retaliate to Saddam Hussein's aggression on Kuwait? Is that an acceptable position for a country like ours to refuse to implement the fundamental principles set out in the UN's Charter of rights which states that it is illegal to cut off water supply and deprive people of food, especially civilians?

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out to my colleague that our party's position is clearly stated in the first part of our release.
We explained why we agreed with the government on one point, taking up what I consider to be a very positive
stand. We also discussed the points on which we were at variance regarding the sanctions the hon. member referred to. The validity of that measure may be debatable, but our position should not be rejected on the basis of a detail regarding the implementation of the sanctions. We must take a global approach. It is true that, from an ideological point of view, we are taking two different stands. There is the position of the hon. member's party that war is the answer, and there is ours that sanctions are the answer.
We need more time to prove that political and economic pressures are the key to finding the appropriate solution. If my colleague wishes to go into the merits of this proposal, I am prepared to examine them with him. I am convinced that together we could come to an agreement.

There is some concern about proportionate representation of speakers and I wonder if hon. members would just give me a moment to consider it. I want to be very fair here.
