Keeping in mind the number of members, the number of members of parties, and the number of Independents and members of the bloc who have taken part in the debate-and I know the hon. member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie would co-operate with the Chair-I am going to call the member for Okanagan-Shuswap, followed by the hon. member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie. We will then move over to a Liberal member.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap, and then the hon. member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie.
January 17, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate your judicious judgment this evening.
It goes without saying that the last few days have indeed been difficult days for every member of this House, and I speak in a very non-partisan manner on this. This issue has faced Parliament over the last few days. When we initiated the debate on this resolution, we were in fact not yet in a situation of war. Since then, the situation in the world has preceded the debate in the House of Commons. Suffice it to say that the issue was whether or not Parliament should in fact be sending Canada's young men and women into battle and now the extension of the debate is to decide just what the extent of that commitment should be.
It is a very deep personal and moral issue that every member of the House has been struggling with over the the past week. That is why the New Democratic Party, in its wisdom, with regard to members voting on this resolution before the House, had decided to free its members to speak their own conscience and to vote freely as they felt personally. We were disappointed that the government did not see the merits of a free and unhindered vote on such an issue of personal conviction.
As we have debated over the last few days, profound changes have taken place in the world around us. There has been a failure to secure a peaceful and diplomatic solution to the crisis in the Middle East. With this failure, the 28-nation coalition of the United Nations has seen to exercise its final and tragic option. The world is once again at war.
No one can condone the brutal annexation of Kuwait by Saddam Hussein. I think I speak for all members to say that dictators like Hussein must never be allowed to oppress other nations. We made the mistake in the Second World War, and I think all nations were very concerned that we do not make that mistake again. That is why the 28-member coalition of the United Nations moved to turn back that aggression. That is why the international embargo against trade with Iraq was implemented. That is why the United Nations served notice that Hussein must withdraw from Kuwait. That is why the economic blockade was implemented.
This brings me to a critical point, the economic blockade. The economic blockade against Iraq was in fact beginning to bite and beginning to bite hard. Striking
Government Orders
evidence was given back in December by the United States Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, Mr. William Webster, that the Iraqi exports had in fact at that time been slashed by some 97 per cent. That was even greater than the cuts that were made to the imports to Iraq, which were at that time slashed by some 90 per cent.
U.S. Defence Secretary, Dick Cheney, a few months ago said that the sanctions and the embargo were beginning to have an impact. It was back a couple of months ago. He admitted that the UN trade embargo had clearly been effective, and I quote, "in closing off the spare parts in military supplies".
The Baghdad regime was inexorably running out. It was running out of the commodity which it so desperately required, the commodity of money. Its oil reserves are the drip-feed of Baghdad's life support system. Without them, without the ability to sell its oil and use that cash to purchase armaments and supplies, I submit that the dictatorship would have ultimately perished.
It begs the question which has been asked time and time again in this House also why the decision was made to draw an arbitrary line in the sands of time on January 15 and say that at that date negotiations would cease and the trigger would be pulled. Why was that deadline imposed? Why was President Bush not prepared to allow time for the sanctions to bite harder?
There have been many arguments presented in the House with regard to that critical point. Some members have stated that it would take too long for the embargo to take hold. Others have said that it would be unlikely that the coalition of nations could have held together for that long. It would begin to disintegrate and therefore it would be emasculated. It has been said elsewhere that it would be too costly to maintain that embargo, but how costly is the price of war? How costly is the price of human life?
There have been other arguments, I submit valid arguments, that given time would also have allowed Hussein to muster the forces, to reinforce the troops, and to dig in even deeper. I am not a military strategist and I do not know the answers to these questions. It may be correct; it may not be. I am not in a position in terms of a military strategy to argue the truth of these points.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
The fact remains that sufficient time was not given for those sanctions to take hold.
I heard an argument earlier this evening from one of the members on the government side that the economic blockade was in fact hurting the poor, the lower income earners, and the women and children of Iraq. Is bombing them more humanitarian and more humane? I submit that it is not.
The critical point that I want to make-and it has been made by other members of my caucus and it has been made by members of the Liberal opposition-is that insufficient time was given to exhaust all possible diplomatic and economic actions before that final tragic decision had to be made. Time was not given to squeeze Hussein until he finally realized he had to leave.
The war which now engulfs the Middle East may well have been inevitable. Perhaps waiting longer may have made it worse, but we will never know the answer to that question. I cannot help but feel that we may have moved in too fast. For the love of God, we should have waited longer. The price of human life is simply too precious to sacrifice. This war was premature and this war is also incompatible with the long-term interests for the area of the Middle East. It is incompatible with the restoration of peace in the area.
Canada's involvement with the economic blockade is very much justified and its continued involvement unfortunately now jeopardizes its traditional and historical role as a peacekeeping nation. It has tarnished our reputation. It has bloodied Canadian hands.
Having said that, I want to say: Don't get me wrong on this. No one can condone the actions of Saddam Hussein. No one can condone the atrocities that were perpetrated upon Kuwait. No one can justify the military annexation of another country. No one can tolerate the pillaging that took place, the plundering of villages, and the raping of women and children. No one can tolerate that kind of inhumane action. Hussein had to be stopped. That is, indeed, the bottom line.
Let us also remember that the apocalyptic scenario of modern warfare, with the chemical and biological weaponry, and the potential for nuclear retaliation, serves as a
potent reminder that diplomacy has always been and will always be the best possible solution.
The economic sanctions were working. Given time, we could have ground Hussein into an abject and bloodless surrender, but the decision was made to discontinue the diplomatic path, to pull the trigger.
I want to submit to the House that it is really ironic when we look at it. It was the Americans themselves who armed Iraq, who trained Iraqi soldiers, who assisted Iraq in its fight with Iran, and who taught it the technology of modern warfare. Now we see the sleek missiles supplied by the Americans are in fact being launched against them. I think that fact alone speaks volumes about the ultimate consequences of the international arms trade.
We should keep in mind that the enemy is not the Iraqi people. The enemy is a dictatorial tyrant by the name of Saddam Hussein. I fear for the Iraqi people tonight for they are the ones who are to be the most devastated in this tragedy.
It is ironic that the technological wizardry of modern warfare has made it ever more deadly and pin-point accurate. Surgical is a word that has been used-and the same technology that has brought about modem warfare brings it right into our living rooms. We can turn it off. We can watch commercials. As we are having dinner, we can see the surgical strikes. It is in fact sanitized. It is a sanitized war. People have been clustered about their televisions watching commanders explaining surgical strikes and neutralizing targets, kicking ass, high-tech style.
It has eliminated the human element of war, the human tragedy of war. While it is very crucial we have the information through the media, at the same time I fear that it has desensitized this nation and will desensitize us further. It makes it easier to accept war the next time.
I want to put it into context with a passage written by Mr. Christopher Black, a Toronto lawyer and freelance writer. He writes of war, saying: "This country, for reasons still veiled behind platitudes of freedom and standing up to aggression, has begun the journey into a world of unimaginable terror, a world of disciplined and sanctioned murder, of gaping wounds and blackened burned flesh, of young men screaming in agony, of the inferno of flame-throwers, napalm, disintegrating planes
January 17, 1991

Government Orders
and tanks blazing in the desert night, a world of spilled intestines and swollen, stinking death". That is the reality. That is the human element of war and that is why all war is wrong.
This war need not have been, at least not yet. It was premature. It was unnecessary, but now that the trigger has been pulled it is no longer our choice. We are involved. I want to make it perfectly clear that in that context Canada, as a member of the United Nations has agreed to abide by these decisions.
Now that push has come to shove, it is my personal perspective that Canada should continue to play an active role within that United Nations alliance. But what should our role be? Should it in fact be an offensive role, a role of attack and destroy? I submit that it should not. Apart from the F-18s, Canada really does not have the kind of military muscle and the technological acumen to participate in offensive action.
Canada has a moral obligation as a nation known for its peacekeeping abilities to work within the alliance in a very positive way to seek an end to the tragedy of warfare. It can, and it should, play a vital role in the provision of medical and humanitarian aid. It can, and it should, continue to provide defensive cover for the ships in the gulf.
There is a role for Canada in this theatre of war. We simply cannot cut and run. But our role should be a role of humanitarian medical aid and defensive cover. It should not be offensive. It should reflect our continued resolve to right what has become a terrible wrong.
I have no doubt the resolution of this crisis will prove crucial to the collective future of the United Nations and in fact crucial to the future of world democracy.
As I close, I want to state again that dictators such as Saddam Hussein have to be stopped. That is the bottom line. That is the final option.
In addition to that comment, I can only say that it is tragically unfortunate that to do so the world community had to exercise that final option and enter the theatre of war. I hope and pray that we do not have to do so in the future.

I want to congratulate my hon. colleague on his excellent speech. I must remind him, however, of the efforts, unprecedented in the history of Canadian diplomacy, that were made to prevent this war in the Persian Gulf.
The fact is that, in the 16 weeks before the Gulf war started, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, had over 50 bilateral talks with various key players. If we ou add to that the other 50 or so multilateral meetings he attended, as well as the Prime Minister's many meetings and efforts, this certainly is the largest diplomatic move ever undertaken by Canada. It may even be larger than that undertaken during WWII or when Canada provided assistance to the UN in the Korean war.
Canada did make these efforts, but it would seem that members on his side of the House do not recognize the incredible efforts Canada made so that this tragedy could be avoided. I wish my colleague would at least recognize these facts and praise the government for these unprecedented efforts.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly recognize the member's comments in terms of the historical action that Canada has played in both world wars and the Korean conflict. We did play a very proud role. Many Canadians never returned to their homeland as a result of sacrificing their lives in the cause of world freedom. There is no question about that. We all recognize that and do so every year when we attend Remembrance Day ceremonies throughout this land.
At the same time I would submit to my colleague opposite that the world is entering a new arena, where the active participation in warfare will someday no longer be required. Canada has to provide a leading role. As a traditional peacekeeping nation, as a nation that has sought to find the diplomatic option at all costs, Canada has to continue to provide that role in whichever way it can, even when other nations are in active war. We are in this war. Let us recognize it. We do have a role to play, but I do not think our role is necessarily an offensive military role.
Let us face it, we are not a superpower nation. Admittedly, we do not have the technological acumen and the training for offensive action that the U.S. troops

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
and the troops of Great Britain have. Traditionally we have played a different role in modern times. I think that we have to continue to do that.
Particularly in light of the conflict that is facing us in the Persian Gulf, we have to recognize that there is going to be great need for medical assistance. We are setting up a field hospital a few short kilometres from what could be described as the front line. We fully support that. The provision of medical aid is going to be a critical necessity if the war ends up being a protracted war. There is going to be a great need for humanitarian aid. With Jordan opening its borders to refugees, there is going to be a flood of refugees out of the Middle East. Canada must play a vital role in providing assistance for those refugees.
I recognize the fact that we had to seek the military option in previous years, but that does not mean that it commits us to an offensive military option in modem times.

As I rise to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker, Canada is at war and the prevailing sentiment is deep concern.
Those who were for war are wondering how long it will last, how many lives will be lost, and what will happen after that. Those who were against are wondering whether there is anything that can be done against that war. Should they give up and passively let the current carry them? And, like the others, they also wonder how many lives will be lost. Just where can this war lead us? Was it worth it, particularly when we see and hear since the beginning that an attack against Israel might very well trigger retaliation, and Israel would have every reason indeed to defend herself and protect her people against an attack?
That, however, would completely alter the course, the scope, and the intensity of the war. What would happen in Jordan, Syria, Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria under pressure from their people? Would they side with Saddam Hussein? And Mauritania and Turkey, are they not making Saddam Hussein the hero of the Arab world? Did the world, our planet, deserve to be drawn into such a risky endeavour, on the eve of the year 2000, in year one after the cold war?
Many hopes have been lost now, particularly among younger people. Polls show that Canadians are against war and want peace. I am glad to see these thousands of people throughout the world, even in the United States; I think about the 300,000 men and women demonstrated in Germany, and the many Canadians who took to the street in Quebec and Montreal marched for peace.
Right now that is the most encouraging indication for the future. That feeling of peace must now become the foundation of the new international order where state-to-state relations will be governed by right rather than might, something which, as early as the 18th century, Emmanuel Kant kept hoping for and called the universal republic. In this morning's Le Droit, Adrien Cantin wrote that we must prepare for post-war times right now.
It aptly sums up what I feel and what I think today. I did not rise to while time away, for as an elected member I believe that in such circumstances we do have a role to play. We have every indication that the people of Quebec and other Canadians want peace. Since the past is oftentimes our garantee for the future, it would be appropriate to examine our conscience. Questions have to be addressed to the government right here in the House. Why are we at war? How come we have reached this point?
We all know that the United States, Japan and the European Economic Community had domestic policy priorities with respect to this war, particularly their oil supplies. We all know as well that the United States play the role of policeman in the world, and is always closely linked to ever stiffer international competition to find and maintain new markets.
But does Canada have such domestic policy priorities? Oil? I doubt it, considering that Canada is an oil producing country. For example, Quebec gets only 1.2 per cent of its oil supplies from the Middle East, from Saudi Arabia. It could not be argued that this is an absolute strategic requirement. We also know that Canada has never used strong-arm tactics to secure a place on international markets, which explains our country's excellent reputation.
This is certainly why, when trying to justify our Armed Forces' involvement in this war, the Mulroney government never put forward any other argument then Canada's good name.
January 17, 1991

Again, there are more questions than answers. In what have Canada's best interests been better served since August 2, than since January 16, when the war started. Finally, has Canada a policy for the Middle East and, if so, what is it? How could the Canadian government drag us so deeply in to this war without being politically and morally responsible for the men, women and children who will die? How could it fail to explain to us, without being asked, what situation is likely to develop after the war?
Has Canada a policy for the Middle East? Has Canada recognized the need to call a peace conference for the Middle East, on the basis of all and I emphasize the word all-UN resolutions concerning that area? What is its opinion about the political stability of that area? Has it many proposals to make?
How does it think it will be possible, should the allied forces prevail, to ensure Kuwait's security? Does it know how long our Armed Forces will remain there? Does it feel that Canada's good name in the world has been enhanced by this diplomacy which does not reflect in any way our country's strategic interests and resemble much too closely, for instance that of the United States?
If Canada had actively pursued a new diplomatic approach for the Middle East, an approach based on the need for an international peace conference in that area, which would recognize the absolute necessity, definitely solve the Palestinian issue, to create a Palestinian state, I sincerely believe that Canada would have been better served, that its reputation would have been enhanced and that peace could have been maintained.
When I arrived here, my position was this: Denounce Iraq's aggression against Kuwait and demand the withdrawal of Iraqi forces; maintain the economic sanctions against Iraq with the participation of our military forces; oppose all active involvement of our Armed Forces in actual combat; and finally support as much as possible all diplomatic efforts which might result in an international conference on the Middle East situation.
This conference should deal with the problems of Kuwait, Lebanon, Cyprus, Palestine, as well as the whole issue of the relations between Israel and its Arabs neighbors. If we really want to see the light at the end of the tunnel in that region, taking into account the need to protect the strategic interest, of western countries and
Government Orders
above all, the need to recognize the legitimate aspirations of these people, this international conference should address the following issues: first, the immediate withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait; second, the participation of all Middle East countries and nations, including the PLO; third, the PLO's recognition of Israel's basic right to exist as a state; fourth, Israel's recognition of a Palestinian State.
I wish to emphasize that all these conditions are contained in resolutions already adopted by the United Nations, an organization which would be called upon to play a vital role as'the chairman of this conference. If we want to have a fighting chance at achieving our purpose, we should avoid at all costs the temptation of trying to identify the good and the bad. Refusing all absolutism, we should refrain from trying to interpret reality in black and white.
Saddam Hussein is neither the champion of the Palestinian cause, nor the saviour of the Third World, nor a martyr to the cause of Islam. He is a dictator who for a long time enjoyed the support of Western powers, including the United States. For that matter, George Bush is not a peace and justice loving man who is adverse to all forms of aggression. He has quite a track record, from Grenada to Panama in his support of a great many dictators, including precisely Saddam Hussein.
On the other hand, we should not overlook the fact that the U.S.S.R., an important member of the Security Council, took advantage of the Middle East crisis to crush violently the legitimate aspirations of the Baltic States. It is not by resorting to such analyses, therefore, that we will be able to grasp the full meaning of reality. The only possible understanding should be based on the recognition that all men and women have the right to live their lives to the fullest, that all people have the right to express themselves, and that all countries have the right to exist. These are high ideals, but they are the only ones on which to base a true international order which would guarantee the greatest possible social justice for all.
We should not overlook the fact that in the Middle East context such Israeli leaders as Menahem Begin and Yitzhak Shamir were once terrorists themselves and that, more recently, that it was only on the express order of the supreme court of that country that the Israeli government reluctantly agreed to give out gas masks to

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Palestinians in the occupied territories, and only one per family at that.
As we must prepare for the after war period, Canada should position itself now on that basis, for this war will not eliminate the causes of the current conflict. I came here feeling that I could not support this war not because I am in principle against all wars, but because, in my heart of hearts, I felt that this war would not change anything in the gulf crisis, and the outbreak of the war has not made me change my mind.
Of course, my heart is with the men and women of Quebec and the rest of Canada who are directly involved in the war and who have been risking their lives every moment since last Wednesday. I fully support them and I sincerely hope that this war will soon be over for them. The Mulroney Government has never had and will never have my support for his action since last August 2.
We should not fail to see the forest for the trees. There are circumstances when people should not act against their principles, especially when these principles, rather than war harbour true and viable solutions for the future.
For these reasons, I will not support the government's proposal.

Mr. Speaker, I have a quick comment to make and a question to ask.
I was quite impressed by the member's speech and discourse. I was impressed by the emotion with which he spoke about Canada. Would the hon. member be good enough to speak briefly on what he thinks Canada's role should be in this war, rather than the one suggested by the government?

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the government would be well advised now to step up its diplomatic effort, for it is wrong to support that diplomacy ends in time of war. As a matter of fact, it becomes actually more intense, although it might not necessarily be visible for all to see.
Moreover, I suggest that the government should put pressure on the Americans who are definitely the true force behind the United Nations' resolution. They are in charge. Again, I suggest that the government should put pressure on the Americans and remind them that the intended objective, at least judging from the UN resolutions, is not to crush Iraq, but to ensure that the Iraqi forces leave Kuwait. Otherwise, not only would they not respect the spirit and the letter of the UN resolutions, but they would completely destabilize that area, and cause a ground swell of hatred against both the United States and the whole Western world. Canada should guard against that. I suggest that this is the type of action Canada should take at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for asking a question, because after 12 hours in the House, I want to be right next to the member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie. It's pretty hard to run to your seat to ask a question, so I appreciate the hon. member's initiative. I don't want the kids to think there is more than one of us when they see us first in one corner of the House and then somewhere else.
This is the first time I have heard the hon. member, a colleague from Quebec, speak to a matter of such importance. I am always disappointed that members generally show so little interest in international affairs. I am disappointed because I always said that one of the main reasons I was attracted to Ottawa, in addition to defending Quebec and my own identity, was my abiding interest in international affairs, and I think that as federal members our focus should be international as well as national. We don't belong at this level of government if we have no thoughts on the matter to offer our fellow Canadians.
My point is that I was pleasantly surprised by what the hon. member said. I was of course delighted, but not just because we seem to share the same views. After all, I have always respected colleagues who do not share my views, when they express them with a great deal of eloquence, intelligence and vigour. In the circumstances, some of the good speeches I have heard in the House so far included two by Bloc quebecois members. The hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean made a remarkable speech,

January 17, 1991

and in fact, in caucus I and several other members recommended that our colleagues read it very carefully. And this is certainly not someone who shares our political philosophy.
In the same vein, the hon. member for Laurier- Sainte-Marie provides a fresh and new outlook on this very dramatic situation. Another great speech we heard this afternoon was by the hon. member for Esquimalt- Jean de Fuca from British Columbia. I say, because it is getting late, and I wish people-I am not referring to members of my own party but to members of other parties-would read it. There is a man who must feel incredibly torn. He said himself: "I am a Jew." In any case, I felt I had to draw your attention to his speech, one of the great speeches like the one I just heard.
I do not really have any questions, except that I would like the hon. member to expand for a few minutes on the international conference which has never materialized. What does the hon. member think this conference would do for problems in the Middle East, since he referred to it in his speech?

I think that if the UN has a role to play, and people are talking about a new world order, there is a role here for an international organization. I think that role should be played by the UN. It should be made possible for Mr. Perez de Cuellar to hold such a conference.
Furthermore, as I pointed out this conference would include the PLO, provided it deletes from its Charter the statement that it does not recognize Israel's right to be a sovereign state. That is imperative. Similarly, I think Israel has an important role to play. What if Israel were to say: "We agree to having a peace conference and to having the PLO at the conference, we agree to a Palestinian State as provided in the resolutions passed long ago at the UN, provided the PLO recognizes Israel"? It is impossible to negotiate when one party is against the continued existence of the other party. I think that is obvious.
I think that is where we should look for a solution to these problems. Until there is a conference-today, there is a problem with Iraq. In 1967, it was Egypt, and again in 1973. There were problems in 1948. In 1956 it was Suez, and I forgot Cyprus and Lebanon-until there is a conference it is like a puzzle with a piece missing. At least at a conference, people will talk to each other.
Government Orders
The UN will be able to provide for ways to enforce its decisions, and I am thinking of economic sanctions, properly supported and applied by all countries, based on the legitimate status of the UN. I think that is how we must see international relations in the future, and not the way Foglia described this morning in La Presse, where he said he had the impression the Americans were high-tech to their fingertips but with as much brains as King Kong. That kind of approach is dangerous. It is very dangerous to let intellingence be thrust aside by technology. I am not blaming the American people. I respect them just the same. None of us is better than the next person, but we must let diplomacy take precedence over the tools of destruction. I think that is essential.
I want to thank the hon. member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie. The hon. member for Mississauga East.

Mr. Speaker, the lives of hundreds of Canadian men and women in the Persian Gulf may be snuffed out by the decisions made by this government. Politicians sitting in relative comfort and safety will again decide the fate of the soldiers on the front lines.
Cicero stated with moral authority that one should never cease to advocate for peace, for even peace-unjust as it may be-is better than the most just war. History has taught us that war involves such a train of unexpected and unlikely circumstances that no one can predict its conclusion or its consequences.
The aggression of Saddam Hussein most certainly merits the condemnation that he has drawn from Canada and the international community. We have been told of the atrocities committed against the people of Kuwait but there is no greater atrocity than war itself. Many of the same Kuwaitis whom we hope to free may not even survive their liberation. Iraqi civilians have already died and just hours ago Israeli civilians, who are far removed from the conflict in Kuwait, were struck by Iraqi missiles.
Our Prime Minister has said there was no other way. He could not wait any longer. He could not give peaceful measures any more time. The Prime Minister has told us that Canada must abandon its traditional peacekeeping role and join the assault on Iraq. Unlike the Americans,

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
the Canadian Parliament is not voting on a clear resolution taking our country into war.
For the past five and a half months this government has been creeping closer to war while denying at every step that it was going in this direction. It is the leaders of this government who are waging war, but it is the Canadian people who will suffer, particularly those in the Armed Forces and their families.
The United States Congress debated fully the arguments for war and the arguments for peace. By only a handful of votes, the United States Senate chose to press their nation into battle. Our own government, unfortunately, is not honest enough to debate the real issue at an appropriate and useful time. It was not until the day before the bombs started falling that the Prime Minister allowed debate on his government's decision to go to war. We are here tonight debating whether the UN should have given its permission for war to be waged when we know that war is already well under way.
The ministers of this government never told the Canadian public in a direct and honest way that they were dragging the nation into its first war since Korea. Once again, this government has looked south of the border for instruction. Once again the Canadian public has been bushwhacked.
The Prime Minister has said that the question before the House is a simple one. It may be simple for the government, but for the families of the Canadian men and women who will needlessly die or be maimed this question is not so simple. They will have to pay the real price of this war, not the Prime Minister.
The only noble war is the one that is never fought, that is prevented by leaders whose prime interest is the protection of human lives and who have an absolute commitment to the avoidance of unnecessary conflict. No such commitment has been shown in the Persian Gulf.
The experience in Southeast Asia taught us that, like pawns on a chess board, soldiers will be sacrificed. But the real players will shake hands and move on to the next game.
Barely 17 years ago, U.S. troops pulled out of Vietnam. Nearly 60,000 Americans had been killed and thousands more left maimed, paralysed, or psychologically dysfunctional. When the wounded returned home, they found themselves in veterans' hospitals that can only be described as slums. They faced a public that had already come to realize that the war they fought was immoral and wrong. Many of the same veterans sit in wheelchairs today and remember the role they played in the conflict that left one million Vietnamese dead and a landscape petrified by napalm and years of constant bombardment.
Vietnam was called a noble war, but there is little that is noble in killing hundreds of thousands of desperately poor people, people with few assets and no foreign interests. Today a new generation of soldiers, too young to remember the futility of Vietnam and inspired by Rambo and Schwartzneggar, are being sent to the new killing fields.
American forces are again fighting to restore a division of people imposed by another western nation decades before. Once again the enemy is a population that is overwhelmingly poor, people who will benefit the least from any spoils of war. These are the people who will be shot by American and British soldier, and bombed by allied, perhaps Canadian, planes.
The Prime Minister continues to cite human rights abuses by Iraq as a motivation to commit the greatest abuse of human rights possible, the atrocity of war. The Prime Minister allowed Canada to import $250,000 of oil each day before August 2, knowing full well that Saddam Hussein had used chemicals weapons against his own civilian population.
It is hypocritical for this government now to claim to be overcome by an attack of principle, when events no more horrendous took place in Kuwait. The decision taken by the U.S. to go to war over Kuwait is particularly unfortunate in view of the success that sanctions were having in punishing Iraq.
The problem with sanctions was that there was no guarantee Hussein would be out of Kuwait before the U.S. presidential campaign gets under way next year. All political leaders remember well how Margaret Thatcher used the Falklands war to propel herself to a second electoral victory.
Repeatedly, the Secretary of State for External Affairs asked if there was any evidence that sanctions were working. Surely he knows that the director of the CIA
January 17, 1991

reported in December that continued sanctions would have an increasingly damaging effect on the Iraqi military: the virtual depletion of Iraq's foreign exchange reserves by spring, the shut down of nearly all but energy related and military industries by the summer, a decrease in the Iraqi air forces's ability to fly regular missions after three to six months, and a deterioration of Iraq's ground and air forces after just nine months.
Contrary to what the Prime Minister told us, waiting for sanctions to work could have only made Iraq weaker and poorer, thereby saving Allied lives if military force were ever genuinely necessary. The war option is the most damaging of all possibilities for the region and the allies.
Let us not be fooled about the duration or the human cost of war. So far, 45,000 body bags have been sent to the region. The U.S. military must believe 45,000 could die there. The tragedy is that western culture has glorified war, the leaders who led their nations into battle, and especially those who died in combat. I wish we could attach as much reverence to those who manage to avoid conflict.
Today our nation has seen the results of the first two days of war. The first day, many thought that a U.S. victory would be an easy one. We saw an attack that looked and sounded like a scene from Star Wars. We did not see the carnage on the ground, the 150,000 people who at least one source said, were killed. Now Israel has been hit, once again fearing the use of poison gas against its people and their families. Saudi Arabia has been attacked. Turkey has visions of claiming the oilfields in northern Iraq. Both Syria and Iran are wondering what opportunities a crippled Iraq will offer them. A lasting peace seems less likely than ever.
The government has accepted responsibility for those Canadians killed and those killed by Canadians. For that is all that war involves, killing and being killed. There has never been a good war or a bad peace. Our nation, like a sailor tossed overboard by a captain intoxicated by the glories of war, has no option but to swim to shore, to see the war to its conclusion.
Our brave men and women in the gulf will do our fighting for us and deserve all the respect and assistance we can offer.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I have just a couple of comments and possibly a question. I take exception to a couple of things said by the hon. member and would like to clear the record.
At the beginning of her speech, the hon. member mentioned that the decision by the Canadian government to become involved in war would cost hundreds of thousands of lives. I just want some clarification on that, because I think the member knows full well that it was a collective action taken by the United Nations and not by Canada alone. In other words, Canada did not make the decision to start a war.
Also, I would like the member to comment on some remarks made by her former leader-in fact the leader under whom she ran under as a candidate in the last election. He dismissed the relationship that the member attempts to make between the Vietnam war and the Persian Gulf War. I want her to comment on the issue because he spoke very well on that and dismissed any connection or parallel between those two wars.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra told us that he dismissed totally the accusation that this is simply a U.S. war and that the U.S. has, in a sense, drawn every other country into it. He dismissed that totally. He told us that it is very much a UN sanctioned war in a sense. It is not a U.S. war, not an American war. He is very, very strong on that. I will quote his speech at page 17133 of Hansard of January 16, 1991:
Nobody pushes the United Nations around, not even the United States. Not one nation, especially not the United States, is able to impose marching orders on that institution.
He goes on to say:
No, this is not an American adventure. It is an United Nations action in collective security, one of the greatest historic developments of our time, certainly in my lifetime-
Perhaps the hon. member could comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question. I believe I said hundreds of Canadian men and women. I note that the member asks me about hundreds of thousands of Canadian men and women who will lose their lives. Whether it is 100 or 100,000 lives, 100 are just as important as hundred of thousands Canadian men and women who might lose their lives. So I think we are quibbling about numbers.

Government Orders
I put an equal value or weight on a hundred lives as I do a on hundreds of thousands of lives. But as I mentioned in my speech, I do not see how the hon. member can say with such certainty the exact number of Canadians lives that will be sacrificed to a war which Canadians were not even aware was creeping up on them.
The hon. member asks me about my difference of opinion with the former leader of the Liberal Party. Obviously the former leader has his opinion and I have mine.
In return, I would like to ask the hon. member if he would be good enough to answer a question about a statement that the defence minister made on November 16, when I understand he was visiting the armed forces in the gulf. He told reporters that Canadians might consider participating in an attack on Iraq even without the sanctions of the UN. I quote: "Our preference is that if force is needed there would be a resolution endorsed by the United Nations, but we have not ruled out Canada's support of force outside the United Nations".
That is quite a cheeky comment to make, I would suggest to the minister.
I would like to ask a second question, if the Speaker would allow me to. What was the big rush to get Canada involved in this war? Where is Canada's national interest? Why did the Prime Minister, in an interview on December 28, say: "We are not getting ready for war," he kept insisting, "we are trying to secure peace. Should that change, we are going to know long in advance".
Subsequently he said: "I will go to the House of Commons and explain it and examine with them certain alternatives for Canada".
What alternatives did the government examine before launching Canada into the war?

Mr. Speaker. I would like to reflect upon an interesting observation. I wonder if the member might care to comment on it.
One thing that I have noticed just prior and subsequent to the war being called is that many, students in my riding of Okanagan-Shuswap have gathered together and have spoken very strongly with a united voice that
Canada and the nations of the UN, the allied nations, should do whatever they can to find a peaceful resolution to this conflict, to give more time for the economic sanctions to work.
I just want to reflect on a letter that was written to me. Unfortunately it was the very day that the war was called that it arrived. It says: "Your constituents in the Okanagan-Shuswap gathered at the cenotaph in Salmon Arm on Wednesday in a silent prayer for peace. We would like you to send the attached message to the Government of Canada". It says: "A message to the Government of Canada via our MP Lyle MacWilliam: Hold off on military action. War as a solution is unacceptable to us. Give us sanctions, negotiations, and give peace a chance".
These are many residents in the Okanagan-Shuswap area. There has been a number of petitions from high schools throughout my area. Obviously the students, the young people in Canada, are becoming very concerned about the whole aspect of Canada's involvement in military action. I view it as a very positive sign that our young people are becoming involved and interested in these affairs and speaking out with a very strong voice. They are saying: "give peace a chance, utilize whatever efforts you can to find peaceful resolutions before exercising that final tragic option". I wonder if the member is finding the same thing in her constituency and if she has any comments she would like to make.

I thank the hon. member for his question and his commentary. I think it is quite safe to say that we are kindred souls in this regard.
During the Christmas holidays I had the occasion to visit many of the schools in my riding. The number one topic was the Persian Gulf and the number one concern among the young ones was conscription. All of them, unequivocally, even at that time said that this government was bent on sending them to war. They were astute enough to realize that at that early date. Their number one concern was that they feared they would be drafted.
I would very much like to seek the assurance of this House that this government has no such intent on drafting young individuals who have never had explained to them the merits of this war, why we went to war, or what the national interest of this war is. Many of these young ones should be listened to. I also believe that this

government has turned a total deaf ear to what Canadians are thinking.
My office is continuously inundated with calls from people who fear that we have been misguided and have stumbled into a war that we should never have been into in the first place. I can say with great certainly that had we been the government, we would never have found ourselves in this situation to begin with.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to make my speech although I have a severe cold. Still I hope I will be able to deliver all the remarks I have prepared. I want to join the debate because it has to do with an important issue.
The wide variety of opinions expressed in this debate is testimony to the democratic character of our parliamentary system where each of us is a living link. In these democratic precincts I want to make my contribution as a member, as a Canadian from Quebec. I am proud of the reputation our country has gained the world over as peacekeeper. Canada did achieve notable success by participating in the United Nations peacekeeping operations and peacefully settling various conflicts through diplomatic channels. This important factor must be kept in mind during the debate.
Unfortunately, diplomacy has been silenced and what we hear now is the roar of cannons or, more properly, missiles. Being Jewish, I will not hide the fact that the threats hanging over Israel tonight, right now if the news is correct, are present in my mind.

As a Jew, I have a deep and abiding concern for the welfare of Israel. Of course, this does not make me oblivious to the aspirations of others. I consider myself first and foremost a citizen of the world. Rabbi Harry Stern of Temple Emmanuel in Montreal used to say that there is only one race, the human race. I also know that Israelis yearn for peace with their Arab neighbours and with the Palestinians.
After hearing of last night's attack on Israel, my first thoughts were for friends in Israel. I hoped that they and other Israelis had not been hurt. We now know, of course, that innocent civilians died and our hearts go out
Government Orders
to them and their families. We hope that Israel and Israelis will be spared further attacks.
This unprovoked aggression reminds us of the tremendous price Israel pays simply to exist. I am sure that everyone in this House supports Israel's absolute right to defend itself.
The Liberal Party opposed going to war on January 15.
That does not mean that we would always oppose war. Our leader said clearly in his speech to this House that we opposed going to war at that time. We believed that sanctions ought to be given more time.
I am not a pacifist. It cannot be said that the Liberal Party is pacifist in the sense that we believe that it is possible to 'do away with war under all circumstances. Unfortunately, that is probably not something that the human condition will ever attain.
Our position does not mean that we are opposed to the collective security provisions of the UN Charter. It does not mean either that, as some have suggested in this House, we are prepared to condone Saddam Hussein's aggression. Quite the contrary. We supported a wide variety of measures to make him pay for his aggression. The question is when to use the ultimate recourse of war, when to exercise the security provisions of the charter.
Last week, 47 members of the United States Senate and a good number of congressmen-I forget the exact number-voted against the use of force at that time. Our position is no different from those members of the U.S. Congress. War, the ultimate recourse, should only be used after carefully weighing a whole host of competing factors. Were the conditions right on January 15 or 16? Historians and political scientists will debate this question for years.
In debate in this House, we have heard arguments on both sides of the issue. On the one hand, the Prime Minister, when he spoke in the House, argued that with time and wealth Saddam Hussein would strengthen his arsenal. While sanctions had affected Iraq's exports and living conditions, Saddam would ensure that his armed forces received top priority. I do not think anybody in this House doubts that.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
The Prime Minister also mentioned that Saddam Hussein had demonstrated limitless tolerance for the suffering of his people and there was no evidence that sanctions had caused a groundswell of discontent.
On the other side of the argument, the leader of my party observed that in September and October, President Bush, Secretary of State Baker and the Director of the CIA, Mr. William Webster, had all said that sanctions were working. I am sure that we have heard these figures many times in this debate. More than 90 per cent of Iraq's imports and 97 per cent of its exports had been stopped. Industrial production had declined by 40 per cent. The flow of spare parts and military supplies from the Soviet Union and France had stopped. My leader said that the United Nations Security Council should report on the effectiveness of sanctions. He argued that the use of force should be the last resort after all other avenues had been completely exhausted, sanctions and diplomacy included.
To try to gain some perspective on these questions, I spoke some weeks ago to a reputed national affairs analyst. She told me that she was not optimistic that sanctions would work within three or four years. Sanctions are premised on the assumption that the target population will rise up and overthrow its leader. Iraq was an ideal case from an economic standpoint, but perhaps the worst case in the sense that it has a ruthless leader with a powerful security apparatus.
Further, Saddam Hussein has shown his ability to build down his economy or, in other words, to reduce the standard of living of Iraqis. That was done during the eight or nine year war with Iran.
This analyst believed that there were really only two choices: one was to leave Saddam Hussein in Kuwait for three or four years; the other was the option that we are faced with now, namely war. These are both terrible choices.
The best thing you can say about leaving Saddam Hussein in Kuwait is that the status quo would have been preserved. In the view of the analyst I spoke to, Hussein would have had difficulty building his military capability. He would not have had great capacity to do further damage in the region.
Then there is the option of war.
No one can say where war may lead, how long it will last, how many lives will be lost or how many countries will be involved. Apart from the human costs, many agree that the political consequences will be equally terrible. War will bring with it political destabilization. Many questions must be asked about the peace that will follow. Here are just a couple: Will Iraq survive as an independent country or will it be divided between Syria and Iran? Will war lead to a Shiite government?
We have not begun to address these and countless other questions.
What I am saying is that war will bring with it human devastation and political consequences that may be worse than a prolonged occupation of Kuwait would have brought. That is, as I said earlier, a terrible conclusion to come to when we think of the devastation of Kuwait and its people. But again, we are weighing two terrible choices.
I would ask, had the opposite case been made, was war necessary to avoid even greater death and destruction that will result from war? Was Saddam Hussein in a position to do further damage?
With Operation Desert Shield, with several hundred thousand allied troops in Saudi Arabia, would Saddam Hussein have risked attacking Saudi Arabia or any other neighbour?
The argument has been made that war was necessary to stop Saddam Hussein from going nuclear. If we had evidence that Iraq was close to possessing a deliverable nuclear weapon, my view and that of our party would clearly have been different.
In November, The New York Times published a report in which it cited intelligence estimates that Iraq would require two to ten years to develop a nuclear arsenal. In an editorial, The New York Times offered the opinion that the Iraqi nuclear threat did not itself justify a military strike at this time. The editorial continued:
The only long-term solution, short of unending military occupation, must be diplomatic. In the final resolution of the gulf crisis, the nuclear issue must be high on the agenda. All shipments of bomb-making material to Iraq should be embargoed, international inspections should become far more aggressive, and Iraq should be pressed to forgo building facilities that could be rapidly converted to bomb production.
Some may say that this is the view of a newspaper, The New York Times, albeit a fairly authoritative newspaper. It may or may not be right. However, before going to

war, I believe that we require persuasive evidence, which I do not believe was presented to this Parliament, to the U.S. Congress or to the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker. I rise this morning to engage in a debate that I never expected I would be participating in. Certainly, it is a debate that I never thought I would see the Parliament of Canada undertake. In fact, until the word came down on Wednesday night that we were in a situation of war and that missiles were actually flying toward Iraq, I never believed it. I never believed that Canada would actually go to war.
I believe that is a position many members of the House had. In the hours following that first announcement, while wandering the halls of Centre Block, I ran into
Government Orders
many members who were dumbfounded, who were awestruck, who could not believe that this had actually happened.
Over the last two days, I have had time to think about it and I have been asking myself what is Canada's role in this regard. Why is Canada at war? Why are we going to war? What justification can there possibly be for that war? I have to come to the conclusion that there is no justification for Canada to be involved in a war at this time.
President George Bush has said,-and the Prime Minister has also acknowledged and indicated-, that economic sanctions simply were not working and we had to go to war. The economic sanctions that were being imposed have been the most comprehensive economic sanctions in the history of the world.
Last week there was a very eloquent debate taking place in the United States in which speaker after speaker, mostly Democrats, rose to point out the evidence that in fact economic sanctions were taking hold and that they were having an effect. There was evidence such as the report from the CIA which said that the war machine of Saddam Hussein was beginning to break down and, if economic sanctions continued for a few more months, they would begin the cannibalization of Saddam Hussein's war machine as the Iraqis would take parts from equipment to put on other equipment to keep it going. This is very sophisticated equipment and, without parts that were not coming in, the machinery would break down. The Gross National Product, as we have heard many times, was being strangled. It was a country that was having severe economic problems. Yet, we have gone to war. What has been the result of that war?
I was listening to a briefing from the Pentagon today as I was watching television. The general who was giving the briefing indicated that the war was going as expected. He said that in the 45.5 hours since they commenced the hostilities, they had conducted over 1,000 sorties per day. They had conducted 2,000 missions in the 45.5-hour period. He indicated that it was like two consecutive D-day operations. On D-day there were air raids of astounding proportions and he said they had two consecutive D-days. Presumably, there will be another one tonight, another one tomorrow night, and for the next few days.

The American pilots who are interviewed on television coming back from these missions have indicated that they have found virtually no resistance or very little resistance. In fact, they have made their raids and come back. We have heard rumours-unconfirmed, of course-that, besides knocking out strategic points, anywhere from 150,000 to 350,000 Iraqis have been killed, annihilated. They have ceased to exist. That is something that has to hit every Canadian right in the pit the stomach. In 45 hours, we have wiped out perhaps 350,000 people. Mr. Speaker, that is astounding.
What has been Iraq's response? The so-called coalition has lost perhaps eight planes. They are not sure if they have been shot down, if they have run out of gas, or what happened to them, and a few missiles have been lobbed into Israel. Granted, their response of lobbing missiles at Israel is not justified, but the response of Iraq has been extremely minimal compared to the impact that the American coalition has had on Iraq.
It leads me to believe, especially when they say it is going as expected, that in fact members of American intelligence knew what to expect. They knew full well that the Iraqi war machine, such that it is, was not a threat. They knew what the response was going to be. They did not know whether they were going to lose 8,12, or 15 planes, but they knew they were going to have a devastating impact on Iraq. And yet they went ahead.
They went ahead despite the fact that economic sanctions were working. They went ahead despite the fact they knew that they were going to blow the hell out of hundreds of thousands of people in Iraq.
What was the reason for this? It was not a war intended to solve problems in the Middle East. The resort to war was not the last resort. It was not a war that was necessary to get rid of Saddam Hussein. This is a war that I believe was chosen by George Bush not to get rid of a madman-which certainly Saddam Hussein is-but rather to help George Bush get elected in the next election. Some crass politics, I am afraid to say, that are taking place.
A few years ago there was the situation of Margaret Thatcher who won a political victory as a result of her military victory in the Falkland Islands. George Bush is trying to repeat it here.
And so is Brian Mulroney.

I am afraid to say that my colleagues are right. The Prime Minister is using the same sort of political belief and the same sort of mentality that George Bush is proceeding with.
Despite the rhetoric that has been taking place, the U.S. has to take responsibility for a lot of the situation that exists in the Middle East right now. The U.S. has to take responsibility for Saddam Hussein. He is in many ways a creature of the United States, much as Noriega was in Panama.
We have heard a lot of talk about an international peace conference for years. To a large extent-not totally, but to a large extent- it is because that peace conference has never taken place. For George Bush to stand up now and say that he has to get rid of this madman, in a self-righteous fashion, to save the world. There is a lot of talk coming out of both sides of his mouth.
What has been the Canadian role in this? We have this 28-nation coalition that exists. Canadians have fourth-largest contingency, behind the British and the French. Of some 500,000 allied troops, the Americans have 450,000. Canada has about 1,700. We have about three World War Il-class ships and 25 planes, and that is our role. The role of Canada in this war effort is minuscule. If the Canadian troops and the Canadian planes are not there, there would be virtually no effect on the outcome of this war. Yet, why are we there? Certainly, we are not going to win the war or lose the war. That is for certain.
If one wants some crass politics-and I am sorry I have to tell my hon. friend opposite this, but this is the only thing that makes sense of why we are in this war- it is that the Prime Minister is getting something out of this. He is getting Canada a seat at the Mexico-U.S. free trade talks. Also, he is at 12 per cent in the polls and he is hoping to take advantage of the Margaret Thatcher-Falklands episode and gain some political points. He has nothing to lose. My friends opposite have nothing to lose at 12 per cent in the polls. They are trying to wrap themselves in the Canadian flag in order to gain something out of this.

What makes me very sad is that, although the Prime Minister has not resorted to the rhetoric of George Bush, where George Bush is going to go "kick ass", he has come very close. He is now talking of escalation. Last night, after the attack on Israel, the Prime Minister commented that perhaps Canada will have to escalate its forces.
If the rumours of sending 5,000 troops are true, how is that going to help the situation? They are certainly not going to knock out the Scud missiles going into Israel. They certainly are not going to have any effect in knocking out Saddam Hussein. It can only be for political advantage. When a government, a Prime Minister, or a President uses political advantage and uses crass politics and plays politics with the lives of human beings, that is about as low as one can go in politics.
Hear, hear.

I am afraid that that is where this government has dropped to.
The New Democrats have been very clear on this situation. Our troops should not be there. They should have pulled out at the first indication that George Bush was going to enter into war. And make no mistake, it is not a United Nations war. It is an American war under the guise of the United Nations. It is not a coalition. Some people like the term "allies" because it brings up patriotic feelings. It is not an ally. It is an American-led attack with a few extra people along. That is what this war is. Let's make no mistake about it.
At the first word of any military action by George Bush, the New Democrats would have advised Mr. Bush that at the first bullet fired Canadian troops are pulling out of the region. We agreed with the economic sanctions and we are willing to take part in that. We think that Saddam Hussein has to be removed, but not through blowing the hell out of Iraqis. At the first indication of any shot, we would have indicated to George Bush that we are out of the region.
We should be taking a different role. We should be there as peacekeepers.
After the bombs stop, there is going to be a tremendous need for the reconstruction of people's lives in that region. Of the 350,000 people-or whatever the figure
Government Orders
might be-some are soldiers, but many are families. They are children, women, men, and families just trying to survive in an area where, through no fault of their own, the world gone mad.
Canadians should be there to help in reconstruction. We should be taking our traditional role. There will be buildings collapsing after the bombs stop falling. There will be contaminated water. There will be bombs that hit the ground and did not explode blowing up. There are going to be all sorts of ongoing problems. There will be people who have been maimed for life through losing arms and legs and their sight.
Canadians should be taking a traditional role of peacekeeper. We should be willing to that. We should be sending in engineers and medical teams and have them ready to take on the role that Canada can best do.
We have no business being in this war. We will have no effect on the final outcome of the war. We can play a role as peacekeepers. We have destroyed our reputation as peacekeepers by taking part in this war and for that I am personally truly sorry.
Before I finish, I want to say that although we did not support it, the reality is that there are Canadian troops in the gulf. My thoughts go out to those troops and their loved ones. I know that all of us hope that those people come home. We certainly hope that there will be no more Canadian personnel sent over to the region.
I want to close by saying that when historians write their accounts years from now they are going to conclude that this war was a grievous error. When they look at Canada's role in it, I believe that it will be seen as a very large blemish in the history of our nation.

Mr. Speaker, when I turned on my television in the early hours of Wednesday evening and saw that my world was at war and realized that very soon my country would be at war, I was filled with a sense of despair. I really could not believe that at this time in our history, as what we call civilized people, we still thought that the way to solve world problems was to bomb, to destroy, and to kill.
I had to phone my children one by one to say: "I am sorry. I am sorry we have failed. We have failed all of you and there is nothing I can do about it."
Like all their generation, my children are wonderful young people. They are healers, they are builders, they are innovators, raised and educated to live in a world that values healing and building and using the mind to solve problems. They grew up believing that their country, as perhaps no other, stood for a new era, an era when the resolution of human conflict would be achieved to the greatest extent possible by the application of human ingenuity, determination, and compassion.
I do not know which I consider the greatest tragedy: that Canadian men and women and those of other nations with all the potential they hold are in danger of dying far from home, or that they are being called upon to kill others. Either is a tragedy. But they have been ordered to do so not by a vote of this Parliament, but by fiat, by a handful of men and women who sit safely here in Ottawa and put the lives of others at risk.
Our thoughts and our prayers are with them. I say to each and every one of them the Irish prayer: "May God hold you in the palm of his hand", and may you return safely to the family and friends you left behind. We admire and respect you and know you will give the
Government Orders
utmost in skills and talent to the difficult job you have been assigned.
I pray too for the men and women of Israel and for the children who faced the last two nights and will face the nights to come with fear. We hear tonight that five more bombs have been dropped on Tel Aviv with even more destruction and even more fear. I express my deepest admiration for the handful of Israeli leaders who have resisted the natural urge to retaliate for the damage and devastation being done to their people. Instead of reacting with weapons, they have reacted with restraint, with courage and with wisdom. I agonize for those in the Jewish community in Canada who fear for their loved ones and their friends.
While I feel despair and a sense of tragedy, I also feel utter disdain for this government which has felt that the potential for destruction and death it was prepared to unleash was so inconsequential that the right of Canadians to speak out on this crucial situation through their elected members in Parliament could be ignored and shunted aside. As the world moved inexorably toward a war deadline, our Prime Minister silenced my right and the right of all members of this House to speak on behalf of those who sent us here. Barely 12 hours before the clock struck midnight on Tuesday, we were allowed to come back to do what it is our sworn and sacred duty to do.
What could be more crucial than to speak for our constituents on the issue of war and peace? Yet the Prime Minister waited until it was too late for more than a handful of us to speak before that horrible deadline. Why? Why did he wait? Why did he delay? Why did he deny the voice of Canadians when democratic assemblies around the world were meeting and debating?
The train of events is clear. He waited for the American Congress to meet. He waited for the American Congress to have its debate. He waited for the American Congress to hand the American President his mandate for war and he waited while the emissary from the American President came and got him on side. He waited until after the commitment of Canadian lives had been made to war before he came to this Parliament.
Parliament was locked out while he waited and the voices of Canadians were not heard. Only when the decision was already made and communicated to the United States were the voices of Canadians through

their elected members of Parliament allowed to be heard.
Even then the Prime Minister would not let this House debate the real issue. In his contempt for Parliament, he refused to put his intentions clearly before House. He refused to say that the question before the country is: Shall Canada go to war? In the aftermath, who can doubt that was and is the question? He continued to dissemble, to divert, to duck, to dodge and to deceive with some vague, abstract pretension that we were somehow, in principle, endorsing the United Nations. It was left to the Official Opposition to put the question squarely before Canadians, to state clearly our belief that Canada should do everything possible to enforce the removal of Saddam Hussein from Kuwait by economic sanctions, that if hostilities broke out in the Middle East, our troops should be brought home and Canada should prepare for its role as peacemaker and peacekeeper.
We believed and we still believe that the time had not yet arrived when war was the only possible means to force Saddam Hussein from Kuwait.
Even now, with bombs flying and people dying, with the lives of Canadians, Iraqis, Kuwaitis, Israelis, Saudis, Jordanians and those of numerous other nations at stake, the government refuses to be honest about its purpose.
On Thursday at noon, defence department officials provided us with a briefing. They were asked specifically what mission was the base for the strategic and tactical decisions they were participating in. Was it to get Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait, or was it to destroy the war machinery of Iraq?
We were told by those responsible for Canada's war effort that the mission was in line with the United Nations' resolution to get Hussein out of Kuwait. And yet this afternoon the Prime Minister said in this House that "We are engaged in a campaign to make sure that his, (Hussein')s, war machine can never again be used". And then tonight again, on radio, I hear the Minister of National Defence saying in response to the same question, that our mission is to get Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. What is the honest story for the people of
Canada? Is it not time we heard it? The Prime Minister, should tell Canadians the truth.
Tonight I heard the spokesperson for the Soviet Union regretting that missiles made in the U.S.S.R were used against Israel last night. The missiles may have been stamped "Made in the U.S.S.R.", but what is the country of origin of the droplets of nerve gas that may strangle the children? What is the country of origin of the biological warfare that the Secretary of State for External Affairs says may be unleashed against allied forces and innocent civilians?
From whence come the nuclear technology and the components of nuclear bombs that threaten the chain reaction that can destroy the world for human habitation? Who are the nations that for over a decade have armed the madmen of the world? Who are the governments that have based their economies on weapons and technologies of destruction and death, where every year their economies prosper on a new toy and markets have to be found for last year's models? Where are the nations who put international trade above the safety of the world and refuse to control the movement of arms?
Who are the merchants of death who do not care where their products end up as long as their dividends are up, who put profits above the sanctity of human life?
Let there be no mistake, about my intentions. The men and women who stretch the frontiers of science and technology deserve nothing but our greatest admiration. Their talent and their creativity are essential to the maintenance of mutual deterrence and the delicate balance that can preserve peace in our world. Their contribution to the advancement of human health and safety is incalculable. They are not the ones who have shirked the responsibility to stop the spread of the products of their labour getting into the hands of those who would use them in the mad pursuit of power. It is others. It is all of us, the lawmakers, who bear the responsibility for killing thousands of blameless bystanders to destroy the monsters we have created and armed.
And at what costs? What risks do we take when we decide not simply to remove Hussein from Kuwait but to obliterate his nuclear production facilities? Whose lives do we jeopardize when we bomb the plants that produce chemical weapons?
