How do we destroy the capacity to produce deadly biological weapons without releasing untold agents of harm on unsuspecting people who want nothing more than to wake up tomorrow, to toil for a meagre living, to feed and clothe their children, and hope for a better world for the next generation? To what extent has it been in the interests of the superpowers for well over a decade to maintain the tensions in the Middle East, to ignore the plight of Palestinian people without a home, and to refuse to work for the kind of climate in that territory that would lead the nations of that region to be able to sit down and resolve their differences?
Saddam Hussein is a blip in the history of Baghdad. Countries, provinces, states and kingdoms come and go but cities endure. The centres of population for people endure. Baghdad goes back 10,000 years to the dawn of civilization, yet we in our arrogance have assumed the right in our brief stay on this earth to blast it to smithereens.
Does the 24-hour TV docudrama we have witnessed since Wednesday show us any of this reality? Have we seen one dead child? Have we seen one drop of blood? Do we know how many people have died? Have we been allowed to see the reality of this war? No.
What we have seen is sanitized science fiction, Star Trek with bright lights flashing off into the universe. The Enterprise goes off into the darkness, sparkling explosions fill the sky, with patterns of lights pretty as the stars, but obscuring the reality of thousands of living beings, breathing in a living city. People quiver in fear. The flight deck of the Enterprise is now the CNN newsroom where people risk their lives to satisfy our insatiable armchair curiosity to catch one more siren or the colours of one more blast out the window.
It has be?n said that Canada has lost its innocence. I know I have lost some of mine this week. In my newly honed cynicism I have listened to the Secretary of State for External Affairs admit that the cordon of sanctions is more like a sieve, with the resources of oppression continuing to pour through to Saddam Hussein. I ask myself: how far the potential for war in their hands since November has weakened the determination and the organization of the United States and its allies to tighten
Government Orders
the cord of sanctions, to pull the strings so tight that Saddam Hussein would strangle to death?
I have listened to the excuse that the embargo wreaks hardships on the Iraqui and Kuwaiti people but not on the military. I ask myself: What greater hardship there could be than being dead tomorrow morning? I ask myself: How many wars do we need to end wars? We say it with every war we have.
I watched and listened to the verbiage about the United Nations and I ask myself: Why Canada's commitment to enforce the embargo and our commitment of forces was made to the U.S. weeks before the UN announced an embargo? Why did the Prime Minister's announcement of CF-18s going to the gulf follow within hours on the heels of the announcement by a senior American air force officer that they would destroy Baghdad with bombs? Why is it not the United Nations which has made the crucial determination that sanctions could not work and that the time had come for force?
I have listened in vain for months for one single independent Canadian position, for one single Canadian initiative to reach a peaceful solution. I have listened for Canada to call for the final decision to be made not in Washington but in New York by the United Nations, for this action against Hussein to be under the clear and unequivocal direction of the Security Council of the United Nations. I have listened for the voice of Canada to be the voice of strength, restraint and peaceful resolution. I have not once heard anything but the echo of President Bush.
We have lost more than our innocence. We have lost our stature and the respect the world has had for us as peacemakers and peacekeepers. The world has lost an independent honest broker for sanity and a better way for the future.
This week has been a betrayal of the new hope for the next century which we all felt at the beginning of the last year. It has been a betrayal of the gains made for democracy and freedom by those brave individuals who stood up to oppression by the tens of thousands in eastern Europe, many of them at the risk of and at the loss of their lives. It has been a betrayal of the hope we all had that the billions of dollars that had been going into the weapons of destruction could now be diverted to saving children, saving our environment, building a better world. Yet here we are again, with one nation

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
spending half a billion dollars a day killing, maiming, destroying, not building.
I make no apology tonight for choosing passion over dispassionate analysis. It is a time for passion. It is a time for reason when the lives of thousands are at stake. The possibility of a world without conflict and oppression deserves our passion.
I make no apology for saying the voices of women are needed in our legislatures. I make no apology for saying it is time to put away the centuries of thinking that reason only defines us as human beings when we know that reason and passion make us human. I make no apology for reporting to this House that when the Gallup poll recorded that 59 per cent of Canadians were against war, by a ratio of nearly two to one, 59 per cent were women rather than men.
I make no apology for personalizing the horrendous situation that faces Canada and the world, for saying that what I want for my own children I owe to every child of the world, the right to grow up safe, healthy, secure and free, to develop their talents and contribute to a better world in the third millennium. We have done irreparable damage to that right this week.

Mr. Speaker, I would very much like to congratulate the previous speaker on a magnificent speech. In my observations of the debate in this House, some of the finest speeches that have been made in favour of peace, and the endurance of human values, have been made by women. It certainly speaks very strongly for more women legislators in this place.
I have just a couple of comments. It is apparent to me that this House cannot resolve the desire of the majority of Canadians to find a peaceful route for Canadian involvement in this issue. I am just wondering whether it is not time for the women in this House to join together and to set a different course. Although it is only one drop of water, it tends to gather speed and greater mass as time goes by. There is an extremely strong desire in this country for peace. The majority of people do not want us there killing Iraqis. They see a much more positive and constructive role.
The first question I would put to the hon. member is this. Does she see that the government is fixed and all of its members cannot leave the direction the Prime
Minister has established? Maybe it is time for the women in the opposition to gather together and with a unified voice put together the individual voices that they have so strongly put before this House and see if they cannot gather more and more people in the cause of peace. Perhaps they could focus on the rest of the legislators here, lead them, gather other citizens behind them and try to overpower what has happened to us on this side of the House.
The second thing is your mention of the creation of madmen. I have been here for more than a decade now and I have heard this side of the House speak constantly against the creation and the use of the madmen in the world by the nation to the south of us. Eighty thousand people have been murdered in El Salvador and they have been murdered by U.S. dollars and U.S. advisers. Nobody ever talks of invading that country. They talk about continuing it. It certainly depends who is killed.
Maybe when this is over and all the preaching about atrocities from the other side of the House is finished, we can reflect this back to them and say: Now what do we do about those? Obviously the United States will never let us see a military overthrow of that.
The third thing the hon. member mentioned that was so effective is: Once this is over, what do we do about the dirty hands of all the nations in this business? I have been here for more than a decade and I have heard this side of the House rail against the West Germans selling chemical plants to manufacture nerve case, about the French selling reactors from which fissionable material is extracted to build nuclear weapons. It is time that we reflected this back to the government and say that many nations, including our own, have, very dirty hands in selling arms and selling the wherewithal to kill people.
I thought that was a tremendous speech. I certainly think that those three items show the capacity of the opposition to come together. We have been motivated in our desire to see Canada move in a peaceful direction. Maybe the women on this side of the House can begin the process of pulling us together and pulling the rest of the people together to achieve what she has articulated. She mentioned dirty hands. Our hands are as dirty as those of other nations in building this monster and
January 17, 1991

others. Let us get rid of the El Salvadors and the insanity that has gone there.

The members questions and comments would require another 20 minutes to answer, but I will not impose on the House. I think he cannot beg off that easily. He cannot leave it to the handful of us in this House who happen to have the power to create life and therefore perhaps value it more highly. It is time for the men in this House to start saying that the fate of the world matters to them and the fate of the world's children and the fate of every single human being on this earth matters to them, more than money and more than power and more than property.
That is what we need, for you to start listening to us. We are doing our bit to change the values on which we make decisions, but frankly I do not have a lot hope for my country when I see it under this government slipping more and more into a value system based on might and power. Those who have will have more. Those who haven't will have less. Those who are strong will survive and thrive at the expense of those who are weak, and the weakest of all are our children.
I do not have a lot of hope when I see resources being taken from those who most need to be heard in our democratic society. I do not have a lot of hope when there is not enough money to clean up our rivers and lakes, but there is enough money overnight to destroy. I do think that Canada has lost immeasurably in this situation and in the last few years in our ability to be seen to be forging a different way for the world, to be turning our technological and communications expertise into productive and positive environmental technologies, which by the way are just as economically profitable as destructive technologies. I do see us as having lost a great deal of ability to contribute positively and independently in this world and I regret it.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for doing me the kindness of allowing me to briefly to echo the words of the hon. member from Vancouver. My only regret is that it is so late. It is now two o'clock Saturday morning, and we have been debating since ten o'clock Friday morning. Personally, never in my life will I regret not leaving this House earlier, because the speeches are getting better by the hour.
Government Orders
What an incredible collection of well thought out, informative and non partisan pieces of work. I did not know what the hon. member was going to say at this time, nor how she would vote. This is what true debate is all about.

It is a true House of Commons debate. It is not to be told, bang, one side will vote this way because all of the other side will vote the other way so argument is totally irrelevant. I regret there are not more people here. I am not talking about the people in this House because, by tradition, I cannot mention how many people there are, but it is regrettable. The importance of the speech and the argument put forward by the hon. member for Ottawa West is something to reflect upon. I would hope the debate will not end. Members may say, "how come the debate is not finished" and "who spoke", and then they will read the comments. In any case, I will make sure in my own speech that her comments will not be forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, this is my first speech since my return to the House of Commons from the recent by-election in York North. I never believed, however, that upon my return to the House of Commons I would be debating, in my first speech, war, indeed Canada at war.
Throughout that period I always held a deep belief and faith that governments throughout the world, including Canada, would be able to reach a peaceful settlement to the serious gulf crisis, a crisis that has shocked, saddened and profoundly affected Canadians. I continued to believe that we, as a democratic nation, could, through principled diplomacy and through the pursuit of every possible avenue, arrive at a resolution to this international crisis.
This morning it is obvious that my dreams as a young Canadian for a peaceful resolution to the crisis have been shattered. War measures have taken precedence over a peaceful resolution. Canada is at war in the Persian Gulf. This is a serious time and a serious issue with serious repercussions and unimaginable implications for international peace, order and security.
Like all Canadians, I condemned the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its illegal annexation. I believed it was wrong, unjustified and completely contradicted the emerging

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
new spirit of co-operation among the nations of the world.
I believe that the imposition of mandatory economic sanctions against Iraq, if given more time, might have been the peaceful resolution to the crisis. As a parliamentarian, I would have liked to have participated, to have been given the opportunity to participate and hear the highest forum of the land on this very important issue, and to have participated in the debate long before the present reality of war. I think that our contribution in that case might have been more meaningful.
This morning, as I speak, however, I realize that the hypothetical questions of the past do not address the reality of the present. The post-mortem of the war may answer some of these questions.
What is important tonight is to come to grips with our role in the gulf as young Canadian men and women offer their lives for democratic principles that have been the cornerstone of Canada's involvement in international affairs. We must offer our unequivocal support to them, as they, through their efforts, must achieve the goal shared by every one of us in this House, and indeed everyone across this nation to bring peace and order to the Middle East and to the world.
I can perhaps spend hours describing the failures of this government in dealing with this crisis, but I think that perhaps we can underline the most basic evidence of their failure and that is the fact that we are at war.
War is failure. The political leadership of this nation, like many others, has failed to arrive at a peaceful resolution. From this morning on we will be judged on how we move toward the attainment of peace. I might suggest that this morning in the House of Commons we meet at a crossroads, not a point of arrival but a point of departure. Where do we go from here?
I would like to take this opportunity to call upon this government, all members of Parliament and all governments throughout the world to move quickly in seeking the ultimate goal of peace. We must actively pursue peace talks. Peace talks must replace bullets and bombs. We cannot afford to lose human lives because of our
inability as political leaders to find a solution. We are elected to seek solutions and we must find them.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member spoke for only five minutes; I understand that he will split his time with another colleague.
Yes, that is correct, the member for Hamilton Mountain.

Mr. Speaker, all my life I have admired people who, at all political levels, have served their fellow Canadians. I have always had a very special attachment to the House of Commons and the democratic process.
Two years ago I was privileged to be elected to this House by the citizens of Hamilton Mountain. I have dedicated all my time and energies since then to serving them and I have enjoyed every minute of it. Every time I have addressed this House, I have felt proud. I never expected that circumstances would be such that I could not say it is a pleasure to participate in this debate, but this is not the case today.
Indeed, it is not with pleasure but with a broken heart that I rise to talk not about peace, but about war. Up to the very last moment I had hoped that our call for peace and patience would be heard, but this government chose not to listen.
I have always felt that the responsibility of a political leader is to solve problems, to negotiate solutions, to work out compromises. We have to recognize today that we have failed in these responsibilities.
Canada has had an extensive and honourable history of working toward peace on the international stage. The role that this government has orchestrated for Canada in the events taking shape in the Middle East over the last months deeply compromises this tradition. Rather than providing a much needed voice of reason and support for negotiations, this government has abdicated the Canadian tradition of peacemaking to follow the path of violence.
To what end? Will the world be a better place? Is this region of the world going to be more democratic, more peaceful?
There are no winners in war, only losers. War is not a solution to human conflict, but a stark example of human failure. I strongly feel that the Canadian government
January 17, 1991

should have given sanctions more time to work. As a Canadian, I deeply regret that we have abandoned the peaceful and proud legacy of Lester B. Pearson.
The scale of human suffering that will result from this confrontation is horrible to contemplate. We have not seen any of it yet, but soon the horrors of war will be on our television for everyone to see. Analysts in the United States were speculating today that there might already be thousands of deaths after only 50 hours of war. Let us hope that they are wrong.
As I anxiously watch the events unfolding in the Persian Gulf, the faces of Canadian servicemen and women keep flashing through my mind. We hear politicians and military advisers discussing the grand strategies involved in Operation Desert Storm, as they call it. We must remember that the bottom line in war is always human suffering.
Political choices have been made. They are not mine. However, I strongly support the courageous efforts of our servicemen and women and I pray for their safe return from the Persian Gulf. For those with loved ones in the gulf, my thoughts are with you, as we hope for a quick return to peace in the region.
I also hope for the safety of those residing in the gulf region who have found themselves caught in the middle of this conflict.
I want to repeat that it was with a sad heart that I saw diplomacy and negotiations give way to bullets and bombs. With the end of the cold war, I had hoped that we would find peaceful solutions to the world problems. I truly hope that this does not represent the new world order that so many international leaders have spoken of over the past few months.
While everyone feels a sense of attachment to their country, we are all ultimately citizens of the world. I take no pleasure in watching reports of the successful bombing missions inflicted on the people of Iraq. The devastation and human suffering caused by the gulf war will be enormous.
Canada must take a leadership role in searching for the restoration of peace and in looking for ways to deal with the horrendous consequences of war. A lasting peace must be achieved. I pray that in the days to come peace will be restored in the gulf region and that all Canadian servicemen and women will safely return to their families at home. Then, with a sense of both
Government Orders
sadness and a renewed mission, we can begin again to search for a lasting peace and a new world order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, naturally all Canadians are still in a state of shock at the reality that we are at war. I think most of us still find it unbelievable. A country that has for so long prided itself on being recognized globally as peacekeepers finds itself now involved in a horrible battleground in and around the Persian Gulf. Bombers are flying, people are dying, and the sad part of it, of course, is the message that we just received from the Canadian Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War and the United States Centre for Defence Information predicting that at least 200,000 people will die and another 500,000 people will be seriously injured. The sad point of all of this is that 80 per cent will be civilians and the largest group of civilians will be children.
Let me be perfectly clear at the outset of my remarks. We all recognize that the perpetuator of this process, Saddam Hussein, is indeed a brutal dictator, a barbaric aggressor, first into Kuwait and more recently into the state of Israel. Some people have referred to him as a psychotic personality, a madman, someone who has violated human rights as have few other countries, and has killed off his own people by the thousands in a form of a unmitigated savagery. We deplore the atrocities, of course, that have occurred time and time again in that country as a result of his decisions.
We also must recognize that while we are dealing with Saddam Hussein, there are millions of children and the parents and grandparents of those children who, like us, have no interest in involving themselves in this horrible war.
I speak tonight as a father of two sons, both of draft age. I must say it certainly focuses one's attention. We are discussing here whether or not we ought to be involved. To think that certain decisions may in fact result in their participation. I cannot for the life of me feel comfortable with that as a father of two young boys.
I want to say that when we look at this war the sad part is that we have to admit we have all failed. This is a symbol of defeat, a symbol of failure. It is a mistake. It is wrong. It is unjustified. I think we have simply admitted that we as a species have failed when we find ourselves involved in such a horrible situation, such a brutal and barbaric situation. To think that as we speak here in the House of Commons, hundreds and hundreds oi flights

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
are occurring over Iraq and thousands and thousands of tonnes of bombs are being dropped, and thousands of people are being killed or maimed.
One can only wonder as one looks around the House and you notice that most of us are at an age that has never known war. Our parents and our grandparents have, but to most, war is something that we have only read about or seen on television screens or in movie theatres. We have to wonder if in fact, as historians have reminded us, it appears that every generation must repeat the errors of the previous one. Here we are involved in the unthinkable. I think we are still in shock by the reality that we are involved in a horrible war.
We all, as we speak today, recognize that the men and women in our forces are serving in the gulf region, we pray for them and we hope for a quick return to their homes, their families, and their friends, and of course a return in good health.
I have been almost shocked at the tremendous response by constituents from 1 out of 295 ridings in the country, the riding of Kamloops, with a host of phone calls, letters, telegrams, faxes, delegations, almost universally condemning our participation in this war. I have in my hands petitions from Cariboo University College, Kamloops Secondary School, Logan Lake Secondary School, Westsyde Secondary School, North Kamloops Secondary School, Clearwater Secondary School, Bar-riere Secondary School, Chase Secondary School, a large number of junior secondary schools and a number of elementary schools. Petitions as well have come from the communities of Chase, Penetan Lake, Paul Lake, Raleigh, Heffley Creek, Barriere, Clearwater, Deadman's Creek, Savona, Little Fort, North Thompson Indian Band, Logan Lake, Kamloops, Dallas, Barnhart vale, Brockelhurst, Westwold and a whole host of other communities, as well as a number of churches and many community organizations. They all say that Canada should not be involved in this conflict.
I believe very strongly that getting involved as our government has committed us was a serious error. To have the United States lead an attack on Iraq was in fact an error. Before any country involves itself in these kinds of hostilities, surely to goodness it would explore all
other avenues before it initiated the kind of slaughter and horror that we are seeing now hour after hour.
I must say I felt badly as a Canadian to see our government responding so quickly to the American initiative in terms of involvement militarily in the area of the Persian Gulf. I feel our own foreign policy it is no different from that of the state of Montana. We are essentially now an extension of American foreign policy because immediately, when the United States said that it was becoming involved in an aggressive way in the Persian Gulf, our Prime Minister within seconds said: Aye, aye, sir, we are there with you.
There were no discussions with the people of Canada, no debates in Parliament. The oddity of it all is that today we are debating the issue of our involvement in the Persian Gulf when we have nearly 2,000 troops already in the Persian Gulf and when we have aircraft committed to the Persian Gulf and ships committed to the Persian Gulf. It is a little after the fact. The horse is out of the barn. I say that this has been a very sad moment for Canadians, seeing our foreign policy, particularly when it involves this type of aggression, essentially being led by President Bush of the United States. When we look at whether or not we had exhausted all peaceful possibilities to encourage the brutal Saddam Hussein to get out of Kuwait, we can only say that we did not.
We failed. Look at diplomatic efforts that could have been initiated sometime ago. Granted there was a flurry in the last few hours leading up to the January 15 deadline. We can well admit that much more could have been done. What we did do and we are proud of the fact was we committed to involve ourselves with a sanctions initiative in the Persian Gulf, an attempt to strangle the economy of Iraq sufficiently to require Saddam Hussein to remove his troops and back off from the occupation of Kuwait. But, did we give sanctions a chance to prove themselves? We did not.
Look at the evidence that we have in terms of the successes that were there. I have to simply quote a few people that I think we would all recognize. They are certainly respected, knowledgeable people who understand the role of sanctions. I can quote people like William Webster of the United States Central Intelligence Agency. He said before the United States Congress less than two months ago that 90 per cent of Iraq's imports and 97 per cent of its exports had been stopped.
January 17, 1991

James Schlesinger, former Secretary of Defence for the United States, said that we needed approximately one year for the trade sanctions to work. We allowed them, as we recall, only four or five months.
The Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs, in a letter dated December 28 of last year stated that these were the most effective and comprehensive sanctions ever applied by an international community. Of course, sanctions is not a new technique to encourage countries to do certain things. There are 115 cases of sanctions that have been applied around the world. We know that it takes at least one to two years before they can be effective in terms of strangling the life out of an economy sufficiently to require the government of that country to make what we believe are the appropriate decisions.
Let us go on. General Schwarzkopf, Commander of the United States forces in the Persian Gulf, issued a statement in support of continued economic sanctions.
A study of over 100 cases of sanctions that have been applied around the world, indicated that these sanctions will bite, and bite deeply, and bite soon. This is most encouraging. I could go on and quote others. I will just quote two more because I think it is important Canadians recognize that the sanctions were working.
Admiral William Crowe, former Chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, appearing before a Committee of the United States Congress said: "The embargo is biting heavily. In my judgment, given the standard of living Iraq is used to and the increasing sophistication of Iraqi society, it is dead wrong to say that Iraq is not being hurt. It is being damaged severely and also I believe that goes for the Iraqi military which depends on outside support".
General David Jones, former Chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, said: "The risk is that the problems inherent in maintaining the offensive military option would create are too problematic." He points out that Saddam Hussein is losing $20 billion to $30 billion in hard currency every year. This, of course also suggests that he is not receiving military supplies. We recognize that the only goods coming into the country were being largely smuggled in. Of course smugglers depend on
Government Orders
hard currency. At this rate, currency was simply drying up in terms of foreign exchange.
I have a long list of all sorts of people who have pointed out that the economy was being devastated by these sanctions. The statistics that the American Congress provided the world were to point out that the Gross National Product of Iraq in only four months had been crushed by 48 per cent. If that is not an effective sanction at work, to see the GNP drop by 48 per cent in just a few weeks, I do not know what other information would be required.
The short and the long of all this is that, yes, the sanctions were working. They were very effective and, had they been given time, we can only conclude that they would have driven Saddam Hussein from Kuwait. But we saw that the United States was not prepared to wait. I say the United States because I think we can all recognize that there almost seemed to be an enthusiasm that the American administration had made a decision, for whatever set of reasons-and we all heard them-not the least of which is the reliance of the American military industrial complex either to be preparing for war or in a war.
Someone succinctly pointed out the other day that the best way to get rid of inventory was to blow it up. We see that that is indeed one of the ways that the American economy is driven. It was decided for a whole set of reasons. If Kuwait was a country of palm trees, date palms and bananas, would American forces by the tens of thousands be involved in reinstating a sheikh, with his family, once again to lead a country, an undemocratic nation, a family that had abandoned a Parliament in that country? I doubt it.
Another aspect of this process has concerned many of us. Someone the other day mentioned that the first casualty of war is truth. We recognize that what we are receiving now day by day on our television screens and through newspapers is propaganda. The American led forces have admitted that the news is being laundered, that everything has to move through military censors. If in fact this was a just war, as some of our government members have indicated, surely then we would not be afraid to expose it. With the fact that the American administration does not allow reporters into the various

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
areas, we can only assume that they are hiding something, that they are covering up something, that they are embarrassed and so on.
Think of what else is happening as we watch television to get the propagandized results of the hour-by-hour goings on in the Middle East.
The other day someone suggested a return to play-byplay action. This is what you say about a Superbowl. This is how you describe a football game. Of course, their play-by-play action was the hundreds of sorties of bombers heading out either to carpet bomb the Iraqi forces dug in, in southern Iraq, or the surgical strikes in the city of Baghdad. Surgical strikes, it almost sounds good, a medical term.
Of course, what surgical strikes means is huge concentrations of bombs or cruise missiles into a single restricted area, resulting in countless deaths and maiming. Think of the wordsmiths, Mr. Speaker, who have crafted terms to sanitize our reaction, to make it more acceptable to accept the fact that our forces, our country, along with some others, are engaged in a military combat with Iraqi forces.
For example, they talk about liberating Kuwait. They mean attacking the armies of Saddam Hussein in that area. They talk about body counts. Well, body counts are dead people. These are people who have been killed. They talk about protecting our assets. Our assets are the young men and women who are there in our Armed Forces. These are not assets; these are young men and women. These are human beings that we are talking about. These are people. They talk about Baghdad looking like a Christmas tree. The Christmas tree was the massive bombing that was destroying huge parts of the city.
This is a language that has been crafted to sanitize, as my hon. colleague from Okanagan-Shuswap so adequately described it earlier today, to make us more acceptable of a horrible, bloody and brutal war.
I want to say simply that we are at war. Twenty-eight countries are involved in the United States' coalition, but only a few are there offensively. That is why we are arguing that Canada should not be there in an offensive mode. Other countries are there with coast guard ships, bringing various sorts and types of expertise to the theatre of war. We suggest too that Canada is there with
a role to play and that our forces should be redeployed, providing military support for humanitarian initiatives to assist and protect the growing numbers of refugees in the Persian Gulf region, hundreds and thousands of people who are going to require support and protection as they flee Iraq. Escort humanitarian shipping in the area and provide assistance, if you like, to refugees, food ships, shelter, medical supplies. Another role is Canada's involvement with the field hospital and other forms of medical support. Those are the roles that Canada should be playing, not an offensive one. I join with countries like Argentina, Czechoslovakia, Denmark and Norway and others there, but not in a combat role.
In conclusion, I simply want to say that we find ourselves involved in a war that ought not to have occurred, that we believe need not have occurred. It has really set back the role of Canada as a peacekeeper, has probably jeopardized and hindered our future role as a meaningful peacekeeper certainly in that part of the world, if not other parts, and has set back the United Nations. We had hoped that with the collapse of the cold war the United Nations might be able to carry on in a new style, with new institutions and new approaches, where we could solve these international geopolitical problems in some more creative, modern, humanistic way than simply sending in troops to engage in combat.
Unfortunately, as a world, as a country, we fail. The fact that we are involved in such a horrible, brutal, bloody war is an indication of our inadequacies.
Let us now, rise to the challenge and not rest until we find ways and means of bringing peace to the Middle East.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the hon. member and to other hon. members who have stood up and have spoken in the House.
We as members of Parliament cannot end this war. Our government has decided that we will not only participate in the war in a supportive measure, but it has now decided that we will become offensively involved and through our efforts, we will kill Iraqis.
The absolute majority of people who sit on this side of the House is opposed to it. We have fought it every step of the way. We do not believe that this is a significant,
January 17, 1991

meaningful or useful role for Canadians. I do not personally believe that we have failed.
Our government has failed us. Our Prime Minister has failed us and taken us into a war that we and the majority of Canadians want no part of.
I would put to the hon. member a question. Is it not significant that this Prime Minister and this government enjoy the support of only 12 per cent of Canadians, that 88 per cent of Canadians have absolutely no confidence in this government, that a week ago more than 55 per cent of Canadians and that is a growing percentage wanted absolutely no role in this war that would see the killing Arabs or Iraqis? They felt that Canada did not belong there.
It has indeed been the failure of the Prime Minister to recognize the wishes of the majority of Canadians and to win their confidence. It has been a failure of this government, member after member standing up saying we must support the United States in invading Iraq. The interesting thing that the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs both said is if the UN does not, although we would prefer to go in with the UN, we will go with the U.S. and go it alone. That is a colossal failure. The government does not enjoy the confidence of 88 per cent of the people of Canada. It does not enjoy the confidence of a single member on this side of the House.
We have failed to convince the government of anything. We have failed to convince the government to see reason, to exercise humanity and common sense. That indeed is a failing, but it was an impossible task.
Would the hon. member agree that we in fact have not failed? We have tried to put the case in an honest and forthright manner and it has turned a deaf ear. To 88 per cent of Canadians this government has turned a deaf ear. Maybe now is the time for members in the opposition to begin to organize a committee of legislators for peace and to end the war, and to join with other Canadians who want to do this. We can no longer count on our government and we certainly cannot count on the madman to the south of us, George Bush.
Will the hon. member agree that we really have not yet failed, that the only thing we have truly failed in is to convince the government it has already lost?
Government Orders

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
As usual, my colleague presents a thoughtful argument and raises some very pertinent questions that I suspect most Canadians are asking themselves.
Our government has committed us to this involvement, knowing that 88 per cent of the people of Canada do not support our Prime Minister, knowing that a large majority of Canadians are opposed to our involvement in this war. I remember, as New Democrats were calling for the recall of Parliament before any commitments were made in terms of our participation, that we have a debate in Parliament, hoping that for once the Prime Minister would be sensitive to the views of the people he represents, that just for once he would listen to what Canadians were saying.
Of course, we know from all the polls and all the intelligence that we have received from our own country that overwhelming numbers of Canadians oppose our participation in this war. We even said that when it came to a vote, that it be a free vote to unleash Members of Parliament from the whip, from the lash of the Conservative Party, to represent their constituents on whether or not Canada should be going to war.
I cannot think of a more important decision that this House has taken in the last 50 years than to decide whether or not we should commit ourselves, our country, to a state of war. The Conservative Party did not allow its members to vote on behalf of their constituents. They simply were required to support the Prime Minister in his haste to join his friend, President Bush, in involving ourselves alongside America and American troops. It is a very sad moment for the country.
I want to conclude this statement by simply reading from Hansard of September 8, 1939, a comment made by Mr. Woodsworth, the founder of the CCF, the predecessor of the New Democratic Party. He said:
While we are urged to fight for freedom and democracy, it should
be remembered that war is the very negation of both. The victor
may win, but if he does it is by adopting the selfsame tactics which
he condemns in his enemy.
I think those words are as relevant today as they were back in September 1939.

I certainly acknowledge the very thoughtful response of the member for Kamloops. I would put another question that

follows up on this serious disservice that the media is currently doing to the people of North America.
I recall watching virtually all night last Christmas the American Broadcasting Corporation as described the assault on Panama by the madman to the south of us. We have to remember that the Americans created Noriega. It was not drug interdiction that bothered them as much as his newly adopted position on the Panama Canal. At the moment the Central American dictator began to threaten their ownership of the Panama Canal, it no longer became tolerable to keep him. All other human rights abuses, all other drug trafficking, all other abuses were forgiven until he began to demand control of the Panama Canal.
The American Broadcasting Corporation obviously acted as an agency of the U.S. army, glorifying the activity, glorifying the decision of the President of the United States and indeed distorting the information given to the American people and the way it was picked up by many agencies in Canada. My serious concern is that our media is being roped into that enormous distortion, that denial of information that people need to make rational judgments about this activity.
Part of that strategy is the cutting of the budget to a public broadcasting corporation, one that has a credible record of investigative journalism, absolute responsibility in providing information to the people of this country in a fair and balanced way. This war that George Bush has inflicted and dragged us into by a dog's leash in the Middle East is now being distorted in an even worse manner. I compliment the hon. member on bringing out this enormous disservice about critical broadcasting of American military briefings, and the plot to keep the population in ignorance.
When George Bush said, "we will not enter this war with one arm tied behind us", he was referring in one respect to the absolute denial of any information through a free media about what is going on, the devastation and the information that the population needs to make a reasonable judgment about this war.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of this House, I can honestly say that I deeply regret having to debate this motion, for it is a debate concerning war.
No reasonable individual in Canada or throughout the entire world wanted to see a war in the Persian Gulf or anywhere else, yet tragically since January 17 such a war has occurred and the fragile stability of the Middle East is once again on the line.
For Canada, this tragedy is closer to home this time. The men and women who are representing our country whether on land, at sea or in the air, are carrying out their duties in a very professional and exemplary manner. Our country and our people can be proud of them. We wish each and every one of them a safe and quick return to their loved ones. I know that every member of this House and all Canadians share this wish.
In my riding of Stormont-Dundas, I have received several petitions from constituents who are very concerned about the war in the Persian Gulf. One hundred young students from Newington Public School and 280 St. Lawrence High School students in Cornwall particularly impressed upon me that a generation which has never experienced war does not want to today.
Mr. Brian Ferguson of Cornwall also collected some 500 signatures in the past two days, signatures for peace. I believe these people mirror the views of a majority of Canadians. The people who sign these petitions want an end to the deployment of Canadian Armed Forces personnel in the Persian Gulf. They wish to remind the Government of Canada that Canada has a reputation as peacekeeper and ask that we do not jeopardize this great treasure which Canadians hold so dearly.
We know that Canada has a tradition of being there when needed to help keep the peace. Canadian peacekeeping forces have for some time now been carrying out peacekeeping duties in Cyprus and on the Golan Heights. I hope that should it come about in the days ahead that to achieve a cessation of hostilities, a United Nations peacekeeping force is required, Canada will again be prepared to step forward and offer to participate.
January 17, 1991

The recent missile attack upon the state of Israel has shocked the world. Many felt that Saddam Hussein's threat to launch such an attack on Israel was just that, a threat. Sadly, this was not the case. Nonetheless, we recognize the considerable restraint exercised by Israel not to retaliate.
The world is now wondering and fearing what will happen if Scud missiles with chemical warheads land in Israel. What will happen to the coalition forces against Iraq if Israel counters with a retaliatory strike either by plane or by Jericho missiles? The real potential exists for collapse of the coalition and an escalation to the conflict. The world can only speculate as to what will occur and the ramifications posed by such events. Certainly the Iraqi leadership would relish dividing the coalition by bringing Israel into the war.
Whatever events take place in this war, we can be sure of Canada's resolve to attain peace. Canadians will maintain their commitment to peace. As one of my constituents said in a letter to me and I quote: "peace is the only reasonable alternative to war and that while it is attainable peace can be a difficult goal to achieve."
I believe the United Nations was trying to do the utmost to prevent a war. As well, I think a strong case could be made that this war may well have been avoidable. If the sanctions imposed upon Iraq by the United Nations had been given more time, perhaps this war would never have occurred. Some have argued that Saddam would not have left Kuwait under any circumstances. Perhaps this is true, but war has started. As the leader of our party has said on several occasions, it is easy to start a war but it is very difficult to stop one.
It is the duty of Canadians and all the peoples of the world to work toward ending this war and avoiding any of the catastrophic consequences which this war has the capability of producing. This war, like some have suggested, is not about oil. It is not a result of the United States wanting to attack Iraq. I also believe that there is no wish by the Iraqi people to fight American, British, French, Saudi, Syrian, Egyptian, Canadian or any other nation which is a part of the United Nations coalition in the Persian Gulf.
Government Orders
The coalition is there to remove Iraq from Kuwait since that country was invaded by Iraq. The invasion was condemned by the world community and the decision was made to stand up to this aggression.
It is a mistake to assume that it was absolutely necessary to attack Iraq after the January 15 deadline. Unfortunately, the decision was made and the war was begun.

The Liberal Party's position has been clear throughout this debate. We urged the government to give diplomacy and sanctions time to work. The government did not listen. Although there is no need for war at this point in time, the Liberals are prepared to support our troops, these Canadian men and women who are fighting in the Persian Gulf. We are not going to let them down.

The Liberal Party supports Canada's military effort in the Persian Gulf. This position, however, does not preclude our party from continuing in its efforts to advocate a peaceful and expedient solution to the conflict. Efforts we would seek to end this conflict deserve the full support of Canada.
If the Iraqi leadership is not prepared to comply with the resolutions of the United Nations to end this war, then all the effort and support required to bring about a swift conclusion must be made.
Canadians do not want a prolonged conflict in which the possibility of escalation increases along with the price to be paid in terms of human lives.
One hopes that the Canadian government will do everything within its means to go on the offensive for peace, as much as it is prepared to go on the offensive for war. Canada's respected position in the world must be utilized at every opportunity to lobby for peace.
We have numerous contacts within the western and developing world and we are viewed throughout the Middle East with trust. At the United Nations, Canada has always acted independently and consistently in accordance with the principles and objectives of this international body.
I am sure that all Canadians expect our government to be pro-active in peace efforts. Canada must not ignore the responsibility that is placed upon all nations to take

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
up the cause for peace when war occurs. Every opportunity presented must be followed through in the hope that it brings about peace. The search to bring about peace will indeed be a difficult assignment, but the difficulty of the task in no measure outweighs the rewards of success.
Eventually, this war will come to an end. An assessment will be made on the role this country and others played in this tragic conflict. When it comes to Canada, I hope that we will all be comfortable that our government did take up the cause for peace. If this is not the case, the harm caused to Canada's previous commitment to peace and the security of the world will be among the casualties of this war.
In conclusion, as representatives of the people throughout this country, we have a duty and an obligation to work together outside the sphere partisanship to assist in the efforts to establish peace and bring our Armed Forces safely home. To our soldiers, airmen and sailors in the Persian Gulf go our prayers and our thoughts. They have our steadfast support and that of every Canadian. Let us all hope that before long we will see signs of peace in the Persian Gulf.
