Mr. Speaker,
I want to thank my hon. colleague who stayed this late to express his views on this very sensitive issue. I wonder if he could elaborate on a point that was already discussed, namely the role Canada could now be assuming: Bearing in mind the possibility of an international conference on peace in the Middle East, what role would he see Canada playing now and in the future? In view of this war unfolding under our eyes, doesn't Canada have a role to play right now on both the military and diplomatic fronts? Canada's military involvement was decided by this government. Could the government not decide that we should also do what Canada is renowned for, namely
playing a diplomatic role? Can he briefly express his views on this?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Saint-Denis for his comments and his question. Certainly, I hope to see Canada take a proactive approach to peace, because it is our duty, as parliamentarians-and I encourage all Canadians to propose solutions to this problem facing us now.
On the subject of the international conference on the Middle-East situation, I certainly am for it. As Canadians who value peace and wish that everybody else in the world: could live in peace all as we do, the least we can do-and we try to as often as possible-would be to get together around a table and recognize respectfully that, while we do have differences, we also share some values such as peace. I would find an initiative along that line very comforting. After all, the idea has been around for years in the UN but, for some reason, it was always postponed. Now that the cold war is over, if the UN could get to play a greater role and take its place in the world, this initiative-finding a peace solution for the Middle East-would be among the first it should undertake.

Mr. Speaker, I have been deeply concerned about what has happened these past few days, what has happened the past few weeks and months, as we have seen develop within the world a conflict that is really troubling to many nations. It is a conflict that is not easily resolved and one that has caused a tremendous split in this House and a split in many countries, because decisions have to be made about what should or should not be done when we come into difficult situations.
I have very much had to struggle with what I think is probably the most difficult decision I have ever had to face. That decision affects the lives of many other fellows on this planet, other human beings who are foisted into a conflict which many of us believe should not be.
None of us support what Saddam Hussein has done and we were all horrified when we saw troops go into Kuwait. We saw the atrocities that occurred in that country. We realized what challenges were laid to the democratic world and what challenges were laid to Canada, the United States, Europe and all other countries. I thought to myself, with this conflict coming on in
January 17, 1991

the last few days, we, the Canadian people, have joined a war. What do you say to your constituents? What should we be saying to the Canadian people? What are they concerned about?
It is my opinion that the first message should be given is that we support the troops in this country. We support the families who are very concerned about their loved ones. We pray for a very quick end to this conflict. We hope above hope that all diplomatic means will be brought about by our country and by our government to resolve the crisis, not add to the conflict.
I think that this Liberal view is shared by many. We do not have to go very far to quote some of those who have spoken up in the last couple of days. Reverend Walter Farquharson, leader of the United Church, stated: "We reject the claim of our leaders that there was no alternative". Archbishop Michael Peers, leader of the Anglican Church of Canada, stated: "We reject the notion that war in the gulf is justified". Toronto's Roman Catholic Archbishop stated he was profoundly saddened and would celebrate a special mass for peace on Monday. The Canadian Council of Churches has strongly voiced opposition to this matter.
Why are these people, leaders of the churches in Canada, united on the issue that war could have been avoided? This conflict should not have been as it is.
One only has to think about what the alternative is when war begins. What devastation is caused? What does war cost? Certainly the price of war is very, very high morally, physically and economically. Tens of thousands of lives have a potential of being sacrificed when we hear such terms as carpet bombing.
When I was flying into Ottawa tonight, I flew over several major cities: Windsor, Detroit, London, Toronto, and Ottawa. As I was looking down and seeing the lights of the great metropolitan areas, I thought to myself. "If I were in a bomber flying over here in a B-52 and dropping ammunition and bombs like is going on in Iraq right now, whose life would be hurt?" Fortunately in Canada those bombs are not falling today, but we are authorizing those bombs to fall on other countries. We are authorizing our
Government Orders
own troops to take action which will damage, maim and result in very extreme hardships in Iraq.
Certainly I do not support what Saddam Hussein has done, but I think the action we have taken against him should not have been supported either. Billions of dollars will be spent on our war initiatives. Environmental concerns respecting the use of chemical weapons must be addressed. There is great concern over the bombing in Israel which has just taken place. We all are very much concerned that it is not just going to end with a quick few nights' bombing. The potential of drawing Israel into this conflict and ending up with an Arab war against the western world is there.
We know that escalation could very well happen, and no one should put aside the possibilities of what may happen in the future once action has started. Chemical weapons, if used by Iraq, could cause unlimited damage to citizens living in the Middle East if, as the reports we hear from the gulf suggest, oil is spilled in the Persian Gulf from huge tankers or oil wells and set afire. The environmental damage that could result from that will not be cleaned up for centuries. It would be catastrophic globally. This is on top of the devastation that is now being created by conventional weapons.
There is no question why many world church leaders took a position against war. What other alternatives did we have? We had sanctions in place. We were taking positive measures to hurt Saddam Hussein, not physically with bombs but economically with sanctions, hurt him to the point where his economy had slowed down considerably, hurt him by less violent means, means by which the same end could have been achieved.
It seems to me when we talk about how we handle problems that a society must look at the end results, the long-range results not the short-range ones. There is absolutely no question the war that is going on now will create scars and concerns, one nation against another, not just for a few days or a few years; the scars will be for centuries. I have a concern about the divisions that we are creating by a war of this nature. I strongly believe we are creating divisions among races in this world by this type of action.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
When I read an article by Carole Goar in The Toronto Sun I started to think about the kinds of information we have been given by the Prime Minister and the government. It makes one stop and consider whether we have been told clearly and honestly what the situation has been as it has developed over these past months.
On August 10, the Prime Minister had three ships refitted. The government absolutely had no mandate. They were refitted and sent to the gulf. When asked by reporters and members of Parliament what actions were being taken at that time, he said: "We have no mandate". Two weeks later, on August 25, the UN Security Council announced sanctions against Iraq. Certainly the Prime Minister knew when he talked to the press on August 10 that there were mandates for those ships. However, the Canadian public was not told that, nor was the Parliament of Canada. These ships arrived in Italy on September 11 and they were kept there three days. By September 14 we received another announcement that CF-18s were to be sent to the gulf and the ships were on active duty. It is interesting to note why that September 14 date came about, because it is the responsibility of the Prime Minister to bring back Parliament within 10 days when ships are being sent into an area of possible war or conflict.
In not sending the ships in on September 11 when they arrived, but holding them to September 14, obviously the Prime Minister was trying not to call back Parliament immediately and thereby let the people of Canada know. He waited until September 24 to bring Parliament back.
On November 16, our Minister of National Defence announced that we had not ruled out Canada's support for force outside the UN. He more or less suggested that if the UN did not condone physical support, Canada was considering it anyway. He clearly sent a message that Canada would act independently outside the United Nations and that was the avenue it was taking.
On December 28, the Prime Minister promised that Canadians would have plenty of warning if troops were sent on the offensive. On January 8, the Prime Minister said there is no need to recall Parliament. However, on January 15 Parliament was recalled. The bombs started to fall on January 16. The UN deadline date was up.
Did the Prime Minister fulfil his promise of recalling Parliament and telling Canadians well in advance of Canadian offensive actions? I do not think so. I really believe the Prime Minister went in another direction. He talked with James Baker. He talked with President Bush, and I think he had a clear indication of what hostilities would occur and at approximately what time. He called Parliament back to debate this issue after he had made the decision.
I find it very ironic to stand here today and debate a motion that we voted on on November 29. We are redebating it and we are going to revote on that motion after the action has been taken. I find that wrong. I find it wrong because, if the Prime Minister were going to take action, if he were going to commit the troops, and he knows the Liberal Party of Canada and the New Democratic Party of Canada both voted against the same motion, he should have explained it to the House. Yet, he put it on the floor after the bombs flew to have us vote on it again.
I think it was done for a specific reason. The Prime Minister, in putting forth the motion, may well have been trying to gain partisan ends. I find that wrong. The Prime Minister of Canada and the Parliament of Canada should not be aiming at partisan ends in this particular case. We should be looking at what is right and what is wrong. I do not feel that is the course we are on.
I honestly feel that in each major issue we have dealt with in the last couple of years, the guideline has been to divide and confuse the Canadian public. Free trade is a very dividing issue in this country. Meech Lake is a very dividing issue in the country. The Oka situation, same thing. The propositions he put forth to solve our economic problems, same thing again. With this situation, he has put forth an issue which he knew on November 29 was going to divide this House.
I think the Prime Minister and his cabinet should have put a motion forward which would have stated: We support our troops; we will work toward a democratic end; we will do everything we can to bring a quick end to the war. But no, he puts a motion to support the actions of the government which I think, and he well knows, is only a further division of the country. If any person in

January 17, 1991

this country has a reverse Midas touch, it is our Prime Minister. Everything falls apart when he touches it.
Some strong questions have come forward about the role of the United Nations and whether this Parliament supports the actions of the United Nations. I firmly believe this Parliament has supported the role of the United Nations. All three parties supported the sanctions and voted for them in this House. It came down to a question of whether or not we go to war.
I think everyone here must realize-and it is very evident to many international experts on that the mandate of the Security Council resolution 678 does not fully give power to the United Nations. It says that any independent country can attempt to bring Kuwait back to a status of freedom. In other words it authorized the United States to act independently. It authorized Canada to act independently. It authorized every other country to act independently.
From the questions we have had in this House, it has been clearly stated that Canada is not acting under the UN flag. Canada is acting as an independent nation under the flag of Canada. I believe that Canada is acting as an independent nation. It is not acting for or against, or in any other direction with regard to the United Nations. It is following an option that was left by a resolution in the United Nations.
I guess when I look at it more carefully, and I try to determine what the difference is, it really is clear that each nation involved in this conflict has made independent decisions and that the decision for conflict was not made by the United Nations.
The Secretary-General of the United Nations, when interviewed the night the war began, said he was not aware of the conflict beginning. When the Secretary-General of the United Nations is not aware, it is very clear it was not a United Nations action: It was an action of independent nations through a motion from the United Nations.
Canada still supports the United Nations, and all the parties here support the actions of the United Nations. We just do not agree that Canada should be in a conflict where many of us feel Canada's interest is not. I do not know what our international interest in the Middle East is besides peace and fair treatment to all who are there.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member on a very thoughtful and clearly articulated analysis of the situation. I want to support, as everyone else has, his comments about supporting our Canadian Armed Forces and their families, probably the Canadians most critically involved and under the highest anxiety in this entire country. The support that we can lend their families and to the degree that we can support them, I laud his remarks and identify with them fully.
I would ask how this suggestion sits with him, given his analysis. Anything that is said any longer in this House falls on deaf ears. The government and the Prime Minister have made up their mind on that course of action. I am torn. I heard the comments of the hon. member for Saint-Denis about the value of people on this side of the House thinking through their positions and thoughtfully articulating those honest positions.
We are rapidly coming to the end, I think, of the usefulness of that process. I for one have decided that I am going to get on the telephone tomorrow and spend my time phoning every clergy person, every labour leader, every business community leader, in fact as many people as I can, and asking them in the area in which we live in North Island-Powell River to start forming a committee to end the war. As legislators in this place, we can no longer convince the people who hold the levers of decision-making to end this war.
I am going to ask that committee if it would consider doing that. It was effective over a long period of time in the United States and I think it is important today. I am going to phone the Reform Party leader in that area, the Christian Heritage Party, the Liberal Party, the Conservative Party and ask them to join with us in a non-partisan way in representing the majority of Canadians and indeed the majority of people. The thinking people on this side of the House must begin the process of attempting to end the war.
The first step would be to have this government end the involvement of the Canadian Armed Forces in aggressive attacks on Iraq. The greatest support that we can give to our men and women in the Armed Forces is to pull them back before one of them is killed in this unjust war. That is the greatest thing we could do for their families.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
The second thing I am going to ask that committee to consider is to have the Prime Minister of Canada end Canada's involvement in this war. The most constructive thing our Prime Minister could do is end the international political support to the United States for continuing the war.
We then must move forward and convince other smaller and middle sized nations to convince the United States that this war is wrong. We should work together with all other people in this world not only to end this war, but to make sure it does not start again, nor does another start again.
That is probably the most constructive thing that I can do tomorrow morning. I think every other member of this House should do the same. We can no longer convince the Conservative government of the justice of ending the war and ending the international political support for the United States. This is not a United Nations war; this is an American war.
In the United States, the thing that stopped the Vietnamese war was a general committee across the United States to end the war. We have an obligation to do that in Canada and make it work as quickly as possible. The greatest support we can give to our armed forces and to their families is to make sure that we get them out before one of them is killed.

I would like to thank my colleague for his comments and his positive recommendations, because I think that when we look at situations we must come up with alternative means to reach goals where we cannot reach them traditionally.
It does appear that our abilities to reach the Prime Minister, the cabinet and those in power in this government have been stifled on almost every issue. It does not matter about the outcry of the people in the country. It does not seem to matter about many things.
I believe that some areas could be very important. The hon. member touched upon talking with people who are very concerned about stopping the war. I would hope that those people would take the time to write every one of the Conservative members of Parliament as well as other members of Parliament and to do some lobbying within their own area.
I am not one to say just carry a placard and forget about it, but I try to bring forward some logic, some concern, the feelings of the grassroots people in every constituency. Perhaps members will start listening to the
people. I think that is really the only way we will defeat a blockade at this time.
I really feel we are in a blockade with the government at this point in time. We are unable to get our thoughts through. We are unable to convince the government of what the general population is saying. When 85 per cent of the people oppose many of the policies and still it goes on as though things were normal, when its popularity is so far down that it only represents a very minimum number of people in this country, I have to think that we should be very concerned about the direction we are going, very concerned about the next couple of years.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your patience.

I would like to ask my colleague if he would an elaborate on something that is very important to us in our party, and I am sure in the New Democratic Party. It is an idea that has been floating around for so many years. It has been betrayed for so long, betrayed, yes, betrayed by those who only pay lip service to probably one of the most important points. It was a hope un espoir: the international conference on peace in the Middle East. Would he kindly elaborate on this idea and the kind of role that Canada should have played, and could still play?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague again for the question. In this particular situation it is very clear that over the years Canada has had a very clear role, a role of diplomacy, a role of trying to seek solutions, a role of peacekeeping and attempting to avoid conflict, not at any cost but to avoid conflict because of the hurt that it causes other nations when these situations give way to war.
Canada has been a nation extremely well respected because of our ability to negotiate, to be diplomatic, to rise above the issue and look at it from a perspective of how we can resolve the problem. I do not think for one minute that Canada's role should change. However, I do believe at this present time that is not the predominant role Canada is playing. We have formed a very strong coalition with the country to the south. We have followed along on every turn, not only in economics but also in war.

January 17,1991	COMMONS
Rather than resolve and look for solutions and be very positive about how we deal with the Middle East, we have done just the opposite. We have joined with a country that has a very strong vested interest. That vested interest is the economics of the Middle East. The vested interest of the economics of the Middle East is an interest to the world. However, because of that we do not take out a baseball bat and try to win the problem by taking very crude actions, whether they be carpet bombing or whatever. We are supporting aggression rather than diplomacy. That is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, the government has cheapened everything it has touched since it came to power.
I was a bit hesitant about whether I should refer to free trade and what it has done to the nation. I was a bit hesitant about whether I should refer to the changes to the unemployment insurance provisions in this country and what it has done to the nation. But having heard some previous speakers refer to them, I have now done so as well. I would suggest that it is most appropriate to do so, if for no other reason than to give other examples of what the government has done. Handling the Middle East is no different when it comes to handling the situation in a way that cheapens the coin of the realm. The government sped Canadian forces off before Parliament was consulted. It sped Canadian forces off before the United Nations had made its determination as to what should be done but not before the United States had determined what it thought should be done. It has cheapened the House too and, along with it they have cheapened democracy. This is the first major issue before the House in the last two years where debate has not been terminated by closure.
I rather suspect that at this juncture in the debate the government is only too hopeful that it would in some way be able to do just that. Its actions in denigrating everything it touches has also denigrated politicians and, in the eyes of the public, fouled the reputation of those who have put themselves in the service of this country.
One would have thought a new low had been reached in putting forth the motion because the motion itself is something which is blatantly biased. It goes a long way

Government Orders
toward putting almost the final nail in the coffin of the cheapening of this country.
The motion "that this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait" is obviously a well-crafted motion. The government would have known, as has already been referred to it as something which the Liberals and the New Democrats would oppose. That there would probably be a final vote on it would be forcing the opposition in Parliament to vote against the United Nations. We have heard references in the debate from the other side of the House that that is precisely what they are up to. They have made that accusation already.
But a new low was reached for this government when the Secretary of State for External Affairs joyfully held up the report of Amnesty International to verify the atrocities that had occurred in Iraq and then had the temerity to table the report. There are three crimes in the use of this information. The first is the use of an Amnesty International report. The taking of one quote in context to prove a point as he was doing is a scurrilous way to use information. Second, it cheapens the reputation of perhaps the most exemplary organization in the world because the reference was made to only one country. Third, it cheapens the whole debate because it refers to only one country while there are references in the reports of Amnesty International to other countries as well.
To hold up that one report as an example of how life is being threatened in one country and only one country, is to cheapen human life altogether. It quantifies the value of life and I will tell the House why. There are other entries in other reports, if not this one, of Amnesty International and I will cite one. "Sixteen executions, 2,300 under sentence of death. A supreme court decision allows offenders as young as 16 and the mentally retarded to be executed." That reference is not to some Third World country. That reference is not to some country which we usually consider to be undemocratic or backward. That reference is to the United States of America.
I refuse to be trapped into a numbers game on the value of human life. What Saddam Hussein did, and does, is indescribably vile. But a life in Des Moines or a life in San Francisco is as precious as that in Iraq. Barbarism is to be universally condemned. That was my hope when we entered what has often been referred to

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
in the House lately as the new order. My hope was that the kind of barbarism which is described as coming out of Iraq, or which I have just described as taking place in the United States as well, would have been something that would have brought the world to unite in eradicating, as well as it ought to be. Instead of that we have war.
I do not necessarily mean to just condemn the United States or Iraq because of those references. Almost every country in the world is mentioned in those Amnesty International reports and there is a rather an interesting exclusion from the 1989 Amnesty International report. What if things continue to go much further downhill in this country as I expect they might be? It is this country which I am referring to. Canada is not included in the last report of Amnesty International. That may possibly be a result of our history and some of the things that this country has stood for. It is something to be very proud of, but something also to be very highly guarded and regarded.
Turning to the new order, how hopeful we were a year ago when the Berlin Wall came down. We hoped and saw, as I have indicated, that some of the barbarism which had occurred behind the Iron Curtain and all over the world would somehow or other be put to a halt. We had hoped that the east, the west, the north, and the south would be able to unite as the human race and be able to eradicate this kind of thing.
Instead of that we get arguments from the other side of the House, and what are they saying? They are saying we are in a new order; this is a wonderful time. We had trouble before in this world in bringing nations to justice, the argument being because the cold war prevented the United Nations from carrying out its mandate. That statement is innocuous enough but not when translated into action. We would hope that some of the words the party on the other side of the House uses would be turned into action, but unfortunately they are not.
These words were turned into action and what did it translate into? It translates into them saying: "Now that we did not have to worry about taking action against someone who is an ally of someone on the other side of the Berlin Wall, we could all unite. No one has to worry about taking action against some other country and
having someone on the other side of the Berlin Wall would take it out on them".
Instead of having a world in which we are able at least potentially to be able to conquer this barbarism, we now have a world where barbarism is let loose because we live in a new world order. That is the message I have been receiving from the other side of the House as an interpretation that we live in a new world order.
Can we imagine anyone saying that the cold war prevented the United Nations from carrying out its mandate? God help us if that really does get translated into the mandate of the United Nations being war, and that certainly is the first manifestation that we have seen as a result of the concerted action by the world community after the tearing down of the Berlin Wall.
A lot of interesting quotes seem to have come out of the debate over the last two or three days. I would have to go back in Hansard to see who said it, but someone said that a blind passion for peace led to World War II.
I know who said that and hon. members know who said that, don't they? The Prime Minister said that, at least he quoted someone who said that. I do not know who originally said it, but I do know that the Prime Minister quoted that. He said that a blind passion for peace led to World War II. Someone on the other side of the House then asked, in reference to a similar quote: "Would sanctions have worked against Mussolini, or would they have worked against Hitler?" How on earth is anyone to know whether they would have worked? They were not tried. There have been references on this side of the House to people involved on Mussolini's side of that conflict who said that if sanctions had been applied, "you are doggone right they would have worked, and worked quickly."
There was no intention of ever applying sanctions at the beginning of World War II. The industrial business complex of the world on both sides profited from what was happening in the build-up of arms on both sides of the conflict.
As a matter of fact, a late friend of mine worked in Bermuda during World War II as a censor. Every piece of mail that went back and forth between North America and Europe went through the hands of censors. He said to me, still maintaining his oath of secrecy: "Ron, you would be appalled if you knew what the business leaders
January 17, 1991

of this nation had really been up to during World War II".
I do not really know whether or not sanctions would have worked at the beginning of World War II. I do know that they certainly were not tried.
I would like to make a reference to World War II which I have not heard anyone refer to yet. Others here have said they are not really historians. I do not claim to be an historian, but it seems to me that in the last two world wars, it was the United States who followed Canada into war. To put it another way, certainly the United States got into these conflicts after Canada did. I wonder what has happened in the meantime to put the United States into such a state of haste.
God help us, had the United States followed Canada into this war. We like to pride ourselves as being a "kinder and gentler" nation, although I rather suspect that under the leadership of the present government the probability is that it was pretty much a mutual decision to go into this war. I would suggest that under the leadership of a philosophically different government this nation would have been one which would not have led and would not have followed the United States into war.
When we get into the matter of sanctions, I think the concept of the world order is something which is relevant. As a matter of fact, I may have been a bit unkind when I referred to the glee with which the government marched into the new world order by saying that the whole thrust of the United Nations had been thwarted by the cold war.
The imposition of sanctions was evidence, without a doubt, that that new order had some potential. Under the new order, with almost every nation on earth agreeing that Saddam Hussein was a barbarian and ought to be curtailed in his actions, the countries of Iraq and Kuwait-which he had occupied, admittedly, with no justification whatsoever-were surrounded.
I really have not been in all that many situations where I have been surrounded and wanted to get out, but I do speak the English language. I understand what "surrounded" means and the kind of concerted action that was arrayed against Saddam Hussein. I stand here with full acknowledgement that my party was fully behind the
Government Orders
imposition of sanctions against that dictator and madman, Saddam Hussein. If somehow or other, with the whole idea of the new world order, come to a point peacefully where a madman surrounded, incapable of being able to carry on much longer, is immobilized, he then would most certainly not have been able to succeed for very much longer.
I see that my time is running short, but I would like to say that this whole idea of sanctions having been given a chance is absolute rot. I do not want to over-emphasize it, but if we can give the Government of South Africa 30 years of voluntary sanctions which eventually proved to work, we can certainly impose sanctions against Saddam Hussein which can last much longer than five months. That was an artificial deadline anyway.
There are many more things which could be said, but I would like to close with the thought that comes from a quote from Anthony Star, since we seem to be so fond of making quotations in the House.
Anthony Star says: "With the exception of certain rodents, no other vertebrate habitually destroys the members of its own species." War can only be viewed as the definitive expression of the disposition of the human race. I pray that before long the government comes to its senses and does everything it can to reverse what it has gotten into and what this world has got into.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member on an excellent and insightful speech and solid recommendations to this House. I know he agrees with me that those recommendations, like all those proceeding from this side of the House, have fallen on deaf ears. In fact the Prime Minister of Canada and each and every Conservative member have made up their minds that Canada will become involved in this war, and that we will commit our Armed Forces, with the United States and a limited number of other nations, to attack Iraq.
Would the hon. member be interested tomorrow in beginning the process of joining together with other like-minded legislators and citizens into attempting a different route, possibly creating committees to stop the war? Such committees would be made up of any willing citizen in each of our local areas: people in the clergy, members of organized labour, the business community, local legions, veterans groups, and women's organizations-a broad coalition of people without partisan

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
consideration with a single objective to have this government stop Canadian involvement in the war.
Possibly, we could encourage the peace community in Ottawa to come into our offices, to act as volunteers, to use the telephone services, the mail services and any other services that a member's office could provide, and to help organize these committees in ridings that we possibly do not hold.
Personally I would like to see a committee to stop the war in the riding of every cabinet minister in the government, in the riding of the Prime Minister but ultimately attempt to establish across Canada in the strongest possible fashion to convince the government of the wrong-headed approach that it has taken. It has placed Canada in jeopardy in the world. It has placed the Armed Forces and the members of their families in jeopardy.
Such a committee could act to end Canada's involvement and its Armed Forces in the war. It could end the international political support for George Bush by the Prime Minister and his government. It could convince other smaller nations that have no interest in the kind of butchery that will proceed from the action from this day forth. It could work together with people to stop this war, to end Canada's involvement, and then move to working with like-minded individuals and groups in the United States to stop American involvement in this war.
Such committees could take up the issues that have been dealt with in the House. Canada's nation is a nation with dirty hands in selling arms, nuclear reactors, and the tools of war. It could take up the issue of stopping the assassins that have been put in place, in many cases by the United States, in El Salvador, Central America, Latin America, and southeast Asia.
It could work on a number of issues that we, on this side of the House, have complained about. But it is now almost time to end this debate. There is no point having a vote. It will never convince the government. It will never have an impact on it.
What will have an impact is if the 88 per cent of Canadians who oppose the Prime Minister, the government, and this war band together in an enormous national effort to get us out of the war, and then work to get the Americans out of the war. That is all we can do, I would think.
Would the member not agree, and would he be willing to participate in such an activity?

We sometimes think that people do not watch, but I think we would probably be surprised. We will try to get the other telephone numbers. This is only for our own Opposition Whips, but there is a general telephone number with a lot of telephone lines on it. We will get those.
There are six minutes of my time left. Maybe, before I am finished, we will be able to give out other numbers. The number, again, is 613-995-9557.
How about your home number?

I come from Saskatoon. Of course, the number there is 306-382-3361. It is in the phone book, and everyone knows it.
The answer to the question is, yes, I would become involved in that.
There was an excellent advertisement in the Star Phoenix just last weekend. The fax numbers of the Prime Minister's and Secretary of State for External Affairs were supplied. I would certainly encourage people to do that.
I think we should emphasize that we are not saying that Canada should pull out of the situation altogether. No Canadians would disagree with Canada's involvement in the imposition of sanctions, which we had been involved with before. As the New Democratic Party, we have proposed that there be a pause in the hostilities.
We have been apprised by previous speakers that the news which we have been receiving has been distorted
January 17, 1991

and laundered by the military. So, I suppose that the reports that the Iraqi capability to retaliate and to function has been almost destroyed is probably wrong.
Nonetheless, there is no point in annihilating a nation. It is Saddam Hussein and his army which we are trying to bring to a halt. To continue beyond what is militarily necessary to accomplish that, to continue with an annihilation of the civilian population, and to continue with just an annihilation of even the geographical entity which is Kuwait and Iraq is insanity of the highest order.
There seems to be a tremendous amount of logic to having a pause in hostilities and saying to this madman: "It is time you laid off what you are doing. I have another number here, Mr. Speaker. The area code again is 613-996-7441.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks, I would just like to extend my own personal thanks to you for seeing this debate. I know it has been a very long evening for you and, through you, Mr. Speaker, I would thank the employees of the House of Commons and the people at the table for their perseverance through this very long but very important debate.
As I prepared myself for this debate, I decided I would spend the day back in Winnipeg, inasmuch as it is an issue that concerns the people of my city very much. As I flew back, I was struck by how divided people were.
I went to the Westmister United Church and met with the peace groups and heard views about what this country was all about. If I would talk to my friends at the work-out class around the corner, they would give me other ideas. Yet, if I went to the legion, the first legion in the country, Legion No. 1 on Sargent Avenue, its
Government Orders
members would have a different point of view, as do the members of the Sir General Sam Steele Legion in the north end.
This diversity of views, while at many times is a healthy reflection of a democratic society, is also a reflection of the very divided society that we have right now. When one enters a war theatre in wartime with such divisions, one has to reflect on why that is.
I was saying to myself when I prepared that it is a very odd debate to have. The motion was crafted, thought about, and presented to the House in a time of peace, on the edge of war, but still in a time of peace. Yet, we are winding up the debate today in the middle of a war. In some respects it is hard to believe that it has only been 60 hours since the first guns were fired and the first planes took off and headed into Iraq. It seems like a lifetime ago that we have a chance to save ourselves from war and now we are right in the middle of a very difficult struggle.
Many of us spend our time while we are not debating in the House watching this theatre on television. In some respects, this is the first war that we have been forced into the scene by watching the devastation caused by bomb after bomb. Heavens knows what will happen when the troop movement will begin. However, we are also very removed from it. We cannot reach out to the TV and turn it off. We cannot stop those bullets or bombings. Our democratic societies feel helpless because we do not want to see these actions wished upon anyone. Yet, it is beyond our control. At the very moment we are more involved in a real way through international television, we are made to feel not part of it, but removed and helpless by it.
We have to think of how one contributes thoughtfully to debate such as this one. We are all peace loving, but we have very different strategies for producing peace and making sure that we have a society that continues in peace.
Again, I was struck by the fact that one of the major emotions we have is the emotion of anger. How many times in the House have we had an opportunity to show consensus on the one hand, but on the other were presented with motions and opportunities that would only create division.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
For example, there have been many individual remarks-and I would like to add my own to them-about how thankful we are for the troops and the members of the Armed Forced who are obeying the government and presenting themselves in very difficult situations by going out on the limb and putting their families in fear for their futures and all that goes with war. The House was never presented with a motion to thank these people. What would have been more simple for the government to call for the unanimity of the House to thank those who had volunteered for war? I am sure there would not have been one member from any of party, or from among the Independents, who would have said no to that motion. But were we given to show unanimity as to what this House feels? No. Instead, the government has sought ways to divide us.
When one begins to talk about a situation as difficult as the Middle East, one has to reflect on history. I was reviewing the speeches of my colleagues from the last few days and was amazed by the number of people who have turned to history and found examples to support their cases. What would have Prime Minister Pearson done? What would Prime Minister King have done? What would President Roosevelt have done? Among all three parties there has been support from these famous people for their position. In fact, the Prime Minister managed to find words of Stanley Knowles which buttressed his case. I am sure that the NDP were surprised to find Mr. Knowles on the side of our Prime Minister.
They have each had their own crises and contradictions to deal with. Mr. King had to deal with a depression, the Second World War, the lost generation and the failure of the League of Nations. Mr. St. Laurent had to deal with the recreation of North America and, more important Europe, and a cold war. They had to deal with the beginning of the developing nations and the first of the colonies breaking away from the European powers.
In the sixties, we had the beginning of Vietnam and the threat of nuclear war. In the seventies, we had the oil crisis and the second of the serious battles in the Middle East. In the eighties, we had the beginning of the end of the eastern European bloc. Each one of these decades has created circumstances that should cause us to turn back to these people not as heroes necessarily because they solved problems and they had very difficult times, but to cause ourselves to be reflective on the situation that we find ourselves in.
Often, one approaches the problem by thinking how it began, before beginning to solve it. For example, think of Canada and the trouble we are into.
When you enter a constitutional debate, your answer is largely determined by how you conceive the country: is it two founding nations, is it a country that is 130 years old, is it a country that is older than that and, if so, how much older, is it 10 provinces which have made a deal that they can all then recreate the deal, or is it a series of regions?
That might look like an academic and sort of obtuse question when I am discussing the Middle East, but think of the price that Canada has paid by not thinking through that problem. We now have a constitutional crisis because we did not take the aboriginal people seriously. We thought our history began somewhere between 100 to 200 years ago. The aboriginal leaders said no, that this country began 1,000 years ago; you had better begin to think of how to conceptualize that. We refused to acknowledge that at the bargaining table and what happened? We failed to reach an agreement. If we had thought four or five years ago that the real basis of this country included our original peoples, we would now be in a different situation. So we turn ourselves to the Middle East and say to ourselves: "Where do these battles begin?"
Canada has now entered a front for the first time as a member of a war force. No matter how we want to say it, we are working very closely with our allies, but this is the first time we have really intruded in that region, unless one wants to consider Cyprus, which is part of that region but not as directly concerned. What do we think of that crisis? Do we think it began last August with the invasion of Kuwait? Do we think it began with the oil embargo? Do we think it began with the division of Palestine after the Second World War? Do we think of the divisions after the Great War by the European powers? 'Is its origins in different religions that go back for centuries? It is ethnicity? What is the basis of that conflict?
When you enter into a crisis situation, you better have it pretty clear in your mind what you think the problem might be because you want to come out with a solution. Our party was very reluctant, as this House knows, to see us get involved in this conflict. We saw it as one of a series of problems. Although force has been exercised many times before in the Middle East, and never once has it produced the so-called end solution, the agreement that has solved all problems, the agreement among all agreements, that has never worked. For some reason
January 17, 1991

we have decided that this particular time it is going to work.
In posing this question and opposing what has been taking place, this party has been very careful not to position itself among those people who are simply anti-American or pacifist by definition. There are times when wars have to be fought. Many Canadians have in their families people who have fought in wars for good reasons and have paid the price. We in the Liberal Party respect that and have participated in that and supported that.
There is a very good article by a British journalist, Hugo Young, writing in the Manchester Guardian, last week. He argued that Saddam alone is to blame. What he did in this article is very interesting and is something which I think every politician has to do, and that is to read something which tears apart every one of your arguments so that you are sure of yourself. I thought in preparing for today that this person had read my speech before I began and had an argument against every one of my positions.
The Liberal Party has been very thoughtful behind the scenes in its deliberations and its research. It was able to conceive a position which was consistent with its historical commitment to the United Nations but, at the same time thought that certain steps should be taken before we entered the arena. Since we have done that step, it is very important that we take those mistakes made by this government and try to understand how we should be approaching the problem in the future.
I think one of the most important aspects of this debate this week which has to be put on the table by every parliamentarian who is honest with what he or she has seen in their constituencies is the anger of Canadians that we are in this position. It does not matter whether or not they agree that we should be at war or disagree, they are angry. The reason they are angry is that they became confused after Christmas as to exactly why January 15 was the date on which war had to be begun. Why had Canada found itself so closely allied to a position which Canadians themselves were not sold on?
Government Orders
We go back and we say that the government has failed to communicate with Canadians and that the price that is being paid is that we enter into the war without a consensus in this country that this war is going to be a benefit. The government failed to identify the interest of Canada in the Middle East. There are very real interests and ones that we should be fighting for. It failed to open up the debate to Parliament during the summer. It failed to have ongoing debate on this issue. It failed in Question Period to answer these debates openly. It failed to provide briefings to Canadians who were interested. It refused to go out and discuss the issues honestly with peace groups. It refused to consult widely. It ended up with this bull-headed attitude that they knew what was right, cabinet knew what was right, the senior civil servants knew what was right, and they were going to get Canada in there no matter what.
Now history is being recreated. Those of you who like to watch media spins and the media spin doctors, as they are called in the trade now, will recognize that since the decision was made, in fact beginning last Thursday before the decision was made to commence the offence against Iraq, all of a sudden we got news that this government had been out seeking peace constantly. For six months they said nothing but "we have to stick by that deadline, we have to push, push, push." Then all of a sudden we find out they are whispering: "No, no, no. We really, really were trying to do something much different. We were really trying to be on the side of peacemakers here. We just said those other things because that is what is expected of us".
How do you end up expecting people to believe that they have to be there on the war front when in fact the government says that it tried everything so that it would not have to be there on the war front. For the last sue months government members were saying they had to be there in the war front by January 15. And you ask why Canadians are confused. It is because the situation presented to them was confusing and totally manipulative.
That has to be part of the public record because we cannot generation after generation disappoint people who think that the base of this country should be peaceful. As they enter into a situation which frustrates them and they feel manipulated, they get locked out, and that includes particularly younger people and university

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
students, church groups, people who are not normally high profile in the political community. They look around and say: "We do not understand why this is happening. Why do we have to be there?"
There is a good argument to be made, and one that I personally accept, that in a legitimate process involving the United Nations, and in more specific ways with the NATO countries that we are allied with, Canada has a duty, a responsibility, to participate in collective action that preserves our security and preserves world peace. That has been a principle that Canada has adhered to since the original meetings to form the UN in San Francisco. It is a tradition we are proud of. It is a tradition for which we have gone out on the limb in one crisis after another, that people before me have spoken about, many Prime Ministers have faced, and faced with an equal perspective. That is the direction we go in.
However, when you begin to cut corners, you fail to tell people that the UN motion really is not a UN flag type of motion. It really is anybody who wants to get involved can get involved. We are not really going to say it that way. We like you all to help out, but if you do not want to, you do not have to. If that is the way you want to go, that is fine. But be honest. Do not tell Canadians that it is a UN flag operation when they find out too late that we are all there under our own flags and there is a co-ordinator, we think, although we have not really been told this by the Minister of National Defence. We think there is a co-ordinator. We think he might be someone else who is not a Canadian, but we are not too sure of who it is, but we are told it cannot be the UN because co-ordination under the UN will not work. But you say to yourself: "Come on, guys, treat us with some honesty; tell us why we are there under this organization, why you think it is going to work, how we should contribute, and if you think things have to be stepped up to protect our troops and to protect our interests in the Middle East". Obviously things are going to have to be stepped up now-"do not tell us this week, as if you did not think about it last week or the week before, that you are making this decision just now".
Today I heard that we were going to have to move troops into the Middle East. Why are we moving troops into the Middle East? To protect our hospital. Look at the logic.
We are bringing in a hospital to look after the wounded and to protect the wounded. We are bringing in troops instead of honestly saying that we think we should have troops there as part of the allied force. If we want to have troops there as part of the allied force, stand up and say to Canadians that we now have to expand our base, we are going to move in troops. Then we can deal with the issue honestly. We can ask questions in Question Period, we can present motions. We can call the committee together and we can talk about it. But to do it backward, how can any parliamentarian argue against having troops there to protect a hospital? Nobody can. This is the deceit that must drive our Armed Forces crazy, because they have an honest role to play. Canadians respect the Armed Forces. They are committed to seeing Canada play an honourable role. They are proud of the tradition in this country of having an independent foreign policy, one which they feel is formulated in our Canadian Parliament and is developed by the cabinet. There is a set of democratic institutions here second to none in the world, but when ideas and strategies are presented in a convoluted way Canadians pull back.
The government now has the spectre of entering a war with more and more Canadians opposing it. How can you develop a country feeling pride in itself? We are a country with a government that has made it bankrupt. We are in the middle of a recession. We have a constitutional crisis. We have had a crisis of aboriginal people. Now we head into war, and they turn around and they do not know why the country is demoralized. If they went back to their constituencies they would know why people are demoralized. Because they have not seen one thing go right for them for such a long time, they forget what it is like to feel good about themselves. They are not going to feel good about themselves by being in a war they do not understand.
There are some real responsibilities here which I think have been abrogated by this government and I think we are going to pay the price. As we go through this stage, and although I do not share the optimism of some of the commentators that this will be a short war, I think that one thing we have done in the western world, whether we have been involved with the fronts in Asia or whether we have been involved with the fronts in the Middle East, or South America or Central America, we have constantly analysed incorrectly the strength of people who are fighting nationalist fights or fights which they feel strongly about. For religious or historical or fights
January 17, 1991

they have had with others in the region, these battles, have always continued much longer and with much more devastation than we can imagine.
As we commit ourselves to this long battle, we must remember that we not only want to win the battle but we want to win the war. To use a cliche, we want the war's victory to be peace and we want to see peace settled throughout the Middle East. We want to preserve the integrity of many nations there. I know I share with other members, and I am sure they share with me the fear that we have that Israel will be drawn into the battle that it has neither asked for, nor provoked. Every member sitting there watching the television and understanding just how volatile the area immediately around Israel is with long-standing grievances can only hope that it is not drawn into this unfairly.

Mr. Speaker. There is a responsibility among parliamentarians, however, to put on the table ideas to help a government to develop better foreign policy. May I suggest that, first, we take steps starting now to initiate public discussions for a more peaceful world by getting people to understand what is going on in the Middle East. Second, we should try to revitalize any added nations. Third, we should use those components of the NATO agreements to begin to work out political and social plans to involve Eastern Europe before that explodes on us. Fourth, we should develop a military policy which has as its basis the development of a peacemaking function in terms of acquisitions of equipment.
We are in this case right now where we can not respond with peacemaking because we have CF-18s and they do not have a peacemaking role. It does not matter where you are. Fifth, we should establish human rights as a part of our foreign policy. Sixth, we should develop regional plans for peace so that this does not happen again in places like Cambodia, the Philippines and Central America. Seventh, we should have a white paper for peace. Eighth, we should have a parliamentary
Government Orders
committee talking to Canadians about these issues. Ninth, perhaps most important, we should publicly recognize that war is a failure. To enter war is a failure of everything we stand for as a country. We should turn this around, take this failure and make it into a positive benefit by recommitting our country to a peaceful future.

Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things the member touched on that I just want to make a point or two on and possibly follow up with a question.
I was pleased to hear the member touch on collective action and the responsibilities of Canada under the charter of the United Nations to act collectively with the rest of the world. I am pleased that he recognizes that, and I am pleased that he recognizes the need for collective security in the world. I do not believe that we are too far apart on that sense of responsibility on behalf of Canada. I think I have quoted the member accurately on that.
One of the things I do want some clarification on, if possible, is this. He mentioned that we do have interests in the Middle East. Noting that he understands what those interests are, I noted that the member said that those interests are worth fighting for.
We have been told in a sense by the government, but I was hoping that he could tell us this morning what those interests are in his own terms and sense of what they might be.

Mr. Speaker, I think Canadian interests in this case are tied into the development of a long term, peaceful plan for the Middle East. It is the one area of the world that, I guess since I was a student some 23 years ago, I have always worried about. It is the area that could blow up the world because of the combination of economic, historical and national and religious interests coming to converge in a very small area with an intensity that I think we in Canada do not appreciate.
The one principal organization we set up to work on that is the United Nations. One of the major tasks that the United Nations has to undertake is a more honest dealing with Middle East issues. There have been-some members in the House follow this very closely-several

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
resolutions in front of the United Nations which are left unresolved.
With our alliance stretching into Turkey through NATO, we have the commitment through its agreement to stabilize and protect that particular country.
There are other interests that I think are developing. There are economic interests. We have several private and public corporations very active in that region. There are trade interests at stake for us.

As a peacekeeping middle level power, we can show the world what some of those solutions might be.

Government Orders
that everything that had to be decided in order to proceed with the war has been decided.

One of the things that excites me a little bit is the fact that the member from Saskatoon, after his speech and in response to a question and comment from the member for North Island-Powell River, indicated that there was a number in the members' lobby which citizens who are watching this debate all across the country could call and actually tell members who are present in the House tonight precisely what their feelings are. I think, even at four o'clock in the morning, which is only one o'clock in the morning British Columbia time, these people can actually, in watching the debate, help us with information, give us their feelings and have an exchange of feelings with those people across Canada who are so interested in what is happening in the Middle East and in this Parliament that they are actually switching from the news channels to watch the debate here in the House of Commons because now they have an opportunity to interact with members and to tell members what they feel.

made and that I, as a member of the House of Commons, was absolutely powerless. In fact, it makes you feel a bit foolish when the decision has already been made and all you have to do is simply ventilate a little bit about the position that is taken by the government.

To some extent, the government attempted to make fools of the members of the opposition. I think it was the wrong tact taken by the government in this case.
I have read a little bit of history in my time. I know that during periods of war, often the government will contact the opposition parties and attempt to establish a union cabinet or a union approach because of the need to pull the country together and to establish national unity at the time of war. As part of that comprehensive approach to unity, it approaches trade unions for example, that will become involved in the war production effort. They contact municipalities, banks, businesses and financial institutions, the efforts of which it is going to need in order to mobilize the country to prosecute a war.
In this case, as is traditional with this government, it did not even bother to contact the opposition to develop the question that we were going to be debating in this House. I looked at the question that was presented to us by the government as a fait accompli and the question says this: "That this House re-affirms its support of the United Nations in ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait." Nobody in this House could have any difference of opinion with a question like that. We want to support the United Nations. We want to support the
principles of the United Nations as set out in its charter. We are committed as a party and a country to do it. How can we possibly oppose a resolution like this? That is not the reason that this question was placed on the floor of the House of Commons by the hon. Prime Minister.
The reason this was placed on the floor was for a political trap. Basically, this resolution will be interpreted by the government as opposition support for its efforts in the war against Iraq. It is unfair for a Prime Minister to come into a House to present a resolution like this knowing that it is a resolution designed to entrap politically opposition members in this House into voting in a way they do not want to vote. It is manipulation and the kind of manipulation that we have seen far too often by this Prime Minister. It is the kind of manipulation that he himself boasted about when he was talking about delaying the First Ministers' Conference on the Meech Lake Accord until the last possible minute so that the First Ministers of this country would feel compelled by the passage of time to vote quickly to pass the Meech Lake Accord. I think the country rejected that kind of political manipulation. We certainly do not like to see, in an important situation like this, the opposition in this Parliament manipulated into voting for a resolution that is essentially a political trap.
Hear! hear!

Now, I support those members who have stood up, including the leader of our political party. For example, the member for Fraser Valley West I think made an excellent presentation in this House, a compassionate, committed presentation, committed to peaceful resolution of disputes, both in the Middle East and around the world. But the problem is, that when you are presented with a question, and all of the parties in the House of Commons have not had an opportunity through a consultation process to develop, it is almost impossible to allow members on that basis to have a free vote. If you vote yes for this resolution, then the government is going to say you

support the war. If you vote no for this resolution, the government is going to say: "you are in favour of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait" or "you are opposed to supporting the men and women of our military forces overseas." But I want to tell you that I am absolutely opposed to Canada's participation in this war against Iraq. I do not think it is necessary. I think it is pursuing a United States' foreign policy, and I do not think that Canada should be involved in it. I am absolutely opposed to the use of Canadian forces in an offensive way against the Government of Iraq. That is not to say that I do not want Iraq out of Kuwait or that I support Iraq's aggression in Kuwait. What I am saying is that there were alternatives that we should have used and that we should have exhausted before we resorted to war.
I think that those alternatives would have been successful had they been given the opportunity. But other people-and I am thinking of George Bush and the U.S. administration-were motivated otherwise, and I think that has dictated how Canada has become involved in the war in Kuwait.
I agree with my leader that I think Canada's forces should be in the Middle East, but they should be in the Middle East serving ends other than the violent ends being pursued by the United States. I think we should be using our forces to contain the war zone so that the war does not expand. I think we should be assisting in the blockade of war material and other support going to Iraq through the Middle East so that Iraq is ultimately denied the ability to maintain its troops in Kuwait and to maintain a war against the allies there. I also believe that our troops and Canadian personnel should be used for

humanitarian purposes; to provide health, medical and refugee support to those civilians and others who are either injured or become casualties as a result of the war, or who become displaced from their homes as result of the destruction due to this war.
Canada has a tremendous and respected role to play in providing those kinds of humanitarian and support services to those who are injured, become casualties or refugees as a result of this war.
I think that represents the kind of traditional role Canada has played recently in wars around the world. I think that has generated for us a great deal of respect.
I had the opportunity to visit the United Nations as a parliamentary observer just a few months ago. This was an opportunity that I never thought of, growing up as a young child in New Westminster, British Columbia in a very poor family. I never believed that I would be sitting on the floor of the United Nations with delegations from all around the world discussing issues of world importance.
I was almost overwhelmed by the opportunity that was given to me as a member of this Parliament. I have a great deal of personal respect and lend a great deal of support to the United Nations.
For the government to come into the House and tell me as a member of the opposition that if I do not support its resolution, then for some reason I am opposed to the United Nations. I absolutely resent that kind of entrapment and gamesmanship with this resolution. It is absolutely false. I can speak not only for myself by that statement, but also for. . . whole of our caucus.
This caucus has supported the United Nations throughout the history of this political party and throughout the history of the United Nations.
That has not always been the case with some of our allies in the current war effort. For example, I want to talk about an incident that happened recently before the World Court. The Speaker will be aware of what is called the Contra scandal which brought to light the fact that the United States was providing, both legally under American law at times and under its own law at times, weapons, money, material and humanitarian aid to a group called the Contras that would not really exist

without the support of the United States government or its surrogates.
The World Court, back in 1986, heard a case advanced by Nicaragua that the United States was violating international law by supporting the Contras by printing booklets calling for psychological warfare and terrorism against Nicaraguan communities by providing the Contras with weapons with which to kill Nicaraguan civilians, and in fact in instruction manuals on psychological warfare and terrorism actually advocating the murder of non-combatant Nicaraguan citizens. The United States was violating the charter of the United Nations and was engaged in an act of aggression against Nicaragua.
The World Court ruled that by mining the harbours of the Atlantic coast of Nicaragua the United States again was not only violating the treaties it had with Nicaragua but was also in violation of the Geneva articles of war and the charter of the United Nations.
The United States has not been known in recent years, as recent as 1986, to be a supporter of the United Nations. Here, the government is telling us that we should side with the United Nations, and the United States in telling us how we should be giving great respect for the United Nations. I want to know where the Government of Canada was when those violations were taking place, when the United States was hauled before the World Court and found guilty of violating the United Nations charter and international law and participating in an act of aggression.
It is a country of 220 million that was engaged in an act of aggression against a country of 3.5 million people. Why was Canada not standing up on its hind feet? Why was it not seeking allies in the United Nations to prevent this kind of active aggression going on in Nicaragua, which had been identified and condemned by the World Court, an international body which Canada claims to support. Where was our support for the United Nations then?
One of the reasons why I feel almost ashamed as a legislator to be here at 4.45 in the morning talking about a resolution that is virtually redundant is that Canada has already gone to war along with the United States. We really do not have any power on behalf of our citizens.
I have had letters from my citizens all over my constituency saying that they absolutely oppose this war. I represent my citizens and yet can do absolutely nothing because the government has come into this House with its mind made up and members of this Parliament can do absolutely nothing to change its mind.
As I speak, there are two members of the government in the House, cabinet is asleep, and nobody is really listening to Canadians. That makes people like me frustrated.
But there is an opportunity for people to get in touch with this Parliament at this very hour. I would suggest that they call 613-996-7446 and they will reach the opposition lobby.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member on a very effective speech, one that I know will be read and considered. I do not say that lightly or with humour. It raised some factual evidence about the performance of the United States in this world that certainly does no credit to its record and no credit to its support.
One of the things that the previous speaker mentioned was an alternate role for the Canadian Armed Forces. When the Americans finish bombing Iraq back to the stone age, and that the country lays in ruins, its government, administration, and infrastructure destroyed, there will be an enormous number of casualties, absolutely enormous.
But the day the bombing stops, the deaths will accelerate. They will accelerate from gastro-intestinal diseases. People will die from injuries suffered during the war. They will suffer from starvation, famine, disease and exposure. Their water systems will be gone. Their sewer systems will be gone. There will be toxic chemicals and hazardous wastes everywhere. Transportation systems will be destroyed. Throughout their cities there will be dangerous buildings damaged by war. What we need to do is to think seriously about the use of the Canadian Armed Forces who have tremendous expertise, medical corps who can offer treatment to civilian and military casualties. They can treat famine and disease through some of the public health techniques that they have. They can deliver community health care. Women are still going to be pregnant and have babies, people are
January 17, 1991

still going to be suffering from diseases and will need the distribution of antibiotics, medicines and surgery.
We could put a corps of engineers in there to destroy the dangerous and damaged buildings. We could restore transportation systems so that the sick, the injured and the destitute can be brought to medical treatment and to places for shelter and food. We could restore electricity, so that pumps could be run to remove sewage and provide water. We could look into damaged sewer systems, water systems, communications so that the population can gradually be reorganized to protect and provide for itself.
Transportation units out of Trenton, Comox or Cold Lake could provide stores that we already have in place of medicines, food, fuel, shelter and clothing. Many of the people will die of exposure. We think of it as always a hot country, but it is not so.
Our Canadian Armed Forces have stores available and the opportunity to prevent starvation, to prevent death from the simplest diseases of infants and young children, to provide just basic antibiotics that will save more lives than probably anything else. They are ready and competent to deliver those stores, but unfortunately this government has not for one moment considered that.
What lies ahead when this wreckage is finished is the possibility of even more deaths from simple matters of disease and lack of attention, food, clothing, shelter and medicine. Our Armed Forces are far better equipped to deliver that than to make war. Yet in the briefing the other day the two individuals who came forward to give our caucus information said our Armed Forces are not giving consideration to that.
If we are not in there the day the bombs stop dropping, people will begin to die at an accelerating rate. It is going to take money, resources and planning to get in place. I would ask why the Prime Minister, why the Minister of National Health and Welfare and why the Minister of National Defence are not giving this House information about what responsibility we intend to take the day the
Government Orders
bombing stops and when the money and resources are going to be put aside.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for posing those alternatives. It is something that this caucus is concerned about and that the opposition is concerned about. Even as World War II drew to a close, and other previous wars drew to a close, the allies, before and during the war, had some ideas meetings to determine exactly what was going to happen when peace was ultimately restored; who was going to have responsibility for rebuilding the destruction that had been done who was going to have the responsibility for the medical reparations that were going to be required because of the injuries and the losses in particular populations what kind of economic reconstruction was going to take place, who was going to deal with restoring the populations to the economic health that it had before.
I think those discussions have not commenced by the participants in this war and they should certainly commence. I congratulate the member for some of the suggestions he has made so far.
Along the same lines, we should be looking at the future role of Canada's Armed Forces and Canada's military power because I think many Canadians, having seen what has happened in the Middle East, never want to see Canada's military play this kind of role again.
There has been a number of peaceful roles suggested, the role that we traditionally follow in the United Nations as peacekeepers to separate combatants and to restore a peaceful existence between conflicting nations.
I think the Canadian Armed Forces could be used for other purposes. They are already used to some extent off the west coast to watch for oil spills and that kind of thing, and to become involved in the protection of the environment which will be a major concern for the next 10 years. I-think our Armed Forces could be allocated, for example, to help Africa with its elephant poaching problem. That species is under the threat of extinction because those who are going after that species are better armed than the wardens in the national parks in Africa.
