Government Orders
Why are our Armed Forces not offered to that country to beef up the park warden system so that they can protect a declining species? If action is not taken quickly, that species will be wiped out. Why are they not offered to protect the kind of damage that is being done in the rain forests in southeast Asia and in central South America? I think our Armed Forces could be used internally in some countries as police to assist in the maintaining of the natural environment. If we do not protect those elements of the natural environment, then all life on earth could be threatened.
If the Speaker will give me one final moment, I can recall reading a statement by Physicians for Social Responsibility that said there is something like 10 million cases of malaria in the world today, 1 million new cases are developed each year and 1 million people die of malaria each year. We could cure malaria. The cure is now available if we allocated what we spend on arms around the world in the space of two weeks. I think that the Government of Canada should make a commitment to stop spending on military purposes for two weeks and contribute that to an international pool because more people now are now dying of malaria than are dying in wars. They are the true victims of the next war. If we set aside that money and dedicated it to a cure for such diseases as malaria, I think we could save more lives than any other thing we could possibly do. I think Canada should commit itself to that kind of action world-wide which I think will be valuable to people of this generation and to future generations.

It is a
pleasure on behalf of the New Democratic Party Caucus to rise in this Elouse to contribute to the debate. I would like to remind citizens of this country who are concerned about what this has done that there is a telephone number in the lobby here so that they can convey their thoughts to a member of Parliament. I urge them to call 613-996-7446. There are things that citizens must do in order to offset what the government has done so please call.
There are four short questions that I would like to deal with tonight and they are questions that Canadians are asking. How did we get into this mess? How do we get out of the mess? How do we prevent this situation in the future? What should be Canada's role in the future? How did we get into this mess? Without dwelling too long, this government has basically found it necessary to obligate itself completely to the United States.
A great deal of time has been spent by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and members of the Conservative caucus on how great the Americans are as a trading partner with Canada. Many of us have relatives in the United States and very friendly ties with the people of the United States. Very often over this century the United States has taken a tactic in its foreign affairs that is completely abhorrent to what most Canadians believe to be correct.
But the Prime Minister, for whatever reasons, has decided not only to work with the United States, but to obligate himself in a very unhealthy and unwholesome way. That is the reason we are into war. There are those of us who believe that this special relationship must be paid for. Canada has a trade agreement with the United States and whether you agree with it or not, this government was absolutely committed to it. To maintain it I am sure that James Baker told the Prime Minister the night he arrived that: "if you wish to maintain that you will not only back us politically in the international attack on Iraq but you will in fact get blood on your hands." That was the price. It may have been even more. The fact that we can join the United States and Mexico at the table talking about an agreement may in fact be the price. There may be more that will be announced later. But unfortunately, this Prime Minister and this government have attempted to place Canada in a very subservient obligated role to the United States in this very disastrous act.
The Prime Minister and the government do not enjoy the confidence of Canadians. Eighty-eight per cent of Canadians continuously express disfavour with this government, no confidence. Fifty-five per cent of Canadians on the January 7 wanted no action for Canadians in a war against Iraq. That number is growing. The feeling is stronger and stronger. I am sure, now that Canadian Armed Forces have been committed to attacks on the Iraqi population, that number will grow astronomically. There will be no glory for this government, no glory for this Prime Minister or this country in the acts that are done. Canadian citizens will not support it. There has been a lot of talk about the Canadian Armed Forces. We, on this side of the House, feel that the Canadian Armed Forces need to be supported. They have been placed in an extremely precarious position. Many of us feel that that position is not morally right and that in fact we feel the best kind of support for them and for their families is to withdraw immediately. This is not our war. This is not
January 17, 1991

our kind of action. Our Armed Forces have a far better role to play.
How do we get out of this war? Many Canadians are asking that question on the phones tonight. The government has to attempted to rationalize to the people of Canada in as strong a voice as it can-every member of cabinet, the Prime Minister, and every other member who has spoken in this House-why we need to join with the United States and attack Iraq, why we have to commit our Armed Forces in an offensive way to kill Iraqis. The rationale is extremely weak.
There are probably now close to two billion people, with the assets of almost all of the developed world aimed at a nation of 17 million people. The sanctions would have stifled them. The price of rice is $42 a kilogram and rising. It has gone up 90 times. Soon Iraqis will not be able to eat if those conditions continue. Certainly, their armed forces could not continue. The production of oil and the obtaining foreign currency would be virtually impossible.
How do we get out of it? We simply ask the Prime Minister to end Canadian involvement in the war, to withdraw the troops from actively attacking Iraqis.
My colleague from Comox-Alberni made a very reasoned suggestion that the government could use the troops that are there for containment. Why allow an attack outside the borders of Iraq? Why not contain the theatre of war? That is a reasonable suggestion and a reasonable role. We have effective, well trained members.
I am very upset that this government and our Armed Forces have not begun planning for the mission to take place as soon as the bombs stop and the guns go silent. What about our involvement in rescue and reconstruction? More people could likely die in the aftermath of the war with the chaos, the disease, the lack of sustenance, and the exposure that could happen. We have the talent, the capability, and the resources within our Armed Forces to deliver enormous aid. Down the road, Iraqis may in fact see us as friends again and trust us if we were to play that role. We may be individuals who are

welcomed as citizens of the world in that part of the world if we offer a helping hand.
That is not going on right now. That has been confirmed by the Armed Forces. I would honestly like to hear the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the Minister of National Defence saying that they have heard messages from the opposition and have plans in place for rescue and reconstruction the minute the bombs stop. We will join with Japan and other nations committed to that route as their contribution in this very unfortunate conflict.
What do we do to prevent this situation? How do we get out of the war? I am more and more convinced that we cannot do anything more in this House of Commons. The motion, as has been pointed out, is now irrelevant. The debate has largely been members thinking on their feet of what can be done.
Many people in this House have come to some conclusions. There is no point in having a vote. There is no point in continuing the debate much longer. The government has made up its mind and the opposition has made up its mind. The citizens of Canada can find a vehicle. Such a committee representing the entire community can approach the government and the Prime Minister and place enormous political pressure asking the government to end Canadian involvement but not stop there. Ending Canadian involvement means becoming reinvolved in the traditional way that Canadians have been involved before and reorganizing the approach of the Armed Forces to rescue, rehabilitation and construction. We can also become involved in containment, the blockade, and the sanctions as a continuing measure until a peace treaty and co-operation can be developed. Many roles can be played, other than an offensive attack on the Iraqi people.
Such a committee to end the war in Canada can then extend its efforts to assist committees in the United States to stop George Bush and stop the American armed forces from bombing this country back into the stone age and from the enormous casualties that will accrue from a land war in that country. A committee to stop the war can spread out to smaller countries or other

Government Orders
medium sized countries such as the Nordic countries. They are not in this combat, killing Iraqis. They are looking at offering far more constructive ideas than Canada. It could discuss joining with those nations and asking them to co-operate in stopping the war.
This could happen on a much broader scale. If and when that war stops, when Canada makes a nobler contribution than we make today, the committee could become involved in attempting to motivate politically whoever forms this government and the next government that follows to prevent Canada from having dirty hands in this business. We are a substantial seller of arms and equipment in the world, which sustains armed forces of governments that are absolutely abhorrent to our way of life.
What is going on in Central America is completely disgusting. We should be influencing the United States to try to clean its hands of the blood it has gathered there over the years. Down the road, we should look at how we can enhance our contribution to making this a safer and a more humanitarian world in which to live. On the issue of sanctions and collective security, it strikes me that Canada has become an expert in the area of peacekeeping. Canadian Armed Forces members have placed themselves in a dangerous position between belligerents. Over the years, they have become experts in monitoring the flow of arms and in winning the confidence of both sides so both sides would accept the peacekeeping responsibility.
Maybe we will have to move into a new generation of contribution to the world community. I think we have the talent, the commitment, the courage, and the expertise to do that. In the business of sanctions, an interesting role for Canada would be to develop, through our diplomatic channels and the use of our Canadian Armed
Forces, mechanisms to enhance the use of sanctions. When we have a peacekeeping situation, we cannot get in between belligerents in a hot war, but once they decide they want to stop shooting and they need a neutral force to stabilize the area, possibly an unarmed force to stabilize the area, Canadians are able to execute those diplomatically, maintain the diplomatic context in which that must happen, separate the belligerents, stop arms flow, and generally contribute in a very positive way.
If we were to do the same thing with sanctions, we should encourage nations around the boundary of a country that has had sanctions imposed on it to co-operate in support of the world community. With our diplomatic initiatives, if we are trusted and we are seen as a nation that can be trusted, we may in fact be able to win the co-operation which the United States, Israel or other nations with blood on their hands cannot do. We may be able to do that.
We can develop the expertise for monitoring the flow of goods on which there is an attempted interdiction. We could develop those techniques and develop expertise in making sanctions work so that nations do not have to resort to armed forces. Outlaw nations could be brought to the table before there is a resort to massive bloodshed.
The role that Canadians could play, not only in peacekeeping, could be a very forward looking one in which Canadians could become experts at operating sanctions. Canada is a trusted nation, a nation without blood on its hands and without an axe to grind but with a major history of contribution to the world community behind it. Canada has a willingness to foster peace and the friendship of nations through means other than resorting to violence.
Perhaps I would like to apologize to the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte for the disruptions I caused in the points of order at the beginning of the evening. I think it was an expression of the kinds of frustrations that have developed here. I regret that. Over the course of the evening I have appreciated the contributions of all colleagues who have spoken. The thinking on their feet by everyone here has left us with a fresh crop of constructive ideas to use in going forward. We felt frustration over the difficulty of this government in giving credence to the opposition in any way, shape, or
January 17, 1991

form. Certainly it has had a great deal of difficulty in terms of any modification of its position.
I accept that it has taken the decision to attack Iraq. It is going to defend it to the end of its caucus, and that is fine. It is over. There is no point in a debate continuing on this motion or a vote. I think we in the opposition have to move forward together, bind Canadians together, and pressure the government to politically change its position.
It has been a very useful exercise and one that will lead to something very positive.

Mr. Speaker, I came into this House somewhat despondent, depressed, saddened, and sickened by what was happening in the world today.
Over the last half hour or so, since the member for Saskatoon-Dundurn gave out the phone number of the opposition lobby, I have been involved finally in participatory democracy. I have been thrilled to be able to talk to people from all across Canada who are phoning in, on their dime, to tell us as parliamentarians what they think.
I would like to give them a voice right now in the House of Commons before I start into my remarks. I spoke to a gentleman from Calgary, Alberta who said he was still up and thrilled to watch the debates in the House of Commons, especially the members of the opposition. He was disappointed in the government's position, but he said that because of what he had heard from the members of the opposition he had confidence in Canada. He thought members of the opposition were showing a good deal of leadership in this debate.
I took a call from a woman from Victoria who said there were three in her family who were totally disheartened. She said it was a damned shame that Canada was in this war.
A gentleman from Tillsonburg, Ontario, said that he was frustrated members of Parliament were forced to toe party lines. He wished people in Canada could have a say. I am pleased to give him that opportunity today to have his say in the House of Commons.
Government Orders
Further, I took a call from a gentleman in Montreal who said he was disheartened by the government's approach to the Middle East situation and that he was sickened by the whole thing. I share that with him.
Before I go on to the next person, I would like to give that number out again. It is 613-996-7446. We have members of Parliament waiting on the lines to take calls.
Another person from Vancouver phoned and said that his position was that we should remain as non-aggressive, that we had to stay in the area and remain in a role of aiding, not in a role of attacking.
A woman from Toronto said that she was opposed to the Canadians being in the gulf and getting involved in the war. She felt and wished that they were peacemakers.
A woman just phoned me prior to my coming into the House from Calgary, Alberta. She said that she had not been able to sleep since this war started. She is worried about Canada being in the war. She said tonight that before her grandchildren went to bed they lit candles lor peace. She would like us to reach that peace, a lasting peace.
Those are some of the comments of people from across Canada. That number again is 613-996-7446. We appreciate the calls from across Canada.
The motion before the House should be set out in my remarks. Once again, it is:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
Let us not make any mistake about what we are in fact debating in this House of Commons right now. We are debating whether Canada should be involved in the war in the Middle East. We are debating whether Canada should be taking an aggressive role in that war. That is what we are debating.
There is no doubt about it. Every member in this House of Commons and people across Canada have always supported the United Nations in its peacekeeping role. Over the last 45 years we in Canada have been proud of our Canadian forces and their role in the United Nations and in the world as peacekeepers and peacemakers. That has changed now, as of a couple of days ago, with Canada's role in the Middle East.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
That is very disappointing to me. I was born just prior to the end of the Second World War and I have watched Canada build that reputation. I remember being in the United Nations Club when I was in high school and hearing guest speakers talk about the sleeping giant on the world scene. That was prior to the days, or around the time, I suppose, when Lester Pearson won his Nobel Peace Prize for his initiatives in the Middle East, in the Suez Canal crisis. I thought, as a young Canadian, that I could be proud of my country taking that position. This was a position that all Canadians could be proud of. All of our military and service people could be proud of their part in the world or global scene.
I was greatly saddened when I heard the sabre-rattling of the Bush administration and within hours I heard the sabre-rattling of our own government. That was not the Canada that I knew. That was not the Canada that I had become proud to be a part of. That was not a Canada that the people in my riding were telling me that they were proud of. Taking such an aggressive role in a military situation was totally foreign to me as a person born and raised in Canada. I was unused to that role. I still feel very uncomfortable with the role of Canada as an attacking nation. It is a role that I feel is untenable to all of us as Canadians.
Just prior to Christmas I visited a number of classrooms throughout the riding of Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt, in Penticton, Oliver, Osoyoos, from grade 5 right up to grade 12. At that stage I was being asked questions such as the following ones. Why are we doing this? Are we going to be drafted? Is this going to lead to a third world war? What will be left of the world? Will they use the atomic bomb?
We have been told that we are fear-mongers for even talking about this, but these implements of war are present in the world. We would be ostriches with our heads in the sand if we did not approach and answer the questions. I wish I had the answers. I wish I could assure these children that there would not be a major conflagration, that this is a very localized war. I wish I believed that myself, but I fear greatly for all the world when I see the type of weaponry involved in this conflict and watch what has happened in Iraq and in Israel over the last couple of days.
The fire power is there to destroy the world we know. I cannot make light of that. I do not want to have a part in that. I want to go back to a world in which I can feel comfortable raising my two daughters. When I leave home to return to Ottawa and have a 12-year old ask me if there is some other way than flying, it touches me in a small way, but that small way is substantially smaller than how it is touching the people who are actually present in the conflict in the Middle East. Can we imagine what it is like being in Baghdad right now or Tel Aviv or Jerusalem, not knowing what is going to happen, not knowing whether in fact there is going to be chemicals and chemical warfare? My heart goes out to the people who are involved in this conflict.
I am not the only one who is concerned. Prior to the recent situation I received a number of letters and a number of calls. By far the majority of them, as with the calls I have earlier read into my remarks, is against a position of aggression by Canada.
The resolution sent to the Prime Minister by the city of Grand Forks, in the boundary country in my riding, says a lot of how the people in my riding think. I will read it into the record:
The council for the city of Grand Forks unanimously pass the following resolution:
Bearing in mind Canada's traditional policy of supporting the United Nations and cognizant of Canada's international reputation as a peacekeeper and aware of our responsibilities regarding the welfare and security of our citizenry as municipal legislators, the Council of the Corporation of the City of Grand Forks in open meeting assembled beseeches the government of the Prime Minister Brian Mulroney to exercise patience and restraint with respect to the commitment of Canadian forces to the current conflict in the Persian Gulf and urges the Government of Canada to spare no effort to effect a peaceful resolution of the present crisis and to establish, within the framework of the United Nations, lasting peace, justice and security in the region.
On behalf of the citizens of Grand Forks, their mayor takes the opportunity to urge the Prime Minister and the Government of Canada to consider this community's position regarding the role of the Canadian forces in the Persian Gulf. Some of the remarks and the resolution of the city of Grand Forks are reflected in some of the letters I have received. A letter from North Vancouver reads:
Please consider, before committing Canada to war, evety other possible censure and weapon against Hussein. So far, my impression of the international military response is that this is some form of military party, that no wants wants to miss.
January 17, 1991

He goes on in another paragraph and says:
Don't let the majority of Parliament rubber stamp the decision without honest debate; our Parliament has been (almost unanimously) tragically wrong in the past. On February 25,1941, Angus Maclnnis was the only MP to speak out against repressive measures against the Japanese. And we ail know how wrong that decision was.
A woman from Summerland, British Columbia in my riding, writes:
I am an old woman and have lived through two terrible world wars, but realize that they were very small as compared with what will happen if we keep on this ridiculous way of dealing with the present situation.
A letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs from Kaleden, British Columbia in my riding, reads:
It is time our leaders realized that Canada is in a position to be a peace negotiator. We do not always have to follow the lead of the United States. We can be the country that leads towards finding creative, non-destructive methods to solve our differences. We can be the country that finds a peaceful end to this crisis.
I echo the words spoken by this couple in Kaleden, British Columbia. I agree that we can be that catalyst which brings about peace if we have the will.
In further remarks from a woman in Penticton, she states:
Rather than be pushed by the United States to the brink of war, cannot we take the lead in striving for a peaceful solution? Canada has always gained world-wide respect as a peace seeking nation.
In the final paragraph she says:
There must be a solution to solving world crises other than by going to war, resulting in the death of thousands of innocent people and leaving to mourn countless parents, widows and fatherless children.
Finally, the Penticton United Church of Canada has written a letter to the Prime Minister. I would like to read part of it. It indicates:
Should war take place, the innocent civilian population, from infants to elders, will be subjected to mass slaughter. Those who survive will live through miseries we can barely imagine, in a land laid waste. Are we willing to deal with the increasing flood of refugees, physically or mentally maimed, that would result? If we support war, we must also take responsibility for the results of war. We do not believe our government has considered this.
When we watch or listen to the media, we realize that a "war fever" has been building. The almost hysterical reaction of many is not only terrifying, but shows we have learned little from the past. Painting war in glorious colours has not yet been replaced by sober consideration. What would we be defending here? Certainly not democracy. And no nation should risk a bloody altercation over the availability of oil and gasoline.

Because of modern weaponry, including chemical and nuclear attack, war, no matter how limited to start with, has terrifying potential to engulf all nations and perhaps the planet itself. War has become obsolete as an acceptable method of settling international disputes.
He beseeches the Prime Minister and urges that the government reconsider its strategy and press for peace by all possible alternative action.
These remarks of various people throughout the province of British Columbia, mainly within my riding, are ones that I could not have written better. That is why I have chosen to give those people a voice within Parliament tonight, as I have tried to give to the people who have phoned in a voice. I will tell the people who have been trying to phone in to keep up their calls. If there is no answer when they call, we ask them to keep calling. The number again is 613-996-7446.
To Shirly McKee from Penticton, I appreciate your call of support earlier this evening. We do appreciate those calls from all of you letting us know what your thoughts are on this most important matter and to give you, the people of Canada, a voice in the House of Commons through us, the members of the New Democratic Party. So keep the calls coming.
I would just like to wind up with a couple of extra comments that bring home to me why Canada should pursue, together with the United Nations, some common solutions to this conflict through international diplomatic co-operation. The Government of Canada must take the necessary steps to promote an international peace conference on the Middle East to start achieving common security. Without that common security we have little hope for the security of our children into the future. Most of all, that is what I want. I want to leave Parliament at the end of my term knowing that I have not failed as a politician, that I have not been part of leading this country into a conflagration. I want to be able to say that I have had a part in creating world-wide peace.

Mr. Speaker, at 5.30 in the morning, Eastern Standard Time, I had managed to catch a few winks during the night while the other eye was switching between the parliamentary channel and the news channel in an

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
attempt to keep track of the events unfolding in the wee small hours of the morning.
Certainly, the news from the last few hours has been more than a little distressing. I could not help but think what is taking place is not really surprising, because once the genie is out of the bottle, then no one is in control. The politicians are not in control. The generals are not in control. The people are not in control. No one is in control; everything is out of control.
Once Saddam Hussein let the genie out of the bottle in August last year and once George Bush and the coalition made the decision to open active hostilities a few days ago and commence their action, the genie was released once again. So now we have two genies floating around and the situation is doubly out of control.
With the second launching of missiles towards the State of Israel, we are all waiting with bated breath. There is little we can do but wait to see if the remarkable restraint shown by that state last night can be repeated. I think the preponderance of opinion is that it is not likely to be able to show that same degree of restraint again for a multitude of reasons.
If that should happen, the hostilities that now exist between the partners of the coalition on one side and the State of Iraq on the other may well be twisted, turned, and broadened so that some of the allies become opponents and a set of factors move and take on their own momentum, which may result in a conflagration covering the entire Middle East area of a nature that all of us, throughout the world, must surely shudder to consider. That is what happens once the genie is out of the bottle.
In the debate that has taken place over the last few days and certainly in the hours of last night and this morning, a few thoughts struck me. One is that we cannot pretend that what has happened has not happened. Whatever our recollection and interpretation of history, we cannot rewrite it and we cannot change it. We have to start from where we are; we cannot go back and try again, as much as we would like to. So while we may wish to recall certain events to see what we can learn from our mistakes, in order to try not to repeat them in the future, we cannot change them. We are still making
mistakes but maybe it is not too late to correct some of them.
It is said by some that Saddam Hussein is a madman, a lunatic. That has been repeated many times in this House. Maybe he is, but, unfortunately, his is not a unique kind of lunacy. I am sure that a number of members will recall the lunatic theory espoused by Henry Kissinger and Richard Nixon in Mr. Kissinger's book on Vietnam and Cambodia. The theory was, and I will just try to paraphrase it briefly, that if you persuade your enemy that you are a lunatic or will act in a lunatic manner without regard to consequences, then your opponent may fail to put you to the test out of fear of an irrational or lunatic response and then you win. Was Heniy Kissinger a lunatic? Was Richard Nixon a lunatic? Is Saddam Hussein a lunatic?
It is like the allegorical story that was repeated on television a few weeks ago by David Suzuki, the story of two drivers playing chicken. If you really want to win, the story went, you throw away your steering wheel and destroy your brakes. The theory is, when the other guy knows you cannot turn away, he will chicken out and you will win the game. The catch is, what happens if your opponent does not know or does not believe or, even worse, he has thrown away his steering wheel as well. We know what will happen and it just did. It happened on August 2,1990 and it happened again this January. There are no winners and depending on what happens in the next few hours, we may all be losers and very serious losers.
I listened with a great deal of interest to some of the debate tonight, and one of the lines I wanted to pursue was pursued in a great deal of depth by a colleague not of my own party, the member of Parliament for Ottawa South. It was a very well developed argument on the changing nature of power structures in the world today and the lessons that we, perhaps, ought to draw from them. I am not going to go on at length. I would recommend to anybody in the nation that his remarks were very much worth reading.
One of the phrases he used concerning the current situation and the current action undertaken a few days ago was, and I think I am quoting him correctly: "The wrong action at the wrong time by the wrong force." That was at 10.15 last evening Eastern Standard Time. One of the things that concerns me, because of the way things were done a few days ago, is that we have wasted an opportunity to do things right. We could have set up a
January 17, 1991

United Nations operation and command in a way and a manner that would pave the way for effective and acceptable peacekeeping and peacemaking in the post cold war world. The checks and balances of the balance of terror are gone. While it makes many of us very uncomfortable I am also glad that they are gone.
I am sure many Canadians will recall the days in 1962 when those of us who were leaving work on a particular evening when the threats of the Cuba missile crisis were heavy, said goodbye to each other in a different way than we usually do because none of us knew if we were going to be coming back the next morning. The buses home after work that day were very silent. The difference is that most of us in most of the world are reasonably assured that whatever happens, most of us will be seeing each other the next day and that is refreshing. There are no longer two people in the world with their fingers on the big button. That, in itself, presents new and very real dangers.
We must begin to construct new mechanisms, hopefully through the United Nations, which can deal with matters of aggression and major violations of human rights and national rights. The world is dominated by a single superpower which has not demonstrated that it is the most responsible force on the face of this earth. This is little if any more acceptable or welcome than the regime of the balance of terror from which we are now emerging.
A lot of silly things has been said in this debate on both sides of the House. I hope I will not add to their number. The present conflict did not start in January of this year. It started last August. There are members on both sides of the House who appear to sound so virtuous and self-righteous that all they do is enrage others and increase the level of mutual intolerance of which there is enough already, both here in Canada and throughout the world.
The motion before us reads:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
The New Democratic Party asks that this be a free vote for very good and valid reasons. The government said no but it is free for us. The government and its spokesper-
Govemment Orders
son have made it clear that it would interpret a yes vote as support for their policy and that I cannot support, and it is not a cop-out. But neither can I vote against a motion that says what this motion actually says. That only leaves me one other option and that is to abstain. That is not something I care to do. But because of what I regard as the mischievous attempt to manipulate this House of Commons by this kind of phraseology and this kind of interpretation, it leaves me no other course.
However imperfect the design of the current United Nations sanctioned policy is, the only hope for the future lies in a subsequent formation, perhaps for later conflicts, of a permanent UN command that can act reasonably quickly in later phases of this conflict or, more likely, in future actual or potential conflicts. That is the only hope for freedom, justice and peace in the single superpower world in which we are now located for better or worse.
I do not kid myself that a single superpower will agree to be bound by the same rules that apply to the rest of us any more than these rules applied to two superpowers. That is not the way superpowers behave. We have to work slowly and methodically to expand the application and acceptance of this kind of genuine international action because international action must be governed and managed. It must not be merely international in name or it will never be accepted and will never be effective over the long haul. That is the only hope for the future and we have to start now.
The conflict in which we have been engaged since last August and since early this week is a tragedy. We can only hope that it will be brought to a conclusion soon without a wider war and with a minimum loss of life on the part of all concerned. We must move soon to bring the nations of the Middle East to the peace conference table and work to construct stable and secure nations and stable and secure boundaries in that area.
Any of us who lived through the period of the last 40 or 50 years recognize that the Jewish people in the State of Israel had to have a homeland. But because of the duplicity of the British war office and the British foreign office in the early part of this century when the same lands were promised to two different peoples, we have had a continuing problem that is a running sore which

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
threatens the peace not only of that region, but of the world.
Any of us who witnessed the events prior to and during World War II will know that we in Canada as well as the rest of the world are guilty. When Jewish people from Germany and Europe were attempting to find a place to go, we all shut our doors. Their desire and necessity for a homeland was understandable.
No matter how evil the State of Israel has acted on many occasions in recent years-and it has, despite some of their origins and despite some of the earlier beliefs, they have adopted many of the same ethics and practices that their oppressors practised during World War II upon them. We still have to understand what made them what they are. We must also find some way that the Palestinians can be secure in a homeland of their own, while allowing some secure and stable boundaries of at least the original State of Israel. We must begin to build a Middle East that has something of lasting value. We must have some hope that that region will not tear itself apart to the detriment of all of us. As there often are in the world there are two rights and two wrongs. We must take the opportunity that surely will come when this immediate conflict concludes to assist in drawing all the parties together and provide whatever assistance and assurances we can to try to build some long-term security for all of the peoples of the Middle East.
We heard the remarks of the member for Saint-Denis earlier today. They were passionate, serious and deserved an audience. I trust that when he makes his major address he will repeat some of them. I also listened to the former premier of British Columbia, the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. Like the member for Saint-Denis, I was impressed by the obvious feeling and the knowledge of that member as he attempted to describe some of the events that had taken place and some of his hopes and his fears for that region and for the world.
This is not a simple issue and I have never pretended to have all the answers. I hope I know some of the right questions. But I am sure the people of this country are committed to attempting to build an international world order and international mechanisms that can be trusted and can be respected. I only hope that the actions which this government has been a party to over the period of the last few weeks and months will not prevent us and
the rest of the world from constructing such a mechanism. That is my hope and my prayer. I am sure that the majority of the people of my own area and I hope the majority of the people of Canada will agree with me on it.

Mr. Speaker, it is approaching six o'clock in the morning. Some of us have been here since ten o'clock yesterday morning. I feel more vigorous than if I just got up.
I have been here 27 years. I do not consider this a Conservative issue. It is not an NDP issue. It is not a Liberal issue. I will say in English and French it is not a Quebec issue. I am Catholic, a strong believer, but this is not a Catholic issue. This is a moral issue. I never believed that after 27 years in this House people would start to understand. I really liked what the hon. member has just said. It prompts me to make a short comment. At long last we are addressing the real issue. We are going back to the causes of the problem of today.
I will repeat again, even to the point of maybe embarrassing my friend and colleague from British Columbia, the member for Epquimalt-Jean de Fuca. He is not in my party. He does not speak my language. He is not from my religion. Yet he made an unbelievably moving speech. He asks what is wrong. It was a very ordinary speech. It was not because it was important, a deeply felt speech.
When we want to solve a problem, it is not enough to govern.

You have to anticipate. You have to have vision. You cannot push people around. You cannot humiliate them. You cannot torture them and expect them to take it forever. However, it would be so easy.

That is what the member is prompting me to say. It would be so easy. I do not understand. People see it as so difficult, and I see it as so easy. I must be at fault. I must be totally wrong. I see it as an easy way. It is a question of respecting people regardless of skin colour, religion, rich and poor, black or anything. Just as long as you breath.
We are all the sons and daughters of the same God, because there is a God. That God today is looking at us and saying: "They are my children. Are they not intelligent enough to make peace with each other instead of
January 17, 1991

killing each other? Are we so deprived of grey matter that we are totally unable to find solutions?
I want to thank the member because I do not feel alone any more when I talk about the Palestinians, and peace between Israel and the Palestinians. I have given 26 years of my life to conferences. In my party, I have been pushed and pressured. The pressure is still going on at this late hour this morning to ask us to vote in favour of this motion.
The pressure is by powerful people I respect, but I do not give in easily and I will not. I hope my colleagues will reflect. We will listen to the other speeches, but I really am so full of energy suddenly because I see so many people who realize that yes, maybe we should have paid more attention to that part of the world.
It could be exploding. The news is not good. It will not be a macho Stallone style of war where we go in, clean up and that is it. No. The hate is profound. I do not want Canada to be hated. We have no reason to be hated, because people love us. They think of us in ways that even we do not know ourselves. We should kiss the floor everywhere we go in this country of ours.
Everybody likes Canada. Sometimes I really wonder if we deserve it.

Mr. Speaker, again I find myself for about the third or fourth time in the last 15 hours touched by the comments of the member.
It is not necessarily germane to this particular debate that we have tonight, but I just want to say that it does renew one's faith in this business in which we are engaged to see someone who has been involved for as many years-I say that in a respectful way-as the hon. member for Saint-Denis. He still has that degree of enthusiasm, commitment and belief that something can be done. It is a business that sometimes increases the level of cynicism-it is almost certain to-but to maintain that degree of passion and commitment is something welcome to behold.
Leaving that aside, the one further comment I would like to add to what I have already said is that there are many things I did not say because my colleagues and other members touched on them, particularly the reputation of that great superpower to our south. I do not
Government Orders
feel comfortable in that kind of single superpower world any more than I did in the two superpower world that preceded it.
Even though I am uncomfortable with that, the evil that was done by one nation to another last August, the occupation of Kuwait, and what happened in Kuwait since that invasion and that transgression, the catalogue of infamy that took place in Kuwait, as recorded by Amnesty International and other observers, almost made the record of the Nazi invasion and occupation of Denmark-a history with which I am somewhat acquainted-pale in significance. That was a civilized invasion and occupation compared to what happened there. I cannot forgive that, but neither can I forgive an action that threatens to blow up that whole area and cause it to move back into the dark ages and remove perhaps any chance we have to reconstruct a stable, secure, and just order in that portion of the world. That is the fear I have and that is why we have to find some way to get those two genies back in the bottle.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks, I want to commend our brave young people in the armed service who are currently carrying out the policy of the government of the day in the Persian Gulf. This debate is not about them directly. It is about the decision by the government to commit them to war.
I would like to make my position very clear today. I am opposed to Canadian offensive participation in the gulf war for three reasons. First, I would prefer to see Canada play a significant humanitarian and diplomatic role, rather than a symbolic offensive military role that may restrain our future ability to play an active role to bring about peace in the Middle East.
Throughout the night as this debate is taking place, we are receiving phone calls from across Canada. We are urging people to phone in with their concerns to area code 613-996-7446, to express their concerns. I know there are many people out there who feel as devastated as I do by what is taking place.
I believe that other avenues at least had the potential to bring Saddam Hussein to his knees. I will not commit my vote to a war until I, as a member of Parliament, am convinced that no other options exist. I would like to remind the House that the New Democratic Party did

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
not support the headlong rush into war represented by and I Security Council resolution 678.
As we debated that resolution, we talked about our concerns about a deadline and how it would be seen and would be effective. Throughout that debate, the government kept insisting that that was only a date and that we could continue sanctions. It did not mean that war would break out at that date. Less than 14 hours after that date came about, Canada was at war.
I want to say how devastated I was when I heard that, after hearing the comments from the Prime Minister and from the Secretary of State for External Affairs every day as we questioned them in the House with regard to sanctions and asked them for proof that they were not working. Not one single time did the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Prime Minister put forward any concrete evidence to the House that these sanctions were not working. They kept telling us that the sanctions would continue and that it did not necessarily mean that we would be going to war.
We voted against that resolution. I had hoped and prayed that I would not have to come into the House and say what I am going to say at this moment and that is, we told you so. The Prime Minister, the Secretary of State, and the members of the government who voted for that resolution have now got the conscience 14 hours after the deadline of putting Canada at war.
There is a fundamental question that all members of the House have to ask. . . as they formulate their position. We are all appalled by the brutality of the Iraq invasion and the occupation and the suffering of the people of Kuwait. But what is the trade-off? Would seven or ten more months of sanctions, sanctions that many experts felt had a good possibility of working, be a fair trade-off for what may be the loss of hundreds of thousands of lives? The answer I could arrive at is yes. The risk of sanctions not working was preferable to the risks of war. The uncertainty of sanctions working is no less than the uncertainty of where this war could take the world.
What is the most appropriate role for Canada? I would like to take the opportunity to expand on each of my three points. There are many countries that strongly oppose Iraq which are not playing an offensive military role in the gulf. There are many countries that have
contributed to all the military build-up in the gulf which strongly oppose Saddam Hussein and have abided by that UN sponsored programs and sanctions. It is very important to consider the question of why some countries support the United Nations have chosen to become involved in this war in an offensive manner and why some have hesitated. It is fair to assume that each country's decision is based on an evaluation of tradition, capability, history, and its perception of what the best course of action is.
Our government has decided that the act of military engagement is the best and most appropriate of action. I fundamentally disagree with it. I believe that Canada has a tradition: a view of war as the last possible resort. I must say that this is a tradition that differs from that of our neighbours' to the south.
There has a been a lot said about the role played by Lester Pearson in developing this tradition. This precedent has served us so well and I, too, would like to acknowledge his enormous contribution.
I too, would like to acknowledge the vital role played by John Diefenbaker during the Cuban missile crisis, because I believe it is important to point out the non-partisan history of our Canadian experience. Mr. Diefenbaker could have enthusiastically backed the military effort of the U.S., but he insisted that Canada would make military decisions on its own and only as a last resort. Mr. Diefenbaker could have committed Canada to participating in the U.S. sponsored trade embargo against Cuba, but he did not.
Through his actions, Mr. Diefenbaker said forcefully and courageously that Canada, although it agreed about the threat posed by missiles in Cuba, would make its own military decisions.
Canada has a tradition of military caution and of looking for non-military solutions to conflict. I believe this current government has broken with this tradition.
The next question, and one I think all members who opposed the government's decision have a responsibility to answer is: What should Canada's role be?
I suggest the number of actions that should be considered, including the use of our military personnel for what could be best described as humanitarian roles, such as medical personnel, refugee and relief operations, and
January 17, 1991

the preparation for possible peacekeeping operations following the war.
Canada should also be pursuing a very resolute and non-combatant diplomatic effort, as we did in Vietnam.
I must say that I do recognize the efforts made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs prior to the start of the hostilities. I do appreciate the fact that he has allowed Iraq diplomatic representation to remain in Canada. But what happens if Jordan, Syria, Iran, or Yemen join the battle against our allies? Who is going to be in a position to negotiate? Who will be able to lead a diplomatic initiative if the whole region goes to war?
I believe that an active military role by Canada will end any chance of Canada filling this essential role and, frankly, I fear it will reduce our options to simply increasing our military commitment to fight other enemies.
In returning to my second point, the abandoning of sanctions, I would like to point to the experts who have offered the opinion that sanctions are working. Senator George Mitchell, Senator Wellstone, former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff Admiral William Crow, Georgetown economist and sanctions expert, Dr. Gaiy Hufbauer, and the list goes on and on. These people say that sanctions had-and I use the past tense-a reasonable chance to achieve their objectives.
Many of my colleagues from the Liberal and Conservative parties have said that this issue is now irrelevant, that sanctions are dead. It is clear there is some twisted logic at work when people, who three days ago said that we must stay the course with sanctions, now say that they support offensive actions in a war they did not support.
It was a mistake by the allies to go to war three days ago. It was a mistake by our government to support the January 15 deadline. It was a mistake to give up on sanctions and the policies that all agreed were hurting Iraq. It is an horrendous mistake to argue that because war has started it is now right to support an offensive role by Canada.
It is obvious that we will not know the casualty totals for some time, but no one would argue that if this war goes on the death total could reach into the hundreds of thousands. That is what war really is, death and destruction.
Government Orders
What is the cost of 100,000 lives? One month? Two months? Three months? I cannot pretend to know that answer. But I can say this, it is more than five months and that is all that we gave sanctions time to work.
I will not-I cannot-vote to commit our brave young people to fighting a war that our politicians have not taken the time to resolve. This is the most important decision I have ever had to take in six years in the House. I will not vote for Canada's offensive participation in a war just because it has already started.
In finishing, I would like to restate the fact that the New Democratic Party warned against supporting the deadline because of the fear that the exact scene we are seeing today, an unnecessary early war, would happen. That is what we are faced with. The fact that the worst has happened is not enough to force me to vote for war.
Before I conclude, I would like to read into the record a few letters and petitions that I have received from my riding regarding this very sad and dreadful decision we have made.
This first letter is addressed to me, with copies to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It was dated January 16 and is from constituents in Fernie, British Columbia. It states:
Dear Mr. Parker,
The only heartening thing within the events of the last days has been the strong, sane position of the New Democratic Party and Audrey McLaughlin's forceful statements of that position. The failure of the United Nations to find a peaceful solution is an enormous setback to the establishment of lasting world peace. Canada should not back the United Nations in their erroneous decision. We are extremely angry at our elected government committing our country, our friends, and our family to war. We can only hope that all Canadian young people will understand the insanity and immorality of war.
I have another letter from a constituent in Grasmere, British Columbia addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the NDP, the hon. member for Burnaby- Kingsway, and myself. It states:
Dear Sirs,
With all of my mind and being, I object to Canada's involvement in the gulf situation to further maximize profits for multinational corporations. An economy based on an arms race and war is an unforgivable failure of our government's foresight and leadership.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Truth and non-violence are timeless. One can never cease to be amazed that so many continue to passively accept the anxieties and crumbs handed down from an affluent society to gamble off lives in applying the ultimate sacrifice in unbearable pain and suffering.
I also have a petition from 65 residents of Cranbrook, British Columbia dated January 16, and I am not going to read off all the names. It states:
Dear Mr. Parker,
We are a group of concerned citizens in your constituency who strongly and proudly support your stand and your efforts for peace at this very crucial time.
We feel Canada's role in the world should be one of leadership in making and keeping peace. We, as Canadians, do not support aggressive military action as a way to stop, mend, or prevent aggressive actions of others.
We hope that you will continue to be adamant in this view and that Canada will accept and follow this view so that we will not be engaged in offensive action in the Middle East.
Before I sit down, I plead with the government, government members, and all members of the House of Commons to find a resolution to this deadly war and to bring about peace as quickly as possible so that there will be less suffering and less damage throughout the world.

Madam Speaker, I would like to point out that there have been numerous phone calls to parliamentarians tonight with people expressing their opinions on this, and I would urge those calls to continue to 613-996-7446.
The opinions of Canadians who have been flowing in here tonight have been incredible. The number of people who are awake and have said they cannot sleep since this thing has started, the suggestions that have come in over the phone, and the absolute commitment are enormous.
The one thing I want to raise with the hon. member and every other hon. member is the problem with the action of the Prime Minister-an individual who enjoys the antipathy of 88 per cent of Canadians and the hostility of the majority of Canadians-and his cabinet declaring a state of war with Iraq.
It has been said that nobody, individually or collectively in a small group, should be allowed to make war on behalf of Canadians. The suggestion has been that there should be a division of power and some checks and
balances in this matter. A vote of this House should be the only authority to declare a state of war to exist with another nation and to authorize the use of armed forces aggressively against them.
Would the hon. member support the concept that we members who support the idea that a Prime Minister and cabinet cannot make a decision to attack another nation offensively and to declare a state of war to exist, should go forward and put together a private member's Bill and seek to have every member of the House endorse it? It would see the power to declare a state of war removed from cabinet and the Prime Minister, and the only authority that could declare war on behalf of this country would be this House by a full vote of every member.
Would the hon. member support that proposition so that that we could move forward and this decision could not be made by a Prime Minister obligated to the United States, or a small group of Canadians called the cabinet could not make that decision?
We are not talking about defensive action. We are talking about aggressive action in a state of war. That would be decided by a full vote of the House. We should put together a private member's bill and attempt to sell that bill to every member of the House so that we never have to face an entrapment motion such as the one that has been placed before us in this situation.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the question. It is an excellent opportunity. This is one of the things I noted in the House as we started to debate this, as the tragedies unfolded, and as we were watching television. I heard and saw the devastation of each member on all sides of the House at the destruction and capabilities for it taking place out there.
I heard many of them talking to one another saying that decisions were being made by a half of the House.
Many of the people across Canada who voted for the government and for these positions gave their support to this side of the House. When a decision of this magnitude is made, that is the type of debate and those are the kinds of policies that should come forward so that when that decision is made, the total commitment of the Canadian people has been debated in a non-partisan way and in a very active way without any commitments of any kind to any other promises that may be made or deals
January 17, 1991

that could be cut with other groups and so on. I am not taking about members of Parliament. I am talking about the kinds of discussions that take place between other countries and other groups in which we are not involved at any time.
I agree with the suggestion that was put forward. I would hope many politicians and many members will get together to try to bring about that kind of policy.

Madam Speaker, first I have a comment.
The member from Powell River has given out a phone number, 613-996-7446. I want to tell the House that those of us who have been participating in this participatory democracy are thrilled at what has been happening. We have been taking calls from coast to coast. So far, to my knowledge, we have had none from Yukon or the Northwest Territories.
I would like to share with the House a comment from a woman in Edmonton who said that this is the first time in all her life-she was quite sincere about this-that she could say something that she felt would be heard. I have assured her that her voice would be heard in the House. She wondered how we had changed our role from one of a peacekeeper to one of a warmaker, and whether we were not simply now, through the government, being the echo of the Bush administration.
I would like to ask the member for Kootenay East the question that she posed to me. In the past and through the years, Canadians have been proud to hold their heads up high when they travelled internationally. They have always gone abroad and have been well respected in the Middle East, the east, and central European countries. Everywhere they have gone, they have worn the maple leaf with pride. Will we, through this, lose our respect in the international community? Would the hon. member respond to that woman from Edmonton?
I remind people that the number is 613-996-7446. Keep the calls coming.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for the question.
Government Orders
It is a remarkable thing that here we are at 6.30 a.m. after a long debate throughout the night. Phone calls are coming in from across Canada expressing Canadians' concerns and desires for Canada to maintain a peaceful role and not an offensive role.
I believe we have lost our tradition. If we continue in this aggressive role, we are going to lose that tradition. But what is even more severe is the fact that, when this war is over and if we have participated in an offensive way, we will also lose the respect, dignity, and trust that we have had for many years as a country that is peaceful and does everything possible to find the avenues of peace.
Not only will we lose our trust as individuals, but as a country. We have worked so hard for that-and I am not going to be political here-not only under Liberal administrations, but also under Mr. Diefenbaker's administration. As I have stated in my speech, not only under the Liberal administration, but also under Diefenbaker's administration New Democrats for years have been known to be striving for peace and ways to maintain peace. I want to say that yes, our tradition as a peaceful nation and one that is respected world-wide is at stake. I would urge the government to reconsider its offensive role to get back to the role of peacemaking and find a solution so that we can get out of this horrible mess.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a number of us have referred to the resolution. I would like to do the same thing so that we will know just exactly what we are supposed to be discussing. It is very short:
That this House reaffirms its support of the United Nations in
ending the aggression by Iraq against Kuwait.
It has been said that it is a resolution that should give the New Democrats any difficulty because we have always been strong supporters and proponents of the United Nations. Had that been the end of the story, there is no doubt that we would have been supporting the resolution.
But, Madam Speaker, you and I were in the House. We heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs say on one occasion in response to a question that the government is not going to be bound by Security Council resolutions because they might make the wrong decision.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
It was only after the Security Council passed the resolution that we are talking about that the government then said: "Well, that is our policy", because it reserved the right to go in Bush's direction if the Security Council was not prepared to go in that direction.
That is why we have trouble supporting this resolution. It is not really the United Nations, position. It is a position that was drafted by President Bush and his advisers. Again, Madam Speaker, you and I have had an opportunity to read the reports of how the President and his people were travelling around the world, calling in all the markers they had, to make sure that every one of the Security Council members supported their resolution. They pulled out all the stops and they got the support. That is not a decision freely arrived at by the Security Council as we see it.
To get to the discussion that we have had, I am not sure how many hours. We are now into the fourth day of it. One loses track of time. I heard someone say in one of the phone calls that they were having trouble sleeping. Some of us might be wondering just what that is. It is half an hour past my usual time of getting up. Like the hon. member for Saint-Denis, I feel more wide awake now than I did some 12 hours ago, so we will see how things go-
I have heard members on the government side of the House say we have to stop Hussein. They describe him with a 22-year record of brutality and terrorism in his own country, a person who has used chemical warfare against his own people, the enemy the people of Iraq have lived under for 22 years. If our motivation is truly one of concern for the people under Hussein's control, if we could wait for 22 years to pay any attention to it, why could we not have waited a few more months or even one more year, if that is what it would take for sanctions to work?
How many children in Baghdad or Tel Aviv or how many adults in or out of the armed services do we have to butcher or maim before we dare agree that it might have been better to have waited and given sanctions an opportunity to work. All the reports I heard were to the effect that the sanctions were working.
Even those who questioned them said that it was just a matter of time, that it could take as much as a year for them to work. We had already invested four and a half
months in the sanctions, why not another of seven and a half months if it took that much, and let sanctions do the job that we are now trying to do by killing?
Some two hours after the news first broke I think it was at seven o'clock on January 16, a poem that I had memorized some 50 years ago and have not looked at, since, forgotten I suppose, came to mind. I attributed it in error to Mr. A.E. Houseman, when in fact it was written by Thomas Hardy. The third verse, as I recall it, goes something to this effect:
Quaint and curious war is.
You shoot a fellow down.
You treat, if met when any bar is,
Or help to half a crown.
War is quaint and curious. War must be mankind's greatest folly. War settle no problems. They exacerbate old ones and create new ones. They settle no problems. Wars are easy to start, but sometimes can be very difficult to stop.
This resolution states that we are working through the United Nations. This is a United Nations effort but, again, you know and I know that when President Bush talks about the war effort and when the Prime Minister of our country talks about the war effort, they talk about the allies. They talk about the coalition. They never talks about the United Nations force because it is not a United Nations Force. It has the backing of resolutions, yes, but it is an American force that is almost totally supported by a few of the allies or coalition.
Canada's role as a peacemaker was universally accepted and highly regarded until it started to weaken in 1984, the occasion of the present Prime Minister's election to that position. From then on our role as one separate, either economically, internationally, politically or culturally, has been so merged with the United States that we are now recognized more and more as nothing but a vassal of the present Bush administration, or a poor 51st state in the Union of the United States.
No one would doubt, no one would question, whether or not it is Bush who is calling all the shots and that we are following them-trying to anticipate them perhaps, but certainly following them. We have abandoned our role as a peacekeeper. That is a loss to us but it is also a loss to the world as a whole.
January 17, 1991

It is easy for politicians sitting in comfortable places far removed from any place of danger to vote in favour of war. We get to vote. The young people who go to the front lines have no vote. That should make us a bit more responsible in voting in favour of war, and yet we seem to do it so easily, so lightly, and not even because it serves our own interests best, but rather because it serves the interests of the American president.
"War is the ultimate human folly. This is something I collected some time ago but it is still valid. The money required to provide adequate food, water, education, health and housing for everyone in the world has been estimated at $17 billion a year. That is a huge sum of money, Madam Speaker. Just about as much as the whole world spends on arms every week of the year, to put it into perspective. One week's spending on arms would be enough to accomplish all those things".
I am going to read another quotation.
Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired, signifies in the final scene a theft from those who hunger, and are not fed, those who are cold and are not clothed. This world in arms is not spending money alone. It is spending the sweat of its labourers, the genius of its scientists, the house of its children... This is not a way of life. Under the cloud of war, it is humanity hanging on a cross of iron.
This is signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower.
Currently Canada spends some $13 billion a year. That is before we got involved in this campaign of invasion into Iraq, $13 billion a year to be prepared for war. Not fighting, but simply to be prepared for war; to be ready to kill, should the occasion rise. We are spending some $3 billion a year to try to help developing nations help themselves, not to give them relief but to try to help them to pick themselves up by their own bootstraps.
Canadians have fought in two world wars and have handled themselves very well, each of them a war that was designed, intended and described as a war that was going to end all wars. Canadians participated well and still are participating in many areas of the world in peacekeeping forces. Today, for perhaps the first time in our history, we are participating in a war as one of the aggressors again, supposedly in the interest of peace.
Government Orders
Canada has failed as has the rest of the world; we joined in the failure. What we have been doing has not worked. We have been fighting wars, wars of defence and, currently, a war of aggression to preserve the peace and none of it has worked. Certainly out of this war, if peace comes it may be 1,000 years down the road. There has to be a better way and I suggest that there is.
I am not a pacifist. I spent five years in the air force during the war and that was a war that had to be fought; the mistakes were made long before war started, there is no question about it. I am not saying that this one is much different. The mistakes, again, were made over a 22-year period. But there has to be a better way and we have to start before we get into war, not after.
When I was in high school, I was impressed by a teacher who, years later, became a columnist for The Ottawa Citizen and is retired here in Ottawa now, Ronald Grantham. He won an international prize for writing a letter or paper on unilateral disarmament.
What I am proposing now as the better way, the only way that can work, because what we have done up till now has certainly failed humanity totally, is for Canada to disarm totally and unilaterally its armed services, do away with our defence spending and concentrate on using that money to help those nations that need it to help themselves. Let us use our money to build peace rather than to arm to fight wars because fighting wars never has and never will produce peace. There may be a cessation of hostilities but we never get peace by fighting wars. Let us disarm and show that there is a better way.
I am not proposing this to the world as a whole. That, I hope, will come, but I am saying that there is one country in the world which can do it alone. There is one country in the world that is big enough. If we abandoned our defence spending, the amount of money and the effort that we could put into a program for peace would be large enough that it would be noticed around the world. We can do it because, although we are very large, very rich in resources, a very productive people with a very strong economy, there is no possibility of our defending our borders against either an aggressor from the south or one from the north. It is totally impossible for a nation of some 30 million people to defend some 10,000 or 15,000 miles of border; it is just not possible.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
We could abandon our defence spending. We are not going to defend ourselves. The amount of money that we are spending on defence, some $13 billion a year right now, of money that is being spent, is but a pittance out of the total amount internationally, of over $1,000 billion a year. Our $13 billion is such a small portion in comparison to the total, it would not be noticed in the total world pool of defence spending. But the contribution that we could make to international aid and development would be noticed. And hopefully, working through the auspices of the United Nations-and as I said before we have always supported the United Nations and would love to be doing it in this case if we thought it was a decision freely arrived at-and selecting countries that would benefit from this kind of assistance, countries that were prepared to forswear spending their scarce resources on national defence as well, on the condition that they had a guarantee from the United Nations organization that their borders would remain intact, perhaps we could widen the circle of nations that would be prepared to leave security of their borders to collective security, as provided by the United Nations.
Canada is unique. We can give up defence since we cannot even pretend to be able to defend our own country. The experience we have had with our armed services this year has been such that we know they are exceptionally good at organization. They could well be used to do the kind of work throughout the world that I feel would be building for peace as opposed to fighting wars and killing people, and hoping that we can kill enough so that the next war will be a little further delayed than it might have been otherwise. Canada is one country that is unique enough in that it cannot defend itself so it might as well give it up. Yet, it is important enough economically that it can make a significant contribution to the kind of program that I have been describing.
We are now participating as an aggressor. We have abandoned our peacekeeping operation. We no longer have that kind of a reputation. Let's take another look at it and go at it from a different direction. Let us make an effort through economic development, using our exceptionally capable armed services to do the organizing so that we can make a tremendous impression upon the world and show there is a way for human beings to live together. If we go on the way we have been going for
centuries and even for thousands of years, if we do not soon learn to live together, we are going to give up living altogether as a species on this planet.

Madam Speaker, with your indulgence I would like to make a comment and then ask the member a question.
My comment is to thank the people across Canada once again for their participation in this debate throughout the night. It has been most heartening to see that the people of Canada do watch the parliamentary channel, whether it is in British Columbia or St. John's, Newfoundland, regardless of the time of night. We have had calls over the last couple of hours from all across Canada.
Just recently I took calls from about 14 people from Ottawa, a couple of people from St. John's, Newfoundland, and from Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. All these people speak with one voice in saying they do not want Canada in an aggressive role in the Middle East. I want to express my appreciation to all these people who have phoned in. We have made note of all they have had to say and hope that we have been able to use some of that in our speeches this evening.
I would like to go on with another comment and question with respect to a call that I took from Penticton, British Columbia, a couple of days ago. This person worked for 28 years in the military. His position was that the Iraqi war machine should be crushed because of the build-up of arms. We discussed over a period of time what that build-up of arms was and the difficulties that we were going to have as a nation if we moved, as he said, from a war machine led by a madman and wondered who defines the war machine that should be crushed and who defines the madman. Do we go through all of the countries that have built up arms and who is going to be the policeman in this?
My question to the hon. member is this. Is there some way that he sees to cut off the supply of arms to some of the nations that are building up, such as Iraq, which have built up their arms as a result of imports from places like France, Germany, the Soviet Union and the United States? Can he, in his wisdom and with his experience of World War II and his experience since as a legislator, see any way of tightening up the control so that we get to the root of the problem in this arms build-up and the greed
January 17, 1991

of the arms builders. Can he make a comment on that for me please?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to advise the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan that his colleague has left him a minute and a half.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer has to be through the United Nations organization and I mentioned that during my speech. If that organization becomes influential enough, and people agree that it will have the power to resolve disputes and to guarantee borders, then those nations will not have any need for the kind of armaments they are buying now and paying hard dollars for in many cases and bankrupting their countries to do it. They will not have any use for equipment like that. They will not need it to protect themselves and they will not be able to use it to attack anyone else, so there would be no point to it any more.
The answer lies in strengthening the United Nations. I discussed during my speech and suggested how that could be accomplished.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to do something I thought I would never have to do, and that is speak not in the theoretical, but in the real fact that we are a country at war. It is not formally declared, but nevertheless one we are into.
Let me say at the outset that perhaps in some way I am a contradiction in terms of my very existence. I exist because of a war. My father met my mother in Scotland when he visited relatives of his brother-in-law, when he was sent there as a member of the Queen's Own Cameron Highlanders out of Winnipeg. He met my mother.
