They married and then he was shipped off to Dieppe where he was captured and spent most of the remainder of World War II in a Nazi prison camp in Poland, Stalag 8-B. He was released at the end of the war and came back to Canada and I became their first child.
I say a contradiction because when I was 13 he died of the ramifications of his incarceration. So I have mixed feelings about war, recognizing that sometimes we have no choice, recognizing that sometimes major blunders occur in the decisions of war and the decisions to go to war.
Government Orders
I had the honour three years ago to retravel the path my father took as a member of this House, along with the then Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Hon. George Hees, to attend the 45th anniversary of the landing at Dieppe. In a lot of ways that solidified growing feelings in me about war and the stupidity of such means to resolve conflicts between nations.
Not only was it in seeing the reality of Dieppe, a place that should never have been invaded, because it was impossible to attack and win, but also seeing the reality of the tombstones in England and France and thinking back to comments from my parent's generation of newsreels about when the boys came back home. The ages on those tombstones were 18, 19, 20, 21. They were boys. They had to grow up in a hell of a hurry, but they were still boys who died on those battlefields.
At the same time as more and more information about the Second World War was becoming evident because of the release of confidential documents, to paraphrase the words of George Hees at that time when we held an evening remembrance service at the cemetery at Dieppe, was his comment on the generals and the stupidity of the decision by the generals about going into Dieppe.
We made a mistake in Dieppe and as a nation we made a mistake, as a world we made a mistake in going to war before sanctions against Iraq had time to truly work. There is no question in my mind about that. This is a dumb war. This is an unnecessary war. It is also a war where Canada has undermined 20, 30, whatever years as a nation of peacekeepers, of men and women who have been out there around the world keeping combatants apart, whether it is Cyprus or Israel. I visited UN camps in Israel on the Golan Heights.
Men and women along with other nations such as Finland and India, to name just two, have worked very hard to keep combatants and warring nations apart. That is Canada's role. That is what Canada's military is equipped to do. We do not have the equipment, the force in terms of personnel to be an offensive nation, and thank God that we do not. At the same time, I am scared about what will happen to our men and women who are already deployed in the Persian Gulf and those who may soon be deployed.

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
It is now a few minutes before seven o'clock in the morning. Technically, according to the House of Commons, this is still Thursday. Some of us believe it really should be Wednesday. But in the last hours of this debate, I will be the last speaker for my party and my friend the member for Saint Denis will be the last for his. We have been receiving phone calls from across Canada. It has been truly remarkable.
In the time remaining, I would like to try to report to the House about the exchange we have had. As someone who has been staffing the phones in the lobby, I have been talking to people whom I have never met, not one person have I ever met in my life. A lot of the calls were from British Columbia primarily because of the time zone reality. I want to say that I took calls from people in Ontario and Quebec who have not been able to sleep. They have been up all night concerned about what Canada got itself into, worried sick, and they are watching the debate in the House of Commons.
One of the messages they passed on to me is that the reason they are watching the House of Commons channel as opposed to the multitude of news channels is that finally they are hearing something about peace, that they are hearing from members of this House who are saying that this war is insane, this war has: "to stop, we have to find a better way, and they are saying: Thank you, keep up the good work".
A lot of times members of Parliament feel pretty lonely. Certainly, at a time like this when my party has differed with the party positions of the rest of the House and, perhaps, for the short period of time with the position of a lot of Canadians, it gets pretty lonely.
I will tell you, Madam Speaker, the calls we have been receiving have really helped us because we know that we are not alone. We are speaking for hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
Let me give some of the thoughts from these Canadians. A citizen from Burnaby is opposed to the war. He says it is a catastrophic blunder and he is now looking at diverting his tax dollars to the peace tax fund.
Another said: "Totally wreckless", A gentleman from B.C called. He is an immigrant from Yugoslavia who has been here for 20 years. He says that this war is totally wrong, that it is an atrocity.
Another talked about the innocent children, women and old people of Kuwait and Iraq. They did not cause this war. They are going to get hurt and killed. Others made comments about the government. They are so sick of this government. Others said that this is a very interesting debate. They appreciate it happening, and we do not support the war. One physician from Ottawa called about 5 a.m. She just got off night shift at one of the hospitals. A member of Physicians for Nuclear Responsibility called in to express her support.
There is great agreement with what the NDP has been saying. This next comment was quite interesting because a lot of us have been watching the news channels and the scenes. Certainly, the one scene from Iraq, the first pictures to come out of the bombardment with the anti-aircraft weapon response, looked like Star Wars. It looked like something out of a movie.
One individual said: "People think this is just one big Nintendo game." Then he pointed out and said: "These are live players. These are human beings in that Nintendo game. It is not an artificial thing that gets eradicated. It is live flesh and blood".
Others pointed out that we should not fool ourselves, that this is really not a United Nations force. This is an American force with a few other countries participating.
A gentleman from Oshawa called with clear disapproval of the Canadian involvement in the gulf. A gentleman from Downsview said: "This war sickens me." A lady in Vancouver called and said that she had been at a meeting last night organized by the COPE aldermen and 500 young people walked 30 miles from Maple Ridge to Vancouver to the meeting chanting: "We don't want war. We want peace." That is the next generation. It is also the cannon fodder. Let us not forget that.
Others said: "Bring our forces back." One said: "We are ashamed of our country in terms of what it has done." Others reflected what we all know, that this is an emotional roller coaster. They have said that Iraq should not be occupying Kuwait, but they are also ashamed that the Prime Minister chose to give Canada an aggressive role rather than a peacekeeping role under the direct auspices of the United Nations.
A person from Nanaimo said: "I wish there was some way to stop this war". Another said: "Because of what I have heard tonight, knowing that there are people in Parliament who are expressing what I have been thinking, I can sleep a little better tonight and thank you".
January 17, 1991

One asked for a wiser approach to how we deal with these kinds of disputes. A person from Toronto wanted to add their voice to a desire to end Canadian involvement in the war and proud of the NDP for the position that we have taken, and would love a peacekeeping role.
One lady I talked to, who is a former citizen of South Africa, talked at length about the sanctions and how they really were not applied as effectively as they could have been in South Africa. Yet look at what we are seeing happening, where apartheid is ending. She also said that no one can rejoice at the destruction of the human beings in the Middle East.
Another one pointed out that the real soldiers, not in a derogatory way in terms of our forces in the Middle East, were the members of that peace camp, including one Canadian doctor, who positioned themselves without weapons between the coalition forces and the Iraqi forces. Another one just said that it is very emotional, and appreciated what we were doing.
A woman from Sarnia said that we had no right to be there. She pointed out that she was 76 years old, so she has been through a couple of wars already. She said: "We did not accomplish anything in the last one. What is this one going to accomplish? It is just going to lead to yet another war at another point in time". Another interesting phrase that came out is that we can fight for peace. As a political movement, we can fight for peace.
There was great support for the suggestion by my colleague for a non-partisan coalition against the war. One was very angry-in fact two in terms of the calls-with what has been happening in Question Period, that members of the government are laughing at suggestions for peace.
They are also appalled at the media coverage. They did not identify the media, but we have all been watching. It seems to be that the language is a military language and the focus is on the military weapons. We have not seen any pictures of the dead in Iraq or in Kuwait. We have seen pictures of the damage in Israel and we regret that. We think it was insane for Hussein to attack Israel, unwarranted, unnecessary, unconnected with this war, and, God, I hope that Israel is able to keep its act together and not feel bound to retaliate because that will only escalate.
Government Orders
Again, as our speakers have pointed out time and time again, that was one of our fears about going to war in the Middle East. It has always been one of our fears that it will not be a nuclear war started between the U.S.S.R. and the United States; it will be an accident in the Middle East or a similar country.
I know that the time for my remarks is nearing an end. It has been impossible to put in 20 minutes all the thoughts that I have, plus all the comments and thoughts that have been passed on to me this evening. I just want to make two final points, particularly to those people who will be watching the reruns of these debates that when they call there may not be anyone answering the phones. We are going to try to staff the phones in the opposition lobby for the time, if we can predict, when the repeat will be on for the last three or four hours of the debate because we do want to hear from them. I would encourage people out there to call their local member of Parliament and let him or her know where they stand on Canada's involvement.
As I said at the beginning, I never thought, I never expected, I never planned to be in this House to be debating the fact that Canada was at war. As a Canadian who gets deeply emotional when the phrase "we stand on guard for thee" is sung as part of our national anthem, having seen what standing on guard for thee has done, I do not want any more heroes. I do not want any more heroes on the battlefield. I am quite happy to remember the heroes who fought for Canada in World War I, World War II and the Korean war. Please, let us end this war now; let us put our forces back to a peacekeeping role to do what they have done for Canada for years, and made us proud. Thank you, Madam Speaker, and thank you, ladies and gentlemen for watching this debate and letting us know how you feel.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Ati-kokan for his excellent speech on a subject which, I agree is not easy. I would like to remind Canadian people, of one thing if I may. There is great concern today, and rightly so, about the risks the men and women of the

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Canadian Armed Forces are presently facing in the Gulf. We too often forget the tens of thousands of policemen and women who risk there lives daily to enforce the law in Canada. It is sad, but when one of them gets killed it is not cause for a debate in this House. My point is, Madam Speaker, that the role Canada is playing is that of restoring peace. Peace has to be restored before we can maintain it.
One man has led his people without telling them a thing, and they are truly the first victims of what is happening out there. I am talking about the Iraqi people who blindly followed a man with no conscience.
The international law, the international government we call the United Nations, and all its member nations unanimously denounced the aggression on one of their own, and Kuwait called upon its sister nations within the UN to come and free it. Canada, with a 45-year tradition of peacekeeping and defending rights and freedoms, did not depart from the mission it always gave itself by accepting the risks and sacrifices required to bring about a new world order.
I do not like it, when the hon. member and his colleagues claim that we, on this side of the House, are people looking for violence and for war. Quite the contrary; never in the history of Canadian diplomacy was there so much effort to prevent a war.
Over the last 112 days, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has had 50 bilateral meetings and at least another 50 multilateral meetings, while our Prime Minister was attending numerous meetings and having numerous phone conversations, to try to find a peaceful solution to the conflict before we got to this point.
Madam Speaker, Canada has been a leader in the world for the past 45 years. I think Canadian people can be proud of the work their country and their government have done. Of course the present situation, and I will close on that, is the doing of a man who did not recognize the law, the international law and that of the United Nations, which state that every nation on this earth has the right to live freely in its country and to call its neighbours and friends to its assistance after an invasion such as the one Kuwait sustained.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the member opposite for his compliment at the beginning of his statement and question. I also thank him for his question.
It is no surprise that there are fundamental differences in this House in terms of how one achieves peace. The Government of Canada has chosen at this point in time to use military force as a means to attempt to achieve peace.
We have been consistently saying that the time was not there to do that, that sanctions take a while to work. The five-month arbitrary deadline was set at the request of the United States. The coalition forces in the gulf are not wearing the blue helmets of the United Nations, the tradition of any UN force. When the government likes to wrap itself in the UN flag, it is a see-through flag and what we are seeing is the American Stars and Stripes.
A lot has been said about this party in particular being anti-American. It is not true. We just got a call from a Will Williamson from Deforest, Wisconsin. He is a veteran of the Vietnam War, 100 per cent disabled. He is totally disillusioned by what his country has done. He has been watching all night. He phoned to congratulate us on our phone-in set-up. He says it is the single largest advance in democracy he has ever seen.
I also want to remind the House that my leader met with senior American members of the Democratic Party, members of Congress and Senate who oppose the war as much as we do. We are not anti-American. We are anti-Bush administration. We are anti-administration of the Conservative Party of Canada. We are pro-Canada. We are pro-peacekeeping in our traditional role of not beating up the bully but of isolating the bully, cutting off the resources that are needed for the bully to function.
I might add that right now we have a Middle East version of the Hatfields and the McCoys. We have two families fighting over turf, not caring about their people, fighting over lines drawn by Great Britain at the end of World War I. The boundaries have no reference to the people who live there.
January 17, 1991

People who have called me tonight have implored the Government of Canada to rethink what it is doing. The time is not too late. We can revert to our traditional role, not by bringing our men and women back home, but by using them to help the victims, the refugees, the injured, and the families left without parents and homes. That is the role for Canada. That is what we should have been doing all along.
At the same time we should be working through the UN to find a diplomatic solution so that the war and carnage can end before many more people are killed, regardless of race.

Madam Speaker, government involves making decisions. It involves planning and it involves choices. I have chosen to be against this war in which my country, Canada, is involved.
One of the happiest moments of my life was on February 10, 1964, when I was elected for the first time as the member for the riding of Saint-Denis in Montreal.
One of the promises I was allowed to make by Mr. Pearson to my constituents was that even if we were a minority government we would have a distinctively Canadian flag before the next election. First there was a very vigorous debate in the House, but we got our flag.

We got our Canadian flag after a long debate, my first debate in 1964. That was the pride of my day. It has been the pride of my life ever since.
Yes, I come from Quebec. Yes, I am Canadien frangais. Yes, I am from Montreal. Yes, I said the same thing in French.

I see Canada's flag as an image, a dream, a symbol for a world in disarray that is seeking, somewhere on this planet, a relatively peaceful land, a generous land, with open-minded people who may have their minor prejudices, but nevertheless, a land where people can live in peace and understanding.
Government Orders

That is what Canada is all about. It is a hope for the world. What the world has always seen in Canada is the hope of a different place on earth or, as my Indian friend says in English, mother earth. Indians always talk about mother earth. Canada is that. Canada is looked on by the world as a compromise between all kinds of regions, emotions and people who could always provide, not a solution but proposals when there is trouble in the world.
The government of the day has chosen to join with the United States and with many other countries to teach Saddam Hussein a lesson once and for all. The leader of the government-and I will say it in English-is a personal friend of mine.

And I say in French without shame, that he is a personal friend. On Wednesday, October 11, when this Prime Minister, my friend, received His Majesty King Hussein Bin Talal of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, he addressed him in the following terms, very politely of course: "We also celebrate here today the landmark first address to the Canadian Parliament of the leader of an Arab country. Your autobiography and the testimony of many respected world leaders record your dedication, sir, to the cause of peace in the Middle East. In fact, few, if any, have shown greater determination in this cause nor pursued it with greater resolve. As Prime Minister Thatcher has said so aptly of you, Your Majesty, your human qualities, above all your courage and clearsightedness, have earned you both respect and admiration world-wide".
He said a few other things that might be a bit embarrassing, but the point is that the little king, as they call him, warned the world of the tragedy that is now taking place under our very eyes. The Middle East is far more complex than we think.

You could study it for 25 years, as I have done, and still feel humble because you have a lot more to learn. I said in my speech in October that when you go to the Middle East you know how you get in, but you do not know when you will get out and how you will get out. We are in.
It was was not the mission of Canada to be there that way. That country was representing a hope for humanity. It did not respect a big power. La France and Great Britain, I call them my in-laws. It is always pleasant for a

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
person like me and like my three colleagues from Quebec, members of the Conservative Party, friends, to say we would double colonialize, la France and Great Britain.
We are Americanized. We love it, but we are not American. That is what almost half of the world sees in us. Here is a country that was colonized by the French, taking the land away of course from the Indian and the Eskimo, and then colonized again by the British and looked at with envy by the United States. That is why we have our entry everywhere in the world.
The government has chosen. It is not our choice. I am not going to yell. It is 7.30 p.m. Saturday morning. Most of us have been here since ten o'clock Friday morning. As I said earlier, I never felt more full of energy having stayed during every minute of the debate. The outcome is so unbelievable that it gives me a kind of lasting energy to try to convince governments that it may not be too late. Do not look at us and say: "The Liberals seem to be divided". I hope the NDP will vote against this motion. The Gallup poll may be saying something today but a great Roman thinker said: "Reason must prevail over public opinion when it is volatile". I will remember, all my life, the time when the War Measures Act was in force, when 86 per cent of the people were endorsing us. As I said earlier, I voted for it. I still claim I was lied to. I did have the information so I had to do my duty. But I know one thing: 1970 is something that I remember, clearly. The government has chosen. Public opinion, volatile as it is, not having seen yet the massacre taking place, says it is right, Okay.
On this question, as I said earlier, I make it a moral issue not a Gallup or a poll issue. I remember also, in 1972, the same people who were supporting us at 86 per cent almost defeated us, less than 18 months after, so one does not go by polls, polls, and polls. I would like, at this time, to say that I, Marcel Prud'homme, feel-I hope that is a good expression in English-so much for our young Canadians who are, at the moment, right in the middle of accomplishing their duty because they signed, they are military. They are proud and they obey. The government of the day says: "You are going to do that" and they are doing it.
In this sense, I am positive we will not deprive them of all the essentials so that they come back to this country safely. That is one issue. But the true issue is: why did we not go on? Why did we not convince the United States to be patient in that region of the world? What was predictable is happening. This is Saturday morning at 7.30. Look at what is going on in Jordan. Look at the masses in Algeria, a country with a population of 30 million, 70 per cent of whom are young people. Look at what is going on in my dear Lebanon; there are demonstrations. Poor Lebanon that was just about to get back on its feet, after 16 years of abandonment by the west, the big power. In Jordan, a neighbour of Israel, there are demonstrations. The cabinet is meeting and the Parliament is meeting at this moment while I am talking. What will happen? Do we not know the Arab mind? Do we not have scholars who will tell us that over there they do not function as they do in Europe, they do not feel as they do in Europe. They have been pushed around, insulted and betrayed.

-They had every reason in the world to be suspicious. And this evening, all that seems to have come to a head throughout the Middle East.
Those who thought they could go to the Middle East, do a clean-up operation and get out quickly are mistaken. I am putting my reputation on the line. If I am wrong, I will get down on my knees and thank God. But I doubt it. I think I am going to be right. And I regret that. But couldn't we predict something that was so obvious?
I talked about our Canadian forces. Of course I also want to talk about Israel.

I am a member of the International Parliamentary Union. I spoke to Arafat personally: "Recognize the State of Israel and its right to live in peace", multiple times, while I had Canadian parliamentarians who forced us to vote, if we were going to listen to Arafat, not to be in agreement with him; just to listen to him. Arafat was at the United Nations in November 1974. He came and asked, begged: "Please don't let me down". We did not listen. Every leader in the Middle East asks for justice, peace and understanding.
January 17, 1991

Government Orders
When you do not produce results, you end up with tougher, more fanatical leaders: Hussein today, Khomeini yesterday, Assad from Syria tomorrow. Why is it that the west always ends up with the Marcos and the Duvaliers? I never understood, or I understand too well: interest, honour, favour, money. We always end up with the rotten.
Of course Saddam Hussein will lose. Of course, the alliance will win, but at what price? I am not a pacifist. He was cornered. He did not have any right to go into Kuwait. He had no right to make the people of Israel scared, hoping they would retaliate. He has no right. We all know that. We all agree. But he was cornered.

What is the matter with us politicians? Are we too proud to be wrong? Are heads of State too proud to admit they are not always right? What about history? Eisenhower, a great U.S President, warned that the greatest threat to U.S. peace was the United States defence establishment.-He could have substituted the West for United States- the arms manufacturers that are making a profit by corrupting developing countries.
Today, my dear colleague and Quebecer to the hilt, young Canadians and Quebecers may be killed with weapons manufactured in this country. Does that make sense? Can we accept that? When is the world going to wake up? When will we understand that all nations are seeking the same thing: dignity?

Should I spell it in English, dignity? As powerful as people think they are, they have no more right to dignity than

the humble of this earth, the people who have been tortured and humiliated, all that is unacceptable. And anyone who knows anything about human psychology, as you do, Madam Speaker, knows that someday things are going to explode. Perhaps not today, but surely tomorrow. So we are indeed in a pretty pickle. I can see hon. members who are about to say it is shocking that some of those Liberals and New Democrats are not only against war but against our soldiers over there. It would be monstrous to think we feel that way.
The government has made a decision as it is entitled to do. We do not agree with that decision. However, we believe that everything must be done to give these young Canadians and Quebecers-

Madam Speaker, given the fact that the speaker is the last speaker of the evening and the last speaker in the debate, and given his long time service to this country, could we extend his time to speak in appreciation of the people who are watching this debate and of the calls that I got on the hotline?

speechtext:
I am sure members of the House were quite prepared to extend, for a reasonable time, the time allowed to the hon. member for Saint-Denis. I realize that what has prompted the hon. member to rise was that I did signal, as was my duty, in trying to make things easier for the hon. gentleman. I thank everyone for their co-operation.

The hon. member for Saint-Denis may wish to conclude his speech in a few minutes.
The hon. member for Saint-Denis has the floor, and I apologize for the interruption.

Madam Speaker, you were doing your job, and I respect that fact as I respect this institution.

I will not abuse this but I can feel Canadian feeling quickly. I was in the lobby. To be frank, I will give you one. He is waiting for me to mention his name. It is Todd and he is from Regina. He is in agreement with the government and I have to be honest and say it.
People are watching us on satellite from Wisconsin and Saginaw, Michigan. Nine people phoned while I was in the lobby. I have listened. The NDP was too busy so I did. I was trying to catch the eye of some of my colleagues. I say to the members from Thunder Bay-Ati-kokan. I can read and I can listen. They are from Don Valley West, from British Columbia, a Rose Marie. Within a few minutes there were others from New

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
Westminster, British Columbia, John from Stoney Creek and another a Rose Marie. Suddenly people are having an interest in world affairs. They are saying: "Wait a minute, I did not know what was going on. Who made that decision? How was this decision made and why?"
The Prime Minister will come back on Monday and we will be here. What kind of diplomatic gesture is he going to offer? Right now you can be at war and be part of it. It will be more difficult but at the same time you can carry the Canadian flag again, the flag of pride, offer some solution. Are we totally finished here? Do we have nothing to offer to the world that is begging parliamentarians, statesmen, and church leaders? They are all saying: "Do something. It makes no sense".
I do not like to be partisan. Hon. members know that. I am not partisan, but I say: "Mr. Prime Minister, Mr. Secretary of State for External Affairs, work night and day."
It was unbelievable over Christmas when all the foreign ministers of the world were trying initiatives there. But, when one makes initiatives, one has to have a soul, a soul that understands others. There is no master servant on earth in foreign affairs.

If you treat people with contempt because they are Arabs well, Arabs are like Mr. Plourde or Marcel Prud'homme or Mrs. Champagne. They are human beings who want to be treated fairly and with respect. They expect that, and they always hoped that is what they would get from Canada.
I am sorry, but I think we failed miserably in this respect. I have a pile of notes here. I have been following this debate for days. I have been collecting facts for years, and when I get up to speak, I am afraid I get disconcerted from time to time.

I am not well-disciplined. Over the years I have accumulated what I would like. I have tried every angle to convince colleagues to take an interest and to make government understand. When I travel around the world, I talk about peace in the Middle East because it
will blow up some day. But now that we are in it, there is still a possibility to recuperate our tradition as Canadians.
My last word, Madam Speaker, would be to thank you and my colleagues for your patience. It is a call to Canadians in both French and English.

Let me tell you what I saw last night and this morning, my Lebanese taxi driver-

This is not Canada. This is not my Canada. This is not my Toronto, my Ottawa, or my Montreal.
I hope Canadians who will have a difficult time discussing this issue will not start by being paranoid as soon as they see dark-skinned people, as if immigration officers.
Being from Iraq, Palestine, or any other part of that world does not mean you are not a loyal Canadian. There are laws in this country. People know how far they can go and how much they can do. If they do not behave as good Canadians or as good future Canadians, they know the law is there.
Let us not start insulting these people in a disgusting way, as some are now starting to do. It is too dangerous. Let us understand each other.

We must be very careful. Later on, I will get back to this new economic order, this new world order everyone is talking about. If the new world order exists, what are we waiting for? We could tell our new ally, who has always been a friend, the President of Turkey: "Now listen, there a new economic order and there is a new world order. Couldn't you get out of Cyprus?"

Why do they not get out of Cyprus? There is a new order now in the world. What are they doing occupying north Cyprus?
My colleague from Scarborough-Agincourt said that, well, of course, there is no oil there so that will become a preoccupation of the United Nations very late.
January 17, 1991

Suddenly, the United Nations is becoming so important that the United States government, which forgot to pay its dues to the United Nations for many years, now finds it important again. Can it give the $500 million it owes to the United Nations? Suddenly, the United Nations has become important again.
I rejoice, but I do not want anybody to use the United Nations for his or her own purposes. The United Nations is there to find solutions to world problems.

Madam Speaker, I don't know whether I managed to convince my colleagues, but I can assure you that Canadians who are listening are going to ask questions. The Quebecois and Quebecoises-and I am not discriminating but I happen to like the word,-are going to ask questions. I don't care about being popular. I don't care about the polls. When we come back in a month or two we will see what Canadians and Quebecers think about this debate, a debate that started far too late because it should have been held before or around August 2, not today. The deed is done, so we will try to do the best we can, but it won't be easy. You know as well as I do it will not be easy.

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment very briefly. First of all, I would like to say that I admire and envy the talent and experience of the hon. member for Saint-Denis, especially in the House, and the depth of emotion in his speeches. When I have spent as many years in the House as the hon. member-if my constituents are willing-I may be able to speak with some of that same eloquence and emotion. The hon. member made a number of points which I think are fundamental.
Not so long ago, I was able to go over there and see what it is like in an Arab State, to see the proud bearing of these people, their pride in what they are. However, what I felt was a certain fear that someday someone would want to take over, with total disregard for their sovereignty. Their system may not be perfect. I agree some political systems are not exactly the way we would like them to be, but there is something in the hon. member's speech that bothers me.
People say that the Americans do this and the Americans do that- All I can say is that I was really impressed when a few months ago, Mr. Gorbachev told Mr. Bush and the world: The cold war was over. The cold war
Government Orders
between the two blocs is over and done with. Let us consider all the problems. Hon. member will agree that all the problems in the Middle East were due to the fact that to all intents and purposes, we had two enemies who were both trying to take advantage of the situation in that area and finally, what happened? The result is the shambles we have now. I think the hon. member will agree on that point. However, we had hope, at least I did. I may be naive, and I agree that I am a political novice. I may have been naive to hope that finally, now the cold war was over, all countries large and small, whether they were in the Soviet bloc or in the U.S. bloc-in any case those blocs no longer exist at least would finally without exception, be able to express their views.
In any case, I would appreciate it if the hon. member would answer this question. Would he agree that by attacking Kuwait, Mr. Hussein created an explosive situation and tried to destroy what the whole world was starting to build in an attempt to do something worth while in this area and to give these people, whom I also admire a great deal even if I do not know them as well as the member does dignity by giving them the means to develop their region?

Madam Speaker, of course I said that Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait was unacceptable. In French this is very strong: inacceptable. There are rules. We disagree on how to deal with a situation that is unacceptable. According to the statements by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, by all the religious communities, all the pacifists movements-and I urge them to keep up the good work and keep us all on our toes-there are other ways of doing what we are doing now. That is where we disagree. This is unacceptable. Yes, I say this with a great deal of emotion.

Yes, God dammit, I have emotion. I am talking about the planet, human relationships, human emotions and people who are going to die and are dying. Of course I am emotional, but I am cool.

I can see a few reporters who have been chasing me for quite while saying: "In a long emotional speech-". Well, let them, but I wish they would come and see me after my speech and realize that I am-rational I might get upset, but emotional, I don't mind a bit. In Quebec we are not a distinct but a different society. We think differently, and we act differently. We have different

January 17, 1991
Government Orders
emotions. We are good Canadians just the same, although we are different and we express ourselves in a different way.
This is my way, and I do not intend to change. It takes a lot of physical stamina but the debate is over.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my congratulations to the hon. member. He has been in this House for 27 years. He has sat on the external affairs committee and chaired it longer than I have probably been here. Tonight, he has demonstrated the reason this House has had such great confidence in him.
As a summary in the last speech in this House, he has done a tremendous job. He has given a very stem warning that we have enormous responsibilities for the people of Canada and, indeed, for the people of the world. He has been an articulate spokesperson for the Muslim communities of this world, especially the Palestinian community, for justice, recognition and dignity.
I must say how much I truly respect the contribution that he has made.
The second thing, as a great many people in here have said, is that there has been a failure on the part of this place. Indeed, I have changed my mind tonight. This has not been a failure. People who are here have gone through an agonizing process clarifying their own thinking on it. There have been some very constructive presentations.
Some of the women in this House have made some of the finest speeches that I have ever heard in the 12 years that I have been here. They have made the strongest appeals. I think when we leave here today that all of us will leave with a clearer notion of where we are going with this issue.
Unfortunately, it strikes me there is a division down the middle of this House. It cannot be reconciled. The government feels that it has taken the correct choice, that it is the necessary support for the United Nations. This side feels it is the most inappropriate thing that could have been done.
I think we as legislators do represent constituencies and millions of Canadians and that it is time to move it into the hands of the people. I think that, from our side, organizations across this country that have committees to stop this war are an absolute must. On the government side, they must plead their case to Canadians. God help them.

Madam Speaker, as graciously as possible, I would like to thank the hon. member for his kindness. I would like to make just a slight correction.
Yes, I am a defender of the Palestinians. I will not talk about that, because you will be here for the next 10 hours. I will feel like a Palestinian until the day they, like me, have a passport. Then I will feel like another one who is suffering.
The hon. member mentioned Muslims and Palestinians. I also have great place in my heart for people of the Jewish faith. To me, what we should be working for is getting these three peoples together. Remember that 25 per cent of the Palestinians share our majority faith: Christian, Catholic. If we could only dream.
I said I had a dream. That will be my last dream. If we could only have the reality of putting the leaders of these three great faiths together, who have their Holy Land in places no bigger than 10 times the size of this Parliament. This miracle can take place, but you need people to push people. You need to have initiative.
I call on my colleague to push the government. That is all we can do.

It is physically exhausting, but we have the responsibility. We have had a long debate. We are at war, I agree. I don't challenge that any more, but we have to take steps immediately, and that is where hon. members with whom I have more in common have a great role to play. From now on, night and day, we must keep working, wake up the nation, keep moving, let ourselves be moved by the peace groups. I like these groups because they prick my conscience, they are like gadflies, and that is why I like them. Young people complain there is a lack of imagination in this Parliament. Women, the majority of women in Canada, say: "We don't want war but what can we do?" So it is up to you, my dear colleagues; you are the government!
January 17, 1991



The hon. member is part of the government. Push on the government, not only on the war effort. Saddam Hussein will be taken care of. But push other initiatives to stop that monstrosity taking place in front of our eyes.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it looks as if Thursday is finally drawing to a close.
I would like to take this opportunity on behalf of all members of the House to thank all employees of the House of Commons who have assisted us in this very lengthy debate: the translators, clerks and their associates, the console operators, the senior pages, broadcasting, security people, the Sergeant-at-Arms, bus drivers, Hansard staff, cafeteria staff and our own staff from each political party.
I also want to thank the members who stayed through the night and those who have come back in the wee hours of the morning, like you, Madam Speaker. We all appreciate that. It has been a very exciting debate. It is probably one of the finest hours this Parliament has seen in a long time.
May I also add my compliments to my good friend who was the final speaker for his excellent remarks. I think it is something we should all contemplate. Madam Speaker, thank you to all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank my hon. friend, the Whip of the New Democratic Party for bringing to
Government Orders
the attention of the House our appreciation for all of those who serve this institution and allow us to go on at great length, as we have done in this case. I am sure no one at home would understand that this is still January 17. I am sure, if I told most of them, they would say:. "Yes, you are a member of Parliament; I would believe that". On behalf of the government members, I want to indicate that we too appreciate all the help we have received.
I want to compliment the House on the debate. It had tremendous emotion, tremendous tension, tremendous divergence of viewpoints. The House has risen to the occasion and members have participated in a debate that I hope a few of those Canadians across the country did tune in to and did enjoy.
